If someone invokes the words, “I have been commanded to fight the people until they say, ‘There is no god but Allah,’” as an excuse, does this excuse him from punishment for abandoning prayer, or not? What must rulers and those in authority do regarding those under their authority who abandon prayer? Are their efforts in this regard among the greatest forms of jihad and the foremost avenues of righteousness?

He answered:

Praise be to Allah. Whoever refuses to perform the obligatory prayers deserves severe punishment, by agreement of the leading Muslim scholars. Indeed, according to the majority of the Muslim community, including Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad and others, he must be called upon to repent and, if he does not repent, be executed. Indeed, one who abandons prayer is worse than a thief, a fornicator, a wine-drinker or one who consumes hashish.

Everyone in a position of authority must command those who obey him to pray, even children who have not yet reached puberty. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Command them to pray at seven, beat them for neglecting it at ten, and have them sleep in separate beds.”

---

## Page 11088

Anyone who has a minor in his care—whether a slave, an orphan, or his own child—and fails to command him to pray is to be punished for failing to command the child. The adult is to receive severe disciplinary punishment for this, because he has disobeyed Allah and His Messenger.

Likewise, anyone who has adult slaves, attendants tending horses, camels or falcons, chamber attendants, bābiyya attendants who wash bodies and clothes, servants, a wife, a concubine or female slaves must command all of them to pray. If he does not, he is disobedient to Allah and His Messenger. Such a person does not deserve to belong to the Muslim troops, but rather to the Tatar troops. The Tatars pronounce the two testimonies of faith, yet fighting them is obligatory by the consensus of the Muslims.

Likewise, any group that refuses to abide by even one of the known prescriptions of Islam, whether outward or inward, must be fought.

If they say, “We bear witness, but we will not pray,” they are to be fought until they pray.

If they say, “We will pray, but we will not pay zakat,” they are to be fought until they pay zakat.

If they say, “We will pay zakat, but we will neither fast nor perform Hajj,” they are to be fought until they fast Ramadan and perform the pilgrimage to the House.

If they say, “We will do this, but we will not give up usury, drinking wine or shameful deeds; nor will we fight in Allah’s cause or levy the jizya tax on Jews and Christians,” or anything similar, they are to be fought until they comply.

As the Most High says:

“Fight them until there is no more persecution and all religion is for Allah.”

The Most High also says:

“O you who believe, fear Allah and give up what remains due to you of usury, if you are believers.”

“If you do not, then be warned of war from Allah and His Messenger.”

---

## Page 11089

And usury was the last thing Allah prohibited. The people of al-Tā’if had embraced Islam, prayed and fought in Allah’s cause, yet Allah made clear that if they did not desist from usury, they would be among those who waged war against Allah and His Messenger.

It is related in the two Sahīh collections that when the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, died and some of the Arabs disbelieved, ‘Umar said to Abū Bakr:

“How can you fight the people when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah and that I am the Messenger of Allah. Once they do so, their lives and property are protected from me, except by right’?”

Abū Bakr replied: “Did he not say, ‘except by right’? By Allah, if they withheld from me an ‘iqāl that they used to render to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, I would fight them over it.”

‘Umar said: “By Allah, as soon as I saw that Allah had opened Abū Bakr’s heart to fighting, I knew that it was right.”

It is also related in the Sahīh that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, mentioned the Khawārij and said:

“Any one of you would consider his own prayer insignificant compared with theirs, his fasting compared with theirs, and his recitation compared with theirs. They recite the Quran, but it does not pass beyond their throats. They pass out of Islam as an arrow passes through its quarry. Wherever you encounter them, kill them, for whoever kills them will have a reward with Allah on the Day of Resurrection.”

So if those who stand in prayer at night, fast by day, and recite

---

## Page 11090

the Quran were to be fought on the orders of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, because they had departed from the Sunnah and the Muslim community, then what of those groups who do not adhere to the laws of Islam, but merely follow their kings’ bāsāq (1) and the like? And Allah knows best.

He was asked:

People tell a man to pray, but he does not pray. What is incumbent upon him?

He answered:

If he does not pray, he is to be called upon to repent. If he repents, well and good; otherwise, he is to be put to death. And Allah knows best.

He was asked:

If someone deliberately omits a single prayer, intending to make it up after its prescribed time has ended, does his action constitute a major sin?

He answered:

Praise be to Allah. Yes, deliberately delaying a prayer beyond the time when it must be performed is a major sin. Indeed, ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, said: “Combining two prayers without a valid excuse is a major sin.” Al-Tirmidhī also narrated this from Ibn ‘Abbās, attributing it to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, stating that he

> **Footnotes:**
> (1) Thus in the original.

---

## Page 11091

said:

“Whoever combines two prayers without a valid excuse has entered one of the gates of major sins.”

He attributed this to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, although that attribution is open to question. Al-Tirmidhī said: “This is the practice followed by the scholars.” The report is well known, and scholars have cited it approvingly, not rejecting it.

In the Sahīh, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever misses the afternoon prayer, his deeds have come to nothing.”

Such a warning—that one’s deeds will come to nothing—is given only for the gravest major sins. Moreover, missing the afternoon prayer is more serious than missing any other prayer, for it is the middle prayer, singled out by the command to observe it diligently. It was prescribed for those before us, but they neglected it; whoever observes it diligently will therefore receive twice the reward. It was also this prayer that Solomon missed, whereupon he did what he did to the horses.

It is also narrated in the Sahīh that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever misses the afternoon prayer, it is as though he has been bereft of his family and wealth.”

Someone bereft of his family and wealth is left deprived, with neither family nor wealth to benefit him. His condition is like that of someone whose deeds have come to nothing.

Furthermore, Allah Most High says:

“So woe to those who pray—those who, with regard to their prayer,

---

## Page 11092

are heedless.”

Thus, He threatens woe to those who neglect prayer until its appointed time has passed, even if they perform it afterward. Likewise, Allah Most High says:

“Then there came after them successors who neglected prayer and followed their desires; so they will meet with ruin.”

When Ibn Mas‘ūd was asked what neglecting prayer meant, he replied: “It means delaying it until its appointed time has passed.” They said: “We thought it meant nothing other than abandoning it.” He replied: “Had they abandoned it, they would have been disbelievers.” Ibn Mas‘ūd would say of certain governors of Kufa in his time, “What has your successor done?” because they used to delay prayer beyond its appointed time.

His words,

“and followed their desires,”

include everyone who pursues what he desires at the expense of observing prayer at its appointed time. This applies whether the desired things are forbidden—such as forbidden food, drink, sexual relations, or things to listen to—or permissible, though excess in them is forbidden, or anything else. Whoever is distracted from performing prayer on time by games, entertainment, conversation with his companions, strolling in his garden, developing his property, conducting his business, or anything else has neglected that prayer and followed his desires.

Allah Most High says:

“O you who believe, let neither your wealth nor your children distract you from the remembrance of Allah. Whoever does so—it is they who are the losers.”

Anyone whose wealth and children distract him from performing the obligatory prayer at its appointed time falls within this warning and is therefore a loser.

Describing those whose conduct is the opposite, Allah Most High says:

“Therein, morning and evening, He is glorified by men

---

## Page 11093

whom neither commerce nor trade distracts from the remembrance of Allah, establishing prayer, and giving zakat.”

Since He, glorified be He, has threatened those who neglect prayer beyond its appointed time and follow their desires with ruin, and since anyone who delays prayer beyond its time because he is occupied with what he desires is neglecting it and following his desires, this shows that doing so is a major sin. Such a warning is issued only for a major sin. This is further supported by His describing such a person as a loser: loss does not result merely from minor sins, which are expiated by avoiding major sins.

Furthermore, no … (1) [one disputes that] whoever deliberately prays without ritual purification or facing a direction other than the qiblah, and intentionally omits bowing and prostration, recitation, or any other requirement, has thereby committed a major sin. Indeed, one may cautiously refrain from declaring him a disbeliever if he does not deem that lawful. If, however, he deems it lawful, he is undoubtedly a disbeliever.

It is well known that observing the appointed time for prayer takes precedence over these obligations and others. Muslims do not dispute that a traveller who has no water, but knows that he will find it after the prayer’s appointed time, may not delay the prayer in order to perform it afterward with ablution or a full ritual bath. Rather, that is what is obligatory. Likewise, regarding someone unable to bow, prostrate, or recite: if he deems it lawful, he is undoubtedly a disbeliever.

> **Footnotes:**
> (1) A blank in the original.
> I—Usāma ibn al-Zahrā’—say: The “Harf” electronic version reads:
> “Furthermore, no one disputes that whoever prays without…”

---

## Page 11094

It is well known that even if he knows that, after the appointed time, he will be able to pray with full bowing, prostration, and recitation, he must pray within the appointed time, since he is able to do so.

As for the statement of some of our fellow jurists, “It is not permissible to delay prayer beyond its appointed time except for someone who intends to combine it with another prayer or is occupied with fulfilling one of its prerequisites,” no earlier jurist of our school said this, nor did anyone from any other Muslim school—except perhaps some of al-Shāfiʿī’s followers, though I am uncertain about that. There is no doubt that, by Muslim consensus, this statement cannot apply generally and without qualification. Rather, it concerns a familiar kind of case: someone reaches a well and can lower a rope to draw water, but will not finish until after the appointed time; or someone without clothing can sew himself a garment, but will not finish until after the appointed time; and similar cases.

Even so, what this jurist said concerning these cases contradicts the established position of Ahmad and his followers, as well as the position of the body of Muslim scholars among the Hanafīs, Mālikīs, and others. I know of no one who agrees with him on this except some of al-Shāfiʿī’s followers. Whoever holds this view is refuted by the Muslim consensus that merely being occupied with fulfilling a prerequisite does not permit delaying prayer beyond its legally prescribed time.

If the appointed time begins and someone can search for water but will not find it until after that time has ended, he may not delay the prayer, by agreement of the Muslims, even though he is occupied with fulfilling a prerequisite. Likewise, if someone without clothing can go to a village to buy himself a garment, but would not pray until after the appointed time has ended, he may not delay the prayer; there is no disagreement about this.

---

## Page 11095

Likewise, someone who cannot recite al-Fātihah must pray within the appointed time if he could learn it but would not finish doing so until that time had ended. Similarly, someone unable to learn the takbīr (declaration of Allah’s greatness) and tashahhud (seated testimony of faith) must, when time is short, pray as best he can without waiting. Likewise, even if a woman’s non-menstrual bleeding would cease after the appointed time, she may not delay the prayer in order to pray in a state of ritual purity after that time. Rather, she must pray within the appointed time as best she can.

Where combining prayers is permissible, however, the two prayers share a single time, and someone who delays a prayer is not delaying it beyond the time in which it may lawfully be performed. Indeed, according to one of the two views, combining prayers does not require an intention to do so, as Abū Bakr stated. The same applies to shortening prayers; this is the position of the majority, including Abū Hanīfah and Mālik.

Likewise, the prayer in circumstances of fear must be performed within the appointed time, even though delaying it would allow the worshipper to avoid turning his back to the direction of prayer, making extensive movements during the prayer, falling one unit of prayer behind the imam, separating from the imam before the concluding salutation, making up what he has missed before the concluding salutation, and other such actions performed during the prayer in circumstances of fear. These concessions are made only to preserve the appointed time; otherwise, the prayer could be performed in its complete form after that time, even at night.

Likewise, someone uncertain of the direction of prayer may not delay the prayer until he reaches a town where he can ascertain that direction, even if he is able to do so. Disagreement has arisen only where someone could learn the signs indicating the direction of prayer but would not finish learning them until the appointed time had ended. This disagreement is

---

## Page 11096

the newly introduced, anomalous view mentioned earlier.

As for the well-known disagreement among the imams concerning someone who wakes near the end of the appointed time and cannot perform the prayer before sunrise if he first performs ablution: should he pray with dry ablution, or perform ablution and pray after sunrise? There are two well-known views:

The first is Mālik’s view, which gives consideration to the appointed time.

The second is the view of the majority, including Ahmad, al-Shāfiʿī, and Abū Hanīfah. This is the issue that has led some to mistakenly suppose that a prerequisite takes precedence over the appointed time. That is not so, for the appointed time for someone who has been asleep begins when he awakens. As established in an authentic hadith, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever sleeps through a prayer or forgets it should pray it when he remembers it, for that is its appointed time.”

Thus, he made the time at which Allah requires His servant to perform the prayer the time when he remembers or awakens. Accordingly, whoever performs it at that time, attaining the required ritual purity to the extent that he can, has performed it within its appointed time. He has neither been negligent nor neglected the prayer. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“There is no negligence in sleep; negligence occurs only when one is awake.”

This differs from the case of someone who is awake from the beginning of the appointed time, for he is commanded to perform the prayer within that time. If he deliberately delays it beyond that time, he has neglected it and been negligent. Thus, if he is kept from performing it by attending to one of its prerequisites

---

## Page 11097

he has thereby delayed it beyond the time in which he was commanded to perform it. Were he not commanded to perform it within that time, he could permissibly delay it while going somewhere to obtain water for purification or a garment to borrow, or attending to something similar. This, however, contradicts the consensus of the Muslims.

Rather, someone who awakens near the end of the appointed time need only perform ablution just as someone who awakens within that time does. But if he were to delay the prayer because he would find water at midday, for example, that would not be permissible.

Moreover, the scholars have explicitly stated that when the time for prayer arrives and a person does not pray, he is to be put to death, even if he says, “I will make it up later,” just as he is to be put to death if he says, “I will pray without ablution or facing a direction other than the qiblah.” If he deliberately omits any obligatory requirement of prayer upon which there is consensus, he is to be put to death for omitting it, just as he is for abandoning the prayer itself.

If we hold that he is to be put to death when the time remaining for the second or fourth prayer grows short, the matter is as stated. The same applies if we hold that he is to be put to death when the time remaining for the first prayer grows short—which is the correct view—or for the third. This depends on whether he is to be put to death for abandoning one prayer or three; there are two transmitted opinions on this.

If we hold that abandoning one prayer suffices, must one wait until the time of the following prayer, or is it enough that the remaining time for the neglected prayer grows short? There are two juristic views on this.

There is also a third view, which distinguishes between a pair of prayers that may be combined and other prayers.

The fact that prayer remains valid after its appointed time, unlike the case with its other obligatory requirements, does not contradict what we have stated. Once the appointed time has passed, it cannot be recovered, so he cannot

---

## Page 11098

perform it except after its time has passed. The sin of delaying it remains one of the major sins that repentance and similar means can erase. As for the other obligatory requirements, they can still be fulfilled when making up the prayer.

As for the rulers who used to delay the prayer beyond its appointed time, whom the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, forbade fighting: if it is said that they merely delayed the prayer until the end of its time, there is no issue. But if it is said—and this is the correct view—that they let its time expire, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, commanded the Muslim community to pray within the appointed time, saying:

“Make your prayer with them a voluntary prayer.”

He forbade fighting them, just as he forbade fighting rulers when they appropriated things for themselves, wrongfully withheld people’s rights, and transgressed against them, even though major sins were committed in the course of this.

Anyone who delays the prayer beyond its appointed time is guilty of flagrant sin. Rulers are not to be fought merely because of their sinfulness, even though an individual within the authorities’ power may be put to death for certain forms of sin, such as unlawful sexual intercourse and the like. Not every act punishable by death therefore permits fighting rulers who commit it, for the harm caused by fighting is greater than the harm caused by a major sin committed by the ruler.

For this reason, some scholars among the followers of Ahmad and others explicitly stated that voluntary prayers may be offered behind sinful prayer leaders. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, commanded people to pray behind rulers who delayed the prayer until its time had expired. Such leaders are guilty of flagrant sin, yet he commanded that the prayer be offered behind them as a voluntary prayer.

---

## Page 11099

The point is that incurring the status of a flagrant sinner by allowing a prayer’s time to expire is well recognized among the jurists.

But if someone were to say, “The major sin consists in continually missing prayers, for that constitutes persistence in a minor sin,” the response would be:

The evidence already presented shows that the threatened punishment applies to missing even a single prayer. Furthermore, persistence means resolving to repeat the sin. Someone who commits a minor sin, repents of it, and then returns to it has not thereby committed a major sin.

Moreover, whoever stipulates that prayers must be missed continually needs to provide a precise criterion. If he means continually throughout one’s entire life, those previously mentioned would not fall into this category. If he means a specified period, he must provide evidence for it.

Furthermore, imposing the death penalty for abandoning a single prayer goes further than classifying it as a major sin. And Allah, glorified be He, knows best.

---

## Page 11100

He was asked:

“Does a Muslim who abandons prayer but performs the Friday prayer deserve to be cursed?”

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah. Such a person has incurred punishment by agreement of the Muslims. According to the majority of scholars, including Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad, he must be called upon to repent; if he does not repent, he must be executed.

Cursing those who abandon prayer in general terms is permissible. As for cursing a specific individual, it is preferable to refrain, since he may repent. And Allah knows best.

## Page 11101

Chapter on the Adhān (Call to Prayer) and Iqāmah (Call to Commence Prayer)

He was asked:

“Is the adhān obligatory or a sunnah? Is it recommended to repeat the two testimonies of faith aloud after reciting them quietly? Should ‘Allah is greatest’ be said four times or twice, the latter being Mālik’s position? Should the phrases of the iqāmah be repeated twice or said once? Should ‘The prayer has begun’ be said once or twice?”

He replied:

The correct view is that the adhān is a collective obligation. The inhabitants of a city or village may not abandon the adhān and iqāmah. This is the well-known position in the school of Ahmad and others. Several groups of scholars have described it as a sunnah without qualification. Some of them nevertheless hold that if the inhabitants of a town agree to abandon it, they are to be fought. The disagreement with these scholars is almost entirely terminological.

Many scholars use the term “sunnah” for something whose omission is blameworthy and punishable under Islamic law. Thus, the disagreement between someone using the term in this sense and someone who calls it obligatory is merely terminological. There are numerous comparable examples.

---

## Page 11102

As for those who claim that it is a sunnah whose omission entails neither sin nor punishment, this view is mistaken. The adhān is the hallmark of the abode of Islam. It is established in the Sahīh that “the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, made the lawfulness of attacking a settlement’s inhabitants dependent on their abandoning it. He would perform the dawn prayer and then wait to see: if he heard a caller to prayer, he would not raid them; otherwise, he would.”

In the Sunan of Abū Dāwūd and al-Nasā’ī, Abū al-Dardā’ reported: I heard the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, say:

“Whenever there are three people in a village among whom the adhān is not called and prayer is not established, Satan gains mastery over them. So keep to the congregation, for the wolf devours the stray sheep.”

Allah Most High says:

“Satan has gained mastery over them and caused them to forget the remembrance of Allah. Those are the party of Satan. Indeed, it is the party of Satan who are the losers.”

As for repeating the two testimonies of faith aloud after reciting them quietly, or omitting this repetition; saying ‘Allah is greatest’ twice or four times; and repeating the phrases of the iqāmah twice or saying them once, Sahīh Muslim and the Sunan contain the report of Abū Mahdhūrah: “The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, taught him the adhān in the year of the conquest of Mecca. The office of calling the adhān in Mecca remained with him and his descendants. It is established that he taught him the adhān and iqāmah, including the repetition of the two testimonies of faith aloud after reciting them quietly.”

His report has “saying ‘Allah is greatest’ twice,” as in Sahīh Muslim, and also “four times,” as in the Sunan of Abū Dāwūd and elsewhere. His report also states that he taught him to repeat the phrases of the iqāmah twice.

It is established in the Sahīh that Anas ibn Mālik said:

“When the people grew numerous”—he said—“they discussed having something recognizable by which to know the time of prayer

---

## Page 11103

and suggested lighting a fire or striking a bell. He therefore ordered Bilāl to repeat the phrases of the adhān twice and say those of the iqāmah once.”

One narration in al-Bukhārī adds:

“Except the iqāmah.”

The Sunan of Abū Dāwūd and other works relate:

“When ‘Abd Allāh ibn Zayd was shown the adhān, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, instructed him to convey it to Bilāl. He did so, and it included saying ‘Allah is greatest’ four times, without repeating the two testimonies of faith aloud after reciting them quietly.”

Since this is so, the correct position is that of the scholars of hadith and those who agree with them: to permit every form authentically established from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, without regarding any of them as disliked. The differing forms of the adhān and iqāmah are like the differing Quranic readings, forms of the tashahhud, and similar matters. No one has the right to regard as disliked anything that the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, instituted for his community.

As for those whose disagreement and division reach the point of forming alliances, showing enmity, and fighting over such matters that Allah Most High has permitted—as some people in the East do—they are among those who have divided their religion and become sects.

The same applies to the views expressed by certain imams—I would rather not name names—including some of them regarding as disliked the repetition of the two testimonies of faith aloud after reciting them quietly, supposing that Abū Mahdhūrah erred in transmitting it and that it was repeated to help him memorize it. Likewise, their opponents regard repeating the phrases of the iqāmah twice as disliked, even though they favor Abū Mahdhūrah’s adhān. The former favor his iqāmah and regard his adhān as disliked, while the latter favor his adhān and regard as disliked

---

## Page 11104

his iqāmah. These are two opposing positions. The middle course is to regard neither form as disliked. Although Ahmad and other leading scholars of hadith prefer Bilāl’s adhān and iqāmah because he consistently used them in the presence of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, this is like preferring particular Quranic readings, forms of the tashahhud, and the like.

Following the Sunnah fully in such matters includes practising one form on some occasions and another on others, and using one form in one place and another elsewhere. Abandoning a practice established in the Sunnah and adhering exclusively to another may lead to treating a sunnah as an innovation and a recommended act as obligatory. This, in turn, may lead to division and disagreement when others practise the alternative form. A Muslim must therefore observe the general principles that ensure adherence to the Sunnah and the unity of the Muslim community, especially in matters such as congregational prayer.

Those with the soundest approach in this regard are the scholars of hadith who have learned the Sunnah and followed it. Some leading jurists have relied on weak hadiths in these matters, while others have relied primarily on the practice they found in their own locality, treating it alone as the Sunnah to the exclusion of other practices—even though the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, allowed latitude in this matter, and all these forms are Sunnah.

Some of them may even have identified Bilāl’s adhān and iqāmah with the forms they found in their own locality, whether in Kufa, Syria, or Medina. Yet Bilāl gave the adhān only rarely after the death of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. Rather, the one who gave the adhān in Medina was Sa‘d al-Qarazī, the muezzin of the people of Qubā’.

---

## Page 11105

Repeating the two testimonies of faith aloud after reciting them quietly in the adhān is the practice preferred by Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī. However, Mālik holds that “Allah is greatest” should be said twice, whereas al-Shāfiʿī holds that it should be said four times. Abū Hanīfah prefers omitting this repetition of the testimonies. Ahmad regards both forms as Sunnah, but prefers omitting the repetition, because that was Bilāl’s adhān.

Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad prefer saying the phrases of the iqāmah once. Nevertheless, Ahmad also holds that saying them twice is Sunnah. The three—Abū Hanīfah, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad—prefer repeating the phrase “The prayer is commencing,” unlike Mālik. And Allah knows best.

Shaykh al-Islām said:

As for the adhān, which is a hallmark of Islam, jurists versed in hadith—such as Ahmad—have adopted all the forms established in the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him. Ahmad approved of Bilāl’s adhān and iqāmah, as well as Abū Mahdhūrah’s adhān and iqāmah. It is established in Sahīh Muslim and elsewhere that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, taught Abū Mahdhūrah to repeat the testimonies of faith aloud after reciting them quietly in the adhān, and to say the phrases of the iqāmah twice. It is also established in the two Sahīhs:

“Bilāl was instructed to say the phrases of the adhān twice and those of the iqāmah once.”

The Sunan collections report that he did not repeat the testimonies of faith aloud after reciting them quietly. Ahmad therefore preferred Bilāl’s adhān, because it was the form regularly used in the presence of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, before

---

## Page 11106

Abū Mahdhūrah began giving the adhān and afterwards, until the Prophet’s death. He also approved of Abū Mahdhūrah’s adhān and did not regard it as disliked. This is a principle he consistently applies to all forms of worship, both their words and actions: he approves of everything established from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, without regarding any of it as disliked, while being aware of these forms and either preferring some or considering them all equal.

Likewise, he permits recitation according to any established Quranic reading, even though he has preferred certain readings.

Examples include the different forms of the adhān and iqāmah, and the different versions of the tashahhud established from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, such as those narrated by Ibn Masʿūd, Abū Mūsā, Ibn ʿAbbās, and others. His preferred version is Ibn Masʿūd’s, for several reasons:

It is the most authentic and best known. Its wording has been preserved without variation in a single letter. Moreover, most of the other versions agree with its wording, indicating that this was the version the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, usually instructed people to recite.

The same applies to the transmitted forms of the opening supplication and seeking refuge in Allah, even though he preferred some of them. It also applies to the points at which the hands are raised during prayer, where they are placed after being raised, and the prescribed forms of praising Allah after declaring that He hears those who praise Him. Further examples include the different forms of invoking blessings upon the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, even though he preferred some of them.

---

## Page 11107

Other examples include the different forms of prayer in times of fear: every form practiced by the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, is permissible, with none regarded as disliked. Likewise, every transmitted form of proclaiming Allah’s greatness at Eid is permissible, although he considers some preferable.

Another example is the number of times Allah’s greatness is proclaimed in funeral prayers. According to the well-known position, four, five, or seven times are permissible, although he prefers four.

The other jurists, however, prefer some of these forms and regard others as disliked. Some, such as Abū Hanīfah, regard repeating the testimonies of faith in the adhān as disliked, while others, such as al-Shāfiʿī, regard omitting this repetition as disliked. Some, such as al-Shāfiʿī, regard reciting the phrases of the iqāmah twice as disliked, while others regard reciting them once as disliked. Matters have reached the point where their followers have fallen into a kind of pre-Islamic ignorance: in some eastern lands, they fight one another over this out of ignorant partisanship, even though all these forms are good and have been enjoined:

“The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, instructed Bilāl to recite the phrases of the iqāmah once and Abū Mahdhūrah to recite them twice.”

Indeed, true misguidance is to prohibit what the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, commanded.

He was asked:

“When the caller to prayer says, ‘Prayer is better than sleep,’ is it Sunnah for him to turn around and look to the side, or should he face the qiblah or the east?”

---

## Page 11108

He replied:

No scholar considers this to be Sunnah. Rather, the Sunnah is to say it while facing the qiblah, just like the other phrases of the adhān and the words, “The prayer has begun,” in the iqāmah. The only exception the scholars make is for “Come to prayer” and “Come to success”: when saying these, he turns to the right and left. He should not reserve these two phrases for facing east. No category of phrases in either the adhān or the iqāmah is specifically assigned to facing east or west.

Anyone who says both repetitions of “Prayer is better than sleep” while facing east or west is introducing an innovation and departing from the Sunnah of the adhān, by scholarly agreement.

The scholars have differed over whether the caller should turn around in the minaret, with two well-known views on the matter. Whoever does so has acted within an area open to scholarly judgment. Even so, if he turns around when saying, “Prayer is better than sleep,” he would have to turn around twice, and no scholar advocates this. If he singles out the east for both repetitions, he departs even further from the Sunnah. Thus, he must say both while facing the qiblah. And Allah knows best.

The Shaykh—may Allah have mercy on him—said:

When I travelled by the postal relay, we used to combine the two prayers. At first, I would give the adhān at sunset while riding. Then I reflected and found that when the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, combined the prayers on the night at Jamʿ (Muzdalifah), they did not give the adhān for Maghrib on their way; rather, he delayed the adhān

---

## Page 11109

until he dismounted. So I began doing the same, because when prayers are combined, the time of the second prayer becomes the time for both, and the adhān announces the time for prayer. This is why we hold that the adhān should be given for a missed prayer, just as Bilāl gave it when they slept through Fajr: that is the time for it, and the adhān announces the time when the prayer is performed, not the time when it becomes obligatory.

He was asked:

If someone has begun a voluntary prayer with the opening takbīr and then hears the caller to prayer, should he interrupt his prayer and repeat what the caller says? Or should he complete his prayer and repeat what the caller says?

He replied:

If someone hears the adhān while praying, he should complete his prayer without repeating what the caller says, according to the majority of scholars. However, if he is outside prayer, engaged in recitation, remembrance of Allah, or supplication, he should pause that and repeat what the caller says. This is because responding to the caller is an act of worship whose appointed time will pass, whereas these other forms of remembrance can be resumed later. Interrupting their continuity for a religiously sanctioned reason is permissible, just as one may interrupt

---

## Page 11110

their continuity by speaking when necessary to address another person, enjoin what is right, or forbid what is wrong. The same applies to interrupting their continuity with a prostration of recitation or the like. Prayer, however, is different: its continuity is not interrupted for another reason. Thus, if someone hears another person recite a verse of prostration, he does not prostrate while praying, according to the majority of scholars. Nevertheless, there is well-known disagreement on this matter. And Allah knows best.

## Page 11111

Chapter: The Conditions of Prayer

He—may Allah have mercy on him—said:

Section

When they begin their discussion of prayer with its prescribed times, the jurists of hadith have drawn upon all the texts reported from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, concerning the permissible times and the preferred times.

The time for Fajr extends from the appearance of true dawn until sunrise. The time for Zuhr extends from the sun’s passing its zenith until the shadow of each object equals its height, excluding the shadow present at the zenith. The time for Asr extends until the sun turns yellow, according to the apparent position of Ahmad’s school. The time for Maghrib extends until the twilight disappears. The time for Isha extends until the midpoint of the night, according to the apparent position of Ahmad’s school.

This is precisely what the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, stated in the hadith

---

## Page 11112

which Muslim narrated in his Sahīh from ‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Amr. It has also been transmitted from Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him. No hadith conveying the Prophet’s own words concerning the five prayer times is more authentic than this. Its meaning is likewise authentically established through several accounts of the Prophet’s practice in Medina, narrated by Abū Mūsā and Buraydah, may Allah be pleased with them both. Its details also appear separately in several hadiths. Most jurists have acted upon most of these reports.

The well-known position of the scholars of Iraq is that the time for Asr does not begin until the shadow of each object is twice its height. The scholars of the Hijaz—Mālik and others—recognize only a single time for Maghrib.

Section

Likewise, we affirm what the Sunnah and transmitted reports establish concerning combining two prayers when travelling, because of rain or illness—as in the hadith concerning the woman with non-menstrual bleeding—or because of other valid excuses.

We also affirm what the Book, the Sunnah, and transmitted reports indicate: that prayer times fall into two categories—times of choice, comprising five periods, and times of necessity, comprising three periods. For this reason, the Companions—such as ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn ‘Awf, Ibn ‘Abbās, and others—instructed

---

## Page 11113

a woman whose menstruation ended before sunset to pray Zuhr and Asr, and, if it ended before dawn, to pray Maghrib and Isha. Ahmad agrees with Mālik, may Allah have mercy on him, on these matters, and goes further on the basis of transmitted reports. Al-Shāfi‘ī, may Allah have mercy on him, does not go as far as Mālik in this regard. Abū Hanīfah’s position on combining prayers is well known.

The same applies to the preferred times for prayer. The scholars of hadith generally recommend praying at the beginning of the prescribed time, except where delaying it serves a greater benefit, as established in the Sunnah. Thus, they recommend delaying Zuhr in hot weather without qualification, whether people are gathered together or dispersed. They also recommend delaying Isha so long as this causes no hardship. All of this is established by authentic reports from the Sunnah that cannot be dismissed. Each of the jurists agrees with them on some or most of these points.

Abū Hanīfah recommends delaying all prayers except Maghrib. Al-Shāfi‘ī recommends praying early without qualification—even Isha, according to one of his two positions, and even in hot weather when people are gathered together.

{Yet the authentic hadith of Abū Dharr relates that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, instructed them to delay the prayer until it became cooler, although they were gathered together.}

---

## Page 11114

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah sanctify his soul—said:

Section

“A General Principle”

On the Number of Rak‘ahs in the Prayers, Their Times, and Related Matters of Combining and Shortening

Many scholars who write scholarly works customarily discuss the times, number, and names of the prayers in the chapter on prayer times. Some then discuss shortening and combining prayers in two separate chapters, alongside the prayers of those with valid excuses, such as the sick and those in fear. Others discuss combining prayers under prayer times, while devoting a separate chapter to shortening them. Since travel alone is the reason for shortening prayers, it is appropriate to discuss the traveller’s prayer alongside the prayers of those in fear and those who are ill.

As for combining prayers, there are several reasons for it; it is not confined to travel. We shall devote a comprehensive section to each of these matters.

---

## Page 11115

As for their number, it is well known that there are five prayers: three of four rak‘ahs, one of three, and one of two. This applies when not travelling.

As for travel, the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, made nearly thirty journeys and would pray two rak‘ahs during his travels. No scholar has ever reported that he offered an obligatory prayer as four rak‘ahs while travelling. Even during the Farewell Pilgrimage, his last journey, he led the Muslims in prayers of two rak‘ahs each. This is common knowledge, widely transmitted through so many channels as to establish certainty, and unanimously reported by all his Companions and those who learned from them.

The hadith narrated by al-Dāraqutnī from ‘Ā’ishah, that “the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, would shorten his prayers while travelling and also offer them in full, and would break his fast while she would fast,” is false regarding offering the prayers in full, even if it is authentic regarding breaking the fast. It contradicts the widely transmitted, mass-attested accounts. Nor was this ever mentioned afterward.

How could this have happened, when the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, always led the obligatory prayers during his travels? The exception was once during the expedition to Tabūk, when he was delayed for a time while purifying himself. They appointed ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn ‘Awf to lead, and the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, joined the prayer behind him for part of it.

Had he led them in four rak‘ahs while travelling, this would have been among the things they had the strongest reasons and greatest eagerness to report, since it would have departed from his consistent Sunnah and habitual practice—just as they reported that he sometimes combined two prayers. Since none of them reported such a thing, it is known with certainty that he did not do it.

---

## Page 11116

For this reason, Ibn ‘Umar said:

“The prayer during travel is two rak‘ahs. Whoever opposes the Sunnah has disbelieved.”

That is, whoever believes that praying two rak‘ahs is neither prescribed by the Sunnah nor sanctioned by Islamic law has disbelieved.

Likewise, ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb said:

“The prayer during travel is two rak‘ahs, the Friday prayer is two rak‘ahs, the Eid al-Adhā prayer is two rak‘ahs, and the Eid al-Fitr prayer is two rak‘ahs—complete, not shortened, as declared by your Prophet.”

‘Ā’ishah—may Allah be pleased with her—said:

“When prayer was first prescribed, it consisted of two rak‘ahs. The prayer during travel was left unchanged, while the prayer when not travelling was increased to its full length.”

Al-Zuhrī said: “I asked ‘Urwah, ‘Why, then, does ‘Ā’ishah offer the prayer in full?’ He replied, ‘She adopted an interpretation, just as ‘Uthmān did.’” This was recorded by al-Bukhārī and Muslim in their Sahīh collections.

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Allah has relieved the traveller of fasting and half the prayer.”

Furthermore, when the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, performed the Farewell Pilgrimage, he shortened his prayers throughout his stay in Mecca and at the pilgrimage sites. He entered Mecca on Sunday, left it for Minā on Thursday, stood at ‘Arafāt on Friday, and remained in Minā until Tuesday evening. He spent the night preceding Wednesday at al-Muhassab and performed the farewell circumambulation that night.

Earlier, during the campaign to conquer Mecca, he had stayed in Mecca for nineteen days, shortening his prayers. He also stayed at Tabūk for twenty days, shortening his prayers.

---

## Page 11117

As for the hadith narrated from ‘Ā’ishah, that she travelled with the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, from Medina to Mecca to perform ‘umrah, and upon reaching Mecca said:

“O Messenger of Allah, may my father and mother be sacrificed for you! You shortened your prayers while I offered mine in full, and you broke your fast while I fasted.”

He replied: “You have done well, ‘Ā’ishah.” She said: “He did not reproach me.”

This was recorded by al-Nasā’ī. Al-Dāraqutnī narrated:

“I set out with the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, for ‘umrah in Ramadan. He broke his fast while I fasted, and he shortened his prayers while I offered mine in full.”

He said: “Its chain of transmission is sound.”

Even if this report were authentic, it would contain no evidence that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, offered his prayers in full. “It would establish only his permission to offer them in full. Moreover, this version of the hadith is not authentic.” Rather, it is erroneous for several reasons:

First: Al-Bukhārī and Muslim narrate from ‘Ā’ishah that “the prayer during travel is two rak‘ahs.” Her nephew, who knew her better than anyone else, explained that she offered her prayers in full during travel only on the basis of an interpretation she adopted, not an explicit text she possessed. It is therefore clear that she possessed no explicit text on this matter.

Second: The hadith states that “she set out with him to perform ‘umrah in Ramadan—the ‘umrah of Ramadan—and she was fasting.” This is false by scholarly consensus, for the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, never performed ‘umrah in Ramadan. All his ‘umrahs were in Shawwāl. Since he never performed ‘umrah in Ramadan, and none of his ‘umrahs took place when fasting was obligatory for him, this hadith is invalid.

---

## Page 11118

Third: The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, travelled in Ramadan only for the campaigns of Badr and the Conquest of Mecca. None of his wives accompanied him at Badr, nor was ‘Ā’ishah with him. During the campaign of the Conquest, he fasted at the beginning of his journey and then broke his fast, contrary to what this fabricated hadith states.

Fourth: Whether ‘Ā’ishah performed ‘umrah with him is itself open to question.

Fifth: ‘Ā’ishah would not have fasted and offered her prayers in full throughout her journey to Mecca, departing from his practice without his permission. Rather, she would ask him for a ruling before acting, for undertaking such a thing without doing so is impermissible.

This mass-transmitted Sunnah thus establishes that the prayer during travel consists of two rak‘ahs, just as the prayer when not travelling consists of four. The number of rak‘ahs is learned only from the Prophet’s practice, peace and blessings be upon him, which he instituted for his community. This disproves the view held by some followers of Ahmad and al-Shāfi‘ī that four rak‘ahs are the norm and that two are merely a concession.

On this basis, they maintained that a person shortening the prayer must intend to shorten it at the outset of the prayer. This was stated by al-Shāfi‘ī and is also the view of al-Khiraqī, al-Qādī, and others.

Rather, the correct view is that of the majority of scholars, also preferred by Abū Bakr and others: shortening the prayer does not require a specific intention to do so. A traveller begins the prayer just as a person who is not travelling does. Indeed, even if

---

## Page 11119

a traveller intended to pray four rak‘ahs, doing so would be disliked for him, and the Sunnah would be to pray two. Imām Ahmad’s explicit statements support precisely this view.

The scholars have differed over offering four rak‘ahs while travelling: is it forbidden, disliked, merely a departure from what is preferable, or preferable? There are four views:

The first is the view of Abū Hanīfah and one view reported from Mālik.

The second is another view reported from Mālik, and also from Ahmad.

The third is a view reported from Ahmad and the sounder of al-Shāfi‘ī’s two views.

The fourth is another view held by al-Shāfi‘ī. This fourth view is unquestionably mistaken, and the third is weak. The tenable position is that offering four rak‘ahs is either forbidden or disliked. Some of the Companions used to offer four, and the others would disapprove, but not as they would disapprove of someone committing a forbidden act; rather, their disapproval was that shown towards someone doing something disliked.

As for the words of Allah Most High:

“When you travel throughout the land, there is no blame upon you for shortening the prayer if you fear that those who disbelieve may harm you.”

Here He made shortening conditional upon two causes: travelling through the land and fearing harm from those who disbelieve. This is because shortening, in its unrestricted sense, encompasses both reducing the number of rak‘ahs and abridging the prayer’s actions and essential elements, such as gesturing for bowing and prostration. This form of shortening is prescribed only when both causes are present.

---

## Page 11120

Each cause entails its own form of shortening: travel entails reducing the number of rak‘ahs, while fear entails abridging the prayer’s essential elements.

It would also be a sound interpretation to say that the shortening made conditional here concerns the prayer’s essential elements, since the traveller’s prayer consists of two rak‘ahs, complete rather than shortened. Hence Allah says:

“But when you are secure, establish the prayer.”

This makes clear that shortening prayers cannot be placed on the same footing as combining them. Shortening is the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the practice he prescribed for his community. Indeed, offering four rak‘ahs while travelling has an even weaker basis than combining prayers while travelling.

It is established that he sometimes combined prayers while travelling, whereas he was never reported to have offered four rak‘ahs during travel. The imams disagree about both practices: they disagree over the permissibility of offering four rak‘ahs and over the permissibility of combining prayers, while agreeing that shortening prayers and offering each prayer separately are permissible. Thus, neither disputed practice should be equated with the Sunnah established through mass transmission, which the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, consistently observed during his travels and upon which the community has agreed. [One should therefore not adopt] (1) the view that what he did on several occasions during his travels [is unanimously agreed upon] (2), when the community has disputed it.

Section

As for prayer times, the governing principle is that, in the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, they are of two kinds: a time of choice and ease, and a time of need and necessity.

> **Footnotes:**
> (1, 2) The text in square brackets is absent from the printed edition, and I have not found it in Safeguarding Majmūʿ al-Fatāwā against Omissions and Scribal Errors.
> Usāma ibn al-Zahrā’ — book coordinator for the al-Shāmila Encyclopedia.

---

## Page 11121

In the first case, there are five prayer times; in the second, there are three. The two nighttime prayers and the two daytime prayers are those that may be combined and shortened, unlike the dawn prayer, which is neither combined nor shortened. Each has its own distinct time—the time of ease and choice—while the two prayers in each pair share a time in circumstances of need and necessity. However, no daytime prayer may be delayed until night, nor any nighttime prayer until day.

This is why particular emphasis was placed on safeguarding the middle prayer, the afternoon prayer. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said concerning it:

“Whoever misses the afternoon prayer, his deeds have come to nothing.”

He also said:

“It is as though he has been deprived of his family and wealth.”

This principle is further supported by the fact that Allah mentions the prayer times in His Book sometimes as three and sometimes as five. The three are mentioned in His words:

“Establish prayer at the two ends of the day and in the early hours of the night.”

And in His words:

“Establish prayer from the sun’s decline until the darkness of the night.”

And His words:

“And glorify your Lord with praise when you rise, and glorify Him during the night and as the stars fade away.”

As for the five, He mentions them as four in His words:

“So glorify Allah when you reach the evening and when you reach the morning—to Him belongs all praise in the heavens and the earth—and in the late afternoon and when you reach midday.”

And His words:

“So be patient with what they say, and glorify your Lord with praise before sunrise and before sunset. And glorify Him during the hours of the night and at the ends of the day, so that you may be pleased.”

And His words:

“And glorify your Lord with praise before sunrise

---

## Page 11122

and before sunset.”

“And glorify Him during the night and after prostration.”

It is the Sunnah that has explained this, clarified it, and established its precise details.

Mass-transmitted reports establish that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to perform the five prayers at five separate times while residing in Medina and during most of his travels. Even during the Farewell Pilgrimage—his final journey—he performed each prayer at its own time, offering two units of prayer. He combined only the noon and afternoon prayers at ‘Arafah, and the sunset and night prayers at Muzdalifah. Hence Ibn Mas‘ūd said:

“I never saw the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, perform a prayer outside its time except the sunset prayer on the night of Jam‘ and the dawn prayer at Muzdalifah.”

He said this only because the Prophet offered the dawn prayer very early, while it was still quite dark. Jābir explained in his account that he performed it when dawn broke. Thus, Muslims agree on combining the prayers at ‘Arafah and Muzdalifah, because his combining these prayers during the Farewell Pilgrimage, but not the other prayers in which he led the Muslims at Minā or Mecca, is established through public, mass-transmitted, and widely circulated reports.

It is also established that he demonstrated the prayer times through his actions to someone who asked him about them in Medina, as Muslim related in his Sahīh through the reports of Abū Mūsā and Buraydah ibn al-Husayb. Gabriel explained the prayer times to him in Mecca, as narrated by Jābir and Ibn ‘Abbās. Muslim also related in his Sahīh the prayer times as stated by the Prophet

---

## Page 11123

—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—in the report of ‘Abdullāh ibn ‘Amr. This is the best of the hadiths concerning prayer times, because it explains them in the Prophet’s own words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“The time for the dawn prayer lasts until the sun rises; the time for the noon prayer lasts until the shadow of each object equals its height; the time for the afternoon prayer lasts until the sun turns yellow; the time for the sunset prayer lasts until the twilight glow disappears; and the time for the night prayer lasts until the middle of the night.”

Something similar has been narrated from Abū Hurayrah, attributed to the Prophet, though this report is open to question. Imam Ahmad relied on these hadiths because of his extensive knowledge of the Sunnah. Other imams received some of these hadiths but not others, so they followed what had reached them. Whoever follows what has reached him has done well, and no blame attaches to those who do good.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in more than one hadith:

“There will be rulers who delay the prayer beyond its proper time. So perform the prayer at its proper time, then let your prayer with them be a voluntary prayer.”

This proves that it is not permissible to delay the first prayer until the time of the second, nor to combine prayers without a need. Those rulers did not delay daytime prayers until night, or nighttime prayers until day. At most, they delayed the noon prayer until the time of the afternoon prayer, the afternoon prayer until the sun turned yellow, or the sunset prayer until the twilight disappeared. As for the night prayer, delaying it until the middle of the night would not be disliked. No one used to delay it beyond that, nor is that something rulers do.

---

## Page 11124

As for the three prayer times, authentic hadiths narrated by Ibn ‘Umar, Anas ibn Mālik, and Mu‘ādh ibn Jabal establish:

“He would combine the noon and afternoon prayers, and the sunset and night prayers, performing them at the time of the second prayer when he was pressing on with his journey during the time of the first, or was travelling during that time.”

This is agreed upon by those jurists among the scholars of hadith and the scholars of the Hijāz who permit combining two prayers. Likewise, it is narrated from him:

“During the expedition to Tabūk, when he set out after the sun had passed its zenith, he would perform the noon and afternoon prayers together.”

The compilers of the Sunan collections narrated this from Mu‘ādh. Muslim also narrated in his Sahīh from Mu‘ādh:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, combined the noon and afternoon prayers, and the sunset and night prayers, during the expedition to Tabūk.”

They differed only concerning a traveller who remains encamped throughout the times of both prayers. There are two positions reported from Ahmad:

The first is that he should not combine them, because there is neither a Sunnah precedent nor a need for doing so. This is Mālik’s position and the view preferred by al-Khiraqī.

The second is that he may combine them. This is al-Shāfi‘ī’s position, based on a hadith concerning this situation, also narrated by Abū Dāwūd. Ibn ‘Abd al-Barr mentioned that no other hadith on the matter had been narrated.

It is also established by authentic hadiths and by scholarly agreement:

“During the Farewell Pilgrimage, he combined the noon and afternoon prayers at ‘Arafah, and the sunset and night prayers at Muzdalifah.”

It is also established in the two Sahīh collections, through a hadith narrated by Ibn ‘Abbās:

“He prayed seven and eight units of prayer in Medina: the noon and afternoon prayers

---

## Page 11125

and the sunset and night prayers.” Muslim also narrated in his Sahīh from him:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, combined the noon and afternoon prayers, and the sunset and night prayers, in Medina without fear or rain.”

Ibn ‘Abbās was asked, “What did he intend by that?” He replied, “He intended not to impose hardship on his community.” Mu‘ādh ibn Jabal said the same.

The compilers of the Sunan collections narrated two or three hadiths reporting that he instructed a woman experiencing non-menstrual bleeding to combine two prayers, including the report of Hamnah bint Jahsh and others. Thus, prayers were combined in Medina because of rain and for reasons other than rain. Through this, Ibn ‘Abbās also indicated that prayers may be combined because of fear or rain, and while on the move during a journey. Prayers are combined both while staying in one place and while travelling to relieve hardship.

This shows that travel is not the reason for combining prayers in the same way that it is the reason for shortening them: the number of prayer units is shortened when travelling, but not otherwise. As for combining prayers, he combined them when not travelling. During his travels, he combined them when on the move and at places such as ‘Arafah and Muzdalifah, but did not combine them at his other stopping places. He also instructed a woman experiencing non-menstrual bleeding to combine prayers. It is therefore clear that combining prayers serves to relieve hardship. Whenever performing them separately causes hardship, combining them is permissible. This is the prayer time applicable in cases of a valid excuse or need.

For this reason, Companions such as ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn ‘Awf and Ibn ‘Umar said concerning a menstruating woman: if she becomes pure before sunset, she should perform the noon and afternoon prayers; if she becomes pure before dawn, she should perform the sunset and night prayers. The scholars who permit combining prayers, such as Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, and Ahmad, also held this view. This accords with the “principle of combining prayers”: the time is shared by the two prayers being combined in cases of necessity

---

## Page 11126

and in the presence of an impediment. Whoever catches the last part of the shared time has caught the time for the two prayers [both of them] (1).

Some of our scholars and others maintain that combining prayers is permissible if, and only if, the journey permits shortening them. They have consequently prohibited pilgrims in Mecca and others from combining the noon and afternoon prayers or the sunset and night prayers. I know of no reliable proof for their position. Rather, it contradicts the Sunnah established with certainty from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

We know that he did not instruct any of the Meccan pilgrims accompanying him to delay the afternoon prayer until its exclusive time, nor to bring forward the sunset prayer and perform it before reaching Muzdalifah, whether at ‘Arafah or near al-Ma’zimayn. This is known with certainty, and no one has claimed otherwise. Rather, Ahmad’s statements and explicit rulings indicate that everyone attending the pilgrimage should combine the two prayers and delay the sunset prayer, as established by the Sunnah. This was also the position chosen by a number of his followers, including Abū al-Khattāb in matters of worship, Abū Muhammad al-Maqdisī, and others.

One must therefore say either that combining prayers is connected with travel generally, whether short or long—either without further qualification or because one is on the move—or that combining prayers at Muzdalifah is connected with the pilgrimage rites, as some of our scholars and others maintain. In my view, the former is more correct and more consistent with Ahmad’s principles and explicit rulings. He expressly permitted combining prayers when not travelling because of an occupation; it is therefore all the more appropriate when someone is pressing on during a short journey.

Furthermore, rulings connected specifically with travel are confined to travel, such as shortening prayers, breaking the fast, and wiping. As for those applicable on both long and short journeys, such as praying on a mount, performing dry ablution, and eating carrion,

> **Footnotes:**
> (1) In the printed edition: kilāhumā (both of them).
> Usāma ibn al-Zahrā’ — book coordinator for the al-Shāmila Encyclopedia.

---

## Page 11127

these concessions were granted to meet a need and are likewise permissible when not travelling. Combining prayers belongs to this category: it was permitted because of need in general, not travel in particular. Hence, a concession tied to travel may be dispensed with, whereas one tied to need may become an unavoidable necessity. The former is exemplified by a traveller’s breaking the fast, and the latter by a sick person’s breaking it. The same distinction applies here. And Allah knows best.

Another verse resembling this one in its general and comprehensive scope, though its meaning may be unclear, is His saying, Exalted is He:

“When you travel through the land, there is no blame upon you for shortening the prayer if you fear that those who disbelieve may attack you.”

He permitted shortening the prayer subject to two conditions: travelling through the land and fearing the disbelievers.

Thus, many people, believing that shortening the prayer meant merely reducing the number of prayer units, found this problematic. Some proponents of innovation maintained that shortening the prayer was permissible only in a state of fear, until the Companions related mass-transmitted reports from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, concerning his shortening the prayer during journeys undertaken in safety. Ibn ‘Umar said: “The traveller’s prayer consists of two units. Whoever opposes the Sunnah has disbelieved.” For some of the Khawārij reject a Sunnah that conflicts with the apparent meaning of the Quran, despite knowing that the Messenger established it.

Hārithah ibn Wahb said: “We prayed two units with the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, while he was in complete safety.”

‘Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd said: “We prayed behind

---

## Page 11128

the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, at Minā, performing two units, and two units behind Abū Bakr, and two units behind ‘Umar.”

When Ya‘lā ibn Umayyah asked ‘Umar about the verse, ‘Umar said: “I wondered about the same thing that surprised you. So I asked the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and he said: ‘It is a charity that Allah has bestowed upon you, so accept His charity.’”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, thus explained that shortening the prayer during safe travel is a charity from Allah. He did not say that it contradicts the apparent meaning of the Quran.

We therefore say: shortening in its full, unrestricted sense comprises both reducing the number of prayer units and shortening the essential acts. Reducing the number means performing a four-unit prayer as two units. Shortening the essential acts means shortening the standing, bowing and prostration, as in prayer offered under conditions of intense fear or lesser fear.

Travel is the reason for reducing the number of units, while fear is the reason for shortening the essential acts. When both occur together, both the number of units and the essential acts are shortened. If only one of these two reasons is present, only the corresponding shortening applies. Thus His saying, Glorified is He:

“that you shorten the prayer”

is unrestricted, encompassing both kinds of shortening. The Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explains what the Quran leaves unelaborated, clarifies it, indicates its meaning and gives expression to it. It explains the Quran rather than contradicting its apparent meaning.

A similar example is found in a reading of His words:

“And wipe your heads and your feet.”

Here, wiping is unrestricted in meaning and includes wiping with flowing water, which is washing

---

## Page 11129

and wiping without flowing water, which is wiping without washing.

“The Quran commands wiping without qualification, while the Sunnah establishes that the head is wiped without flowing water, whereas the feet are wiped with flowing water. Thus, it explains the Quran rather than contradicting its apparent meaning. One should therefore reflect upon the Quran and understand its various aspects.”

For most passages whose apparent meaning people imagine has been contradicted are not so. Rather, they convey meanings understood by those whom Allah has granted understanding of His Book. This yields five benefits:

First: establishing rulings through evidence from the Quran.

Second: demonstrating the agreement between the Book and the Sunnah.

Third: showing that the Sunnah explains the Quran rather than contradicting it.

Fourth: clarifying the meanings and explanations contained in the Quran.

Fifth: showing that scholarly consensus accords with the Book and the Sunnah. And Allah knows best.

He was asked about the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“The best of deeds in Allah’s sight is prayer at its prescribed time.”

Does this mean the earlier or the later part of its time?

---

## Page 11130

He replied:

The prescribed time includes both its beginning and its end, and Allah accepts the prayer throughout that time. However, its beginning is preferable to its end, except where the Lawgiver has made an exception, such as delaying Zuhr in intense heat, or delaying ‘Ishā’ when this causes no hardship to the congregation. And Allah knows best.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

Must the night extend until sunrise? And what is the shortest interval between the time of Maghrib and the beginning of ‘Ishā’, measured in lunar mansions?

He replied:

The time for ‘Ishā’ begins when the red twilight disappears. Among buildings, however, one should take the precaution of waiting until the white twilight disappears, since walls may conceal the redness. Once the whiteness has disappeared, one can be certain that the red twilight has gone. This is the position of the majority, including Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī and Ahmad.

Abū Hanīfa, however, holds that twilight means the whiteness. Astronomical calculators say that its duration is two lunar mansions. But this is not a consistent measure, for the mansions are identified by stars, some of which lie close to the actual mansion, while others lie far from it. Moreover, the interval before ‘Ishā’ varies in length with the day, so it becomes

---

## Page 11131

longer in summer, just as the interval of dawn varies with the night and is therefore longer in winter.

Anyone who claims that the interval before ‘Ishā’ equals the interval of dawn in both winter and summer has made an error contradicted by sensory observation, as everyone agrees. His error arises because light depends on vapours. In winter, vapours are more abundant at night, so light appears earlier, whereas in summer there are fewer vapours at night. In summer, vapours make the atmosphere hazy during the day, whereas it is clear in winter, because the sun has dispersed the vapour and the rain has settled the dust.

Furthermore, both lights depend on the sun: one precedes it and the other follows it. They must therefore vary with the sun. In winter, the sun remains absent longer, so the light associated with it lasts longer.

As for equating these two intervals, claiming that dawn lasts longer in summer and the interval before ‘Ishā’ lasts longer in winter, making dawn correspond to the day—lengthening in summer and shortening in winter—and making twilight correspond to the night—shortening in summer and lengthening in winter—this turns sensory observation, reason, and revealed law on their heads. The appearance of darkness is not delayed beyond sunset. And Allah knows best.

---

## Page 11132

He was asked:
“Is it better to offer Fajr while it is still dark or to wait until it grows light?”

He replied:
Praise be to Allah.

Praying while it is still dark is preferable, unless there is a reason that calls for delaying it. The numerous authentic hadiths reported from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, show that he used to offer Fajr while it was still dark. Thus, in the two Sahīh collections, ‘Ā’ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said:

“Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to offer Fajr, and some believing women would attend with him, wrapped in their cloaks. They would then return to their homes, and no one could recognize them because of the darkness.”

There were no lamps in the Prophet’s mosque, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. As related in the two Sahīh collections from Abū Barzah al-Aslamī:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to recite between sixty and one hundred verses during Fajr and finish the prayer when a man could recognize the person sitting beside him. This recitation amounts to roughly half or a third of one of the Quran’s thirty parts. He would finish the prayer when a man could recognize the person sitting beside him.”

It is likewise authentically reported through other chains that he used to offer Fajr while it was still dark, as did his rightly guided caliphs after him. After him, there were rulers who delayed the prayer beyond its appointed time. Under their rule, jurists emerged who observed

---

## Page 11133

their practice and assumed that delaying Fajr and ‘Asr was preferable to offering them earlier. This was a misunderstanding of the Sunnah. They cited as evidence what al-Tirmidhī narrated from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Offer Fajr when it grows light, for that brings greater reward.”

Al-Tirmidhī graded this hadith authentic. Yet even if it contradicted those reports, it could not stand against them, for they are recorded in the two Sahīh collections and are widely known and widely transmitted. When an isolated report contradicts widely known and widely transmitted reports, it is anomalous. It may also have been abrogated, since praying Fajr while it was still dark remained the Prophet’s practice until his death, and was the practice of the rightly guided caliphs after him.

Al-Tahāwī, a follower of Abū Hanīfah, and others, such as Abū Hafs al-Barmakī, a follower of Ahmad, interpreted his words:

“Offer Fajr when it grows light”

as referring to finishing the prayer when it grows light—that is, prolong the Fajr prayer until you finish it as daylight appears.

Another interpretation is that growing light here means becoming clearly discernible: offer the prayer when dawn has become distinct, apparent and clear. For in the two Sahīh collections, Ibn Mas‘ūd said:

“I never saw Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, offer a prayer at a time other than its usual time, except Fajr at Muzdalifah and Maghrib at Jam‘. He offered Fajr that day only after dawn had broken.”

This is how it is reported in Sahīh Muslim, from Jābir, who said:

“He offered Fajr at the first gleam of

---

## Page 11134

dawn.” What ‘Abdullāh ibn Mas‘ūd meant was that he would delay Fajr beyond the first appearance of dawn until it became distinct, clear and apparent. On that day, however, he offered it earlier. Understood in this way, the meanings of the hadiths of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, are reconciled.

If, however, someone delays the prayer for a reason that warrants doing so—for example, someone who ordinarily performs dry ablution delays it so that he can pray toward the end of its time after performing ablution with water; someone praying alone delays it so that he can pray in congregation toward the end of its time; or someone will be able to pray standing toward the end of its time but can only pray sitting at the beginning—or for similar reasons whose merit outweighs that of praying at the beginning of the time, then delaying it for that reason is preferable. And Allah knows best.

He was asked about the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Offer Fajr when it grows light, for that brings greater reward.”

He replied:

As for the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Offer Fajr when it grows light, for that brings greater reward,”

it is an authentic hadith. Yet it is widely reported of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“He used to offer Fajr while it was still dark, so that the believing women would leave wrapped in their cloaks, and no one could recognize them because of the darkness.”

For this reason, they interpreted that hadith in two ways:

---

## Page 11135

First: he meant that it should be light when the prayer is completed. In other words, prolong the recitation until you finish the prayer when it has grown light. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to recite between sixty and a hundred verses in it—roughly half a hizb.

Second: he meant that dawn should become clear and distinct, so one should not pray merely on the basis of a strong supposition that it has begun. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to pray after dawn had become distinct, except on the day at Muzdalifah, when he offered it earlier than was his custom. And Allah knows best.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

A man from among those who profess Islam abandoned prayer for two years, then repented and began performing it regularly. Must he make up the prayers he missed or not?

He replied:

Someone who omits a prayer or one of its obligatory elements may have done so out of forgetfulness, having previously known it to be obligatory; out of ignorance of its obligation; because of an excuse which he believes permits delaying it; or knowingly and deliberately.

As for someone who forgets a prayer, he must perform it when he remembers it, in accordance with the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah

---

## Page 11136

may Allah bless him and grant him peace, which is widely transmitted from him; the imams are agreed on this. He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever sleeps through a prayer or forgets it must perform it when he remembers it. There is no expiation for it other than that.”

It is also widely reported in the Sahīh and elsewhere:

“He and his Companions slept through the dawn prayer while travelling, then offered both its Sunnah and obligatory prayers after sunrise, with an adhān (call to prayer) and an iqāmah (call announcing the prayer’s commencement).”

Likewise, someone who forgets to purify himself from ritual impurity and prays in that state must repeat the prayer after purifying himself. There is no disagreement on this. Even if the person who forgot was leading the prayer, he must repeat it, whereas those who prayed behind him need not repeat it if they were unaware. This is the position of the majority of scholars, including Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, according to the well-known position explicitly reported from him.
