Third, he prevents some people but not others. If he argues that those others recite because of the endowment established for them, whereas this person is not among its beneficiaries, that excuse would be even more reprehensible than the exclusion itself. Someone who recites the Quran seeking Allah’s reward is more deserving of assistance than someone who recites because of an endowment. The founder of an endowment has no right to change Allah’s religion. Merely establishing an endowment does not give its beneficiaries any right within the mosque that they did not previously possess.

Thus, if the founder wished to reserve a spot in the mosque for his endowment in such a way as to exclude others from it, he would have no right to do so. Even if he designated a spot in the mosque for the recitation, teaching or similar activities he had stipulated, that particular spot would not become binding, just as it does not become binding in the case of

---

## Page 11236

a vow. If someone vows to pray and observe a devotional retreat in a particular spot in the mosque, that spot does not become binding upon him; according to the scholars generally, he may pray and observe his retreat anywhere else in the mosque. But must he offer expiation for breaking an oath? There are two views within Ahmad’s school. The other three imams do not require expiation.

This is because a vow makes obligatory only something that would constitute obedience even without the vow. A vow does not turn something that is not worship into worship. The person making the vow is obliged to dedicate only what constitutes obedience to Allah, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever vows to obey Allah, let him obey Him; and whoever vows to disobey Allah, let him not disobey Him.”

Thus, if someone vows to do something forbidden or disliked, or something permissible that is neither preferable to perform nor to omit, he is not obliged to fulfil that vow. There are two opinions concerning expiation: Ahmad requires it according to the well-known position reported from him, whereas the other three imams do not.

The same applies to conditions stipulated by the founder of an endowment, a seller or anyone else. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“What is the matter with men who stipulate conditions that are not in Allah’s Book? Whoever stipulates a condition that is not in Allah’s Book, it is invalid, even if there are a hundred conditions. Allah’s Book has greater authority, and Allah’s condition is more binding.”

All of this is so

---

## Page 11237

because no one has the right to alter the law with which Allah sent His Messenger, introduce into Allah’s religion anything He has not authorized, or change the rules governing mosques from what Allah and His Messenger have prescribed. And Allah knows best.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

Is it permissible to sleep and talk in the mosque, and to walk in sandals in the areas used for prayer?

He replied:

Sleeping there occasionally is permissible for someone who needs to, such as a stranger or a poor person who has no home. People are, however, told not to make it their regular place for sleeping at night and resting at midday.

Speech that Allah and His Messenger love is good in the mosque. Forbidden speech is even more strictly forbidden there, and disliked speech is likewise more objectionable there. Excessive talk, even about permissible matters, is disliked in the mosque.

Walking in sandals is permissible, just as the Companions used to walk in their sandals in the mosque of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. However, when someone comes to the mosque, he should do as the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, instructed: inspect his sandals, and if there is anything unclean on them, rub them against the earth, for the earth purifies them. And Allah knows best.

---

## Page 11238

He was also asked:

Is it permissible to use a tooth-stick and comb one’s beard in the mosque?

He replied:

As for using a tooth-stick in the mosque, I know of no scholar who regarded it as disliked. Indeed, reports indicate that the early generations used tooth-sticks in the mosque. A person may spit or blow his nose into his clothing while in the mosque, by agreement of the imams and according to the reliably established Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Moreover, according to the majority of scholars, performing ablution in the mosque is permissible without being disliked. If ablution is permissible there, even though using a tooth-stick is part of ablution, and prayer is permissible there, even though a tooth-stick is used before prayer, how could using a tooth-stick be disliked? And if spitting and blowing one’s nose into one’s clothing are permissible there, how could using a tooth-stick be disliked?

As for combing the beard, some people regarded it as disliked only on the grounds that human hair, once detached, is ritually impure, and nothing ritually impure may be left in the mosque; or on the grounds that it is like a piece of litter. The majority of scholars, however, hold that human hair detached from the body is ritually pure. This is the position of Mālik and Abū Hanīfa, the apparent position of Ahmad’s school, and one of the two views within al-Shāfiʿī’s school. This is the correct view, for the Prophet

---

## Page 11239

may Allah bless him and grant him peace, “had his head shaved, gave half of his hair to Abū Talha, and distributed the other half among the people.”

In matters of ritual purity and impurity, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, shares the same rulings as his community. Indeed, the basic principle is that he is their example in all rulings, except where evidence establishes that a ruling applies exclusively to him. Moreover, the correct view, held by the majority, is that the hair of animals that die without lawful slaughter is ritually pure. Indeed, according to one of the two scholarly views—the apparent position of Mālik’s school and one of the two reported positions of Ahmad—all hair is ritually pure, even pig hair. According to either view, there is nothing wrong with combing one’s hair if one gathers the fallen hair and does not leave it in the mosque. Leaving one’s hair in the mosque, however, is disliked even if it is not ritually impure, for the mosque should be kept free even of a speck that might get into someone’s eye. And Allah knows best.

He was also asked—may Allah have mercy on him—about sacrificial animals:

Is it permissible to slaughter them in the mosque? May the dead be washed and fetuses buried there? Is it permissible to alter a mosque’s endowment without any benefit accruing to it? Is it permissible to cleanse oneself after relieving oneself or to bathe in the mosque? If this is not permissible, what is the punishment for

---

## Page 11240

one who does this, does not obey Allah’s commands, and does not refrain from what he has been forbidden? Even when a scholar gives him a ruling, he insults him. Is the ruler obliged to restrain and stop him and restore the endowment to its former state?

He replied:

No animals may be slaughtered in a mosque, whether sacrificial animals or otherwise. How could this be permissible when prayer in a slaughterhouse specifically set aside for slaughter is deemed objectionable—either prohibited or merely disliked? How, then, can a mosque be made to resemble a slaughterhouse? This would contaminate the mosque with blood, something from which it must be kept free.

Likewise, no deceased person may be buried in a mosque, whether a child, an adult, a fetus, or anyone else. Mosques must not be made to resemble cemeteries. Altering an endowment without any benefit is also impermissible, as is cleansing oneself after relieving oneself in a mosque.

As for performing ablution in a mosque, scholars disagree over whether it is disliked. The stronger view is that it is not disliked unless accompanied by blowing one’s nose or spitting in the mosque. Spitting in a mosque is a sin, and its expiation is to bury the spittle. How much more objectionable, then, is nasal mucus!

Anyone who does not obey what Allah has commanded or refrain from what He has forbidden, but instead rebuffs those who enjoin good and forbid evil, is to receive a punishment prescribed by Islamic law that will compel him and others like him to fulfil their obligations and refrain from prohibited acts.

---

## Page 11241

Nor may the dead be washed in a mosque. If changes are introduced into a mosque that harm those praying there, whatever harms them must be removed, and measures must be taken to serve their interests, either by restoring it to its original condition or by improving upon it. And Allah knows best.

He was asked:

May someone who teaches children in a mosque spend the night there?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. The mosque must be protected from anything that harms it or disturbs those praying in it, including children raising their voices, soiling its mats, and similar conduct. This is especially so during prayer, for such conduct is among the gravest wrongs.

As for spending the night there, if this is to meet a need—as in the case of a stranger who has no family, a poor stranger who has no home, or someone in similar circumstances—there is no harm, provided he stays there only as long as needed and then moves elsewhere. But taking it as a regular place to sleep at night and rest at midday is not permissible.

---

## Page 11242

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

In a mosque where Quran recitation and oral instruction take place morning and evening, witnesses at the entrance talk excessively, disturbing those reciting. Is this permissible or not?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. No one may disturb those in the mosque who are praying, reciting, remembering Allah, supplicating, or engaging in similar activities for which mosques were built. No one may therefore do anything inside a mosque, at its entrance, or nearby that disrupts them. Indeed, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, came out to his Companions while they were praying and reciting aloud, and said:

“O people, each of you is conversing privately with his Lord, so do not raise your voices over one another when reciting.”

If he forbade someone praying from raising his voice over another person praying, how much more does this apply to others? Anyone who does something that disturbs those in the mosque, or does something that leads to such disturbance, must be prevented from doing so. And Allah knows best.

---

## Page 11243

He was asked:

Is begging in the congregational mosque lawful, forbidden, or disliked? And is it more incumbent to refrain from it than to engage in it?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. The basic ruling is that begging is forbidden, both inside and outside the mosque, except out of necessity. If someone is in such necessity and begs in the mosque without harming anyone by stepping over people or otherwise, without lying in what he relates about his circumstances, and without raising his voice in a way that harms people—such as begging while the preacher is delivering his sermon, or distracting people while they are listening to religious instruction, and the like—then it is permissible. And Allah knows best.

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—said:

Section: “Facing the Qiblah”

There is no disagreement among the scholars concerning what is obligatory in this regard, and the dispute between those who require facing its direction and those who require facing the Kaaba itself has no real substance. Allah Most High says:

---

## Page 11244

“We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward heaven, and We will surely turn you to a qiblah with which you will be pleased. So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque. And wherever you are, turn your faces toward it.”

Up to His words:

“And wherever you set out from, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque. And wherever you are, turn your faces toward it.”

Shatrahu means “toward it” or “in its direction,” as the poet said:

Umm Zinbāʿ, turn—turn the pale camels
To face Banū Tamīm.

He also says:

“For everyone there is a direction toward which he turns.”

Wijhah means the same as jihah (direction), just as ʿidah (promise) and zinah (weight) were originally wiʿdah and wiznah. Thus, the qiblah is what one faces, while the wijhah is what one turns toward. Allah, glorified be He, commanded him to turn his face toward the Sacred Mosque. The “Sacred Mosque” means the entire Sacred Precinct, as in His words:

“So let them not approach the Sacred Mosque after this year of theirs.”

This is not restricted to the Kaaba. This bears out the transmitted report: “The Kaaba is the qiblah for the mosque; the mosque is the qiblah for Mecca; Mecca is the qiblah for the Sacred Precinct; and the Sacred Precinct is the qiblah for the earth.”

It is established in the two Sahīh collections that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prayed two units of prayer facing the Kaaba and said: “This is the qiblah.”

It is also established in the two Sahīh collections that he said:

“Do not face the qiblah when defecating or urinating, nor turn your backs toward it; rather, face east or west.”

He thus forbade facing the qiblah when defecating or urinating, and commanded facing it in prayer. Hence, the qiblah which he forbade people to face

---

## Page 11245

or turn their backs toward when defecating or urinating is the same qiblah that he commanded worshippers to face in prayer. He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“What lies between east and west is qiblah.”

Al-Tirmidhī said: “This is an authentic hadith.”

Several Companions likewise stated this, including ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, ʿAlī ibn Abī Tālib, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn ʿUmar, and others. No disagreement on this matter is known from any of the Companions. The imams of the established schools of law also explicitly stated this, and their statements on the matter are well known.

Later jurists have reported two positions on this matter within the school of Ahmad and other schools. I have examined Ahmad’s statements on this subject and found them consistent, without any disagreement. Differences are likewise reported within the schools of Mālik, Abū Hanīfah, and al-Shāfiʿī, but upon careful examination, these do not constitute a real disagreement.

Rather, whoever says that a person should use his best judgment to pray toward the Kaaba itself, or that his obligation is to face the Kaaba itself according to his best judgment, is correct. Whoever says that a person should use his best judgment to pray in the direction of the Kaaba, or that his obligation is to face the qiblah, is also correct.

This is because they agree that whoever can see the Kaaba must pray facing it. They also agree that the closer worshippers are to it, the shorter their row will be compared with the rows of those farther away. This holds true of anything one faces. Thus, the row close to the Kaaba does not extend beyond its width. If it were longer,

---

## Page 11246

those extending beyond its width would be praying toward something other than the Kaaba. The row behind it is longer, and so on. Thus, when the rows are beneath the mosque’s covered galleries, they curve sufficiently for the worshippers to face the Kaaba: they are praying toward it and in its direction as well. When people are far from it, they pray in its direction and are also praying toward it. Even if a row extends beyond the width of the Kaaba, their prayer is valid by the agreement of the Muslims, even when the row is straight, provided they cannot see it.

It is evident that, if one were to walk straight ahead toward it from these rows, the portion extending beyond its width would lie outside its alignment. Whoever imagines that a worshipper must pray in such a position that, were he to walk straight ahead, he would reach the Kaaba itself has therefore erred. Whoever interprets the obligation to pray toward the Kaaba itself in this way and makes this obligatory has erred. Even if a jurist exercising independent judgment has held this view, it is erroneous and contrary to the explicit texts of the Quran and Sunnah and the consensus of the early generations—indeed, the consensus of the Muslim community. For the community agrees that the prayer of a long row extending many times beyond the width of the Kaaba is valid, even if the row is straight, without any bend or curvature.

If it is objected:

At a distance, bending and curving are not needed as they are at close range. Similarly, when people face the crescent moon, the sun, or a mountain, they face it even though they are numerous and scattered, whereas if it were close, they could not face it

---

## Page 11247

unless they were few and gathered together. The reply is:

There is no doubt that the bending and curving required at a distance are less than those required nearby. The greater the distance, the less the curvature; the nearer one is, the greater it becomes, until the row nearest the Kaaba has the greatest bend and curvature. Nevertheless, some bending and curving would still be necessary at a distance if the aim were to establish a straight line between the worshipper and the Kaaba, such that, were he to walk along it, he would reach the Kaaba. The curvature, however, would be very slight. It has been said, for example, that if a row were a mile long and situated in Greater Syria, each person’s bend would amount to the measure of a barley grain. This was mentioned by someone who explicitly stated [that] (1) facing the Kaaba itself is obligatory, but said that such slight curvature may be overlooked.

The reply to him is:

This is precisely what we mean when we say that the obligation is to face its direction: one is exempt from having to aim for such bending and curving. The disagreement thus becomes merely verbal, without any substantive difference. The point is that whoever prays in its direction is praying toward the Kaaba itself, even though he is not required to aim for such precision. It should not be said that someone who prays in this manner is mistaken in reality but excused. Rather, he faces the qiblah in reality as well as outwardly, and this is what he has been commanded to do. Thus, when the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, built mosques in the various cities, some were such that, if a straight line were projected from them toward the Kaaba, it would miss it. Yet the Muslims’ prayers in them were valid by the agreement of the Muslims.

> **Footnotes:**

## Page 11248

This also clarifies the claim made by those who say:

“For anyone near it or near the mosque of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the qiblah must lie along a straight line, since the Prophet would not be left in error.”

The reply is:

These people assumed that such an orientation towards the qiblah would be mistaken. It would only be mistaken if the obligation were to seek an alignment along a straight line between the centre of one’s nose and the Kaaba. That is not the case; rather, the texts of the Quran and Sunnah cited above establish the contrary.

A similar example is the statement of some that if people mistakenly perform the standing at ‘Arafah on the tenth day, it suffices for them. The correct view is that this is the Day of ‘Arafah, both in reality and outwardly, and there is no error in that. Rather, the Day of ‘Arafah is the day on which people perform the standing at ‘Arafah. Likewise, the crescent moon only counts as such when people proclaim its sighting; if it rises but they do not proclaim its sighting, it does not count as such. There is, however, a well-known disagreement concerning the crescent: does the term denote what rises, even if its sighting is not proclaimed, or what people proclaim sighting? These are two well-known views within the school of Ahmad and elsewhere, unlike the disagreement concerning facing the Kaaba.

Further evidence for this is that, if it were said that a person must seek an alignment along a straight line between the centre of his nose and forehead and the Kaaba, the reply would be that there must then be a means of knowing this. For Allah has not made anything obligatory without providing evidence by which it may be known. Yet it is well known that only a select few know how to determine this, despite their disagreements and their frequent errors in doing so, whereas the obligation to face the qiblah is general

---

## Page 11249

for all Muslims. The knowledge required of them cannot therefore be obscure, attainable only through a lengthy, difficult and perilous method, when acquiring such knowledge is impossible or difficult in most circumstances.

This is why those who have followed this method speak without knowledge, while disagreeing among themselves about it. Their familiar points of reference are al-Jady and the celestial pole. Some of them say:

“The pole is al-Jady, and it is a faint star.”

This is wrong in three respects: the pole is not al-Jady; al-Jady is not a faint star, but a bright one; and the pole is not a star at all.

Others say:

“Al-Jady is a faint star.”

This too is mistaken. Most of them say that the pole is a faint star, and report two opinions concerning whether the pole revolves or not. This is a confusion of distinct things. The pole, which is the centre of rotation, does not shift from its position, just as the spindle of a millstone does not shift from its position. There is, however, a small, faint star near it. If this star is called the pole, it is so named because it is the nearest star to the pole. This star does revolve: the stars unquestionably revolve, while the centre of rotation, which is their pole, unquestionably does not. Reporting two opinions on this matter is therefore the speech of someone who has failed to distinguish between the two.

The readily visible point of reference is al-Jady. Using it to establish exact alignment with the Kaaba is possible only at certain times, not at all times. For when the sun is in the middle of the sky, when shadows are at their shortest, the pole is aligned with the Syrian corner of the House, which lies to

---

## Page 11250

the right of someone facing the door. Those whose homeland is aligned with this pole, such as the people of Harrān and others, thus pray towards that corner. Hence their qiblah is said to be the most accurately aligned. Those whose homeland lies west of them—such as the people of Syria—turn slightly eastwards in proportion to their distance from this line: the farther away they are, the more they turn. Those who live east of them—such as the people of Iraq—adjust their qiblah in the opposite direction. Thus, the inhabitants of those lands keep the pole and what lies near it directly behind their heads. The people of Syria turn slightly, keeping it between the left ear and the hollow at the nape, or behind the left ear, depending on how near or far their homeland is from those people. The people of Iraq keep it behind the right ear. It is well known that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the Companions never instructed anyone to take account of the pole, anything near it, al-Jady, Banāt Na‘sh, or anything else of this kind.

For this reason, Imam Ahmad objected to those who instructed people to take account of these things. He instructed them not to determine the qiblah by al-Jady, saying:

“The hadith makes no mention of al-Jady. Rather, whatever lies between east and west is qiblah.”

This is indeed correct. Had determining the qiblah in this way been obligatory or recommended, the Companions would have known it best and been the first to do so, and the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would have explained it. He left nothing pertaining to the religion unexplained. How, then, could this be so when he expressly stated that whatever lies between east and west is qiblah, and forbade facing the qiblah or turning one’s back towards it when defecating or urinating? It is unanimously agreed among

---

## Page 11251

Muslims that the prohibition in this regard is not limited to the person relieving himself being aligned with the Ka‘bah along a straight line. Rather, the prohibition is broader than that. Facing the qiblah is commanded in one circumstance, just as it is forbidden in another. Although a prohibition may encompass what a command does not, this is consistent with his saying:

“Whatever lies between east and west is qiblah.”

Moreover, making religion dependent on this leads the Muslim community into disputes and disagreements over its religion, whereas Allah has forbidden division and disagreement. Most people have no precise knowledge of this; they merely follow those who have determined it approximately. Exact determination in this matter is either impossible or exceedingly difficult, and the Sharia does not impose such requirements.

Among those who claim expertise in calculation and knowledge of this matter, you will find that most make erroneous statements. When asked for evidence for their claims, they fall back on unverified premises and reports from people whose accounts cannot be trusted. The jurists who have mentioned some of these matters received them from those people without examining them rigorously. Thus, the followers of both groups ultimately rely on others in a way that involves error in many instances. One then claims that the qiblah he has determined is correct, rather than the one determined by the other, while the other claims the opposite. Eventually, people split into factions and groups. All of this is among the things Allah and His Messenger have forbidden.

The reason for this is that they have introduced into their religion what does not belong to it and prescribed religious practices for which Allah has given no permission. They have therefore disagreed over the innovation they themselves prescribed, because it

---

## Page 11252

has no fixed standard, just as those who seek to determine the appearance of the new crescent or the onset of dawn by calculation disagree. There is no consistently valid mathematical proof for this; rather, it is fraught with contradictions and discrepancies. These people have turned away from the latitude afforded by religion and from the proofs of the Sharia, falling into various forms of ignorance and innovation despite their claims to knowledge and expertise. Such is how Allah deals with those who abandon what He has prescribed in favour of innovations and go to excessive lengths in religion.

It is authentically reported in Sahīh Muslim, from al-Ahnaf ibn Qays, from Ibn Mas‘ūd, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Those who go to extremes are doomed.”

He repeated this three times. Ahmad and Abū Dāwūd also narrated it.

Furthermore, Allah said:

“So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque.”

And He said:

“Everyone has a direction toward which he turns,”

meaning, a direction he faces. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“This is the qiblah.”

The qiblah is that which one faces. He also said:

“Whoever prays as we pray, faces our qiblah, and eats what we slaughter is a Muslim, with the same rights and obligations as us.”

Muslims unanimously agree that, as a general rule, a person praying must face the qiblah. What is commanded, then, is to face the qiblah and turn one’s face toward the Sacred Mosque. The question is whether facing it and turning one’s face toward it require that the centre of one’s face be directed

---

## Page 11253

toward it—that is, the centre of the nose and the corresponding parts of the forehead, chin, and so forth—or whether a person is considered to face something when he turns his face toward it, even if the centre of his face is not aligned with it. This is the crux of the issue.

It is well known that people are prescribed to turn their faces toward the preacher and are forbidden to face the qiblah when defecating or urinating. In these and similar cases, facing something does not require alignment with the centre of the face and body. Rather, a slight deviation does not mean that one is no longer facing it. If a term has a defined meaning in the Sharia, that meaning is authoritative; otherwise, its meaning in language and customary usage is authoritative. Here, what constitutes facing something is established by the Sharia, language, and customary usage.

As for the Lawgiver, he said:

“Whatever lies between east and west is qiblah.”

It is well known that someone in Medina, Syria, or similar regions who places east to his left and west to his right is facing the Ka'bah with his body, such that a straight line could extend from his face to the Ka'bah, and likewise from his chest and abdomen. That line, however, may not extend from the centre of his face and chest. Thus, facing something with one’s face is broader than facing it with the centre of the face alone. And Allah knows best.

## Page 11254

He was asked:

Regarding the intention for purification, prayer, fasting, Hajj, and other acts of worship: does it reside in the heart or on the tongue? Is stating the intention aloud obligatory or recommended? Has any Muslim said that unless a person does so, his prayer or other act of worship is invalid?

Has anyone said that the prayer of someone who states his intention aloud is better than that of someone who does so quietly, whether he is leading the prayer, following an imam, or praying alone? Is expressing the intention verbally obligatory or not?

Has any of the four imams, or any other imam of the Muslims, said that a person’s prayer is invalid unless he expresses his intention verbally? If this is not obligatory, is it recommended? What was the practice of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the Rightly Guided Caliphs?

If someone persists in stating his intention aloud, believing this to be prescribed, is he an innovator who contravenes Islamic law, or not? Does he deserve discretionary punishment if he refuses to desist? Please give us a detailed answer.

He replied:

All praise be to Allah. The intention resides in the heart, not on the tongue, by agreement of the imams of

---

## Page 11255

the Muslims in all acts of worship: prayer, purification, zakat, Hajj, fasting, freeing slaves, jihad, and so forth. If a person says something contrary to what he intends in his heart, what counts is his heartfelt intention, not his words. If he speaks without forming an intention in his heart, that does not suffice, by agreement of the imams of the Muslims. Intention is a form of purpose. Hence the Arabs say, “May Allah have good in store for you,” meaning, “May He intend good for you.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Actions are only according to intentions, and each person shall have only what he intended. Whoever emigrates to Allah and His Messenger, his emigration is to Allah and His Messenger; and whoever emigrates for worldly gain or to marry a woman, his emigration is for that for which he emigrated.”

By “intention,” he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, meant the intention in the heart, not on the tongue, by agreement of the imams of the Muslims—the four imams and others.

The occasion of this hadith also indicates this. A man emigrated from Mecca to Medina to marry a woman called Umm Qays, and so he became known as “the emigrant for Umm Qays.” The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, then delivered a sermon from the pulpit and mentioned this hadith. This man’s intention was in his heart.

Stating the intention aloud is neither obligatory nor recommended, by agreement of the Muslims. Rather, anyone who does so believing it to be prescribed by Islamic law is an innovator who contravenes that law. He is ignorant and misguided and deserves discretionary punishment, or otherwise punishment, for doing so if he persists

---

## Page 11256

in doing so after he has been informed and the matter has been explained to him, especially if he disturbs those beside him by raising his voice or repeats this time after time. For this he deserves severe discretionary punishment. No Muslim has said that the prayer of someone who states his intention aloud is better than that of someone who voices it quietly, whether he is leading the prayer, following an imam, or praying alone.

As for voicing the intention quietly, this too is not obligatory according to the four imams and all the other imams of the Muslims. None of the imams has said that voicing the intention is obligatory for purification, prayer, fasting, or Hajj.

A person praying is not required to say, “I am praying the dawn prayer,” or to specify the noon or afternoon prayer, or whether he is leading the prayer or following an imam. Nor must he say “an obligatory prayer,” “a voluntary prayer,” or anything else. Rather, it suffices that his intention be in his heart, and Allah knows what is in people’s hearts. Likewise, for a ritual bath following sexual impurity and for ablution, the intention in the heart suffices.

The same applies to the intention to fast in Ramadan. No one is required to say, “I will fast tomorrow,” by agreement of the imams. Rather, the intention in his heart suffices. Intention follows knowledge: whoever knows what he wants to do necessarily intends it. Thus, if a Muslim knows that tomorrow is a day of Ramadan, and he is someone who fasts Ramadan, then he will necessarily

---

## Page 11257

intend to fast. If he knows that tomorrow is Eid, he will not intend to fast that night.

The same applies to prayer. If he knows that the prayer being held is the dawn or noon prayer, and knows that he wishes to perform the dawn or noon prayer, then that is necessarily the prayer he intends. He cannot know that it is the dawn prayer yet intend the noon prayer. Likewise, if he knows that he is praying as an imam or following an imam, he necessarily intends that. Intention necessarily follows knowledge and belief: if he knows what he wishes to do, he must intend it.

Thus, if he knows that he wishes to perform the noon prayer, and knows that this prayer is the noon prayer, he cannot intend another prayer. Even if he believes that its time has ended, his prayer is valid by agreement of the imams. Likewise, if he believes that its time has ended and therefore intends to perform the prayer after its prescribed time, but it turns out that he performed it within its time, his prayer is valid by agreement of the imams.

If he intends to offer the funeral prayer for the deceased before him—whoever that may be—and thinks the deceased is a man when it is a woman, his prayer is valid despite the discrepancy with what he intended. But if he intends to offer the funeral prayer only for someone he believes to be a particular person, and he prays over someone he believes to be that person, only to discover that it was someone else, then in this case he did not intend to pray over the person before him.

---

## Page 11258

The point here is that none of the imams holds that verbalizing the intention is obligatory. However, one of the later scholars derived a view within the school of al-Shāfiʿī that it is obligatory, and the overwhelming majority of al-Shāfiʿī’s followers judged him mistaken. His error arose because al-Shāfiʿī had said, “Something must be uttered at the beginning of the prayer.” This scholar mistakenly thought that al-Shāfiʿī meant uttering the intention. All of al-Shāfiʿī’s followers corrected him, explaining, “He meant uttering the opening takbīr (declaration of Allah’s greatness), not the intention.”

But is verbalizing the intention recommended or not? The jurists have two well-known views on this. Some recommended it, including certain followers of Abū Hanīfa, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad. They said that verbalizing it reinforces the intention, and recommended doing so for prayer, fasting, Hajj, and other acts of worship. Others did not recommend verbalizing it, including certain followers of Mālik and Ahmad, and others. This is the position explicitly reported from Mālik and Ahmad. Ahmad was asked, “Do you say anything before the opening takbīr?” He replied, “No.”

This is the correct view. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not say anything before the opening takbīr, nor did he verbalize the intention for ritual purification, prayer, fasting, Hajj, or any other act of worship. Neither did his caliphs. He never instructed anyone to verbalize the intention. Rather, he told the man whom he taught to pray, “Say ‘Allah is the Greatest,’” as reported in

---

## Page 11259

the Sahīh, where ʿĀ’isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would begin the prayer with the takbīr and begin his recitation with ‘Praise be to Allah, Lord of all worlds.’”

He did not verbalize an intention or anything else before the takbīr, nor did he teach any Muslim to do so. Had this been recommended, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would have done it, and the Muslims would have known about it. Likewise, in Hajj, he would begin ihrām (pilgrimage consecration) with the talbiya (pilgrimage invocation), and he prescribed that Muslims recite the talbiya at the beginning of Hajj. He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to Dubāʿa bint al-Zubayr:

“Perform Hajj and stipulate a condition, saying: ‘Here I am, O Allah, here I am; I shall leave ihrām wherever You prevent me from proceeding.’”

Thus, he instructed her to stipulate her condition after the talbiya. He did not prescribe that anyone say anything before the talbiya. One should not say, “O Allah, I intend to perform ʿumra and Hajj,” or “Hajj and ʿumra.” Nor should one say, “So make it easy for me and accept it from me,” “I have intended both together,” “I have entered ihrām for Allah,” or anything else of this kind in any act of worship. One says nothing before the talbiya; rather, he made the talbiya in Hajj equivalent to the takbīr in prayer.

He and his Companions would say, “So-and-so pronounced the talbiya for Hajj,” “He pronounced it for ʿumra,” or “He pronounced it for both together,” just as one says, “He pronounced the takbīr for prayer.” Ihlāl means raising one’s voice with the talbiya. In his talbiya, he would say:

“Here I am for Hajj and ʿumra,”

intending what he wished to

---

## Page 11260

do after the talbiya, not before it. All forms of verbalizing the intention that people have introduced—before the takbīr, before the talbiya, in purification, and in all other acts of worship—are religious innovations that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not prescribe.

Every addition introduced into prescribed acts of worship that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not prescribe is an innovation. Indeed, he consistently refrained from such additions in his worship. Thus, performing them and persisting in them constitutes innovation and misguidance in two respects:

One is the belief that this is prescribed and recommended—that doing it is better than leaving it undone—even though the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, never did it at all. The real implication of this claim is that what we have done is more complete and better than what the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did.

A man once asked Mālik ibn Anas about entering ihrām before reaching the designated boundary. Mālik replied:

“I fear that you may fall into temptation.”

The questioner said, “What temptation is there in that? It is only a few additional miles in obedience to Allah, the Almighty and Majestic.”

He replied, “What greater temptation could there be than to think that you have been singled out for a virtuous deed that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not perform?”

It is established in the two Sahīhs that he said:

“Whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me.”

That is, whoever thinks that another way is better than my Sunnah and turns away from what [I have prescribed] (1), believing

## Page 11261

that what he has chosen is better than what he has turned away from—is not of me. For the best speech is the speech of Allah, and the best guidance is the guidance of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, as an authentic report states that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would proclaim in his Friday sermons.

Whoever says that someone else’s guidance is better than the guidance of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, has succumbed to temptation; indeed, he is astray. Allah Most High said—honouring him and affirming his proof against all mankind:

“So let those who oppose his command beware, lest a trial befall them or a painful punishment afflict them.”

That is, a punishment that causes pain. He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded Muslims to follow him, to regard as obligatory what he made obligatory and as recommended what he favoured, and to believe that nothing is better than this. Whoever does not believe this has disobeyed his command. In Sahīh Muslim, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Those who go to excess are ruined.” He said this three times.

That is, those who impose strictness where strictness is unwarranted. Ubayy ibn Kaʿb and Ibn Masʿūd said: “Moderation in following the Sunnah is better than strenuous effort in following an innovation.”

No one may invoke the gathering of people for tarāwīh (Ramadan night prayers) as an argument, saying:

“What an excellent innovation this is!”

For it is an innovation in the linguistic sense, because they did something they had not done in this form during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace; yet it is a Sunnah prescribed in Islamic law. The same applies to expelling Jews and Christians from the Arabian Peninsula and founding towns such as Kūfa

---

## Page 11262

and Basra, compiling the Quran into a single volume, establishing the register of stipends, and other such measures.

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prescribed the Ramadan night prayers for his community and led them in congregation for several nights. During his lifetime, people prayed both in groups and individually. However, he did not regularly gather them into a single congregation, lest these prayers become obligatory for them. When he died, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the revealed law became settled.

When ʿUmar—may Allah be pleased with him—became caliph, he gathered them behind a single imam. The one who gathered them was Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, who assembled the people for these prayers at the command of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb—may Allah be pleased with him. ʿUmar was one of the rightly guided caliphs, concerning whom the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Adhere to my Sunnah and the Sunnah of the rightly guided caliphs after me. Bite firmly upon it with your back teeth.”

That is, the molars, because they exert the greatest force.

In Sahīh Muslim, Ibn ʿUmar is reported to have said:

“The prayer during travel is two rakʿahs. Whoever rejects the Sunnah has disbelieved.”

That is, whoever believes that two rakʿahs do not suffice for a traveller has disbelieved.

The second aspect concerns consistently departing, in acts of worship, from the practice consistently observed by the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. This is an innovation by the agreement of the imams, even if someone supposes that his addition contains some good. An example is the introduction by some earlier people of the call to prayer and the call to commence prayer for the two Eid prayers. They were forbidden to do so, and the imams of the Muslims disapproved of it, just as

---

## Page 11263

would be the case if someone prayed two rakʿahs after the ritual walk between Safā and Marwah, by analogy with the two rakʿahs after circumambulation. Some later scholars of al-Shāfiʿī’s school recommended this. Some later scholars of Ahmad’s school also recommended that a pilgrim entering the Sacred Mosque begin with the prayer of greeting the mosque. In doing so, they contradicted the imams and the Sunnah. Rather, the Sunnah is for someone in the state of ihrām to begin with circumambulation, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did when he entered the mosque. This differs from a resident who wishes to pray there without circumambulating: it is good for him to offer the prayer of greeting the mosque.

In short, Allah perfected the religion for the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his community, and through him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, completed His favour upon them. Anyone who declares an act obligatory when Allah and His Messenger have not made it obligatory, or [disliked] (1) when Allah and His Messenger have not deemed it disliked, is mistaken. The imams of the religion unanimously agree that nothing is forbidden except what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden, and nothing belongs to the religion except what Allah and His Messenger have prescribed. Whoever departs from these two principles has brought upon himself war from Allah.

Whoever institutes religious practices that Allah has not authorized and prohibits what Allah and His Messenger have not prohibited follows the religion of the people of pre-Islamic ignorance who opposed His Messenger. Allah condemned them in Surahs al-Anʿām and al-Aʿrāf and elsewhere for instituting religious practices that He had not authorized. They prohibited what Allah had not prohibited and permitted what Allah had forbidden, so Allah condemned and censured them for that.

Thus, those who believe in Allah and His Messenger hold as part of their religion that the five legal rulings—declaring something obligatory

## Page 11264

, recommended, permissible, disliked, or forbidden—are to be derived only from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Nothing is obligatory except what Allah and His Messenger have made obligatory, and nothing is lawful except what Allah and His Messenger have made lawful.

On some of these matters the imams of the religion agreed; on others they differed and referred them back to Allah and His Messenger. Allah Most High says:

“O you who believe, obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you. If you disagree over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you believe in Allah and the Last Day. That is better and best in outcome.”

Anyone who speaks ignorantly and in opposition to the imams must be prohibited from doing so and disciplined if he persists, as others like him among the ignorant are treated. No leader of misguidance is to be followed in anything that contravenes the revealed law, even if he is renowned for his knowledge. As one of the early generations said:

“Do not look at the jurist’s conduct; rather, ask him, and he will tell you the truth.”

Allah knows best. All praise is due to Allah.

He was asked:

Does someone who leaves his home intending to purify himself or pray need to renew that intention when he actually purifies himself or prays, or not? And is verbalizing

---

## Page 11265

the intention a sunnah practice or not?

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds. Imām Ahmad was asked about a man who leaves his home to pray: must he form his intention at the time of prayer? He replied: “He already formed his intention when he left.”

For this reason, leading scholars among his followers, such as al-Khiraqī and others, said that it suffices to form the intention before the opening takbīr (declaration of Allah’s greatness), as early as the beginning of the prayer’s appointed time. If he keeps the intention consciously in mind until he prays, that suffices by scholarly agreement. Scholars also agree that the intention need not be verbalized.

It is common knowledge that anyone who pronounces the takbīr in prayer necessarily intends to pray. If he knows that he is praying the noon prayer, then he intends the noon prayer. Whenever someone knows what he wishes to do, he necessarily intends it. But if he does not know, or forgets, the intention escapes him; this is rare.

There are two views within Ahmad’s school and elsewhere as to whether verbalizing the intention is recommended. His explicitly stated position is that it is not recommended. Abū Dāwūd said: “I asked Ahmad, ‘Does the worshipper say anything before the takbīr?’ He replied, ‘No.’”

He was also asked:

“Must the intention coincide with the takbīr? Please explain to us how it is to coincide with the takbīr, since al-Shāfi‘ī stated that prayer is not valid unless

---

## Page 11266

the intention coincides with the takbīr. This is difficult.”

He replied:

Regarding the intention’s coinciding with the takbīr, scholars hold two well-known views. The first is that it is not obligatory . . . (1).

The concurrence stipulated as a condition may be understood to mean pronouncing the takbīr immediately after forming the intention. This is possible and presents no difficulty; indeed, this is how people generally pray. It is inevitable: were they required to refrain from doing so, they would be unable to.

It may also be understood as extending the intention so that its end coincides with the end of the takbīr, with its beginning coinciding with the beginning of the takbīr. This is not valid, because it entails the complete intention being absent at the beginning of the prayer, leaving the beginning of the prayer without the required intention.

It may also be understood as keeping the entire intention consciously present throughout the final part of the takbīr. Scholars have disagreed over whether this is possible. Some have said that this is impossible and beyond human capacity, let alone obligatory. Even if it were held to be possible, it would be so difficult that the requirement would be waived on account of hardship.

## Page 11267

Moreover, what invalidates both this interpretation and the preceding one is that the person pronouncing the takbīr should reflect upon it and grasp its meaning. His heart should therefore be occupied with the meaning of the takbīr, not distracted from it by consciously calling the intention to mind. Furthermore, intention is a condition of worship, and conditions precede acts of worship and remain legally effective until their completion, as is the case with ritual purity. And Allah knows best.

He was asked:

Does the “intention” required when beginning acts of worship, such as prayer and other observances, need to be spoken aloud—for example, by saying, “I intend to fast” or “I intend to pray”? Is this obligatory or not?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. The intention for ritual purification—whether through ablution, ritual bathing, or dry ablution—and for prayer, fasting, pilgrimage, zakat, expiations, and other acts of worship does not need to be spoken, by agreement of the imams of Islam. Rather, they agree that the intention resides in the heart, not on the tongue. Thus, if someone mistakenly says something contrary to what he intends in his heart, what counts is his intention, not his words. No one has reported any disagreement on this, except that one of the later scholars of al-Shāfiʿī’s school—may Allah have mercy on him—derived a contrary opinion, but the leading scholars of his school judged him mistaken.

His mistake arose because al-Shāfiʿī said:

“Prayer necessarily requires a spoken utterance

---

## Page 11268

at its beginning.”

By this, al-Shāfiʿī meant the obligatory opening takbīr. This mistaken scholar, however, thought that al-Shāfiʿī meant stating the intention aloud, and all the scholars of al-Shāfiʿī’s school judged him mistaken.

The scholars did, however, disagree over whether it is recommended to state the intention quietly. The jurists hold two well-known positions on this.

A group of scholars from the schools of Abū Hanīfah, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad held that stating it is recommended because it reinforces the intention.

A group from the schools of Mālik and Ahmad, and others, held that stating it is not recommended, because this is an innovation not reported from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, or his Companions. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, never commanded anyone in his community to state the intention, nor did he teach any Muslim to do so. Had this been a recognized, prescribed practice, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his Companions would not have neglected it, especially when it concerns something the community encounters every day and night.

This is the soundest position. Indeed, stating the intention betrays a deficiency in both reason and religion. As for religion, it is an innovation. As for reason, it is like someone who wants [to] (1) eat some food and says: “My intention in putting my hand into this vessel is that I want [to] (2) take a morsel from it, put it in my mouth, chew it, and then swallow it to satisfy my hunger.”

This is like someone saying: “I intend to perform, as an obligation, this prayer which is obligatory upon me

## Page 11269

at this time, offering four units in congregation within its prescribed time, for Allah Most High.” All of this is foolishness and ignorance. For intention extends as far as knowledge does: whenever a person knows what he is doing, he necessarily intends it. It is rationally inconceivable for someone to act knowingly without intention; likewise, intention cannot exist without knowledge.

The imams agree that stating the intention aloud and repeating it are not prescribed. Indeed, anyone who habitually does this should be disciplined sufficiently to deter him from worshipping through innovations and disturbing people by raising his voice. For the hadith states:

“O people, each of you is conversing privately with his Lord, so do not raise your voices over one another in recitation.”

What, then, of someone who disturbs people with words other than recitation? Instead, he says: “I intend to pray, to pray such-and-such obligatory prayer at such-and-such a time”—among other practices that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not prescribe.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked about a man who was told: “It is not permissible to state the intention aloud in prayer, nor did the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, command it.”

The man replied: “It is true that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, neither did it nor commanded it. However, he did not forbid it, and the prayer of someone who states it aloud is not invalid.”

He then said: “We have good innovations and bad innovations,” and cited the tarāwīh prayers as evidence

---

## Page 11270

on the grounds that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, neither gathered people for them nor forbade them, and that it was ‘Umar who gathered the people for them and ordered their observance. Is it as he says? Are the practices established by the Rightly Guided Caliphs to be called innovations? May practices instituted by others be judged by analogy with theirs? Is there any basis for what he says and does?

As for his statement, “The prayer of someone who states his intention aloud—for prayer or other acts of worship—is not invalid,” does someone who objects to him sin or not?

He answered:

Praise be to Allah. Stating the intention aloud for prayer is a bad innovation, not a good one. This is agreed upon among Muslims. None of them has said that stating the intention aloud is recommended or that it is a good innovation. Whoever says this has contradicted the Sunnah of the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the consensus of the four imams and others. Anyone who says this must be called upon to repent. If he repents, well and good; otherwise, he is to be punished as he deserves.

The disagreement concerns only whether uttering the intention quietly is recommended. There are two views on this. The correct view is that uttering it is not recommended, for the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his Companions did not utter it, either quietly or aloud. No one has the right to alter the acts of worship that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prescribed for his community or to introduce innovations into them.

Nor may anyone claim that such things are good innovations, as in the case of the call to prayer that some people introduced for the two Eid prayers. The one who introduced it was Marwān ibn

---

## Page 11271

al-Hakam, and the Companions and those who followed them in righteousness denounced this. They did so even though the call to prayer is a remembrance of Allah, because it is not part of the Sunnah.

Likewise, when people introduced regular gatherings not prescribed by Islamic law—such as gathering for a particular prayer at the beginning of Rajab, on its first Friday night, or on the middle night of Shaʿbān—the Muslim scholars denounced this. If people were to introduce a sixth prayer, gathering for it in addition to the five prescribed prayers, the Muslims would denounce their action and restrain them.

As for “the night prayers of Ramadan,” the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, established them as a Sunnah for his community and led them in congregation for several nights. During his lifetime, they prayed both in groups and individually, but they did not maintain a single congregation, lest these prayers be made obligatory upon them. When the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, died, Islamic law became settled. Then, during the time of ʿUmar—may Allah be pleased with him—he gathered them behind a single imam, Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, who led the people in these prayers at the command of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb—may Allah be pleased with him.

ʿUmar—may Allah be pleased with him—was one of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, concerning whom the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Adhere to my Sunnah and the Sunnah of the Rightly Guided Caliphs after me. Hold fast to it with your back teeth.”

This means the molars, because they exert the greatest force. What ʿUmar did was Sunnah, yet he said, “What an excellent innovation this is!” For it is

---

## Page 11272

an innovation in the linguistic sense, because they did something they had not done during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace—namely, gathering in this manner. Yet it is a Sunnah prescribed by Islamic law.

The same applies to expelling the Jews and Christians from the Arabian Peninsula—that is, the Hijāz, Yemen, al-Yamāmah, and all the lands of the Arabian Peninsula that had not come under Persian or Roman rule; founding cities such as Kufa and Basra; compiling the Quran into a single volume; instituting the state register; introducing the first call to prayer on Friday; appointing a deputy to lead the people in prayer outside the city on Eid; and other practices established by the Rightly Guided Caliphs. Since they established these practices at the command of Allah and His Messenger, they are Sunnah, even if they are called innovations in the linguistic sense.

As for stating the intention aloud and repeating it, this is a reprehensible innovation, not a recommended practice, by the agreement of the Muslims. Neither the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, nor his Rightly Guided Caliphs did this.

He was asked:

About a man who, when praying, disturbs the people in the rows around him by stating his intention aloud. They rebuked him once, but he did not desist. Someone said to him:

“What you are doing is not

---

## Page 11273

part of Allah’s religion, and in doing it you are contravening the Sunnah.”

He replied:

“This is Allah’s religion, with which He sent His messengers, and every Muslim must do this.”

He also recites the Quran aloud behind the imam. Did the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, do this? Did any of the Companions, any of the four imams, or any of the Muslim scholars? If the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, his Companions and the scholars did not do this in prayer, what is required of someone who attributes this to them and practises it himself? Is it permissible for a Muslim to support him with even a single word if he does this, claims that it is part of the religion, and tells those who rebuke him, “Everyone may do whatever he wishes in his religion, and your rebuking me is ignorance”? Are those who rebuke him correct in doing so, or not?

He answered:

Praise be to Allah. Stating the intention aloud is not prescribed according to any of the Muslim scholars. Neither the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, nor any of his caliphs or Companions, nor the early generations of this ummah or its imams, did this. Whoever claims that this is Allah’s religion and that it is obligatory must be instructed in Islamic law and called upon to repent of this statement. If he persists in it, he is to be put to death.

Rather, the intention required for acts of worship—such as ablution, ritual bathing, prayer, fasting, zakat and others—resides in the heart, by agreement of the imams of the Muslims. “Intention” means purpose and resolve, and all rational people agree that purpose and resolve reside in the heart, not the tongue. Thus, if someone forms his intention in his heart, his intention is valid according to the four imams,

---

## Page 11274

and all the other imams of the Muslims, both early and later. There is no disagreement on this among the scholars who are followed and whose views are relied upon in issuing fatwas. Some later followers of the imams, however, claimed that verbalizing the intention is obligatory, though they did not say that stating it aloud is obligatory. Even so, this view is plainly erroneous, contrary to the consensus of the Muslims and to what is necessarily known of the religion of Islam by anyone familiar with the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the practice of his caliphs, and how the Companions and their successors prayed. Anyone familiar with this knows that they did not verbalize their intentions, nor did the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, command them to do so or teach this to any of the Companions. Rather, it is established in the two Sahīh collections and elsewhere that he said to the Bedouin who prayed incorrectly:

“When you stand to pray, say ‘Allah is the Greatest,’ then recite whatever you can of the Quran.”

In the Sunan collections, it is reported that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The key to prayer is purification; its inviolable state begins with the declaration ‘Allah is the Greatest’ and ends with the salutation of peace.”

In Sahīh Muslim, it is reported from ʿĀ’ishah, may Allah be pleased with her:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would begin the prayer with the declaration ‘Allah is the Greatest,’ and begin the recitation with ‘All praise is for Allah, Lord of all worlds.’”

It is established through mass transmission and the consensus of the Muslims that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the Companions would begin the prayer with the declaration “Allah is the Greatest.” No Muslim has transmitted, either from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, or from any of the Companions, that he verbalized his intention before this declaration, whether quietly or aloud, or that he commanded this. It is well known that there would have been ample motivation and incentive to report such a practice if there had been

---

## Page 11275

such a practice, and that those whose reports constitute mass transmission could not, either in the ordinary course of events or under religious law, have concealed reports of it. Since no one has reported it, it is known with certainty that it never occurred.

Thus, later jurists disagree about verbalizing the intention: is it recommended alongside the intention in the heart? Some followers of Abū Hanīfah, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad considered it recommended, saying that it reinforces the intention and gives it fuller expression. Other followers of Mālik, Ahmad, and others did not consider it recommended. This is also the explicitly stated position of Ahmad and others; indeed, they regarded it as a disliked innovation.

They said: Had it been recommended, the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would have done it or commanded it. He explained everything that brings one closer to Allah, especially prayer, whose manner of performance must be learned from him alone. It is authentically established that he said:

“Pray as you have seen me pray.”

These scholars said: Adding this and similar practices to the manner of performing prayer is like introducing any other innovation into acts of worship—for example, adding the call to prayer and the call to commence prayer to the two Eid prayers, or adding two units of prayer on al-Marwah to the ritual walking between al-Safā and al-Marwah, and similar practices.

They also said: Verbalizing the intention is unsound on rational grounds. For someone to say, “I intend to do such and such,” is like saying, “I intend to eat this food

---

## Page 11276

to satisfy my hunger,” and “I intend to wear this garment to cover myself,” and similar intentions already present in the heart, which it is unbecoming to articulate. Allah Most High says:

“Are you informing Allah of your religion, when Allah knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on earth?”

Concerning His words:

“We feed you only for the sake of Allah,”

some of the early generations said: “They did not say this with their tongues. Rather, Allah knew it from their hearts and reported it on their behalf.”

In short, the intention must be present in the heart; there is no disagreement about this. As for verbalizing it quietly, later scholars disagree over whether this is disliked or recommended. Saying it aloud, however, is disliked, prohibited, and not prescribed, by agreement of the Muslims. Repeating it is still more objectionable. This applies equally to the imam, those praying behind him, and anyone praying alone. By agreement of the Muslims, none of them is prescribed to voice the intention aloud or repeat it; rather, they are forbidden to do so.

Indeed, even someone praying alone is not prescribed to recite aloud if doing so disturbs others. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, came out to his Companions while they were praying and said:

“O people, each of you is conversing privately with his Lord, so do not raise your voices over one another in recitation.”

As for someone praying behind an imam, the Sunnah is for him to recite quietly, by agreement of the Muslims. However, if he occasionally raises his voice

---

## Page 11277

with some words of remembrance, there is no harm in that, just as an imam may occasionally let those behind him hear a verse during a prayer normally recited quietly. It is authentically reported from Abū Qatāda that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace,

“would sometimes let them hear a verse during the noon and afternoon prayers.”

It is also authentically reported that some Companions praying behind the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, recited a supplication aloud at the opening of the prayer or upon rising from bowing, and he did not disapprove of this.

Anyone who persists in practising religious innovations and commending them should receive a discretionary punishment that deters him and others like him from such conduct. Anyone who mistakenly attributes something false to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, must be informed of his error; if he does not desist, he is to be punished. No one may speak about religion without knowledge, nor assist anyone who speaks about religion without knowledge or introduces into it something that does not belong to it.

As for the statement, “Everyone may do whatever he wishes in his religion,” this is a grave statement. Whoever says it must be called upon to repent of it; otherwise, he is to be punished. Indeed, persisting in such a statement warrants execution. No one may practise in religion anything except what Allah and His Messenger have prescribed, rather than whatever he wishes or desires. Allah Most High says:

“And who is more astray than one who follows his own desires without guidance from Allah?”

And He Most High says:

“Indeed, many lead others astray through their desires, without knowledge.”

“Do not follow your desires, lest they lead you astray from the way of Allah.”

And He says:

“Do not follow the desires of a people who went astray before, led many others astray, and strayed from the right way.”

And He Most High says:

“Have you seen the one who has taken as his god

---

## Page 11278

his own desires? Will you then be his guardian?”

“Or do you think that most of them hear or understand? They are only like cattle—rather, they are even further astray.”

And He Most High says:

“But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge in their disputes, then find within themselves no unease concerning your judgment and submit wholeheartedly.”

It has been reported that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“By Him in whose hand is my soul, none of you truly believes until his desires accord with what I have brought.”

He Most High says:

“Have you not seen those who claim to believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you? They wish to seek judgment from false authorities, although they were commanded to reject them. Satan wishes to lead them far astray.”

“When they are told, ‘Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger,’ you see the hypocrites turn away from you in aversion.”

And He Most High says:

“Or do they have partners who have prescribed for them a religion that Allah has not authorized?”

And He Most High says:

“Alif Lām Mīm Sād.”

“A Book has been sent down to you—so let there be no unease in your heart concerning it—that you may warn by it, and as a reminder to the believers.”

“Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord, and do not follow any protectors besides Him. How little you take heed!”

And He Most High says:

“If the truth were to follow their desires, the heavens and the earth and all those within them would surely fall into ruin.”

There are many similar passages in the Quran. It is thus clear that a servant must follow the truth with which Allah sent His Messenger, and must not make his religion conform to his desires. And Allah knows best.
