## Page 11279

He was asked:

Two men disagreed about “intention.” One said, “Do not begin the prayer without an intention,” citing the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Each person will have only what he intended.”

The other said, “It is valid without an intention.” Give us a ruling, and may you be rewarded.

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. Prayer is not valid without an intention. However, the intention resides in the heart, by the consensus of the Muslims. It consists of purpose and resolve. If someone intends in his heart something different from what he says with his tongue, what counts is what he intended in his heart.

The scholars differed over whether stating one’s intention is recommended, holding two views. They agreed that neither raising one’s voice when stating the intention nor repeatedly stating it is recommended; rather, the imams unanimously agree that these practices are prohibited. If someone does not state his intention verbally, his prayer is valid according to the four imams and others. Only a few outliers among the later scholars dissented.

---

## Page 11280

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was also asked about the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“A person’s intention is more far-reaching than his deeds.”

He replied:

This statement has been made by several people, and some cite it as traced back to the Prophet. Its meaning can be explained in several ways:

First: An intention unaccompanied by action is rewarded, whereas an action unaccompanied by intention is not. The Quran, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the imams establish that whoever performs righteous deeds without sincerity to Allah will not have those deeds accepted. It is also established in both Sahīh collections, through several chains of transmission, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever intends to do a good deed but does not do it has one good deed recorded for him.”

Second: Whoever intends to do good, does as much of it as he can, but is unable to complete it receives the reward of one who performed it. Thus, it is reported in both Sahīh collections that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“There are men in Medina who have been with you on every journey you have made and in every valley you have crossed.” They asked, “Even though they are in Medina?” He replied, “Even though they are in Medina. A valid excuse has held them back.”

Al-Tirmidhī also graded as authentic the hadith narrated by Abū Kabshah al-Anmārī from the Prophet

---

## Page 11281

may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“He mentioned four men: a man whom Allah granted wealth and knowledge, who uses his wealth in obedience to Allah; and a man whom Allah granted knowledge but no wealth, who says, ‘If I had wealth like so-and-so, I would use it as he does.’ He said, ‘The two are equal in reward.’ Then there is a man whom Allah granted wealth but no knowledge, who uses his wealth in disobedience to Allah; and a man whom Allah granted neither wealth nor knowledge, who says, ‘If I had wealth like so-and-so, I would use it as he does.’ He said, ‘The two are equal in sin.’”

It is also reported in both Sahīh collections that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever calls others to guidance will have a reward equal to the rewards of those who follow him, without diminishing their rewards at all. Whoever calls others to misguidance will bear a burden of sin equal to the burdens of those who follow him, without diminishing their burdens at all.”

It is also reported in both Sahīh collections that he said:

“When a servant falls ill or travels, the deeds he used to perform while healthy and resident are recorded for him.”

There is much evidence supporting this.

Third: The heart is the king of the body, and the limbs are its troops. If the king is upright, his troops are upright; if the king is corrupt, his troops are corrupt. Intention is an act of the king, whereas outward deeds are acts of the troops.

Fourth: According to Ahl al-Sunnah, repentance from a sin is valid even when a person is unable to commit it.

---

## Page 11282

as in the repentance of a man whose penis has been severed from unlawful intercourse, or the repentance of someone whose tongue has been cut out from making accusations of unlawful intercourse and other such sins. The foundation of repentance is the heart’s resolve, and this remains possible despite physical incapacity.

Fifth: Intention is not subject to corruption, unlike outward deeds. Intention is rooted in love for Allah and His Messenger and the desire for His Countenance. This is itself beloved and pleasing to Allah and His Messenger. Outward deeds, however, are subject to many defects and are not accepted unless they are free of them. For this reason, acts of the heart alone are superior to bodily acts alone.

As one of the early Muslims said:

“The believer’s strength lies in his heart, and his weakness in his body; the hypocrite’s strength lies in his body, and his weakness in his heart.”

A detailed discussion of this would be lengthy. Allah knows best.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

A Hanafī man prayed in congregation, keeping his intention private, and then raised his hands with every pronouncement of “Allah is the Greatest.” The congregation’s jurist objected, telling him:

“This is not permissible in your school, and you are introducing an innovation into it. You are wavering: you have neither followed your imam nor taken guidance from your school.”

Does what he did constitute a deficiency in his prayer and a departure from the Sunnah and his imam’s teaching, or not?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. The person who objected to his keeping his intention private is ignorant. Stating one’s intention aloud is neither obligatory nor recommended, neither in the school of Abū Hanīfa nor

---

## Page 11283

in that of any of the Muslim imams. Rather, they all agree that stating one’s intention aloud is not prescribed. Whoever does so is mistaken and acts contrary to the Sunnah, by agreement of the imams of the religion. Indeed, the position of Abū Hanīfa, Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad, and all the other Muslim imams is that if a person forms the intention in his heart without expressing it verbally, either quietly or aloud, his prayer is valid. Verbalizing the intention is not obligatory, according to either Abū Hanīfa or any of the other imams.

Indeed, when one of al-Shāfiʿī’s later followers put forward an inferred opinion that verbalizing the intention is not obligatory, the other followers declared him mistaken, saying: “Al-Shāfiʿī only required the opening declaration of ‘Allah is the Greatest’ to be spoken, not the intention.” As for Abū Hanīfa and his followers, they never disputed that verbalizing the intention is not obligatory. The same applies to Mālik and his followers, and Ahmad and his followers.

Rather, the scholars differed over whether quietly verbalizing the intention is recommended, holding two views.

A group of the followers of Abū Hanīfa, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad said: “Verbalizing the intention is recommended, but not saying it aloud. Neither verbalizing it nor saying it aloud is obligatory.”

A group of the followers of Mālik and Ahmad, along with others, said: “Rather, verbalizing the intention is not recommended, either quietly or aloud, just as it is not obligatory by agreement of the imams. For the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and his Companions did not verbalize their intentions, either quietly or aloud.” This is the correct view, supported by the Sunnah.

---

## Page 11284

As for raising the hands with every declaration of “Allah is the Greatest,” even when prostrating, this is not the Sunnah that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—practised. The Muslim community does, however, agree that the hands are raised with the opening declaration of “Allah is the Greatest.”

As for raising them when bowing and when standing upright after bowing, most jurists of Kufa, such as Ibrāhīm al-Nakha‘ī, Abū Hanīfa, al-Thawrī, and others, did not know of this practice. Most jurists of the other centres and scholars of transmitted reports, however, knew of it, since reports of this Sunnah from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—were widely transmitted. These included al-Awzā‘ī, al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ishāq, and Abū ‘Ubayd. It is also one of the two positions reported from Mālik. Indeed, it is established in the two Sahīh collections, through reports from Ibn ‘Umar and others:

“The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—would raise his hands when beginning the prayer, when bowing, and when raising his head from bowing. He would not do so when prostrating or between the two prostrations.”

This practice is also established from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—in authentic hadith reports from Mālik ibn al-Huwayrith, Wā’il ibn Hujr, and Abū Humayd al-Sā‘idī, the latter in a gathering of ten Companions of the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—one of whom was Abū Qatāda. It is also known through reports from ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib, Abū Hurayra, and many other Companions, from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

Whenever Ibn ‘Umar—may Allah be pleased with them both—saw someone praying without raising his hands during the prayer, he would throw pebbles at him.

‘Uqba ibn ‘Āmir said:

“For each gesture, he is credited with ten good deeds.”

---

## Page 11285

The Kufans base their argument on the fact that ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd—may Allah be pleased with him—did not raise his hands. They are excused until the authentic Sunnah reaches them, for ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd was the jurist whom ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb sent to teach the people of Kufa the Sunnah. Nevertheless, many Companions—may Allah Most High be pleased with them—preserved the Prophet’s practice of raising his hands, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Ibn Mas‘ūd did not explicitly state that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—raised his hands only at the beginning; rather, they saw Ibn Mas‘ūd praying and raising his hands only at the beginning. A person may forget or have a lapse of attention. The matter of pressing the hands together during prayer had also escaped Ibn Mas‘ūd: when praying, he would press his hands together as he bowed, as they used to do in the early days of Islam. This practice was subsequently abrogated, and they were instructed to place their hands on their knees. Ibn Mas‘ūd had not retained this. The disputed raising of the hands does not invalidate the prayer; indeed, one may pray without raising them, though raising them is better and more commendable.

If someone follows Abū Hanīfa, Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, or Ahmad, then finds another imam’s position stronger on certain issues and follows it, he has acted well. There is no dispute that this does not detract from either his religious commitment or his uprightness. Rather, such a person is closer to the truth and more beloved to Allah and His Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—than someone who is partisan towards a particular individual other than the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. This includes someone who is partisan towards Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad, or Abū Hanīfa and considers that particular imam’s position to be the correct one that ought to be followed, rather than the position of the imam who disagreed with him.

---

## Page 11286

Thus, whoever does this is ignorant and misguided; indeed, he may even be a disbeliever. For if he believes that people are obliged to follow one particular imam rather than another, he must be called upon to repent; if he does not repent, he is to be put to death.

The most that can be said is that a layperson may, should, or must follow an imam, without prescribing any particular individual—not Zayd or ʿAmr. But to say that ordinary people must follow this or that particular imam is something no Muslim would say. Whoever is loyal to the imams and loves them, following each of them in whatever appears to him to accord with the Sunnah, is doing well. Indeed, his position is better than that of others, and such a person should not be disparaged as “wavering.”

Rather, the blameworthy waverer is someone who is neither with the believers nor with the disbelievers, but presents one face to the believers and another to the disbelievers. Allah Most High said concerning the hypocrites:

“The hypocrites seek to deceive Allah, but He deceives them. When they stand up for prayer, they stand lazily, showing off before people,”

up to His words:

“And whoever Allah leaves astray—you will never find for him a way.”

The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“The hypocrite is like a sheep wandering between two flocks, going to one at times and to the other at times.”

It is these wavering hypocrites whom Allah and His Messenger condemned, and He said concerning

---

## Page 11287

them:

“When the hypocrites come to you, they say, ‘We testify that you are indeed the Messenger of Allah.’ Allah knows that you are indeed His Messenger, and Allah testifies that the hypocrites are liars.”

He Most High also said concerning them:

“Have you not seen those who take as allies a people with whom Allah is angry? They belong neither to you nor to them, and they knowingly swear to lies.”

These hypocrites who ally themselves with the Jews, with whom Allah is angry, belong neither to the Jews nor to us. Such are those among the Jews, Christians, Tatars, and others who outwardly profess Islam while their hearts remain with their own people. Such a person is neither a true believer nor a disbeliever both outwardly and inwardly. These are the wavering ones whom Allah and His Messenger condemned. Allah has obliged His servants to be believers, neither disbelievers nor hypocrites, but rather to love for Allah’s sake, hate for Allah’s sake, give for Allah’s sake, and withhold for Allah’s sake.

Allah Most High said:

“O you who believe, do not take the Jews and Christians as allies. They are allies of one another. Whoever among you takes them as allies is indeed one of them.”

Then, further on, He says:

“Your allies are none but Allah, His Messenger, and those who believe—those who establish prayer, give zakat, and bow down in worship.”

“Whoever takes Allah, His Messenger, and the believers as allies—then surely the party of Allah will prevail.”

He Most High also said:

“O you who believe, do not take My enemies and your enemies as allies, offering them affection when they have disbelieved in the truth that has come to you,”

and the rest of the verse.

He Most High also said:

“You will not find a people who believe in Allah and the Last Day showing affection to those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, even if they are their fathers, their sons, their brothers, or their kindred.

Those are the ones in whose hearts He has inscribed faith and whom He has strengthened with a spirit from Him.”

## Page 11289

Thus, the imams of the religion follow the path of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all. The Companions were united and harmonious, even when they disputed certain subsidiary rulings of the Sharia concerning purification, prayer, Hajj, divorce, inheritance, or other matters. Their consensus is conclusive proof.

Whoever is partisan toward one particular imam to the exclusion of the others is like someone who is partisan toward one particular Companion to the exclusion of the rest: like the Rāfidī who champions ‘Alī to the exclusion of the three caliphs and the majority of the Companions, or the Khārijite who disparages ‘Uthmān and ‘Alī, may Allah be pleased with them both. These are the ways of the people of innovation and desires, whom the Quran, the Sunnah, and consensus establish as blameworthy and as departing from the law and path with which Allah sent His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

Whoever is partisan toward one particular imam bears some resemblance to these people, whether his partisanship is for Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, Abū Hanīfah, Ahmad, or anyone else. At best, someone who is partisan toward one of them is ignorant of that imam’s standing in knowledge and religion and of the standing of the others. He is therefore both ignorant and unjust. Allah commands knowledge and justice and forbids ignorance and injustice.

He Most High said:

“But man undertook it; indeed, he was unjust and ignorant,”

“so that Allah may punish the hypocritical men and hypocritical women,”

and so on to the end of the surah.

Now Abū Yūsuf and Muhammad were the most devoted followers of Abū Hanīfah and the most knowledgeable about his views

---

## Page 11290

and yet they differed with him on almost countless issues because evidence from the Sunnah and other proofs had become clear to them which they were obliged to follow. Nevertheless, they continued to hold their imam in high esteem. They are not to be called wavering.

Indeed, Abū Hanīfah and the other imams would adopt a view, then discover evidence contrary to it and follow that evidence. Such a person is not called wavering, for a person continues to seek knowledge and faith. When knowledge previously hidden from him becomes clear, he follows it. This is not someone wavering, but someone rightly guided whom Allah has increased in guidance.

Allah Most High said:

“And say, ‘My Lord, increase me in knowledge.’”

Every believer must therefore show loyalty to the believers and their scholars, seek the truth and follow it wherever he finds it, and recognize that whoever among these scholars exercises scholarly judgment and reaches the correct conclusion receives two rewards, while whoever exercises scholarly judgment and errs receives one reward for his effort, and his error is forgiven.

The believers must follow their imam when he does what is permissible, for the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The imam has only been appointed to be followed.”

Whether he raises his hands or does not raise them, this neither impairs nor invalidates their prayer according to Abū Hanīfah, al-Shāfi‘ī, Mālik, or Ahmad. If the imam raises his hands but the person praying behind him does not, or vice versa, this does not impair the prayer of either. Likewise, if a man raises his hands on some occasions but not others, this does not impair his prayer.

No one may make the view of a particular scholar a banner of allegiance, requiring others to follow it and forbidding other practices established by the Sunnah. Rather, there is latitude in all the practices established by the Sunnah, such as the adhān and iqāmah—the call to prayer and the call to commence it. For

---

## Page 11291

it is established in the two Sahīh collections that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace,

“commanded Bilāl to recite the phrases of the adhān twice and those of the iqāmah once.”

It is also established in the two Sahīh collections that he

“taught Abū Mahdhūrah to recite the phrases of the iqāmah twice each, like the adhān.”

Whoever recites the phrases of the iqāmah twice has done well, and whoever recites them once has done well. Whoever makes one form obligatory to the exclusion of the other is mistaken and misguided. Whoever shows allegiance to those who practise one form rather than the other solely on that basis is likewise mistaken and misguided.

Among the reasons Allah gave the Tatars power over the lands of the East was the widespread division and strife among their people over schools of law and other matters. Thus, you find someone affiliated with al-Shāfi‘ī so partisan in favour of his school against that of Abū Hanīfah that he departs from the religion. Someone affiliated with Abū Hanīfah is similarly partisan in favour of his school against that of al-Shāfi‘ī and others, to the point of departing from the religion. Someone affiliated with Ahmad is partisan in favour of his school against one or the other. In the Maghrib, you find someone affiliated with Mālik partisan in favour of his school against one or the other. All this belongs to the division and discord that Allah and His Messenger have forbidden.

All these people who are partisan in falsehood, following conjecture and what their souls desire, and pursuing their own desires without guidance from Allah, deserve blame and punishment.

This is a broad subject that cannot be treated at length in this fatwa. Holding fast to the community and maintaining harmony are fundamental principles of the religion, whereas the disputed subsidiary issue is an obscure matter of detail. How, then, can a fundamental principle be undermined for the sake of upholding a subsidiary matter? Most of these partisans know nothing of the Quran

---

## Page 11292

and the Sunnah, except what Allah wills. Rather, they cling to weak hadiths, unsound opinions, or accounts attributed to certain scholars and shaykhs that may be true or false. Even if they are true, the person concerned is not infallible. They cling to unverified reports from fallible speakers, while claiming authenticated transmission from the infallible speaker—namely, what trustworthy, reliable scholars have transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and recorded in authentic collections. The transmitters of these reports are deemed trustworthy by the unanimous agreement of the leading religious scholars, and the one from whom they transmit is infallible: he does not speak from his own desire; it is only revelation sent down to him. Allah Most High has required all people to obey and follow him.

Allah Most High says:

“But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge in their disputes, then find within themselves no resistance to your decisions and submit completely.”

And Allah Most High says:

“So let those who oppose his command beware, lest a trial afflict them or a painful punishment befall them.”

May Allah Most High guide us and all our fellow believers to the speech, deeds, guidance, and intentions that He loves and is pleased with. Allah knows best. All praise belongs to Allah alone.

## Page 11293

He was asked about an imam of the Shāfiʿī school who says, “Allah is greatest,” repeating this declaration many times while the people stand behind him.

He answered:

All praise belongs to Allah. Repeatedly pronouncing the intention and the declaration “Allah is greatest,” as well as pronouncing the intention aloud, is prohibited according to al-Shāfiʿī and all the other leading scholars of Islam. Whoever does this acts wrongly. If he believes this to be part of the religion, he has departed from the consensus of the Muslims. He must be forbidden from doing so. If he is removed from his position as imam when he refuses to desist, there would seem to be grounds for doing so, for it is reported in Sunan Abī Dāwūd:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ordered that an imam be removed for spitting in the direction of prayer.”

The imam must pray as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to pray. He may not content himself with what suffices for someone praying alone. Rather, he is forbidden to make the prayer excessively long or unduly short. What, then, if he persists in something forbidden to the imam, those following him, and someone praying alone? Allah knows best.

---

## Page 11294

He was asked about a man who, when praying at night, forms his intention and says, “I am praying my portion for the night.”

He answered:

This expression, “I am praying my portion for the night,” has not been transmitted from the early generations of the Muslim community or its leading scholars. What is prescribed is to intend to pray for Allah, whether by night or by day. He is not required to express his intention verbally. If he does express it, saying, “I am offering the night prayer for Allah,” or “I am praying the night vigil,” or something similar, that is permissible but not recommended. Rather, following the Sunnah is preferable. Allah knows best.

He was asked about a man who caught one unit of prayer with the congregation. When the imam concluded the prayer with the salutation, he stood to complete his prayer. Another man then came and prayed with him. Is it permissible to take this follower as one’s imam?

He answered:

As for the first man, there are two opinions concerning his prayer in the school of Ahmad and elsewhere. The correct view, however, is that this is permissible, and this is the view of most scholars, provided that the imam intends to lead and the follower intends to follow. If, however, the follower intends

---

## Page 11295

to follow, but the imam does not intend to lead, there are two opinions:

The first is that the prayer is valid. This is the view of al-Shāfiʿī, Mālik and others, and is also one view reported from Ahmad.

The second is that it is not valid. This is the well-known view reported from Ahmad.

The explanation is that this man was following an imam at the beginning of the prayer, then became someone praying alone after the imam’s salutation. When the other man follows him, he changes from praying alone to leading, just as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, became the imam of Ibn ʿAbbās after initially praying alone. This is valid in voluntary prayer, as illustrated by this hadith and explicitly stated by Ahmad and other leading scholars, although an opinion that it is impermissible has been mentioned within Ahmad’s school.

As for obligatory prayer, there is a well-known disagreement. The correct view is that this is permissible in both obligatory and voluntary prayers, since, by leading, the imam assumes more obligations than he had when praying alone. Thus, there is nothing objectionable at all in someone praying alone becoming an imam, unlike the former case. Allah knows best.

---

## Page 11296

Chapter: The Manner of Performing Prayer

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

A man was walking hurriedly to the Friday prayer. Someone objected and told him, “Walk at an unhurried pace.” The man rejected this advice, saying that Allah Most High has said:

“O you who believe, when the call is made for prayer on Friday, hasten to the remembrance of Allah.”

What is the correct understanding?

He replied:

The striving commanded here does not mean running. It is authentically reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When the call to commence prayer is given, do not come running. Rather, come walking calmly. Pray whatever you catch, and complete whatever you have missed.” Another narration reads: “Make up whatever you have missed.”

Rather, the leading scholars have explained that striving in the Book of Allah means work and action, as Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, your efforts are diverse.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it as he should, while being a believer—it is they whose striving will be appreciated.”

And Allah Most High says:

“When he turns away, he strives throughout the land to spread corruption therein.”

And Allah Most High says:

“The recompense of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger

---

## Page 11297

and strive to spread corruption throughout the land.” And He said of Pharaoh:

“Then he turned away, striving.”

ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb recited: “Proceed to the remembrance of Allah.” Thus, the striving commanded for Friday prayer means proceeding and going to it.

The word “striving” is originally a generic term. In customary usage, when a term encompasses two categories, people often give one category a distinct name, leaving the general term exclusively for the other. For example, “blood relatives” encompasses all relatives: those who inherit prescribed shares, those who inherit as residuary heirs, and those entitled to neither. Once those entitled to prescribed shares and residuary heirs were distinguished by their own names, “blood relatives,” in the customary terminology of jurists, came to refer exclusively to those entitled to neither.

Likewise, the term jā’iz (“permissible”) encompasses acts and contracts that are obligatory or binding, as well as those that are not. Once certain acts were designated obligatory and certain contracts binding, the term jā’iz, in their customary usage, became restricted to the other category.

Similarly, the term khamr (“wine”) is a general designation for every kind of drink. But once drinks made from things other than grapes were given the distinct name nabīdh, khamr came, in customary usage, to refer exclusively to grape juice. Some scholars consequently thought that the term khamr in the Quran and Sunnah referred exclusively to that. Yet hadiths transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, through so many independent chains as to establish certainty demonstrate its general scope. There are many similar examples.

---

## Page 11298

This ambiguity arising from later usage has led many people to misunderstand the language of revelation. The word “striving” is a case in point: originally, it encompasses any going or proceeding, and this is the striving commanded in the Quran. One of its two forms may then be given the distinct name “walking,” leaving “striving” restricted to the other. This is the striving that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prohibited when he said:

“When the call to begin the prayer is given, do not come to it running; come to it walking.”

It is reported that ʿUmar used to recite, “Proceed,” and would say, “Had I recited it as ‘strive,’ I would have run until such-and-such happened.” If this report from him is authentic, it would mean that he understood the word “striving” in its restricted sense.

A similar example is the striving between al-Safā and al-Marwah. One jogs only along the valley floor between the two markers, and the term “striving” is used specifically for this. It may also be applied broadly to the entire passage back and forth between al-Safā and al-Marwah. This, however, appears to be because part of it constitutes striving in the restricted sense. And Allah knows best.

He was asked:

“Some people hasten to the pillars ahead of others, before the rows have been completed, and take places for themselves apart from the row. Is it permissible to remain behind the first row?”

---

## Page 11299

He replied:

It is established in the authentic collection that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Will you not form rows as the angels form rows before their Lord?”

They asked, “O Messenger of Allah, how do the angels form rows before their Lord?”

He replied, “They fill the first row, then the next, and stand close together in the row.”

It is also established in the authentic collection that he said:

“If people knew the reward for giving the call to prayer and standing in the first row, and could find no way to obtain it except by drawing lots, they would draw lots for it.”

It is likewise authentically recorded that he said:

“The best of the men’s rows is the first, and the worst is the last.”

These and similar teachings of the Sunnah indicate that worshippers should complete the first row, then the second. Whoever arrives before the others but stands in a row other than the first has acted contrary to Islamic law. If, in addition, he performs the prayer poorly, engages in unnecessary, disliked, or forbidden speech, or commits similar acts from which the mosque should be kept free, then he has failed to honor the religious ordinances and has stepped outside the prescribed bounds of obedience to Allah.

If he does not acknowledge the fault in his conduct and commit himself to following Allah’s command, he deserves a severe punishment that will induce him and others like him to carry out what Allah has commanded and refrain from what Allah has forbidden. And Allah knows best.

---

## Page 11300

He was also asked:

When worshippers do not straighten their rows, but each person prays on his own, is it permissible for them to pray like this in the marketplaces?

He replied:

No one may pray alone behind the row; rather, people must pray in rows. It is reported in the Sunan collections that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The prayer of one who stands alone behind the row is not valid.”

Their prayer in the marketplace is not valid unless the rows are connected. Rather, they must keep the rows close together and fill the first row, then the next. And Allah knows best.

## Page 11301

Shaykh al-Islām Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

For someone seeking to worship Allah, it may be unclear which practice is preferable in the following matters I shall mention, on which the imams have differed:

In prayers with audible recitation, which is preferable: refraining from reciting the basmalah (“In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful”) aloud, or reciting it aloud?

Which is preferable: regularly offering the qunūt supplication in the dawn prayer, omitting it, or offering it occasionally when beneficial? The same question applies to the witr prayer.

Which is preferable: prolonging the prayer while keeping its parts proportionate in duration and manner, or shortening it according to what people have become accustomed to in these times?

When shortening prayers during travel, which is preferable: regularly combining them, or doing so occasionally as needed?

Is spending the entire night in prayer an innovation or a sunnah? Or is praying for part of the night better than praying throughout it?

Likewise, is fasting on consecutive days preferable, or fasting some days and not others? And what of continuing a fast without breaking it at night?

Is habitually wearing coarse clothing and eating coarse food preferable or not?

Which is preferable during travel: performing the regular sunnah prayers, omitting them, or performing some but not others? The same question applies to other voluntary prayers during travel.

Which is preferable during travel: fasting or not fasting?

And if someone cannot find water, or cannot use it because of illness, or fears harm from using it because of severe cold or the like,

---

## Page 11302

should he perform tayammum (dry ablution) or not? Does tayammum take the place of ritual ablution in the circumstances mentioned, or not?

When the crescent of Ramadan is obscured, which is better: fasting or not fasting? Or is one free to choose between them? Or is one of them recommended?

Regarding everything that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, consistently practised—in his deeds, circumstances, words, movements and moments of stillness, and in all his affairs, whether acts of worship or everyday habits—is consistently following all of this a sunnah for every member of the Muslim community? Or does this vary according to the different ranks and those occupying them? Please give us your ruling; may you be rewarded.

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah. These disputed questions concerning the manner of performing acts of worship fall into four categories.

One category comprises matters in which it is established that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, instituted both alternatives, and the Muslim community agrees that whoever follows either incurs no sin, although they may disagree over which is preferable. This is comparable to the modes of Quranic recitation established from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, which people agree may be used interchangeably, such as the recitations well known among Muslims. A Muslim may recite according to whichever of these he wishes, even if he prefers some of them for one reason or another.

Also belonging to this category are the opening supplications transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace

---

## Page 11303

which he used to recite during the night prayer, and the various supplications he would offer in his prayer at the end of the tashahhud (testimony of faith). All these forms established from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, are permissible by the agreement of the Muslims. However, those he commanded are better for us than those he practised without commanding them.

It is recorded in the Sahīh that he said:

“When any of you sits for the tashahhud, let him seek refuge in Allah from four things, saying: ‘O Allah, I seek refuge in You from the punishment of Hell, from the punishment of the grave, from the trials of life and death, and from the trial of the False Messiah.’”

Offering this supplication is better than saying:

“O Allah, forgive my past and future sins, what I have concealed and what I have disclosed, and what You know better than I do. You are the One who brings forward and the One who holds back. There is no god but You.”

It is also authentically established that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to say this at the end of his prayer. However, he commanded the first supplication. A practice whose obligatory status scholars have disputed is more strongly emphasized than one which he did not command and whose obligatory status scholars have not disputed.

Likewise, a supplication that he repeated frequently, such as:

“Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire,”

is more strongly emphasized than one he did not repeat as frequently.

---

## Page 11304

The Second Category

Matters concerning which the scholars agree that either of the two practices leaves a person’s worship valid and entails no sin, but they disagree over which is better and which the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to practise. This category includes qunūt (supplication) in the Fajr and Witr prayers, reciting the basmalah (the invocation “In the name of Allah”) aloud, the wording used to seek refuge in Allah, and similar matters.

They agree that the prayer of someone who recites the basmalah aloud is valid, as is the prayer of someone who recites it quietly. They also agree that the prayer of someone who offers qunūt in Fajr is valid, as is the prayer of someone who does not. The same applies to qunūt in Witr. Their disagreement concerns whether reciting the basmalah is obligatory; the majority hold that it is not. They also disagree over whether reciting it is recommended; the majority hold that it is.

They further disagree about cases in which the imam omits something that a person praying behind him considers obligatory. For example, the imam might omit the basmalah while the follower considers it obligatory; touch his penis without renewing his ablution while the follower considers ablution obligatory after doing so; pray wearing tanned hides from animals that died without lawful slaughter while the follower holds that tanning does not purify them; or undergo cupping without renewing his ablution while the follower considers ablution necessary after cupping.

The correct position, established with certainty, is that the follower’s prayer behind his imam is valid, even if the imam is in fact mistaken. This is because it is established in the Sahīh that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“They lead you in prayer. If they do so correctly, the reward is yours and theirs; if they err, the reward is yours and the blame is theirs.”

Likewise, if a person prays behind someone who offers qunūt in Fajr or Witr, he should offer it with him, whether

---

## Page 11305

he offers it before bowing or afterwards. If the imam does not offer qunūt, the follower should not offer it either.

If the imam considers something recommended, but those praying behind him do not, he does well to leave it for the sake of agreement and harmony.

Witr is an example of this. The scholars hold three views concerning it:

The first is that it must consist of three joined rak‘ahs, like Maghrib. This is the view held by some scholars of Iraq.

The second is that it must consist of a single rak‘ah, separate from the prayer preceding it. This is the view held by some scholars of the Hijaz.

The third is that both forms are permissible, as is the apparent position of the schools of al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad and others. This is the correct view, although these scholars prefer to separate it from the preceding prayer.

Thus, if the imam favours separating it, but those praying behind him prefer that he perform Witr like Maghrib, he does well to accommodate them in order to bring their hearts together. This accords with what the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to ‘Ā’ishah:

“Were it not that your people had only recently left the age of ignorance, I would have dismantled the Kaaba, set it at ground level, and given it two doors: one through which people would enter and another through which they would leave.”

He thus refrained from what he considered better, lest he alienate the people.

---

## Page 11306

Similarly, if a man considers it preferable to recite the basmalah aloud, but leads people who do not—or vice versa—and accommodates their practice, he has done well. Their disagreement concerns only which practice is preferable, according to their understanding of the Sunnah.

A group of scholars from Iraq believed that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, offered qunūt for only one month, then [discontinued it] by way of abrogating it. They therefore believed that qunūt in the obligatory prayers had been abrogated. A group of L scholars from the Hijaz believed that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, continued to offer qunūt until he departed this world. Some of them believed that he offered it before bowing, while others believed that he offered it after bowing.

The correct position is “the third view,” held by the majority of hadith scholars and many leading scholars of the Hijaz. It is what is established in the two Sahīh collections and elsewhere: he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, offered qunūt for a month, supplicating against Ri‘l, Dhakwān and ‘Usayyah, then discontinued this qunūt. Some time later, after Khaybar and after Abū Hurayrah had embraced Islam, he again offered qunūt, saying:

“O Allah, rescue al-Walīd ibn al-Walīd, Salamah ibn Hishām, and the oppressed believers. O Allah, intensify Your punishment upon Mudar, and afflict them with years of famine like those of Joseph.”

Had qunūt been abrogated, he would not have offered it on this second occasion. It is also established in an authentic hadith that he “offered qunūt in Maghrib and ‘Ishā’.” The Sunan collections report that he used to offer qunūt in all five prayers. Most of his qunūt

---

## Page 11307

was in Fajr. He did not regularly offer qunūt in Fajr or any other prayer. Indeed, it is established in the two Sahīh collections that Anas said:

“He only offered qunūt after bowing for one month.”

As for the hadith reported by al-Hākim and others through al-Rabī‘ ibn Anas, from Anas, who said:

“He continued to offer qunūt until he departed this world,”

this statement, in its context, refers only to qunūt before bowing. Even if this report contradicted the authentic hadith, it would carry no weight, since al-Rabī‘ ibn Anas is not among the narrators of the Sahīh. Yet it does not contradict it at all. It simply means that he always prolonged his standing in Fajr before bowing. As for the claim that he regularly supplicated in Fajr while bowing or afterward, whether audibly or inaudibly, this is unquestionably false. Anyone who carefully considers the authentic hadiths will necessarily recognize this and realize that, had this occurred, the Companions and Successors would have transmitted it. They would not have neglected to report his regular qunūt prescribed for us, when they reported his qunūt that is not prescribed in that exact form, but only in a comparable form. For the Muslims agree that supplicating for those particular individuals and against those particular individuals is not prescribed; rather, comparable supplication is prescribed.

Thus, when calamities strike, it is prescribed to offer qunūt in Fajr and other prayers, supplicating for the believers and against the disbelievers. This is how ‘Umar offered qunūt when he fought the Christians, using his supplication that includes:

“O Allah, curse the disbelievers among the People of the Book,”

and so on.

---

## Page 11308

Likewise, when ‘Alī—may Allah be pleased with him—fought a people, he offered qunūt, supplicating against them. Whoever offers qunūt should use a supplication appropriate to each calamity. It is good to name the believers for whom one supplicates and the disbelievers fighting against the Muslims against whom one supplicates.

As for qunūt in Witr, scholars hold three views:

One view is that it is not recommended under any circumstances, because it is not established that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, offered qunūt in Witr.

Another view is that it is recommended throughout the year, as reported from Ibn Mas‘ūd and others, and because the Sunan collections report that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, taught al-Hasan ibn ‘Alī—may Allah be pleased with them both—a supplication to recite in the qunūt of Witr.

A third view is that qunūt should be offered during the latter half of Ramadan, as Ubayy ibn Ka‘b used to do.

In fact, qunūt in Witr is a form of supplication permissible in prayer: whoever wishes may offer it, and whoever wishes may omit it. Just as a person may choose to offer Witr as three, five, or seven rak‘ahs, and, when offering three, may choose to separate them or join them together, so too may one choose whether to recite the qunūt supplication or omit it. When leading people in the night prayers of Ramadan, one does well to offer qunūt throughout the month, does well to offer it during the latter half, and does well to omit it altogether.

---

## Page 11309

Likewise, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, did not prescribe a specific number of rak‘ahs for the night prayers of Ramadan. He himself never prayed more than thirteen rak‘ahs, whether in Ramadan or at other times, but he would make the rak‘ahs lengthy. When ‘Umar gathered the people behind Ubayy ibn Ka‘b, Ubayy would lead them in twenty rak‘ahs, then offer three rak‘ahs of Witr. He shortened the recitation in proportion to the increase in the number of rak‘ahs, because this was easier for those praying behind him than making each rak‘ah lengthy. Some of the early Muslims later prayed forty rak‘ahs followed by three rak‘ahs of Witr, while others prayed thirty-six followed by three rak‘ahs of Witr. All of this is permissible; whichever of these ways a person follows in the night prayers of Ramadan, he has done well.

The best choice varies according to the circumstances of those praying. If they can bear standing for a long time, it is best to pray ten rak‘ahs followed by three, as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, used to do when praying on his own, both in Ramadan and at other times. If they cannot bear this, it is best to pray twenty. This is the practice followed by most Muslims, being a middle course between ten and forty. Praying forty rak‘ahs, or some other number, is also permissible, and none of these choices is disliked. Several leading scholars, including Ahmad and others, have explicitly stated this.

Anyone who thinks that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, prescribed a fixed number for the night prayers of Ramadan, which may neither be increased nor decreased, is mistaken. So, if there is such

---

## Page 11310

latitude in the very number of rak‘ahs offered in the night prayer, what, then, of prolonging the standing for the Qunūt supplication, or omitting that supplication? All of this is permissible and good. A person may feel energetic, in which case it is better for him to prolong his worship; at other times, he may not, in which case it is better for him to shorten it. The prayer of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, was well proportioned: when he prolonged the standing, he also prolonged the bowing and prostration; when he shortened the standing, he also shortened the bowing and prostration. This was his practice in the obligatory prayers, the night prayer, the eclipse prayer, and other prayers.

People have differed over whether it is better to stand longer, to bow and prostrate more frequently, or whether the two are equal. There are three views on this.

The soundest is that the two are equal. Standing is distinguished by Quran recitation, which is superior to remembrance and supplication, whereas prostration itself is superior to standing. Thus, when one prolongs the standing, one should also prolong the bowing and prostration. This is the prolonged devotion to which the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, referred when he was asked, “Which prayer is best?” He replied, “Prolonged devotion.”

For Qunūt means sustained worship, whether while standing, bowing, or prostrating. As Allah Most High says:

“Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing in prayer”

He thus describes him as devoutly obedient while prostrating, just as He describes him as devoutly obedient while standing.

---

## Page 11311

As for the basmalah (“In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful”):

There is no doubt that some Companions recited it aloud, while others did not, either reciting it silently or not reciting it at all. Most of those who recited it aloud would do so on some occasions and recite it silently on others. This is because a remembrance that the Sunnah prescribes reciting silently may nevertheless be recited aloud for an overriding benefit, such as teaching those praying behind the imam. An authentic report establishes that Ibn ʿAbbās recited al-Fātihah aloud in the funeral prayer to teach them that reciting it is Sunnah.

Scholars have differed over Quran recitation in the funeral prayer, holding three views:

One view is that it is not recommended under any circumstances. This is the position of Abū Hanīfah and Mālik.

Another is that reciting al-Fātihah in it is obligatory, as maintained by some followers of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad.

A third is that reciting al-Fātihah in it is recommended, but if a person does not recite and instead merely supplicates, that is permissible. This is the correct view.

An authentic report also establishes that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb would say:

“Allah is the Greatest. Glory and praise be to You, O Allah. Blessed is Your name, exalted is Your majesty, and there is no deity but You.”

He recited this aloud on many occasions. Scholars agree that reciting it aloud is not a regular Sunnah practice; rather, he did so to teach others. For the same reason, it is reported that one of the Companions used to

---

## Page 11312

occasionally recite aloud the supplication seeking refuge with Allah. If some Companions recited the opening supplication and the supplication for refuge aloud, with the other Companions’ approval, then reciting the basmalah aloud is all the more deserving of the same treatment: it may be prescribed on occasion for an overriding benefit.

However, hadith scholars do not dispute that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not recite either the opening supplication or the supplication for refuge aloud. Indeed, it is authentically reported that Abū Hurayrah said to him:

“O Messenger of Allah, during your silence between the opening takbīr and the recitation, what do you say?”

He replied:

“I say: ‘O Allah, distance me from my sins as You have distanced the east from the west. O Allah, cleanse me of my sins as a white garment is cleansed of dirt. O Allah, wash away my sins with snow, water, and hail.’”

The Sunan collections also report that the Prophet used to seek refuge with Allah in prayer before reciting the Quran. The case for reciting the basmalah aloud is stronger than that for reciting the supplication for refuge aloud, because it is a verse of the Book of Allah Most High, and scholars have differed over whether reciting it is obligatory. They have also differed over whether the opening supplication and the supplication for refuge are obligatory, with two positions on this in the school of Ahmad and elsewhere. Nevertheless, the disagreement over these is less substantial than the disagreement over the obligation to recite the basmalah. The scholars who consider reciting it obligatory are more eminent and more numerous.

Yet it has not been established that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to recite it aloud. Neither the Sahīh collections nor the Sunan collections contain an authentic hadith explicitly stating that he recited it aloud. All the hadiths that explicitly state that he recited it aloud are

---

## Page 11313

weak—indeed, fabricated. When al-Dāraqutnī compiled a work on this subject, he was asked, “Is any of this authentic?” He replied, “As for reports from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, no. As for reports from the Companions, some are authentic and some are weak.”

Had the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, always recited it aloud, the Companions would have transmitted that practice, and the caliphs would have known of it. People would not have needed to ask Anas ibn Mālik after the era of the caliphs had ended. Nor would the Rightly Guided Caliphs, followed by all the Umayyad and Abbasid caliphs, have agreed on not reciting it aloud. Nor would the people of Medina—who knew his Sunnah better than the inhabitants of any other city—have rejected its recitation altogether, whether silently or aloud. The authentic hadiths indicate that it is a verse of the Book of Allah, but not part of al-Fātihah or any other surah.

Scholars have differed over three views: Is it a verse, or part of a verse, of every surah? Is it not part of the Quran except in Sūrat al-Naml? Or is it a verse of the Book of Allah wherever it is written in the copies of the Quran, without being part of the surahs?

The third view is the most balanced and reconciles the evidence. The Companions’ inclusion of it in the copies of the Quran is evidence that it belongs to the Book of Allah. Their separating it from the surah that follows it is evidence that it is not part of that surah.

It is established in the Sahīh that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“A surah has just been revealed to me.” He then recited, “In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy. Indeed, We have granted you abundant good,” continuing to the end of the surah.

---

## Page 11314

It is also established in the Sahīh that when the angel first brought revelation, he said:

“Read in the name of your Lord who created—created man from a clinging clot. Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous, who taught by the pen—taught man what he did not know.”

This was the first revelation; “In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy” had not been revealed before it.

It is also established in the Sunan that he said:

“A surah of the Quran consisting of thirty verses interceded for a man until he was forgiven. It is ‘Blessed is He in whose hand is dominion,’ and it consists of thirty verses excluding the basmalah—the formula ‘In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy.’”

It is also established in the Sahīh that he said:

“Allah Most High says: ‘I have divided the prayer between Myself and My servant into two halves: half is for Me and half is for My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks for.

‘When the servant says, “All praise is for Allah, Lord of all worlds,” Allah says, “My servant has praised Me.” When he says, “The Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy,” Allah says, “My servant has extolled Me.” When he says, “Master of the Day of Judgment,” Allah says, “My servant has glorified Me.”

‘When he says, “You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help,” He says, “This verse is divided into two halves between Myself and My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks for.”

‘When the servant says, “Guide us to the straight path—the path of those You have blessed, not of those who have incurred anger, nor of those who have gone astray,” Allah says, “These are for My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks for.”’”

This hadith is authentic and explicitly establishes that it is not part of al-Fātihah, and it has not been contradicted by

---

## Page 11315

any authentic, explicit hadith. The strongest hadith evidence on this subject indicates only that the basmalah is recited at the beginning of al-Fātihah, not that it is part of it. Thus, some Quran reciters recite it at the beginning of a surah, while others do not. This shows that both practices are permissible, though whoever recites it has adopted the better practice. Likewise, repeating it at the beginning of every surah is better than omitting it, because this means reciting what the Companions wrote in the copies of the Quran. Even supposing that they wrote it to seek blessing, it should then be recited to seek blessing. Otherwise, how could they write something in the Quran that it is not prescribed to recite, when they kept the written Quran free of everything that was not Quran? They did not even write “Amen,” the names of the surahs, markers for every five or ten verses, or anything else of that kind.

Yet it is Sunnah for someone praying to say “Amen” after al-Fātihah. How, then, could they write something that is not prescribed to be said, when they did not write the non-Quranic words that someone praying is prescribed to say? Taken together, the scriptural evidence indicates that the basmalah is part of Allah’s Book but not part of the surah.

The authentic hadith from Anas does not deny that the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), Abū Bakr, Umar, and Uthmān recited it: “I did not hear any of them recite ‘In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy,’” or, “They did not recite ‘In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy’ aloud.” As for the version reported with the wording, “They would not mention ‘In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy’ at

---

## Page 11316

the beginning or end of their recitation,” it only indicates that they did not recite it aloud, because Anas denied only what he knew, and he did not know what the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said quietly.

Nor can it be said that the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) did not pause, but proceeded directly from the opening takbīr to the recitation. It is established in the two Sahīh collections that Abū Hurayrah asked him: “During your pause between the opening takbīr and the recitation, what do you say?”

The interpretation of Anas’s hadith as denying that they recited it quietly has its counterpart in the claim that Anas meant that they would begin with al-Fātihah before any other surah. This, too, is weak, for this is common knowledge and has always been people’s practice. Al-Hajjāj ibn Yūsuf and the other rulers behind whom Anas prayed would recite al-Fātihah before the subsequent surah. No one disputed this, nor was anyone asked about it—neither Anas nor anyone else. There was no need for Anas to report this from the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) and his two Companions. Whoever reports that Anas was unsure whether the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) recited the basmalah or not gives an account consistent with the authentic reports, because Anas did not know whether he recited it quietly; he only denied that he recited it aloud.

Another matter in which scholars agree that either practice is permissible is performing the regular Sunnah prayers while travelling. Whoever wishes may perform them, and whoever wishes may omit them, by agreement of the imams. A prayer that one is permitted either to perform or to omit may sometimes be better performed

---

## Page 11317

because one needs it, while omitting it may be better when one is occupied with something more virtuous than voluntary prayer. However, when travelling, the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) would not perform any of the regular Sunnah prayers except the two rak‘ahs before Fajr and Witr. When he slept through Fajr, he performed both its Sunnah prayer and its obligatory prayer after sunrise. He would pray on his mount, whichever direction it took him, and would also perform Witr on it, but he would not perform the obligatory prayers on it. All of this is established in the authentic hadith collections. As for praying before and after Zuhr and after Maghrib, no one has reported that he did so while travelling.

Scholars have differed concerning the regular Sunnah prayers accompanying the obligatory prayers. Some laid down no fixed prescriptions in this matter. Others prescribed particular practices on the basis of weak hadiths—indeed, hadiths that scholars of hadith know to be fabricated. Such prescriptions include six rak‘ahs before Zuhr and four after it, four before ‘Asr, four before ‘Ishā’ and four after it, and similar practices.

The correct approach in this matter is to follow what is established in authentic hadiths, rather than what contradicts them. Three hadiths are established in the authentic collections:

The hadith of Ibn ‘Umar, who said: “I remember that the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) prayed two rak‘ahs before Zuhr, two after it, two after Maghrib, and two after ‘Ishā’

---

## Page 11318

and two rak‘ahs before Fajr.”

There is also the hadith of ‘Ā’ishah:

“The Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) used to pray four rak‘ahs before Zuhr.”

This too appears in the authentic collection, while the remainder of her report appears in Sahīh Muslim and is similar to Ibn ‘Umar’s hadith. It is likewise reported in the authentic collection, and in a narration graded authentic by al-Tirmidhī, that he prayed two rak‘ahs before Zuhr.

There is also the hadith of Umm Habībah, who reported that the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said:

“Whoever prays twelve voluntary rak‘ahs in a day and night, apart from the obligatory prayers, Allah will build for him a house in Paradise.”

The Sunan collections explain these as:

“Four before Zuhr, two after it, two after Maghrib, two after ‘Ishā’, and two before Fajr.”

Thus, this authentic hadith shows that he verbally encouraged the performance of twelve rak‘ahs. The other two authentic hadiths indicate that he used to pray either ten or twelve rak‘ahs alongside the obligatory prayers. He would also pray eleven or thirteen rak‘ahs at night. His obligatory and voluntary prayers therefore totalled approximately forty rak‘ahs over a day and night. He made his daytime prayers odd in number with Maghrib, and his night prayers odd in number with Witr.

It is also established in the authentic collection that he said:

“Between every call to prayer and the call to commence it, there is a prayer; between every call to prayer and the call to commence it, there is a prayer; between every call to prayer and the call to commence it, there is a prayer.”

The third time, he added, “For whoever wishes,” lest people adopt it as a Sunnah.

---

## Page 11319

It is also established in the authentic collection that his Companions used to pray two rak‘ahs between the call to Maghrib and the call to commence it, while he watched them without forbidding them. If voluntary prayer is prescribed between these two calls for Maghrib, then it is all the more appropriate that it be prescribed between the corresponding calls for ‘Asr and ‘Ishā’, since the imams agree that the Sunnah is to perform Maghrib promptly. This shows that prayer before ‘Asr, before Maghrib and before ‘Ishā’ is among the prescribed voluntary prayers, but not among the regular Sunnah prayers whose number he specified verbally or which he consistently observed in practice.

Anyone who thinks that he had a Sunnah prayer before ‘Asr which he made up after ‘Asr is mistaken. Rather, those were the two rak‘ahs associated with Zuhr: when he missed them, he made them up after ‘Asr. A prayer performed after Zuhr is also before ‘Asr, but the only prayer he made up after ‘Asr was the two rak‘ahs normally performed after Zuhr.

“Prescribed voluntary worship,” such as prayer between the two calls, prayer in the forenoon and similar prayers, is like other voluntary acts of remembrance, recitation and supplication: it may be recommended for someone who is not otherwise occupied with something better, but not for someone who is occupied instead with something better. Consistently doing a little is better than doing much without consistency. Thus, the practice of the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) was steady and continuous. The imams recommended that a man have a set number of rak‘ahs which he rises to pray during

---

## Page 11320

the night, without omitting them. If he feels energetic, he should prolong them; if he feels sluggish, he should shorten them. If he sleeps through them, he should make them up during the day, just as the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) would pray twelve rak‘ahs during the day if he slept through his night prayer. He said:

“Whoever sleeps through his regular portion of recitation, then recites it between the Fajr and Zuhr prayers, will have it recorded for him as though he had recited it during the night.”

The forenoon prayer falls into this category. The Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) did not observe it consistently, as those knowledgeable about his Sunnah agree. Any jurist who claims that the two rak‘ahs of the forenoon prayer were obligatory for him is mistaken. The hadith they cite—“Three things are obligatory for me but voluntary for you: Witr, sacrifice, and the two rak‘ahs of the forenoon prayer”—is fabricated.

Rather, it is established in an authentic hadith, with no report contradicting it, that the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) would pray at forenoon because of a particular circumstance, not because of the time itself. For example, he might sleep through his night prayer and then pray twelve rak‘ahs during the day, or return from a journey at forenoon and enter the mosque and pray there. Another example is the eight rak‘ahs he prayed when he conquered Mecca. They used to call this prayer the “prayer of conquest,” and some commanders would perform it when they conquered a city, for the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) only performed it upon conquering Mecca. Had its occasion been merely the time of day, as with the night prayer, it would not have been specific to the conquest of Mecca. For this reason, there were

---

## Page 11321

some Companions who did not perform the forenoon prayer. However, it is established in both Sahīh collections that Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) said:

“My beloved friend advised me to observe three things: fasting three days of every month, praying two rak‘ahs at forenoon, and praying Witr before going to sleep.”

A version narrated by Muslim states: “And two rak‘ahs at forenoon every day.”

In Sahīh Muslim, Abū Dharr reported that the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said:

“Every morning, charity is due for every joint of each of you. Every declaration of Allah’s glory is charity; every expression of praise to Allah is charity; every declaration that none has the right to be worshipped but Allah is charity; and every declaration of Allah’s greatness is charity. Enjoining what is right is charity, and forbidding what is wrong is charity. Two rak‘ahs offered at forenoon suffice for all of this.”

In Sahīh Muslim, Zayd ibn Arqam said:

“The Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) came out to the people of Qubā’ while they were performing the forenoon prayer. He said: ‘The prayer of those who repeatedly turn to Allah is when the forenoon heat scorches the feet of young camels.’”

These authentic hadiths and others like them show that prayer at forenoon is good and beloved. The question remains: is it better to observe it regularly, as indicated by the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, or is it better not to observe it regularly, following the example of the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace)? This is a matter over which they differed.

The more fitting view is that, for someone who regularly observes the night prayer, this suffices in place of regularly performing the forenoon prayer, as was the practice of the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace). For someone who sleeps through the night prayer, the forenoon prayer serves as a substitute for it.

---

## Page 11322

The hadith of Abū Hurayrah also states that the Prophet advised him to pray Witr before going to sleep. Such advice is given only to someone who does not habitually observe the night prayer. For someone who habitually observes it and usually wakes during the night, praying Witr at the end of the night is better, as established in an authentic hadith from the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace):

“Whoever fears that he will not wake at the end of the night should pray Witr at its beginning. Whoever hopes to wake at its end should pray Witr then, for prayer at the end of the night is witnessed, and that is better.”

It is also authentically reported that the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) was asked:

“Which prayer is best after the obligatory prayer?”

He replied: “The night prayer.”

Section

The third category consists of practices for which it is established that the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) instituted both alternatives, yet some scholars prohibited one of them or deemed it disliked because the report concerning it had not reached them, or because they gave the hadith an interpretation resting on weak grounds. The correct position in such cases is that everything the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) instituted for his community is Sunnah; none of it should be prohibited, even if some forms are better than others.

Examples include the different forms of the tashahhud (the testimony recited while seated in prayer). Ibn Mas‘ūd’s form of the tashahhud is authentically reported from the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) in both Sahīh collections, and there is also an authentic report from him in Sahīh

---

## Page 11323

Muslim of Abū Mūsā’s form of the tashahhud, whose wording is close to that of Ibn Mas‘ūd. Ibn ‘Abbās’s form of the tashahhud is also authentically reported from him in Sahīh Muslim. The Sunan collections contain the forms reported by Ibn ‘Umar, ‘Ā’ishah and Jābir. It is also established in al-Muwatta’ and elsewhere that ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb taught the Muslims a form of the tashahhud from the pulpit of the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace). ‘Umar would not have taught them a form that they accepted unless it was prescribed.

Thus, the correct position according to the meticulous scholarly authorities is that reciting any of these forms of the tashahhud is permissible and is not disliked. Anyone who maintains that using the wording of Ibn Mas‘ūd’s tashahhud is obligatory—as some scholars of Ahmad’s school have maintained—is mistaken.

Another example is the adhān (call to prayer) and the iqāmah (call announcing the start of prayer). An authentic report from Anas states that Bilāl was instructed to recite the phrases of the adhān in pairs and those of the iqāmah singly. It is also authentically reported:

“He taught Abū Mahdhūrah the adhān and iqāmah, repeating the testimonies aloud after first reciting them quietly in the adhān, and doubling the phrases of the iqāmah.”

Some chains of transmission relate that he said “Allah is the Greatest” four times at the beginning, as reported in the Sunan collections; others relate that he said it twice, as reported in Sahīh Muslim. The Sunan collections also report that Bilāl’s adhān, as narrated by ‘Abdullāh ibn Zayd, involved neither such repetition in the adhān nor doubling the phrases of the iqāmah.

Both Bilāl’s adhān and Abū Mahdhūrah’s adhān are Sunnah. Thus, whether the caller repeats the testimonies in this manner or not, and whether he recites the phrases of the iqāmah singly or doubles them, he has done well and followed the Sunnah.

---

## Page 11324

And anyone who says that repeating the testimonies in this manner is obligatory and indispensable, or that it is disliked and prohibited, is mistaken in either case. Likewise, anyone who says that reciting the phrases of the iqāmah singly is disliked, or that doubling them is disliked, is mistaken. Preferring one form over another, however, is a matter of scholarly judgment, like preferring certain Quranic readings or forms of the tashahhud over others.

The various forms of the “prayer in times of fear” performed by the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) also belong to this category, as do the various ways of “seeking rain.” On one occasion, he sought rain in his mosque without performing the prayer for rain; on another, he went out into the open country and led them in two units of prayer. They would also seek rain through supplication without prayer, as his successors did. All of this is good and permissible.

Another example is fasting or breaking the fast while travelling during Ramadan. The four imams agreed that both are permissible. A group of earlier and later scholars, however, held that only breaking the fast is permissible, and that if a traveller fasted, this would not discharge his obligation. They claimed that permission to fast while travelling had been abrogated by his saying:

“It is not righteousness to fast while travelling.”

The correct position is that held by the imams. Nothing in this hadith contradicts his permission for them to fast while travelling, for he denied that it was an act of righteousness, but did not deny that

---

## Page 11325

it was lawful and permissible. An obligation is discharged by performing a lawful, permissible form of the act, provided one fulfils what has been commanded.

What is meant is that fasting specifically while travelling is not an act of righteousness. This is like someone who fasts and makes himself thirsty by eating salty food, or fasts while exposing himself to the sun. One would say, “Fasting in the sun is not righteousness.” Hence Sufyān ibn ‘Uyaynah said, “It means that someone who fasts is no more righteous than someone who does not.”

This indicates that not fasting is preferable, since it was the later of the Prophet’s two practices (may Allah bless him and grant him peace): he initially fasted while travelling, then refrained from fasting while travelling. Whoever thinks that fasting while travelling detracts from one’s religion is a misguided innovator. If he fasts in this manner, believing that fasting is obligatory for him and that breaking the fast is forbidden, a group of earlier and later scholars have instructed him to repeat the fast.

It is authentically reported from the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace):

“Hamzah ibn ‘Amr asked him, saying, ‘I am a man who fasts frequently. May I fast while travelling?’ He replied, ‘If you do not fast, that is good; and if you fast, there is no harm.’”

Thus, if a traveller chooses whichever is easier for him—fasting immediately or postponing it—he has done well, for Allah intends ease for us and does not intend hardship for us.

If, however, fasting while travelling is harder for him than postponing it, then postponing it is preferable. For it is reported in al-Musnad that the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said:

“Allah loves His concessions to be accepted, just as He hates to be disobeyed.”

One of the scholars—either Ibn Khuzaymah or someone else—also included it in his Sahīh. These Sahīh collections rank below the two Sahīhs of al-Bukhārī and Muslim.

---

## Page 11326

As for fasting on a day when the sky is overcast:

If clouds or haze obscure the sighting of the crescent on the night of the thirtieth of Sha‘bān, some Companions would fast as a precaution, while others would not. We know of none of them who considered fasting that day obligatory. Rather, those who fasted did so in an effort to ascertain the correct course and exercise caution. The reports transmitted from them explicitly establish this, including those related from ‘Umar, ‘Alī, Mu‘āwiyah, ‘Abdullāh ibn ‘Umar, ‘Ā’ishah and others.

The scholars hold differing views on this matter. Some forbid fasting that day or regard it as discouraged, as do some followers of Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī and Ahmad. Others consider it obligatory, as do a group of Ahmad’s followers. Still others regard either course as permissible, as in the case of abstaining from food and drink when the appearance of dawn is obscured. This is the position of Abū Hanīfah and the explicitly stated position of Ahmad. Ahmad would fast that day as a precaution, following Ibn ‘Umar and others, not because he considered it obligatory. This is like other acts whose obligatory status is uncertain: performing them as a precaution is recommended, without being obligatory.

If someone fasts that day with a conditional intention—intending that, if it is part of Ramadan, his fast should count towards it, and otherwise it should not—and it then becomes clear that the day was part of Ramadan, his fast suffices according to most scholars. This is the position of Abū Hanīfah and the stronger of the two views reported from Ahmad and others. For intention follows knowledge: whoever knows what he wishes to do necessarily intends it, without having to choose to form that intention. But when someone does not know something, he cannot intend it.

---

## Page 11327

so someone who does not know that a day is part of Ramadan cannot conceivably form a definite intention to fast it as part of Ramadan.

Shortening prayers while travelling and combining two prayers may also come under this heading. The established Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was to shorten prayers when travelling: he would perform every four-unit prayer as only two units. The two senior Companions who succeeded him, Abū Bakr and then ‘Umar, did likewise. He would combine two prayers while travelling only occasionally, when needed. His combining was unlike his shortening: shortening was his regular practice, whereas combining was an occasional concession.

Anyone who reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, performed the noon, afternoon or night prayer as four units while travelling is mistaken. No one has transmitted this from him through any chain of transmission, whether authentic or weak. Some people, however, have narrated a hadith from ‘Ā’ishah, in which she said:

“When travelling, the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would shorten his prayers while I performed them in full, and he would refrain from fasting while I fasted. I asked him about this, and he said, ‘You have done well, ‘Ā’ishah.’”
