Some scholars mistakenly understood this to mean that he himself would sometimes shorten his prayers while travelling and sometimes perform them in full. No one has narrated that. Moreover, the very hadith reporting her conduct is false. Neither ‘Ā’ishah nor anyone else accompanying the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prayed otherwise than as he prayed. No one ever prayed four units with him, whether at ‘Arafah, Muzdalifah or elsewhere, whether they were residents of Mecca or anyone else. Rather, all the Muslims would pray two units with him. During his stay at Minā in the days of the pilgrimage season, he would lead the people in prayers of two units, as did Abū Bakr after him, then ‘Umar

---

## Page 11328

then ‘Uthmān ibn ‘Affān at the beginning of his caliphate. Later, he prayed four units for reasons he considered warranted doing so. People differed over his decision: some agreed with him, while others disagreed.

During the Farewell Pilgrimage, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, combined prayers only at ‘Arafah and Muzdalifah. On his other journeys, however, when pressing on with his journey, he would delay the sunset prayer until after the time for the night prayer had begun, then perform the two together. He would also delay the noon prayer until the time of the afternoon prayer, then perform the two together.

Thus, the correct scholarly view is that a traveller may shorten prayers whether or not he has intended to shorten them. Likewise, when combining prayers is permissible, he may combine them whether or not he intended to do so when offering the first prayer. When the Companions prayed behind the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, at ‘Arafah—two units for the noon prayer, followed by two units for the afternoon prayer—he did not instruct them at the beginning of the noon prayer to intend to combine the prayers. Nor did they know that he would combine them, since he had not done so on any journey other than that one. He did not instruct anyone praying behind him, whether from Mecca or elsewhere, to pray separately from him, either by performing each prayer as four units or by delaying the afternoon prayer. Rather, they offered it with him.

The scholars agree that shortening prayers while travelling is permissible. They also agree that it is preferable, apart from an isolated opinion held by some. Likewise, they agree that performing each prayer at its appointed time while travelling is preferable when there is no reason calling for combining them, apart from an isolated opinion held by some.

---

## Page 11329

Shortening prayers is justified by travel alone and is not permissible outside travel. Combining prayers, however, is justified by need or a valid excuse. Whenever the need arises, prayers may be combined on both short and long journeys. They may likewise be combined because of rain, illness, similar circumstances, or other reasons, since its purpose is to relieve the Muslim community of hardship. Only one hadith reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, combined prayers while stopped during a journey. Hence, those who permit combining prayers—such as Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī and Ahmad—disagreed over whether a traveller who has stopped may combine them. Mālik prohibited this, as did Ahmad according to one of the two reports from him; al-Shāfi‘ī permitted it, as did Ahmad according to the other report. Abū Hanīfah prohibited combining prayers except at ‘Arafah and Muzdalifah.

The same applies to the three forms of Hajj: tamattu‘, ifrād and qirān. The position of the four imams and the majority of the Muslim community is that all three are permissible. A group of earlier and later scholars held that only tamattu‘ is permissible. This was the view of Ibn ‘Abbās and those hadith scholars and Shia who agreed with him. Some of the Umayyads and their followers used to forbid tamattu‘ and punish those who performed it.

The scholars have disagreed over the Prophet’s Hajj, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: did he perform tamattu‘, ifrād or qirān? They also disagreed over which of the three is preferable. Some adherents of Ahmad’s school believe that he performed tamattu‘ in which he came out of ihrām. Another group believes that he entered ihrām for ‘umrah and did not enter ihrām for Hajj until he had performed the circumambulation and ritual walk of ‘umrah.

---

## Page 11330

And some adherents of Mālik and al-Shāfi‘ī believe that he performed Hajj alone and then performed ‘umrah immediately afterwards. Some adherents of Abū Hanīfah believe that he performed qirān with two sets of circumambulation and two ritual walks. Another group believes that he entered ihrām without specifying the form of pilgrimage. All of this is mistaken; none of it was reported by the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. Rather, the Companions’ reports are generally consistent with one another. Whoever attributes disagreement to them on this matter does so because he has not understood their rulings.

The Companions reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, performed tamattu‘, combining ‘umrah with Hajj. This is what most of the Companions reported. Several of these Companions, as well as others, reported that he combined ‘umrah and Hajj as qirān and entered ihrām for both together. They likewise reported that he performed ‘umrah along with his Hajj, while agreeing that he did not perform ‘umrah after Hajj. Indeed, of the Companions accompanying him, only ‘Ā’ishah performed ‘umrah after Hajj, because she had menstruated.

The term “mutamatti‘” in the Quran, the Sunnah, and the statements of the Companions designates someone who combines ‘umrah and Hajj during the months of Hajj, whether he enters ihrām for both together; enters ihrām for ‘umrah and then adds Hajj to it; enters ihrām for Hajj after coming out of ihrām for ‘umrah—which is tamattu‘ in the specific sense used by later scholars—or enters ihrām for Hajj after completing ‘umrah but before coming out of ihrām, either because he has brought the sacrificial animal or even though he has not. They may describe this last person as both someone performing tamattu‘ in its specific sense and someone performing qirān. Alternatively, they may say that he does not fall within tamattu‘ in its specific sense, but is instead performing qirān.

What I have mentioned—that they call qirān tamattu‘—is explicitly stated in hadiths

---

## Page 11331

that are authentic. Some of those who reported that he performed tamattu‘ also reported that he performed Hajj alone, for he performed a single set of Hajj rites and did not leave ihrām because he had brought the sacrificial animal. Thus, his tamattu‘ did not involve leaving ihrām, and in this respect he resembled someone performing Hajj alone.

For someone who arrives during the months of Hajj without bringing a sacrificial animal, it is preferable to leave ihrām by performing ‘umrah, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his Companions instructed during the Farewell Pilgrimage. He instructed everyone who had not brought a sacrificial animal to perform tamattu‘. For someone who has brought a sacrificial animal, qirān is preferable, as this is what the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did. As for someone who performs ‘umrah on one journey and Hajj on another, or performs ‘umrah before the months of Hajj and remains until he performs Hajj, this form of ifrād is not superior to tamattu‘ or qirān, according to the agreement of the four imams.

As for the fourth category, it concerns matters over which scholars disagree: one considers something obligatory or recommended, while another considers it forbidden, and the Sunnah supports only one of the two positions, not both. This is the most problematic of the four categories. In the preceding three, however, the Sunnah permits both alternatives.

An example is their disagreement over reciting al-Fātihah behind the imam while he is reciting aloud. Scholars hold three positions on this matter. One view is that someone who can hear the imam reciting aloud may not recite either al-Fātihah or anything else. This is the view of the majority of the early generations

---

## Page 11332

and later generations. This is the position of Mālik, Ahmad, Abū Hanīfah and others, and one of al-Shāfiʿī’s two positions.

Another view is that both alternatives are permissible, but reciting is preferable. This is reported from al-Awzāʿī, the scholars of Syria and al-Layth ibn Saʿd, and is the view adopted by a group of Ahmad’s followers and others.

A third view is that recitation is obligatory. This is al-Shāfiʿī’s other position.

The majority’s view is correct, for Allah, glorified be He, says:

“When the Quran is recited, listen to it and remain silent, so that you may receive mercy.”

Ahmad said: “There is consensus that this verse was revealed concerning prayer.”

It is authentically established in the Sahīh, in a hadith narrated by Abū Mūsā, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The imam has only been appointed to be followed. When he says ‘Allah is the Greatest,’ say the same; when he recites, remain silent; and when he says ‘Allah is the Greatest’ and bows, say the same and bow. For the imam bows before you and rises before you, so the one offsets the other.”

The hadith continues. This wording has also been transmitted in a hadith narrated by Abū Hurayrah, and Muslim stated that it is authentic.

Allah and His Messenger have thus commanded silence when the imam recites, and the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, made this part of following him. Whoever does not remain silent to listen to him has therefore not followed him. It is well known that the imam recites aloud for the sake of those praying behind him. This is why they say “Āmīn” to his supplication. If they do not listen to his recitation, his reciting aloud serves no purpose. The benefit of following the imam takes precedence over the benefit of what a person praying alone is instructed to do. Do you not see that if someone joins the imam during an odd-numbered rakʿah of his prayer, he does as the imam does, and so recites the tashahhud after an odd-numbered rakʿah

---

## Page 11333

and prostrates after saying “Allah is the Greatest” if he finds the imam prostrating. All this is for the sake of following the imam. How, then, could he not listen to his recitation, when listening brings him the benefit of recitation? For the listener receives the same reward as the reciter.

This is further clarified by their unanimous agreement that, when the imam recites aloud, the follower does not recite along with him anything beyond al-Fātihah. Were he not to receive the reward of recitation by listening silently, reciting for himself would be better than listening to the imam. Since listening silently brings him the reciter’s reward, he has no need to recite himself. His recitation therefore brings no benefit; rather, it is harmful, distracting him from the listening he has been commanded to observe.

They have differed over whether it is preferable for someone to recite or remain silent when he cannot hear the imam because the prayer is one in which recitation is silent, because he is far from the imam, because of deafness, or for some similar reason. The correct view is that it is preferable for him to recite in these circumstances, since he is not listening to a recitation through which the purpose of recitation is fulfilled for him. If he recites for himself, he receives the reward of recitation; otherwise, he remains silent, neither reciting nor listening. Someone who remains silent during prayer, neither listening nor reciting, has neither been commanded to do so nor deserves praise for it. Rather, all the actions of prayer must involve remembrance of Allah Most High, such as recitation, glorification and supplication, or listening to His remembrance.

If it is said that the imam discharges the obligation of recitation on his behalf, reciting for himself is still more complete, more beneficial to him, better for his heart, and more elevating for him in the sight of his Lord. As for remaining silent,

---

## Page 11334

it is prescribed only when the recitation is audible. When the recitation is silent, there is no audible voice to listen to.

Another example of this is performing a prayer occasioned by a specific reason, such as the prayer of greeting the mosque, after Fajr and ʿAsr. Some scholars recommend this, while others consider it either forbidden or merely discouraged. The Sunnah establishes it as either recommended or disliked. The correct view is that it is recommended. This is the position of al-Shāfiʿī and one of the two positions reported from Ahmad, adopted by a group of his followers.

The hadiths prohibiting prayer at these times, such as his statement:

“There is no prayer after Fajr until the sun rises, and no prayer after ʿAsr until the sun sets,”

are general statements subject to exceptions. Funeral prayers are excluded by the agreement of the Muslims. Making up missed prayers is also excluded by his statement:

“Whoever catches one rakʿah of the dawn prayer before the sun rises has caught the dawn prayer.”

It is also authentically established that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, “made up the two rakʿahs of Zuhr after ʿAsr.”

“He said to the two men whom he saw after Fajr at the mosque of al-Khayf, who had not prayed: ‘If you have prayed in your lodgings and then come to a mosque where a congregation is praying, pray with them, for it will be a voluntary prayer for you.’”

He also said:

“O descendants of ʿAbd Manāf, do not prevent anyone from circumambulating this House and praying in it at whatever hour he wishes, by night or by day.”

These explicit texts demonstrate that an exception has been made to that general rule.

---

## Page 11335

As for his statement:

“When one of you enters the mosque, he should not sit down until he has prayed two rakʿahs,”

this is a general command from which no case has been excepted. It may therefore not be restricted by a general statement that is itself subject to exceptions. Rather, a general statement whose scope remains intact takes precedence over one subject to exceptions.

Moreover, praying while the imam is on the pulpit is more strictly forbidden than praying after Fajr and ʿAsr. Yet it is established in an authentic report that he said:

“When one of you enters the mosque while the imam is delivering the sermon, he should not sit down until he has prayed two rakʿahs.”

Since he commanded these two rakʿahs during the period covered by this prohibition, the same applies, with even greater reason, during the period covered by the other prohibition. Furthermore, some of the hadiths prohibiting prayer state, “Do not deliberately choose those times for your prayers.” Thus, he forbade deliberately selecting that time for prayer. Some scholars have also held that the prohibition in these hadiths indicates discouragement rather than outright forbiddance.

Some of the early generations permitted voluntary prayer after ʿAsr without restriction, citing the hadith of Aisha as evidence. For prayer was prohibited only to block a means leading to imitation of the disbelievers, and an act prohibited as a preventive measure may be performed when a greater benefit warrants it. This applies to a prayer tied to a specific occasion, whose opportunity passes when that occasion has passed: unless it is performed at that time, its benefit is lost.

Unrestricted voluntary prayer, however, need not be performed during the prohibited period, since a person does not spend the entire night and day praying. Prohibiting it therefore entails no loss of benefit, whereas performing it at that time entails harm. This differs from voluntary prayer tied to an occasion that can pass, such as prostration upon recitation and the eclipse prayer.

Moreover, if the two rakʿahs following circumambulation are permissible despite the possibility of postponing

---

## Page 11336

circumambulation itself, then a prayer whose opportunity would be lost is all the more deserving of being permitted. Some scholars of our school permit making up the regular sunnah prayers, but not other voluntary prayers, because the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) made up the two rakʿahs after Zuhr, and it is reported that he allowed the two rakʿahs before Fajr to be made up. In response, one may say: if making up a regular sunnah prayer is permissible despite the possibility of postponing it, then prayers whose opportunity would be lost—such as the eclipse prayer, prostration upon recitation, and the prayer of greeting the mosque—are all the more deserving of being permitted.

Indeed, an authentic hadith establishes that an obligatory prayer may be made up during this time, even though postponing it may sometimes be recommended, as in the report:

“The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) delayed making up Fajr when he slept through it during the expedition to Khaybar, and said, ‘This is a valley in which Satan was present with us.’”

If it is permissible to perform what can be postponed, then what cannot be postponed, and whose postponement is not recommended, is all the more deserving of being permitted. These questions cannot be discussed at length in this answer.

Section

As for praying at night and fasting during the day, the best practice is that which authentic reports establish that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) himself followed. He said:

“The best night prayer is that of David: he would sleep for half the night, pray for a third of it, and sleep for a sixth. The best fasting is that of David: he would fast one day and not fast the next, and he would not flee when facing the enemy.”

It is also established

---

## Page 11337

in the authentic collections:

“ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr said, ‘I shall fast every day, spend every night in prayer, and recite the Quran each day.’ The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) told him, ‘Do not do so, for if you do, your eyes will become sunken—that is, recede into their sockets—and your soul will flag—that is, grow weary. Rather, fast three days each month, for that amounts to fasting continually,’ meaning that a good deed is rewarded tenfold. He replied, ‘I can manage more than that.’ He kept asking for more until the Prophet said, ‘Fast one day and do not fast the next.’ He replied, ‘I can manage more than that.’ He said, ‘There is nothing better than that.’ Regarding recitation, he told him, ‘Recite the Quran once each month.’ He kept asking for more until he said, ‘Recite it in seven days.’ He also told him that the best night prayer was that of David, and said to him, ‘Your own self has a right over you, your family has a right over you, and your wife has a right over you. So give everyone their due.’”

The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) thus explained to him that persisting in this practice adversely affects the body and soul, and prevents a person from doing what brings greater reward: fulfilling his obligations towards himself, his family, and his wife.

The best jihad and righteous deeds are those that show the greatest obedience to the Lord and bring the greatest benefit to His servant. If an action harms a person and prevents him from doing what would benefit him more, it is not righteous. It is also established in the authentic collection:

“Some men spoke, one saying, ‘As for me, I shall fast without ever taking a day off.’ Another said, ‘As for me, I shall pray at night and never sleep.’ Another said, ‘As for me, I shall not eat meat.’ Another said, ‘As for me, I shall not marry women.’ The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) then said:

---

## Page 11338

‘What is the matter with men who say such-and-such? I fast and also refrain from fasting; I pray at night and also sleep; I marry women and eat meat. Whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me.’”

The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) thus explained that such misguided asceticism and worship are not part of his Sunnah. Whoever turns away from his Sunnah in favour of these practices, considering them better than his Sunnah, is not of him.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b said:

“Adhere to the path and the Sunnah. Whenever a servant who follows the path and the Sunnah remembers Allah in solitude and his skin shivers with fear of Allah, his sins fall away from him as dry leaves fall from a tree. Whenever a servant who follows the path and the Sunnah remembers Allah in solitude and his eyes overflow with tears from fear of Allah, the Fire will never touch him. Moderate effort in following the path and the Sunnah is better than strenuous effort contrary to the path and the Sunnah. So take care that your deeds, whether strenuous or moderate, follow the way of the prophets and their Sunnah.”

Likewise, 'Abd Allāh ibn Mas'ūd said: “Moderate effort in following the Sunnah is better than strenuous effort in religious innovation.”

Scholars have differed over fasting every day, provided that one does not fast on the two Eid days or the days of Minā. A group of jurists and devout worshippers considered this recommended and regarded it as better than fasting on alternate days. Another group did not regard it as better, but considered it permissible without being disliked, holding that fasting half the time was better. They understood the reports discouraging year-round fasting as referring to those who fast on the prohibited days.

The third view is:

---

## Page 11339

the view of those who regard it as forgoing what is preferable or as disliked—and this is the correct view.

The authentic hadiths from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), such as his prohibition of this practice to 'Abd Allāh ibn 'Amr and his statement,

“Whoever fasts year-round has neither fasted nor broken his fast,”

and other reports clearly indicate that this practice is not prescribed.

Anyone who interprets this as referring to fasting on the five prohibited days is mistaken. Fasting year-round does not mean fasting only five days. Moreover, fasting on those five days is forbidden even if one does not fast on any other days. Thus, fasting on them was not prohibited because it constituted year-round fasting. Nor can a prohibition against fasting for more than three hundred days be understood as referring to just five. This would be like someone saying, “Bring me everyone in the congregational mosque,” while meaning only five of them.

Furthermore, he explained that doing so causes the eyes to become sunken and leaves a person exhausted. This results from fasting continuously, not from fasting on those five days.

An authentic report also relates:

“A man asked him about fasting year-round. He replied, ‘Whoever fasts year-round has neither fasted nor broken his fast.’

“The man asked, ‘What about someone who fasts for two days and does not fast for one day?’ He replied, ‘Who could manage that?’

“He asked, ‘What about someone who fasts for one day and does not fast for two days?’ He replied, ‘I wish I had been given the strength to do that.’

“He then asked, ‘What about someone who fasts one day and does not fast the next?’ He replied, ‘That is the best form of fasting.’”

Thus, they asked him about fasting all the time, then two-thirds of the time, then one-third, and then half.

---

## Page 11340

As for his words:

“Fasting three days of every month is equivalent to fasting year-round,”

and his words:

“Whoever fasts Ramadan and follows it with six days of Shawwāl is as though he has fasted year-round. A good deed is rewarded tenfold,”

and similar statements, he means that whoever does this receives the reward of fasting year-round through the multiplication of reward, without incurring the harm. Thus, whoever fasts three days of every month receives the reward of fasting year-round, apart from Ramadan. Whoever fasts Ramadan and six days of Shawwāl receives, through the two combined, the reward of fasting year-round.

Analogical reasoning would suggest that devoting all one’s time to fasting would be an act of worship, were it not for an overriding consideration against it. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) explained this overriding consideration: neglecting what takes precedence over fasting and incurring harm that outweighs its benefit. Such a person thus forfeits a greater benefit, whether obligatory or recommended, while incurring harm that outweighs the benefit of fasting.

He (peace and blessings be upon him) explained the wisdom behind the prohibition, saying:

“Whoever fasts year-round has neither fasted nor broken his fast.”

For fasting becomes a habit for him, like fasting at night: he gains no benefit from such fasting, and has neither truly fasted nor broken his fast.

Any Companion reported to have fasted continuously held one of these views. The same applies to anyone reported to have regularly spent the entire night in prayer, or to have prayed the dawn prayer with the ablution he had performed for the ‘Ishā’ prayer for so many years—although many such reports are weak.

‘Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd said to his companions:

“You

---

## Page 11341

fast and pray more than the Companions of Muhammad, yet they were better than you.”

They asked, “Why, Abū ‘Abd al-Rahmān?”

He replied, “Because they were less attached to this world and more desirous of the Hereafter.”

As for fasting on consecutive days during part of the year, the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) used to do this. He would fast until one might say that he never stopped fasting, and refrain from fasting until one might say that he never fasted. Likewise, spending certain nights entirely in prayer—such as the last ten nights of Ramadan, or occasionally other nights—is established in the Sunnah. The Companions also used to do this. It is established in an authentic report:

“When the last ten nights of Ramadan began, the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) would tighten his waist-wrapper, awaken his family, and spend the whole night in worship.”

The Sunan collections also report that he spent a night in prayer, repeating a single verse until dawn:

“If You punish them, they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, You are indeed the Almighty, the All-Wise.”

Most of his night prayer, however, was in the middle of the night. He would lead whoever was with him in prayer, as he did one night with Ibn ‘Abbās, another with Ibn Mas‘ūd, and another with Hudhayfah ibn al-Yamān:

“He would sometimes recite al-Baqarah, al-Nisā’, and Āl ‘Imrān in a single unit of prayer, then bow for about as long as he had stood, saying while bowing, ‘Glory be to my Lord, the Magnificent; glory be to my Lord, the Magnificent,’ then rise and remain standing for about as long as he had bowed

---

## Page 11342

saying, ‘To my Lord belongs all praise; to my Lord belongs all praise,’ then prostrate for about as long as he had stood, saying, ‘Glory be to my Lord, the Most High; glory be to my Lord, the Most High,’ then sit for about as long as he had prostrated, saying, ‘My Lord, forgive me; my Lord, forgive me,’ then prostrate.”

As for “continuous fasting without breaking the fast,” it is established that he forbade his Companions to do this, allowing them only to continue until the predawn hours. He explained that he was not like any of them. Some who strove hard in worship would fast continuously: some would go for a month without eating or drinking, others for two months, or for longer or shorter periods. Many of them, however, regretted what they had done, and this became apparent in some of them. For the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) was the most knowledgeable of all creation concerning the path to Allah, the most sincere in counsel to Allah’s servants, the best of all creation, the most obedient to Him, and the most faithful in following His way.

Spiritual states arising from practices that contravene the Sunnah are not praiseworthy, even if they involve disclosures of hidden matters and produce effects. Anyone well acquainted with this subject knows that states arising from acts of worship that are not prescribed are like wealth earned through unlawful means or ownership acquired through unlawful means. Unless Allah comes to His servant’s aid by granting him repentance through which he follows the prescribed path, these things will cause him harm. He may, however, have exercised his judgment and erred, with his error forgiven; or he may have committed a sin that is forgiven because of good deeds that erase it; or he may be tried with afflictions that expiate his sins; or he may be punished by being deprived of those states.

---

## Page 11343

and if he persists in neglecting what he has been commanded to follow of the Sunnah and doing what he has been forbidden, he may be punished by no longer being enabled to perform obligatory duties, to the point that he may become defiantly disobedient or an advocate of religious innovation. If he persists in major sins, there is reason to fear that he may be stripped of faith. Religious innovations continually lead a person from lesser to greater deviations, until they lead him into religious deviation and heresy. This has happened to more than one person who experienced spiritual states involving disclosures of hidden matters and the production of effects. We have known instances of this that this is not the place to recount.

The Sunnah is like Noah’s ark: whoever boards it is saved, and whoever stays behind drowns.

Al-Zuhrī said: “Those of our scholars who came before us used to say: Holding fast to the Sunnah is salvation.”

Generally, when you find someone who possesses a spiritual state involving disclosure of hidden matters or the production of effects, and who uses it to assist disbelievers or the wicked, or employs it in some other act of disobedience, that state is merely the result of acts of worship that are not prescribed. He is like someone who acquires wealth unlawfully and scarcely spends it on anything but disobedience to Allah.

Religious innovations are of two kinds: those involving statements and beliefs, and those involving deeds and acts of worship. The second kind entails the first, just as the first leads to the second. Those who associate themselves with knowledge, rational inquiry, and related pursuits are at risk of falling into the first kind if they do not hold fast to the Book and the Sunnah. Those who associate themselves with worship, rational inquiry, spiritual aspiration, and related pursuits are at risk if they do not hold fast to the Book

---

## Page 11344

and the Sunnah, of falling into the second kind.

Allah has commanded us to say in every prayer:

“Guide us to the straight path—the path of those You have blessed, not of those who have incurred Your wrath, nor of those who are astray.”

Āmīn.

It is authentically reported that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“The Jews have incurred wrath, and the Christians are astray.”

Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah said: “They used to say: ‘Those scholars who become corrupt bear a resemblance to the Jews, and those worshippers who become corrupt bear a resemblance to the Christians.’”

The early generations used to say: “Beware the temptation posed by the wicked scholar and the ignorant worshipper, for their temptation ensnares all who succumb to it.”

Thus, unless a seeker of knowledge combines his pursuit with fulfilling his obligations and refraining from what is forbidden to him, holding fast to the Book and the Sunnah, he will fall into error. Likewise, unless those who pursue spiritual aspiration combine it with seeking the knowledge obligatory for them and holding fast to the Book and the Sunnah, they will fall into error and transgression.

If a man were to hold fast to religious knowledge without doing what is obligatory, he would be wayward. If he were to hold fast to prescribed worship without knowing what is obligatory, he would be astray. Going astray is characteristic of the Christians, and transgression is characteristic of the Jews, although both communities exhibit both error and transgression.

This is why you find that those among the people of spiritual aspiration, worship, spiritual discipline, and the spiritual path who depart from the revealed law concerning commands and prohibitions end up in a state of fanā’ (annihilation) in which they no longer distinguish between what is commanded and what is forbidden, and thus follow their own desires. The form of fanā’ sanctioned by the revealed law, however, is for worship of Allah to efface one’s worship of anything besides Him

---

## Page 11345

and for obedience to Him to efface obedience to anything besides Him, reliance on Him to efface reliance on anything besides Him, asking Him to efface asking anything besides Him, and fear of Him to efface fear of anything besides Him. This is sincere devotion to Allah and worshipping Him alone, without partner. It is the religion of Islam with which Allah sent the messengers and revealed the Scriptures.

You also find that those among people of learning, rational reflection, speculative theology, and inquiry who depart from the revealed law in matters of determinism, negation, and affirmation end up in doubt and bewilderment, just as the former group ends up making wild utterances and outrageous claims. These do not believe the truth, whereas those believe falsehood. Religion is truly realized only by believing the Messenger in everything he has reported and obeying him in everything he has commanded, inwardly and outwardly—in knowledge and states of the heart, and in outward words and deeds.

Whoever extols staying awake at night and going hungry without qualification, and enjoins both without qualification, is mistaken. Rather, what is praiseworthy is keeping vigil and going hungry in accordance with the revealed law. As explained above, keeping vigil in accordance with the revealed law involves prayer, remembrance of Allah, recitation, writing down religious knowledge, reflecting on it, studying it, or other acts of worship. What is best varies from person to person. Some scholars say: “Writing down hadith is better than voluntary prayer.” Some spiritual teachers say: “Two units of prayer that I perform at night where no one sees me are better than writing down a hundred hadiths.” Another leading scholar says: “Rather, it is best to do both.”

What is best also varies according to people’s circumstances. Some deeds are superior in kind, yet may be

---

## Page 11346

at times less meritorious or even forbidden. Prayer, for example, is better than reciting the Quran; reciting the Quran is better than remembering Allah; and remembering Allah is better than supplication. Yet prayer is forbidden at the prohibited times—such as after Fajr and Asr and during the sermon—and occupying oneself then with recitation, remembrance, supplication, or listening is better than praying.

Likewise, although reciting the Quran is better than remembrance, it is remembrance, not Quranic recitation, that is prescribed when bowing and prostrating. Similarly, at the end of the prayer, it is supplication that is prescribed rather than recitation or remembrance.

A person’s religious life may be set right through a less meritorious deed rather than a superior one, making that deed better for him—just as Hajj is better than jihad for women. Some people benefit more from recitation than from prayer; others benefit more from remembrance than from recitation. Others find that striving in supplication, because of their dire need, is better for them than remembrance in which they are heedless. For the same person, one deed may be better at one time, and another at a different time.

An assessment of every individual’s circumstances and an explanation of what is best for each cannot be set out in a book. Rather, guidance is needed through which Allah directs His servant to what is best for him. No servant is ever sincere with Allah without Allah taking care of him.

It is reported in the Sahīh: “Whenever the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, rose at night

---

## Page 11347

he would say:

‘O Allah, Lord of Gabriel, Michael, and Isrāfīl, Creator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the seen, You judge between Your servants concerning that over which they differ. Guide me, by Your permission, to the truth concerning which they have differed. Indeed, You guide whom You will to a straight path.’”

Section

As for food and clothing, the best guidance is the guidance of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. His practice in eating was to eat whatever was readily available if he desired it. He would neither reject what was available nor go to trouble to obtain what was not. If bread and meat were served, he ate them; if fruit, bread, and meat were served, he ate them. If only dates or only bread were served, he ate that. If sweets or honey were served, he ate those too. His favourite drinks were sweet and cool, and he used to eat cucumbers with fresh dates.

When two kinds of food were served, he would not say, “I will not eat two kinds,” nor would he abstain from food because it was delicious or sweet. Sometimes two or three months would pass without a fire being lit in his home, and they would subsist on nothing but dates and water. At times he would tie a stone against his stomach because of hunger. He never found fault with food: if he desired it, he ate it; otherwise, he left it. Food was also eaten at his

---

## Page 11348

table: the meat of a spiny-tailed lizard. He declined to eat it, saying:

“It is not forbidden, but it was not found in the land of my people, so I find it unappealing.”

The same applied to clothing. He wore a shirt and turban, a waist-wrapper and mantle, an outer robe and a farrūj (a type of robe). He wore cotton, wool, and other materials. While travelling, he wore a woollen robe. He also wore clothing brought from Yemen and elsewhere, most of which was made of cotton. They wore garments of Egyptian Coptic cloth, woven from flax. His Sunnah in this regard therefore entails that a man should eat and dress from whatever food and clothing Allah has made readily available in his land. This varies from one region to another.

A group of his Companions had agreed to abstain from eating meat and similar foods, and from marrying women. Allah Most High then revealed:

“O you who believe, do not forbid the good things Allah has made lawful for you, and do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not love transgressors.”

“And eat of what Allah has provided for you, lawful and good, and fear Allah, in whom you believe.”

The two Sahīh collections report that he learned of some men, one of whom had said, “As for me, I will fast without breaking my fast.” Another said, “As for me, I will stand in prayer without sleeping.” Another said, “As for me, I will not marry women.” Another said, “As for me, I will not eat meat.” He said:

“But I fast and break my fast, pray at night and sleep, marry women, and eat meat. Whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me.”

Allah Most High has also said: “O you who believe, eat of the good things We have provided for you, and give thanks to Allah, if you are

---

## Page 11349

worshipping Him alone.”

He thus commanded people to eat of the good things and give thanks to Allah. Whoever forbids the good things is a transgressor, while whoever fails to give thanks is negligent and fails to fulfil Allah’s right.

In Sahīh Muslim, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is reported to have said:

“Indeed, Allah is pleased with a servant who eats a meal and praises Him for it, or takes a drink and praises Him for it.”

Al-Tirmidhī and others report that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The grateful person who eats is of the same standing as the patient person who fasts.”

This way, which the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, followed, is the most balanced and upright of all ways. Deviation from it takes two forms.

Some people indulge excessively in their desires while turning away from fulfilling their obligations. Allah Most High has said:

“Eat and drink, but do not be excessive. Indeed, He does not love those who are excessive.”

Allah Most High has also said:

“But they were succeeded by generations who neglected prayer and followed their desires; they will meet with evil.”

Others forbid the good things and introduce a monasticism that Allah Most High has not prescribed. There is no monasticism in Islam.

Allah Most High has said:

“Do not forbid the good things Allah has made lawful for you, and do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not love transgressors.”

Allah Most High has also said:

“O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds. Indeed, I know well what you do.”

It is reported in the Sahīh that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Indeed, Allah has commanded the believers

---

## Page 11350

to do what He commanded the messengers to do. He Most High said:

‘O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds.’

And He Most High said:

‘O you who believe, eat of the good things We have provided for you.’

Then he mentioned a man who journeys far, dishevelled and dusty, stretching his hands towards heaven: ‘My Lord! My Lord!’ Yet his food is unlawful, his drink is unlawful, his clothing is unlawful, and he has been nourished with what is unlawful. How, then, could his supplication be answered?”

Everything lawful is good, and everything good is lawful, for Allah has made good things lawful for us and forbidden us foul things. What makes something good, however, is that it is beneficial and pleasant.

Allah has forbidden us everything that harms us and permitted us everything that benefits us. This was not so with the People of the Book: because of their wrongdoing, He forbade them good things that had been lawful to them. He thus forbade them good things as a punishment. Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not forbid us any good things.

People’s circumstances differ with regard to food, clothing, hunger and satiety, and even one person’s circumstances vary. Yet the best deeds are those that show the greatest obedience to Allah and bring the greatest benefit to the person performing them. This may be the easier of two deeds, or it may be the harder. Not every difficult deed is superior, nor is every easy deed inferior. Rather, when Islamic law commands us to do something difficult, it commands it because of the benefit it brings, not merely to torment ourselves.

Such is the case with fighting in Allah’s cause, concerning which He Most High said:

“Fighting has been prescribed for you, though it is hateful to you. But perhaps you hate something that is good for you, and perhaps you love something that is bad for you.”

---

## Page 11351

Hajj is the lesser jihad. Hence the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to ‘Ā’ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, concerning ‘umrah:

“Your reward is in proportion to your hardship.”

Allah Most High said concerning fighting in His cause:

“That is because no thirst, fatigue or hunger afflicts them in Allah’s cause, nor do they tread any ground that enrages the disbelievers, nor inflict any loss on an enemy, without a righteous deed being recorded for them on that account. Indeed, Allah does not let the reward of those who do good go to waste.”

Merely tormenting oneself and one’s body without an outweighing benefit, however, has not been prescribed for us. Rather, Allah has commanded us to do what benefits us and forbidden us to do what harms us.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in an authentic hadith:

“You have been sent only to make things easy, not to make them difficult.”

When he sent Mu‘ādh and Abū Mūsā to Yemen, he told them:

“Make things easy, not difficult; give glad tidings, and do not drive people away.”

He also said:

“This religion is easy. No one overburdens himself in practising it without being overcome by it. So make use of the early morning, the late afternoon and part of the night. Moderation, moderation, and you will reach your goal.”

It is also reported that he said:

“The religion most beloved to Allah is the upright monotheistic faith marked by ease.”

Thus, if a person experiences heat, cold, hunger or the like while fighting in Allah’s cause, performing Hajj or undertaking other such deeds, this is something for which he is praised. Allah Most High said:

“They said, ‘Do not go forth in the heat.’ Say, ‘The Fire of Hell is far hotter,’ if only they understood.”

Likewise, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Deeds that expiate sins include performing ablution thoroughly

---

## Page 11352

despite hardship, taking many steps to the mosques, and waiting for the next prayer after each prayer. That is ribāt (keeping watch); that is ribāt.”

As for merely exposing oneself to heat and cold without any religiously sanctioned benefit, going barefoot, uncovering one’s head, and similar practices that some people regard as striving against the self—if these bring a person no benefit and involve no obedience to Allah, there is no good in them.

Indeed, it is established in an authentic hadith that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, saw a man standing in the sun and asked:

“What is this?”

They replied, “This is Abū Isrā’īl. He has vowed to stand in the sun, not to seek shade or speak, and to fast.”

He said, “Tell him to sit down, seek shade, speak, and complete his fast.”

For this reason, he forbade perpetual silence. Rather, what is prescribed is what the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day should speak good or remain silent.”

Speaking good is better than refraining from it, and refraining from evil speech is better than uttering it.

Section

The best course for the imam is to model his prayer on the prayer that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to lead his Companions in. Indeed, this is the prescribed practice that the imams enjoin

---

## Page 11353

as it is established in an authentic hadith that he said to Mālik ibn al-Huwayrith and his companion:

“When the time for prayer comes, give the call to prayer and the call to commence it, and let one of you lead the other. Pray as you have seen me pray.”

It is also established in an authentic hadith:

“He used to recite between sixty and one hundred verses in Fajr.”

This amounts approximately to between one-third and one-half of a juz’, one of the Quran’s thirty divisions. He would recite the longer surahs of the Mufassal section: Qāf, al-Sajdah, al-Mulk, al-Mu’minūn, al-Sāffāt, and others of similar length. In Zuhr, he would recite less than that—about thirty verses—and in ‘Asr, less still. In Maghrib, he would recite less than that, such as the shorter surahs of the Mufassal.

In ‘Ishā’, he would recite surahs such as “By the sun and its brightness” and “By the night when it covers,” and others of similar length. Sometimes he would prolong the prayer and recite more than this, even reciting al-A‘rāf, al-Tūr, or al-Mursalāt in Maghrib.

Abū Bakr al-Siddīq once recited Sūrat al-Baqarah in Fajr, and ‘Umar used to recite Sūrat Hūd, Sūrat Yūsuf, and others of similar length in Fajr. At times, the Prophet would shorten the prayer, either because he was travelling or for some other reason, as he said:

---

## Page 11354

(may Allah bless him and grant him peace)

“I begin the prayer intending to prolong it, but then I hear a child crying and shorten it, knowing how distressed his mother is for him.”

It is even reported that he recited Sūrat al-Takwīr and Sūrat al-Zalzalah in Fajr. The imam should therefore strive to follow the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. If those praying behind him are unaccustomed to his manner of prayer and might be put off by it, he should introduce them to it gradually. He should not begin with something that would drive them away, but should follow the Sunnah as far as possible. The imam must not prolong the prayer beyond its prescribed length unless they choose that. As established in an authentic hadith, he said, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Whoever leads the people in prayer should keep it brief, for among them are the sick, the elderly, and those with pressing needs.”

This was recorded in the two Sahīh collections. He also said:

“When any of you leads the people in prayer, he should keep it brief; when he prays alone, he may prolong it as much as he wishes.”

He used to prolong the bowing and prostration, as well as the standing after bowing and the sitting between prostrations. It is established in an authentic hadith:

“When he raised his head from bowing, he would remain standing until someone might say, ‘He has forgotten.’ When he raised his head from prostration, he would remain sitting until someone might say, ‘He has forgotten.’”

The Sunan collections report that Anas ibn Mālik likened the prayer of ‘Umar ibn ‘Abd al-‘Azīz to the Prophet’s prayer. ‘Umar would glorify Allah about ten times while bowing and about ten times while prostrating. The imam should therefore ordinarily do what the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ordinarily did. If there is good reason to make the prayer longer

---

## Page 11355

than that, or shorter, he should do so, just as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would sometimes lengthen it beyond that and sometimes shorten it.

Section

As for performing ablution whenever it is invalidated, there is the well-known hadith concerning Bilāl, narrated by Buraydah ibn Husayb, who said:

One morning, the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, summoned Bilāl and said:

“Bilāl, how have you preceded me into Paradise? Whenever I have entered Paradise, I have heard you moving ahead of me. Last night I entered Paradise and heard you moving ahead of me. Then I came upon a lofty, square palace made of gold and asked, ‘Whose palace is this?’

“They replied, ‘It belongs to an Arab man.’

“I said, ‘I am an Arab. Whose palace is this?’

“They replied, ‘It belongs to a man of Quraysh.’

“I said, ‘I am a man of Quraysh. Whose palace is this?’

“They replied, ‘It belongs to a man from Muhammad’s nation.’

“I said, ‘I am Muhammad. Whose palace is this?’

“They replied, ‘It belongs to ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb.’”

Bilāl said, “Messenger of Allah, I have never given the call to prayer without praying two units of prayer afterward. Whenever my ablution has been invalidated, I have renewed it immediately and felt bound to offer Allah two units of prayer.”

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, “Keep to them both.”

Al-Tirmidhī said, “This is a good and authentic hadith.” This indicates that performing ablution whenever it is invalidated is recommended, and this is not contradicted by

---

## Page 11356

the hadith in the Sahīh narrated from Ibn ‘Abbās, who said:

“We were with the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, when he returned from relieving himself. Food was brought to him, and he was asked, ‘Will you not perform ablution?’ He replied, ‘I am not about to pray, so why should I perform ablution?’”

This rules out ablution being obligatory, as well as any command to perform it merely for the sake of eating. We know of no one who recommended ablution for eating unless a person is in a state of janābah (major ritual impurity). Scholars differed over whether washing the hands before eating is disliked or recommended. These are two positions, both reported from Ahmad. Those who recommended it cited the hadith of Salmān, in which he said to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“I read in the Torah that washing the hands before and after a meal is among the means of bringing blessing to it.”

Those who disliked it said that it was contrary to the established practice of the Muslims, who did not wash their hands before eating. Rather, this was a Jewish practice, and imitating them is disliked.

As for Salmān’s hadith, some scholars have graded it as weak. It may also be said that this took place in the early days of Islam, when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, liked to follow the practice of the People of the Book in matters concerning which he had received no command. For this reason, he used to leave his hair unparted in conformity with them, but later parted it. For the same reason, he fasted on ‘Āshūrā’ when he arrived in Medina. Then, before his death, he said:

“If I live until next year, I will certainly fast on the ninth.”

He meant alongside the tenth, in order to differ from the Jews.

---

## Page 11357

Section

As for the questioner’s inquiry about consistently observing the practices that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, maintained in his worship and daily habits: is this a sunnah, or does it vary according to the circumstances of those who observe them regularly?

The answer is that we are commanded to obey Allah and His Messenger. We must therefore obey the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in whatever he commands us to do. Allah has mentioned obedience to him in more than thirty places in His Book. He, Most High, says:

“Whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah.”

And He says:

“We did not send any messenger except to be obeyed by Allah’s permission.”

He has guaranteed felicity to those who obey him, saying:

“They will be with those whom Allah has blessed: the prophets, the steadfast affirmers of truth, the martyrs and the righteous. What excellent companions they are!”

He has made felicity and misery contingent upon obedience and disobedience to him, saying:

“Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, He will admit them into Gardens beneath which rivers flow, to remain there forever. That is the supreme triumph.”

“And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and transgresses His limits, He will admit him into a Fire, to remain there forever, and he will have a humiliating punishment.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to say in his sermon:

“Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger

---

## Page 11358

has indeed been rightly guided; whoever disobeys them both harms only himself and will not harm Allah in the least.”

All the messengers called people to worship Allah, fear Him, stand in awe of Him, and obey His messengers. As Noah, peace be upon him, said:

“Worship Allah, fear Him, and obey me.”

Allah, Most High, says:

“Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, stands in awe of Allah, and fears Him—it is they who will triumph.”

Noah and each of the prophets said:

“So fear Allah and obey me.”

Obeying the Messenger in what he has commanded us is the foundation upon which every Muslim must rely. It is the means to felicity, just as failing to do so is the cause of misery. All Muslims agree that obeying his commands takes precedence for us over imitating an action in which he has not commanded us to imitate him. The scholars have not disputed that his commands carry greater weight than his actions, for an action of his may be exclusive to him, or it may be recommended. His commands to us, however, are part of the religion Allah has commanded us to follow.

Among his actions are those which we know he commanded us to emulate, as when he said:

“Pray as you have seen me pray.”

And when, after leading them in prayer while on the pulpit, he said:

“I did this only so that you would follow my lead and learn how I pray.”

And when he performed the pilgrimage, he said:

“Learn your pilgrimage rites from me.”

Furthermore, the Book and the Sunnah establish that whatever he did as a matter of ordinary custom is permissible for us, unless there is evidence that it was exclusive to him. As Allah, Glorified and Most High, says:

“When Zayd had ended his marriage to her, We gave her to you in marriage, so that there would be no blame on the believers for marrying the wives of their adopted sons once the latter have ended their marriages to them.”

Thus He permitted him to marry

---

## Page 11359

the wife of his adopted son, to remove any blame from the believers for marrying the wives of their adopted sons. Thus, we know that what he did was permissible for us to do.

When Allah singled him out for certain rulings, He said:

“And a believing woman if she offers herself to the Prophet, if the Prophet wishes to marry her—a privilege exclusively for you, not for the other believers. We know what We have prescribed for them concerning their wives and those whom their right hands possess, so that there may be no hardship for you. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

When He permitted him to marry a woman who offered herself to him, He made clear that this was exclusively for him, not for the other believers. Thus, no one other than him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, may marry a woman without a dower.

In Sahīh Muslim, it is reported:

“A man asked the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ‘May a fasting person kiss?’ He replied, ‘Ask her,’ referring to Umm Salamah. She told them that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did so. The man said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, Allah has forgiven your past and future sins.’ He replied, ‘By Allah, I am indeed the most mindful of Allah among you and the most fearful of Him.’”

By answering him with his own practice, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, indicated that what was permissible for him was also permissible for his community. Hence, the majority of the community’s scholars held that whenever Allah commands him to do something or forbids him from something, his community is to follow his example in that, unless evidence establishes that it applies exclusively to him.

---

## Page 11360

Among the matters exclusive to him are those peculiar to his prophethood and messengership. No one may follow his example in these, for there is no prophet after him. This includes being obeyed in everything he commands and forbids, even when the grounds for his command are unknown—to the extent that anyone he orders to be killed must be killed. No one after him has this authority. Those in authority, whether scholars or rulers, are to be obeyed provided that they do not command anything contrary to his commands. Hence, Allah made obedience to them subordinate to obedience to him.

Allah Most High said:

“Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you.”

He said, “and obey the Messenger and those in authority,” because obedience to those in authority is subordinate to obedience to the Messenger. They are not obeyed independently or unconditionally. The Messenger, however, is obeyed unconditionally and independently, for:

“Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah.”

And He Most High said:

“Obey Allah and obey the Messenger.”

Thus, when the Messenger commands us, we must obey him even if we do not know the grounds for his command. Obedience to him is obedience to Allah; unlike obedience to anyone else, obedience to him can never entail disobedience to Allah.

Scholars have discussed matters exclusive to him concerning what was obligatory for him, what was forbidden to him, and the honors conferred upon him. This is not the place to discuss them in detail. Some are agreed upon, while others are disputed.

He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was the leader of the community. He adjudicated between them, made distributions, led them in military campaigns, carried out the prescribed punishments, secured the fulfillment of rights, and led them in prayer. Following his example in each capacity must therefore accord with that capacity. Thus, the leader of the prayer and the Hajj follows

---

## Page 11361

his example in that capacity; the military commander follows his example in that capacity; and the one who carries out the prescribed punishments follows his example in that capacity. Likewise, whoever adjudicates or issues legal opinions follows his example in that capacity.

People have disagreed about certain things he did: were they exclusive to him, or may the community also do them? Examples include his joining a prayer as its leader after someone else had led the people, and his declining to offer the funeral prayer for someone who had misappropriated war spoils or for a killer.

Furthermore, when he performed an act for a reason known to us, we can follow his example in it. But when we do not know the reason, or when the circumstances were merely incidental, this is a matter over which people disagree. An example is his stopping at a particular place during a journey. Some scholars consider it recommended to stop where he stopped, as Ibn ‘Umar used to do. They maintain that simply doing the same thing as he did is good, even if his action was incidental, whereas we do it with the intention of emulating him.

Other scholars say that following his example is recommended only when we act on the same basis as he did. If his action was merely incidental, it is not prescribed for us to deliberately pursue something he did not intend. For this reason, most of the Emigrants and the Helpers did not do what Ibn ‘Umar used to do.

Moreover, following his example may sometimes concern the particular kind of action, and sometimes its broader category. He may perform an act for a reason that applies both to that particular kind and to others, rather than for a reason exclusive to it. In that case, what is prescribed is the broader practice. An example is his undergoing cupping, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, for this was prompted by his need

---

## Page 11362

to have unhealthy blood removed. Does following his example, then, apply specifically to cupping, or is the aim to remove blood in a beneficial manner? It is well known that following his example is what is prescribed. Thus, in a hot country, where blood moves towards the skin, cupping is beneficial; whereas in a cold country, where blood recedes into the veins, removing it by opening a vein is beneficial.

Likewise, when he applied oil, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was the purpose specifically to apply oil, or was it to groom his hair? If a country has a humid climate and its people bathe in hot water that makes oil unnecessary, while oil harms their hair and skin, then what is prescribed for them is to groom their hair in whatever manner is best for them. It is well known that the second interpretation is more fitting.

Similarly, he used to eat fresh dates, dried dates, barley bread, and other staple foods of his country. Does following his example mean deliberately choosing fresh dates, dried dates, and barley specifically, so that even those living in lands where dates do not grow and barley is not a staple should do so, although their staples are wheat, rice, or other foods? It is well known that the second approach is what is prescribed.

The evidence for this is that when the Companions conquered the various lands, each of them ate the staple foods and wore the clothing of his own country, without deliberately seeking out the foods and clothing of Medina. Had this latter course been better for them, they would have been foremost in choosing what was better.

---

## Page 11363

This is the basis of the scholars’ disagreement concerning zakāt al-fitr (the alms due at the end of Ramadan): if dates and barley are not staple foods in a particular country, should its people give their own staple foods, such as wheat and rice, or should they give dates and barley because the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prescribed them? For in the two Sahīh collections, Ibn ‘Umar reported:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prescribed zakāt al-fitr as one sāʿ-measure of dates or one sāʿ-measure of barley for every Muslim, young or old, male or female, free or enslaved.”

The scholars hold two opinions on this question, both of which are reported from Ahmad. Most scholars hold that a person should give the staple food of his country. This is the correct view, just as Allah stated concerning expiation:

“From the average of what you feed your families.”

Another example is that he and his Companions generally wore waist-wraps and upper wraps. Is it therefore better for everyone to wear an upper wrap and a waist-wrap, even with a shirt? Or is it better to wear trousers with a shirt, without needing a waist-wrap and an upper wrap? This too is a matter over which the scholars have disagreed. The second view is more clearly correct. This is a broad subject.

This kind of reasoning is not confined to his actions and those of his Companions; it also applies to much of what he commanded them to do and forbade them to do. Some have called this “refining the basis of a ruling.” This is where a ruling has been established concerning a particular case but is not exclusive to it; rather, the ruling applies both to that case and to others. It therefore becomes necessary to identify “the basis of the ruling.”

---

## Page 11364

An example of this is the report established in the Sahīh that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace,

“Was asked about a mouse that had fallen into ghee. He said: ‘Remove it and the ghee around it, and eat the rest of your ghee.’”

There is agreement that the ruling is not exclusive to that particular mouse and that particular ghee; rather, it applies more broadly. The question therefore remains: what is the basis on which the ruling depends? Some scholars claim that the ruling applies exclusively to a mouse falling into ghee. They therefore regard ghee into which a mouse has fallen as impure without qualification, but do not regard ghee as impure when a dog, urine or excrement falls into it. Nor do they regard oil and similar substances as impure when a mouse falls into them. This opinion is unquestionably mistaken.

This does not depend on whether legal analogy is authoritative. The disputed form of analogy involves deriving the basis of the ruling: that is, where it is possible that the ruling applies exclusively to the case addressed by the text. If the ruling could be exclusive to that case, but could also apply both to it and to other cases, someone employing analogy must establish that the feature shared by the original case and the new case is the basis of the ruling. An example is his saying:

“Do not sell gold for gold except in equal amounts; do not sell silver for silver except in equal amounts; do not sell barley for barley except in equal amounts; and do not sell salt for salt except in equal amounts.”

When he prohibited exchanging unequal amounts of commodities such as these, the prohibition could have been based on a shared feature or on a feature peculiar to them.

But when he was asked about a mouse that had fallen into ghee, he gave an answer concerning that

---

## Page 11365

particular incident, and it is clear that the ruling is not exclusive to it. The same applies to all other rulings concerning particular cases, such as that of the Bedouin who said to him:

“I had intercourse with my wife during Ramadan.”

He instructed him to free a slave, fast for two consecutive months, or feed sixty needy people. Muslims agree that the ruling is not exclusive to that Bedouin. Scholars disagree, however, over whether he instructed him to do this because he had broken his fast, because he had intercourse during Ramadan, because he had broken his fast during Ramadan through intercourse, or because he had broken it through an act belonging to the higher category.

Likewise, someone asked him about a person who had entered the consecrated state for ‘umrah while wearing a robe and smeared with saffron-based perfume. He said:

“Remove your robe, wash off the traces of the saffron-based perfume, and do during your ‘umrah what you would do during your Hajj.”

Did he instruct him to wash off the saffron-based perfume because it was perfume, so that anyone in the consecrated state should be instructed to wash off whatever perfume he was wearing? Or was it because this was saffron-based perfume worn by a man? He had forbidden men to apply saffron to themselves; thus, a man is forbidden to use this perfume whether or not he is in the consecrated state.

Likewise, when Barīrah was freed, he gave her a choice, and she chose to leave her husband—according to those who say that her husband was a slave. Muslims agree that the ruling is not exclusive to her. But was she given the choice because she had been freed while married to a slave, thereby attaining full status while her husband remained of lesser status, so that she would not be given the choice if she were freed while married to a free man? Or was the ruling based on her having gained control over her own person, so that she would be given the choice whether her husband was free or enslaved? This is a matter over which they disagreed.

This is a broad subject, encompassing every ruling attached to a particular case when it is known that the ruling is not exclusive to it.

---

## Page 11366

so it is necessary to identify the effective cause on which the ruling depends. Some call this form of reasoning analogy, while others do not. Hence Abū Hanīfah and his followers employed it in cases where they did not employ analogy. The correct view is that this does not belong to the kind of analogy that is open to dispute, just as scholars unanimously agree that ascertaining whether the effective cause applies to a particular case is not open to dispute. These three forms—“ascertaining whether the effective cause applies,” “isolating the effective cause,” and “deriving the effective cause”—together encompass independent legal reasoning.

The first consists in applying the revealed texts and scholarly consensus. A ruling is attached to an attribute, and applying it to a particular case requires establishing that the attribute is present in that case. For example, we know that Allah has commanded us to call upright witnesses from among ourselves, whom we find acceptable. Yet every individual witness cannot be specified, so we must determine whether particular witnesses are upright and acceptable.

Likewise, Allah has commanded spouses to live together honorably, and the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Women are entitled to provision and clothing in accordance with what is reasonable.”

Every individual husband cannot be specified, so individual cases must be examined. Some jurists hold that a wife’s maintenance is fixed by Islamic law. The correct view, however, is that of the majority: it is determined by customary practice, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to Hind:

“Take what reasonably suffices for you and your child.”

---

## Page 11367

Likewise, the Most High says:

“Do not approach the orphan’s property except in the best manner.”

It remains to consider whether entrusting it to this particular merchant in return for a share of the profit constitutes dealing with it in the best manner.

Similarly, He says:

“Charitable alms are only for the poor and the needy.”

The question remains whether this particular person belongs to the poor and needy mentioned in the Quran. Likewise, Allah has prohibited intoxicants and usury in general, but the question remains whether a particular drink is an intoxicant.

Muslims—indeed, all rational people—agree on this form of reasoning: the Lawgiver cannot explicitly state the ruling for every individual case; rather, He speaks in general terms. Our Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was granted the gift of concise, comprehensive speech.

(As for the second type, which they call “isolating the effective cause,” this occurs when a ruling is explicitly stated for particular cases, yet we know that the ruling is not confined to them. The correct view is that this does not fall under analogy, since they agree that it is covered by the text. Rather, the text addresses the category to which the particular case belongs, but that category must be identified.

The case of the mouse in the clarified butter belongs here. The ruling is not confined to that particular mouse and that particular clarified butter, nor to the mice and clarified butter of Medina. Rather, someone asked the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, about a mouse that had fallen into clarified butter, and he answered him. This does not mean that the answer applies only to that person or his question, just as he answered others.

The words “mouse” and “clarified butter” were not spoken by the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, such that he himself could be said to have made the ruling dependent on them. Rather, they were spoken by the questioner, who related what had happened to him, just as he was told by

---

## Page 11368

the Bedouin that he had had intercourse with his wife. Had he had intercourse with his concubine, the same would have applied. Likewise, another man told him, “I saw the gleam of her anklet in the moonlight, so I fell upon her.” Had he had intercourse with her without that circumstance, the ruling would have been the same.

The correct view here is that held by the well-known imams: the ruling concerns any foul substance that Allah has forbidden when it falls into clarified butter or similar liquids. Allah has permitted wholesome things for us and forbidden foul things. Thus, when we base the ruling on this consideration, we are following the Book of Allah. When something foul falls into something wholesome, one discards the foul substance and what surrounds it, and eats what remains wholesome, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded.

This response is not the place to discuss such questions at length. We have, however, drawn attention to this because it bears on following the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in his actions. This, then, is a matter that involves people’s juristic reasoning and inference, and whatever understanding, wisdom, and knowledge Allah grants them. Those closest to the truth are those who connect rulings to the considerations to which the Lawgiver connected them.

This is an area in which people have differed in understanding and disputed: is this derived from the Lawgiver’s words, or from considerations underlying analogical reasoning? Some have claimed that most rulings governing people’s actions are not covered by the Lawgiver’s words, but instead require analogy. Others have claimed that all such rulings are established by the revealed texts, and have gone to excess in their adherence to the apparent wording

---

## Page 11369

to the point of denying the clear implications and indications of the wording. An example is the Most High’s saying:

“Do not say to them so much as a word of irritation.”

They said that this indicates only a prohibition on expressing irritation; no prohibition on striking or insulting them can be understood from it. They also rejected “isolating the effective cause” and claimed apparent meanings for words that those words do not convey. Others sometimes give analogy precedence because the text’s indication is incomplete, or because it is a solitary report. Still others set the text and analogy against one another and give precedence to the text, yet fall into inconsistency.

We have explained elsewhere that sound proofs do not contradict one another. Sound rational and scriptural proofs do not conflict, nor does a sound inference from analogy contradict a sound inference from the wording. Sound analogy is, in essence, treating like cases alike. This is the justice with which Allah sent down the Book and sent the messengers. The Messenger does not command anything contrary to justice, nor does he give different rulings for two equivalent cases; nor can one thing be forbidden while its equivalent is lawful.

We have examined most of the cases in which analogy is said to conflict with the text, and the text’s ruling is said to run contrary to analogy. We have found that whenever the Lawgiver singles something out for a ruling different from that of comparable cases, He does so only because it possesses a distinctive attribute that requires this particular ruling. Such is the special concession for arāyā sales, permitting dates on the palm to be sold for their estimated equivalent in dried dates, because measuring them by volume is impracticable despite

---

## Page 11370

the need to sell. Need requires resorting to a substitute when the original is unavailable.

Thus, when needed, estimation takes the place of measurement by volume, just as earth takes the place of water, and carrion takes the place of properly slaughtered meat when needed. The same applies to the statement that lending, leasing, profit-sharing investment partnerships, tending orchards for a share of their produce, sharecropping, and similar transactions run contrary to analogy. If the speaker means that these transactions possess distinctive features requiring their rulings to differ from those governing transactions unlike them, he is correct. Indeed, this is precisely what analogy requires. But if he means that two equivalent acts have been assigned different rulings, this is an error that even those of lesser rank than the prophets are above committing—may Allah’s blessings be upon them.

Rather, it is these opposing analogies that are unsound, such as the analogy of those who said:

“‘Trade is only like usury.’ But Allah has permitted trade and forbidden usury.”

And the analogy of those who said, “Do you eat what you yourselves have killed, yet refuse to eat what Allah has killed?”—meaning carrion. The Most High said:

“Indeed, the devils inspire their allies to dispute with you. And if you obey them, you will surely be polytheists.”

Perhaps one whom Allah has blessed with understanding and granted knowledge from Himself will find that most rulings known through sound legal analogy are also indicated by the revealed texts, just as the ultimate purport of

---

## Page 11371

the revealed texts accords with the justice sought through sound legal analogy.

Since this is so, discussing the particular circumstances of a person following the spiritual path requires careful consideration of each case and seeking guidance from Allah. Allah has commanded His servant to say in every prayer:

“Guide us to the straight path—the path of those You have blessed, not those who have incurred Your anger, nor those who have gone astray.”

The servant must therefore strive to attain what he asks for in this supplication, so that he may join those whom Allah has blessed: the prophets, the steadfastly truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous. What excellent companions they are!

---

## Page 11372

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—said:

Section: Acts of Worship Prescribed in Different Forms

It has already been explained in several places that when the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, performed an act of worship in different ways, all those forms are prescribed, and none is disliked.
