Examples include the different forms of the tashahhud (testimony of faith recited while seated in prayer) and the opening supplications; performing Witr prayer at the beginning or end of the night; reciting aloud or quietly during the night prayer; the various readings in which the Quran was revealed; proclaiming Allah’s greatness on Eid; including or omitting tarjīʿ (repetition of the testimonies of faith after reciting them quietly) in the call to prayer; and saying the phrases of the iqāmah (final call to prayer) once or twice.

In our response to the Zarʿiyyah questions and elsewhere, we have explained at length that matters over which scholars differ, and concerning which a person wishes to exercise caution, fall into two categories:

The first consists of matters in which they agree that both alternatives are permissible, but differ as to which is preferable.

---

## Page 11373

The second consists of matters in which they disagree over whether one of the two alternatives is permissible. In many such matters, the Sunnah has sanctioned both alternatives. Hajj is an example. Some have said that converting one’s Hajj into ʿumrah is impermissible; some have even said that tamattuʿ (performing ʿumrah followed by Hajj) is impermissible. Others have said that doing so is obligatory. The correct view is that either course is permissible. During the Farewell Pilgrimage, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, instructed the Companions to convert their Hajj into ʿumrah, although he had previously given them a choice between the three forms of Hajj. The caliphs after him performed Hajj without converting it into ʿumrah, as has been explained at length in its proper place.

The same applies to fasting while travelling. Some have said that it is impermissible and that one must refrain from fasting. The correct view, held by the majority, is that both alternatives are permissible. Many of them then said that fasting is preferable, but the correct view is that not fasting is preferable unless there is an overriding benefit in fasting. No scholar has said that refraining from fasting is impermissible, as some ignorant people suppose. This has been discussed at length in several places.

The point here is that practices established in different forms in the Sunnah—such as the call to prayer, the iqāmah (final call to prayer), prayer in circumstances of fear, and the opening supplications—are to be discussed from two perspectives. The first concerns the permissibility of all these forms, without any being disliked. This is the correct view, and it is the position of Ahmad and others regarding all these matters. Some scholars, however, may regard certain forms as disliked or forbidden because they believe that those forms were not established in the Sunnah or that they were abrogated.

For example, some regarded tarjīʿ (repeating the testimonies of faith after reciting them quietly) in the call to prayer as disliked, saying: “He only said it to Abū

---

## Page 11374

Mahdhūrah to teach him Islam, not to teach him the call to prayer.” The correct view is that he made it part of the call to prayer. This is how Abū Mahdhūrah understood it, and both he and his descendants practised it, with the Muslims accepting their practice in Mecca and elsewhere. Some regarded the call to prayer without tarjīʿ as disliked. This too is mistaken, for the established form of Bilāl’s call to prayer contains no tarjīʿ. Another group regarded tarjīʿ in it as disliked. Some regarded prayer in circumstances of fear as disliked unless performed according to the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, while others regarded the form prescribed by that group as disliked. The correct view in all these matters is that no form established in the Sunnah is disliked; rather, all are permissible. This has been discussed at length elsewhere.

Our concern here is the second perspective: when the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, practised something in different forms, then—even if some of those forms are considered superior—following his example by practising one form on some occasions and another on others is better than adhering to one and abandoning the other.

An example is the opening supplication. In the two Sahīh collections, Abū Hurayrah said:

“I said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, during your silence between the opening takbīr and the recitation, what do you say?’ He replied, ‘I say: O Allah, distance me from my sins as You have distanced the east from the west. O Allah, cleanse me of my sins as a white garment is cleansed of dirt. O Allah, wash away my sins with snow, water and hail.’”

Al-Bukhārī included no report concerning the opening supplication other than

---

## Page 11375

this one. It is the strongest evidence for the opening supplication in obligatory prayers, for it explicitly addresses this in the words: “Tell me about your silence between the opening takbīr and the recitation.” This is a question about silence, not about speaking quietly. It is corroborated by the hadith of Samurah and that of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, which state that the Prophet observed two pauses.

There are also several views concerning pauses in prayer.

The first is that there are no pauses, as Mālik held. He did not regard an opening supplication, seeking refuge with Allah, or a pause for the imam’s recitation as recommended.

The second is that there is only one pause, for the opening supplication, as Abū Hanīfah held, since this hadith establishes that pause.

The third is that there are two pauses, as stated in the hadith recorded in the Sunan collections. One version reports that he paused upon completing the recitation, and this is the correct version. Another reports that he paused upon completing al-Fātihah. Accordingly, some followers of al-Shāfi'ī and Ahmad held that three pauses are recommended. The followers of al-Shāfi'ī and some followers of Ahmad considered the pause after al-Fātihah an opportunity for those praying behind the imam to recite al-Fātihah.

The correct view is that only two pauses are recommended, for that is all the hadith mentions. One of the two versions is mistaken; otherwise, there would have been three pauses.

---

## Page 11376

and this is the position explicitly stated by Ahmad: only two pauses are recommended, the second coming at the end of the recitation, to rest briefly and separate the recitation from bowing. As for pausing immediately after al-Fātihah, Ahmad does not consider it recommended, nor do Mālik and Abū Hanīfah. The majority do not consider it recommended for the imam to pause so that those praying behind him can recite.

This is because, in their view, recitation by someone praying behind the imam when the imam recites aloud is neither obligatory nor recommended; rather, it is prohibited. Does reciting along with the imam invalidate the prayer? There are two views within Ahmad’s school. If someone can hear the imam’s recitation, listening to it is better than reciting himself, just as he listens to what is recited beyond al-Fātihah. He thereby attains the purpose of recitation, and listening takes the place of his own recitation. Combining listening with recitation therefore combines the substitute with that for which it substitutes.

For this reason, Ahmad and most of his followers did not consider recitation during the imam’s pauses recommended unless the imam pauses long enough to allow both the opening supplication and recitation. If the pause is too short for both, Ahmad and most of his followers hold that the opening supplication takes precedence over recitation. Indeed, according to one of the two reports from him, he instructs the worshipper to offer the opening supplication even while the imam is reciting aloud.

If the imam pauses after al-Fātihah long enough to allow recitation, then reciting during that pause is better than not reciting. But should it be said that reciting al-Fātihah during it is better, because its obligatory status is disputed, or that reciting another passage of the Quran is better, since he has already listened to al-Fātihah? This is disputed. The explicit statements of Ahmad and most of his followers imply that

---

## Page 11377

reciting another passage is better. It is not recommended for him to recite al-Fātihah when he is listening to its recitation. The disapproval expressed by most of the early scholars concerning recitation behind the imam relates to cases in which he recites aloud. Most imams did not pause for long after al-Fātihah, and few worshippers recited while the imam was reciting aloud. This is prohibited by the Quran and Sunnah, and the majority of earlier and later scholars maintain this prohibition. Whether doing so invalidates the prayer is disputed.

Some scholars, however, hold that the worshipper should recite al-Fātihah while the imam recites aloud. Whether his prayer is invalid if he does not recite it is also disputed. Thus, there is disagreement on both sides. Nevertheless, those who prohibit reciting along with the imam constitute the majority of earlier and later scholars, and their position is supported by the Quran and authentic Sunnah. As for those who require the worshipper praying behind the imam to recite in these circumstances, the hadith they rely upon, narrated by Abū Dāwūd, has been judged weak by the leading hadith scholars.

The wording in the hadith of Abū Mūsā, “When he recites, listen attentively,” was graded authentic by Ahmad, Ishāq, Muslim ibn al-Hajjāj and others. Al-Bukhārī considered it defective because of differences in its transmission, but this does not undermine its authenticity. By contrast, the other hadith was not included in the Sahīh, and its weakness is established on several grounds. It is merely a statement of ‘Ubādah ibn al-Sāmit.

Rather, during the imam’s pause, the worshipper should offer the prescribed opening supplication and seek refuge in Allah. If the imam does not pause long enough for this, or the worshipper misses his pause, should he offer the opening supplication and seek refuge in Allah while the imam recites aloud?

There are three reported positions:

The first is that he offers the opening supplication and seeks refuge in Allah while the imam recites aloud, even though he does not recite, because

---

## Page 11378

the purpose of recitation is fulfilled by listening, whereas he does not hear the imam’s opening supplication or his seeking refuge in Allah, since the imam says these silently.

The second position is that he offers the opening supplication but does not seek refuge in Allah, because seeking refuge is prescribed for recitation, and he is not reciting. The opening supplication, however, accompanies the opening takbīr.

The third position is that he neither offers the opening supplication nor seeks refuge in Allah. This is the soundest view and is held by most scholars, including Mālik and al-Shāfi‘ī, and also Abū Hanīfah, as far as I believe. This is because he is commanded to remain silent and listen attentively, so he should not utter anything else. Moreover, since he is prohibited from reciting, he is likewise prohibited from saying these supplications. Many scholars, among Ahmad’s followers and others, say that prohibiting these supplications is all the more warranted, because recitation is obligatory, yet its obligation is waived through listening. In Ahmad’s school, however, the prohibition against recitation is not more emphatic, since he does not consider recitation obligatory for the worshipper praying behind the imam, whether the imam recites silently or aloud. Even if there is disagreement over whether recitation is obligatory for the worshipper praying behind the imam, there is likewise disagreement over whether the opening supplication and seeking refuge in Allah are obligatory. There are two well-known positions on this within his school.

Among the arguments advanced by those who instruct the worshipper to say both while the imam recites aloud is that both are obligatory and no substitute has been prescribed for them, unlike recitation, for which listening has been prescribed as a substitute. The correct view, however, is that these are not obligatory, and only the person who recites is commanded to seek refuge in Allah. The command to listen attentively to the imam’s recitation and remain silent is stated in the Quran and the authentic Sunnah, and it is

---

## Page 11379

the consensus of the Muslim community regarding recitation beyond al-Fātihah. It is also the view of the vast majority of the early generations, including the Companions and others, regarding both al-Fātihah and other passages. It is one of al-Shāfi‘ī’s two positions, adopted by a number of his most accomplished followers, such as al-Rāzī and Abū Muhammad ibn ‘Abd al-Salām. For reciting while the imam recites aloud is reprehensible and contrary to the Quran, the Sunnah, and the practice of the majority of the Companions. Nevertheless, some of Ahmad’s followers recommended that the worshipper praying behind the imam recite during the imam’s pauses. Some recommended reciting al-Fātihah even while the imam recites aloud; this was the position preferred by my grandfather. A number of scholars, including al-Awzā‘ī and others, likewise recommended this. Some also recommended that the imam pause after al-Fātihah so that those behind him could recite. Ahmad did not recommend this pause, since he did not recommend recitation while the imam recites aloud. A detailed discussion of this belongs elsewhere.

The point here is that the pause for the opening supplication is established by this authentic hadith. Nevertheless, the majority of scholars among the Companions and later generations recommend opening with a different supplication, and most recommend opening with the words:

“Glory be to You, O Allah.”

We have explained the reason for this elsewhere: the superiority of one form of remembrance over another rests on the distinctive merits of the superior form, not on its chain of transmission.

Remembrance is of three kinds: the best is praise of Allah; next come declarations made by the servant or acknowledgments of what he owes to Allah; then come supplications made by the servant.

---

## Page 11380

The first kind includes the first half of al-Fātihah, as well as:

“Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You. Blessed is Your name, exalted is Your majesty, and there is no god but You.”

It also includes glorifying Allah when bowing and prostrating.

The second kind includes his words:

“I have turned my face toward Him who created the heavens and the earth,”

and his words when bowing and prostrating:

“O Allah, to You I have bowed and to You I have prostrated,”

as in the hadith of ‘Alī narrated by Muslim.

The third kind includes his words:

“O Allah, put distance between me and my sins,”

and his supplications when bowing and prostrating. For this reason, a group of Ahmad’s followers deemed forms of praise obligatory, just as they deemed the opening supplication obligatory. Two positions on this have been reported from Ahmad, and Ibn Battah and others favoured the view that it is obligatory. A detailed discussion of this belongs elsewhere.

The point here is that occasionally using a less preferred form—such as the opening supplication narrated by Abū Hurayrah, or opening with “I have turned my face” or “Glory be to You, O Allah,” according to those who prefer the alternative—is better than consistently using one form and abandoning another. This is because the best guidance is the guidance of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. As established in an authentic hadith, he used to say in his Friday sermon:

“The best speech is the speech of Allah, and the best guidance is the guidance of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.”

He certainly did not invariably use a single opening supplication, for the hadith of Abū Hurayrah indicates that he used to begin with this one.

---

## Page 11381

If it is said, “He used to recite it consistently, so consistently reciting it was preferable,” we reply: No scholar, to our knowledge, has said this. Thus we know that he did not recite it consistently.

Moreover, ‘Umar used to recite aloud:

“Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You,”

to teach it to the people. Had the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, not said it in the obligatory prayer, ‘Umar would not have done this with the Muslims’ approval. Similarly, some of them would recite the words of seeking refuge with Allah aloud. It has likewise been said that a number of them recited the basmalah—the formula “In the name of Allah”—aloud to teach people to recite it, just as some recited the words of seeking refuge and the opening supplication aloud, and as Ibn ‘Abbās recited al-Fātihah aloud in the funeral prayer.

The correct view, therefore, is the one explicitly stated by Ahmad: it is recommended to recite these aloud occasionally. Thus, reciting the basmalah aloud on occasion is recommended. Some explicitly reported that Ahmad would recite it aloud when he prayed in Medina. Al-Qādī thought this was because the people of Medina were Shiites who recited it aloud and objected to anyone who did not. For by the time al-Qādī performed Hajj, Shiism had become prominent there, and the Egyptian ‘Ubaydids had gained control over the city and the people of Mecca. They had also prevented pilgrimage from Iraq for a time; al-Qādī himself travelled on pilgrimage from Syria.

The correct explanation, however, is that Ahmad did not instruct people to recite it aloud for that reason. Rather, the people of Medina in his time did not recite it either silently or aloud, in accordance with Mālik’s position. Ahmad therefore wanted it recited aloud, as some of the Companions had done, to teach the Sunnah and make clear that its recitation is recommended in general. Ahmad also recommended, in the case of someone leading people who do not recite the qunūt supplication

---

## Page 11382

in witr and want their imam not to recite it, that he omit it to win their hearts. He thus recommended foregoing what is preferable in order to win their hearts, which accords with al-Qādī’s explanation. Accordingly, reciting the basmalah aloud is recommended when those praying behind the imam prefer this, in order to win their hearts. It is also recommended when doing so makes the Sunnah known, and they learn the Sunnah from him without objecting to his practice.

All of this comes under one comprehensive principle: a less preferable act may become preferable because of an overriding benefit. If something forbidden, such as eating carrion, may become obligatory because of an overriding benefit and the need to avert harm, then a less preferable act may all the more readily become preferable because of an overriding benefit.

The same applies to categories of worship, such as prayer. Prayer, as a category, is superior to Quran recitation and remembrance of Allah. Yet prayer is prohibited at certain times, so recitation, remembrance and supplication at those times are better than prayer. Likewise, supplication at the pilgrimage sites—‘Arafah, Muzdalifah, Minā, al-Safā and al-Marwah—is also better than recitation, as established by textual evidence and scholarly consensus. For the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“I have been forbidden to recite the Quran while bowing or prostrating.”

This appears in al-Sahīh in a hadith narrated by Ibn ‘Abbās. A hadith narrated by ‘Alī also states that the Prophet forbade him to do so. If someone nevertheless recites, does this invalidate his prayer? There are two opinions within Ahmad’s school. Thus, the prohibition of prayer and recitation at the blessed pilgrimage sites … (1).

## Page 11383

For ritual purity is a prerequisite for prayer, but not for that act. Each place has its prescribed form of worship. Likewise, refraining from prayer at the prohibited times is prescribed in every age. As for circumambulation, is Quran recitation during it disliked? Scholars hold two well-known views, both reported from Ahmad. Al-Shāfi‘ī’s position permits it; indeed, he recommends reciting during circumambulation, though not aloud. A treatise is devoted to the other view.

If this applies to categories of worship whose relative superiority is established by textual evidence and scholarly consensus, how much more does it apply to forms of remembrance, especially those concerning which there is disagreement? The standard is undoubtedly the guidance of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. It is established that he used the opening supplication reported in the hadith of Abū Hurayrah. It is therefore best to use this opening supplication sometimes and others at other times. Moreover, each opening supplication meets a need that another does not, so the believer should take his share of every form of remembrance. A person may also need the less preferable act, without the superior act being sufficient for him.

An example is:

“Say, ‘He is Allah, One.’”

This surah is equivalent to one-third of the Quran: that is, whoever recites it receives a reward equivalent to that of one-third of the Quran in amount, but not in kind. For the commands, prohibitions, narratives, promises and warnings contained in the Quran cannot be replaced by

---

## Page 11384

“Say, ‘He is Allah, One.’” Nor is the reward for those passages of the same kind as the reward for this surah, even though the kind of reward for “Say, ‘He is Allah, One’” is superior. The less preferable may therefore be needed where the superior does not suffice, just as a person needs his leg where his eye cannot take its place. The same applies to created things: each has a wisdom for which it was created. So too with acts of worship. Everything prescribed by the Messenger has its wisdom and purpose and brings benefit [in fulfilling] (1) that purpose. Thus, none of the recommended acts he prescribed should be neglected.

Even if another category of worship is said to be superior, a particular act is superior to others at its proper time and place. In those prayers in which he used this opening supplication, his using it was better than using another. This supplication asks for purification, cleansing from sins, and distance from them. It is akin to seeking forgiveness before dawn and to his seeking forgiveness after prayer. He would also offer a similar supplication at the end of his standing upright after bowing, after praising Allah. Thus, he would sometimes begin his standing with it and would also conclude his standing with it. Various opening supplications have been reported from him, most of them in night prayer, as Ahmad mentioned.

It is recommended for someone praying at night to use all these opening supplications. This is better than consistently using one form and abandoning the others, for this was the guidance of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Yet it must also be said: the guidance of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is best, but for some people the best may not be suitable; rather, performing the less preferable act may be

The same may be said here: consistently practising the less preferable form may benefit him more because he loves it, his heart is attentive, and he understands that remembrance. When we say that varying these forms of remembrance is better, we are likewise giving preference to variation as a general practice. What is less preferable may benefit some people more because it suits them, just as its category may be superior under Islamic law in certain places, times, and circumstances. Thus, what is generally less preferable may sometimes be superior without qualification for everyone, as explained earlier. It may also be superior for certain people because they benefit from it more fully. This is the condition of most people: because the less preferable practice suits their imperfect states, they may derive benefit from it that they do not derive from the superior practice, whose demands they are unable to meet.

Section

preferable at a particular time because that form suits the circumstances of that time. Certain forms of remembrance and supplication may likewise be better at certain times. Such is the disagreement over the basmala (“In the name of Allah”): is its recitation obligatory, and should it be recited aloud? Or is reciting it disliked, whether silently or aloud? The former need to present the evidence that it is part of the Quran—an independent verse accompanying the surahs. The latter need to present the evidence that it is not part of the surahs and that its recitation is not obligatory. Both statements are true.

Surah Iqra’ (“Recite”) was the first revelation of the Quran. Both groups have cited it as evidence, and it supports the truth held by each. Those who say that the basmala is not part of the surah argue that when Gabriel came to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, he did not instruct him to recite it. Rather, he instructed him to recite:

“In the name of your Lord who created.”

Had the basmala been the beginning of the surah, he would have instructed him to recite it. This is established in the two Sahih collections through the hadith of ‘Ā’isha.

Those who advocate reciting it argue that He said:

“Recite in the name of your Lord who created.”

This commands everyone who recites to recite in the name of his Lord. Thus, when someone is told, “Slaughter in the name of Allah”

## Page 11387

, “Eat in the name of Allah,” and “Ride in the name of Allah,” it means: mention Allah’s name when you do so. Thus, when He said:

“Recite in the name of your Lord,”

He was commanding the reciter to mention Allah’s name by saying, “In the name of Allah.” This is even more fitting than mentioning his Lord’s name when slaughtering, eating or drinking. He has also commanded seeking refuge when reciting. When someone says, “In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful,” he has fulfilled the command by mentioning his Lord’s name when reciting.

Gabriel did not mention it at the outset only because the Prophet had not yet learned any of the Quran. Instead, he taught him this passage and, through it, instructed him to mention his Lord’s name when reciting. Thereafter, whenever he recited a surah, he would recite, “In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.” Thus, it is established in Sahih Muslim that he said, “A surah has just been revealed to me,” then recited:

“In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.
Indeed, We have granted you abundance.
So pray to your Lord and sacrifice.
Indeed, your enemy is the one cut off.”

Yet this indicates that the basmala accompanies the Quranic passage that is the principal object of recitation, because of the remembrance of Allah it contains. For this reason, it was written in copies of the Quran separately from the surah, not incorporated into it. It is therefore Quran, written in copies of the Quran, but it was revealed as an accompaniment to other passages, which are the principal focus.

This is why it was kept separate in both writing and recitation. In writing, it is written separately; in recitation, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would not recite it aloud. Nor did he include it among the Quranic passages whose recitation is obligatory, as shown by his words in the authentic hadith:

“Allah Most High says: ‘I have divided the prayer

---

## Page 11388

between Me and My servant into two halves: half is Mine and half is My servant’s, and My servant shall have what he asks for. When the servant says, “All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds,” Allah says, “My servant has praised Me.” When he says, “The Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful,” He says, “My servant has extolled Me.” When he says, “Master of the Day of Judgment,” He says, “My servant has glorified Me.”’”—and so on to the end of the hadith.

This is the view of the majority of scholars concerning the basmala: it is a separate verse of the Quran, not part of the surah, and is to be recited silently in prayer. Thus, it is neither excluded from the Quran and abandoned, nor treated like the Quranic text that is the principal object of recitation and therefore recited aloud. In some respects, it resembles seeking refuge with Allah. However, the formula for seeking refuge is not Quran and was not written in copies of the Quran; the Quran contains only the command to seek refuge, whereas the basmala is itself Quran.

Al-Fātiha consists of seven verses by agreement. This is established by His words:

“We have certainly given you the seven oft-repeated verses and the great Quran.”

It is also authentically reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The Opening of the Book is the seven oft-repeated verses.”

Many of the early generations used to say that the basmala was one of its verses and would recite it. Many others did not count it as part of the surah and regarded “You have bestowed favor upon them” as the seventh verse, as indicated by the authentic hadith of Abū Hurayra. Both views are correct: in one respect, it is part of the surah, and in another, it is not. Al-Fātiha consists of seven verses. From one perspective, the basmala is part of it and is therefore counted as a verse. From another perspective, it is not part of it, so the seventh verse is “You have bestowed favor upon them,” because the basmala was revealed as an accompaniment to the surahs.

---

## Page 11389

And the purpose is to begin the Quran by mentioning Allah’s name. Thus, the basmala was revealed at the beginning of a surah as an accompaniment to it; it was not revealed at the ends of surahs. It was written separately in copies of the Quran, but as an accompaniment to what follows it, not to what precedes it. For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, “A surah has just been revealed to me,” and recited: “In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. Indeed, We have granted you abundance.”

It is reported in the Sunan collections that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would not know where a surah ended until “In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful” was revealed to him. Insofar as the basmala accompanies the surah, it is regarded as part of it. But insofar as its purpose is to begin recitation in Allah’s name, just as one performs other actions in Allah’s name, while the Quranic text that is the principal object of recitation is other than the basmala, it is not a verse of the surah. Hence the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“I know a surah of the Quran, consisting of thirty verses, which interceded for a man until he was forgiven. It is: ‘Blessed is He in whose hand is dominion.’”

Some Quran reciters separate one surah from another with the basmala, while others do not. Since the whole Quran is Allah’s speech, the latter do not separate surahs with it, just as someone may mention Allah’s name when beginning to eat and then eat various kinds of food. Others mention Allah’s name at the beginning of every surah. This is better, because it follows the written form of the Quran. It is comparable to one dish being removed and another set down: mentioning Allah’s name at that point is preferable.

---

## Page 11390

Likewise, when someone slaughters one sheep after another, mentioning Allah’s name over each sheep is preferable. As for reciting the basmala at the beginning of al-Fātihah, this means beginning the Quran with it. Hence, two positions are reported from Ahmad on whether reciting it at the beginning of al-Fātihah is an obligatory duty without which the prayer is invalid. Two positions are also reported from him concerning seeking refuge in Allah and the opening supplication; there is thus all the more reason to regard the basmala as obligatory.

Its obligation may be based on its being part of al-Fātihah, but it may also be considered obligatory even if it is not part of al-Fātihah, just as seeking refuge in Allah and the opening supplication may be considered obligatory. For this reason, he does not regard reciting it aloud as a consequence of its being obligatory. Rather, he considers it obligatory while recommending that it be recited quietly. Were it part of al-Fātihah in every respect, reciting some of al-Fātihah aloud but not the rest would be difficult to reconcile with the established principles. If, however, it is regarded as part of al-Fātihah in one respect but not another, the evidence and principles agree, and each matter is given its appropriate characterization. Nor did he say that it is part of the Quran at the beginning of al-Fātihah, even as held by those who do not regard it as part of the Quran anywhere except in Sūrat al-Naml.

Some have said that it is part of the Quran in one recitation but not another, since these recitations have been transmitted through numerous independent chains. The response is:

What has been transmitted in this way is the positive content: the Quran they heard from the Companions and transmitted on the authority of the Messenger. In his time, the Quran had not been written down, nor was arranging the surahs in this order an obligation commanded by Allah. Rather, the matter was left to the Muslims’ choice. Thus, a number of the Companions each had their own convention for arranging its surahs, different from

---

## Page 11391

that of the others. Accordingly, the Messenger taught those who do not recite it without reciting the basmala, while he taught the others with the basmala. This indicates that both practices are permissible, even if one is preferable. It does not indicate that, in one of the two readings, it is not part of the Quran and that he prohibited its recitation. That would combine two contradictory judgments: how could reciting it be both permissible and prohibited? Rather, this indicates that both practices are permissible, just as certain words occur in one recitation but not another, such as “from beneath it” and “Indeed, Allah—He is the Self-Sufficient.” The Messenger permits both including and omitting such words; both are permissible under his law.

This makes clear that those jurists who say that reciting it is obligatory according to the recitation of those who include it, or disliked according to the recitation of those who omit it, are mistaken. Rather, the Quran indicates that both practices are permissible.

Someone who follows a particular recitation is not required to follow it every time he recites. Nor does someone who omits what others recite say that their recitation is disliked. Rather, all of this is permissible by agreement, even though each group may prefer a particular practice.

This also makes clear the error of anyone who denies altogether that it is part of the Quran except in Sūrat al-Naml, and declares those who affirm it unquestionably mistaken, on the grounds that something can only be established as part of the Quran with certainty. He should be told: “Nor can it be excluded without certainty.”

He should then be told: “Those who affirm it are certain that it is established, and certain that those who deny it are mistaken.” Rather, the precise understanding is that whether something is known with certainty or not is a relative matter, and the recitations

## Page 11400

handed down from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, which does not arise after him but was already present in his time, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. It is preserved and safeguarded through its transmission by the Messenger’s successors and the heirs of the prophets.

There are several lines of evidence showing that these fabricated accounts and others have no basis.

First:

When people have compelling motives and incentives to transmit and spread something, it is ordinarily impossible for it to remain concealed. Thus, if only a few report it, this indicates that they are lying. For example, someone who comes out on Friday and reports a major incident in the congregational mosque—such as the preacher falling, his being killed, or people being detained in the mosque—is known to be lying if only one or two people report it. Likewise, someone who reports that there are great cities and numerous peoples along the travel routes is known to be lying if travellers do not report this and only one or two people do. The same applies to someone who reports gold and silver deposits readily accessible to anyone who wants them, in a place known to people, when only one or two people report this. There are many similar examples.

Through rational reflection, analogy, and comparison, one can therefore recognize the falsehood of reports about things which, according to Allah’s established practice, would have become known and widespread had they existed. Likewise, one can recognize the truth of mass-transmitted reports and widely circulated accounts concerning matters about which, according to Allah’s established practice among His servants, people do not conspire to lie. For Allah has endowed the great masses of humanity with a natural disposition to speak truthfully and openly in such matters, rather than

---

## Page 11401

lying and concealment, just as He has endowed them with a natural disposition to eat, drink, and clothe themselves. By nature, a person chooses truthfulness when there is no overriding motive to lie, and prefers to report such momentous events rather than conceal them. People ask one another for news and are inclined to inquire and ask about what happens. Everyone has someone to whom he prefers to speak truthfully and openly rather than lie or conceal information.

Lying and concealment occur frequently among human beings in countless individual cases, just as adultery, murder, death from hunger and exposure, and similar things occur among them. Nonetheless, legitimacy is the norm in their lineage, and survival is the norm in their lives. The point here is that, with mass-transmitted reports, it is known that people have not colluded to lie; and with isolated reports, it is known that people have not colluded to conceal.

(The second line of evidence:

The community’s religion obliges its members to convey, make known, and explain the religion, and forbids them to conceal it. It also obliges them to speak truthfully and forbids them to lie. Their colluding to conceal what must be made clear is therefore like their colluding to lie. Both are among the most reprehensible things prohibited in the community’s religion. This provides a compelling incentive for truthfulness and openness.

Third:

What is known of the uprightness and piety of the community’s early generations, their great eagerness to convey and make known the religion, and their scrupulous avoidance of lying about the Messenger

---

## Page 11402

—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—provides the strongest self-evident certainty that they neither lied in what they transmitted from him nor concealed what he commanded them to convey. This needs-based religious disposition peculiar to them differs from the general disposition shared by all human beings.

(Fourth:

Scholars with specialist knowledge are familiar with the statements of Allah’s Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—obliging them to convey his teachings, with their reverence for the commands of Allah and His Messenger, and with the piety of individuals among them: the caliphs, Ibn Masʿūd, Ubayy, Muʿādh, Abū al-Dardā’, and others down to Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbās, and Ibn ʿAmr. They therefore know with absolute certainty, untouched by doubt, that these men would never conceal the foundations of the religion that must be conveyed to the public, just as they know that they would never lie about Allah’s Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

Hadith scholars likewise know enough about the character of those renowned for this knowledge—such as al-Zuhrī, Qatāda, Yahyā ibn Abī Kathīr, Mālik, al-Thawrī, Shuʿba, Hammād ibn Zayd, Hammād ibn Salama, and others—to know that they would neither lie nor withhold the transmission of these momentous matters. Their very character would have precluded their concealing such matters, had they existed. They have grounds for this knowledge that would take a long time to explain, but establishing it is not the purpose here. The purpose is simply to draw attention to the doubt that has arisen among certain followers of their own desires.

They refer to them by various labels: sometimes ‘the majority,’ sometimes ‘the Hashwiyya,’ and sometimes ‘the common people.’ Having treated this disagreement as precluding the truth from being found in the teachings of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿa, the followers of their own desires each came to adopt one of Satan’s paths.

Thus, the Rāfida claim to transmit from the Prophet’s household reports that have no basis. He fabricated the claim that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—had explicitly designated 'Alī as caliph, that 'Alī had been wronged and denied his right, and that he was infallible. The heretics’ purpose was to use this as a means of demolishing Islam. Thus, Rāfidism became a gateway to heresy and impiety. The Sabian adherents of philosophy and those who adopt some of their ideas or go beyond them—including the Qarmatians, Nusayrīs, Ismā'īlīs, Hākimīs, and others—enter into heresy and disbelief in the Book, the Messenger, and the laws of Islam only through the gateway of Shiism and Rāfidism.

The Mu'tazila and others like them profess adherence to analogy and reason, and impugn much of what Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā'a transmit. They justify this by citing the disagreement already mentioned and similar matters. Some adherents of the religion may even make this a reason to impugn the religion itself and its followers. Thus, some of those who are partisan over these minor matters may be working to demolish Islam’s great foundations.

Section

Once some of the harm arising from this disagreement and division has become clear, we shall explain how it can be removed and what religious duty requires in these disputes. This involves explaining the two principles, namely “the Sunnah and the community”

---

## Page 11405

, both of which are indicated by the Book of Allah. For when the Book of Allah is followed—including its commands to follow His Messenger and to hold firmly, all together, to His rope—guidance and success are attained, and misguidance and misery disappear.

As for the first principle, “the community,” we have begun with it because it is more readily recognized by people generally. They must therefore give consensus precedence over their presumed interpretations of the Book and the Sunnah.

We say: Most of these disputes concern matters that are recommended or disliked, not matters that are obligatory or forbidden. If a man performs Hajj separately after 'umrah, performs Hajj alone, or combines Hajj and 'umrah under a single consecration, his Hajj fulfils the obligation according to the great majority of Muslim scholars, although they disagree over which form is best. Some who depart from the community, however, insist that a particular form is obligatory or forbidden. Thus, some Shia require the first form and prohibit the others, while some Nāsibīs prohibit the first form and do not permit it under any circumstances.

Likewise, the adhān is valid according to all the early scholars of the Muslim community and the great majority of its later scholars, whether or not the two testimonies are repeated aloud after being recited quietly, and whether the opening declaration of Allah’s greatness is said four times or twice. Only a few outliers among students of jurisprudence disagree about this, just as some Shia have disagreed by requiring the inclusion of the call, “Come to the best of deeds.”

Likewise, the iqāmah—the call announcing the commencement of prayer—is valid with its phrases said singly or doubled. Whichever form a person uses, his iqāmah is valid according to the great majority of Muslim scholars, except

---

## Page 11406

for those points disputed by a few outliers. Likewise, reciting “In the name of Allah” aloud or quietly is permissible; neither invalidates the prayer, although some scholars recommend one, dislike the other, or prefer not to recite it. Their disagreement thus concerns what is preferable; otherwise, prayer performed either way is valid according to scholars generally.

Although they disagree over whether audible and quiet recitation are obligatory in their respective places—a well-known disagreement in the schools of Mālik, Ahmad, and others—this concerns prolonged recitation of a substantial amount, such as reciting quietly in the dawn prayer or aloud in the noon prayer. As for reciting a small amount aloud or quietly, no one should declare the prayer invalid on that account, and I know of no one who has done so. Indeed, it is established in the two Sahīh collections that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would sometimes let those praying behind him hear a verse during a prayer normally recited quietly.

In Sahīh al-Bukhārī, Rifā‘ah ibn Rāfi‘ al-Zuraqī reported:

“We were praying behind the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. When he raised his head from bowing, he said, ‘Allah hears whoever praises Him.’ A man behind him said, ‘Our Lord, to You belongs all praise—abundant, pure, and blessed praise.’ When he finished the prayer, he asked, ‘Who said that?’ The man replied, ‘I did.’ He said, ‘I saw thirty-odd angels racing to be the first to record it.’”

It is well known that, had he not said it aloud, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would not have heard him, nor

---

## Page 11407

would the narrator. It is well known that those praying behind an imam are encouraged to say such words quietly. Likewise, it is established in the Sahīh collection that ‘Umar would recite the opening supplication aloud: “Glory and praise be to You, O Allah. Blessed is Your name, exalted is Your majesty, and there is no god but You.” He did this in the presence of the Emigrants and the Helpers.

The regular Sunnah, however, is to recite it quietly. Similarly, some Companions would seek refuge in Allah aloud. It is also established in the Sahīh collection that Ibn ‘Abbās recited al-Fātihah aloud during the funeral prayer and said, “So that you may know that it is the Sunnah.” There are other comparable examples.

Moreover, there is no dispute that some Companions, such as Ibn al-Zubayr and others, would recite “In the name of Allah” aloud, while others, such as Ibn Mas‘ūd, would not. The Companions discussed this matter, yet none declared anyone’s prayer invalid on that account. I know of no disagreement on this point. Although they disagreed over whether reciting it was obligatory, that is a separate question.

Likewise, their disagreement over the qunūt supplication in the dawn prayer concerns only whether it is recommended or disliked, and whether prostrations for forgetfulness are required for omitting or performing it. Otherwise, scholars generally agree that the prayer of someone who omits qunūt is valid and that it is not obligatory. The prayer of someone who performs it is likewise valid, since it involves only briefly prolonging the upright standing and supplicating to Allah in this … (1)

the call to prayer. Thus, if each of the Messenger of Allah’s callers to prayer, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had been instructed by the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace,

> **Footnotes:**
> (1) Omitted in the original.

---

## Page 11408

to use one of the two forms, this would be like his teaching the Quran to ‘Umar in one mode of recitation and to Hishām ibn Hakīm in another: both were Quran whose recitation Allah had permitted. Likewise, tarjīʿ in the call to prayer is established in Abū Mahdhūrah’s call, but is absent from Bilāl’s call as transmitted in the Sunan collections. The same applies to reciting “In the name of Allah” aloud or quietly: authentic reports establish that a group of Companions recited it aloud, that most recited it quietly, and that some did both.

As for what is transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the reports in the Sahīh and Sunan collections indicate that he did not recite it aloud, which accords with the practice of most of his Companions and his community. In the Sahīh collection, the reports of Anas, ‘Ā’ishah and Abū Hurayrah indicate this clearly and unequivocally. The Sunan collections contain other reports, such as that of Ibn Mughaffal and others. There is no hadith in the Sahīh and Sunan collections mentioning that he recited it aloud. All the hadiths explicitly reporting that he did so are weak according to hadith scholars. For this reason, they included none of them in the principal hadith collections. There are, however, reports in the Sahīh and Sunan collections that admit more than one interpretation.

Al-Tabarānī narrated, with a good chain of transmission, from Ibn ‘Abbās:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to recite it aloud when he was in Mecca. When he migrated to Medina, he ceased reciting it aloud and continued thus until he died.”

Abū Dāwūd also narrated it in al-Nāsikh wa-l-Mansūkh (The Abrogating and the Abrogated). This

---

## Page 11409

accords with actual practice, for reciting it aloud predominated among the people of Mecca. The people of Medina, Syria and Kufa, however, did not recite it aloud, nor did most of the people of Basra, though some of them did. This is why they asked Anas about it. Perhaps the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, recited it aloud occasionally, or only softly, if the reports to that effect are reliably preserved. If the hadith collections themselves record that he did one at one time and the other at another, the uncertainty is dispelled.

As for qunūt (supplication during prayer), the matter is clear and leaves no uncertainty upon thorough consideration. It is established in the Sahīh collections:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, performed qunūt in the dawn prayer on one occasion, supplicating against Ri‘l, Dhakwān and ‘Usayyah, then discontinued it.”

His discontinuing it did not constitute its abrogation, for it is established in the Sahīh collections that he subsequently performed qunūt, supplicating for Muslims such as al-Walīd ibn al-Walīd, Salamah ibn Hishām and the oppressed believers, and supplicating against Mudar. It is also established that he performed qunūt in the sunset and night prayers, and in the other prayers, seeking Allah’s aid and victory.

All this, in broad terms, is reliably transmitted from him. However, some scholars of Kufa believed that his discontinuing it constituted abrogation, and thus held that qunūt had been abrogated. Some scholars of Mecca believed that he continued performing the disputed qunūt in the dawn prayer until he departed this world. The position of those versed in hadith is that he performed qunūt for a particular reason and discontinued it when that reason ceased to exist.

---

## Page 11410

Thus, qunūt is an occasional sunnah, not a regular one. It is established that he discontinued it when the occasion for it ceased, then resumed it on another occasion, and again discontinued it when that occasion ceased. It is also established in the Sahīh collections that he performed qunūt after bowing for only one month. This is reliably reported from Anas and others. No one has ever reported that he performed the disputed form of qunūt, either before or after bowing, nor is there anything to that effect in the Sahīh or Sunan collections. Indeed, Companions such as Ibn ‘Umar, Abū Mālik al-Ashja‘ī and others denied this.

It is known with certainty that, had the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, performed qunūt aloud every day, he would have used a supplication that some of the Companions would have transmitted. They transmitted what he used to say in occasional qunūt and in the qunūt of the witr prayer, so there would have been still greater reason to transmit his supplication in a regularly observed qunūt. If, then, the supplication we recommend for it is merely that used in the qunūt of witr, it is clear that nothing concerning this has been transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. This is known with absolute certainty, just as the absence of an explicit text prescribing this and similar practices is known. It is inconceivable that all the Companions neglected to transmit it; such a supposition is certainly false.

Likewise, what is transmitted from Companions such as ‘Umar, ‘Alī and others is occasional qunūt: qunūt offered in times of calamity. ‘Umar’s supplication during it—namely:

“O Allah, punish the disbelievers among the People of the Book,”

and so forth—indicates that he offered it when he was killing Christians. The same applies to ‘Alī’s supplication when he was fighting some of those who face the qiblah in prayer. As for the hadith containing a report from

---

## Page 11411

Anas that “he continued to perform qunūt until he departed this world”: despite its weak chain of transmission and its absence from the Sunan collections, it speaks only of qunūt before bowing.

In the Sahīh collections, Anas is reported to have said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, performed qunūt after bowing for only one month.”

Qunūt before bowing means prolonged standing, for the word qunūt signifies sustained obedience. It may therefore occur during prostration or during standing, as we have explained elsewhere.

As for the Farewell Pilgrimage, although many people have found it confusing, their confusion arose only from terms bearing more than one meaning. They heard some Companions say that he performed tamattu‘, joining ‘umrah to Hajj. Yet these same Companions also say that he performed Hajj alone, while some say that he combined ‘umrah with Hajj. There is no disagreement here. They did not disagree that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, remained in his state of ihrām, that he had brought the sacrificial animals with him and slaughtered them on the Day of Sacrifice, and that neither he nor any of his Companions performed ‘umrah after Hajj that year, except ‘Ā’ishah. He instructed her brother to take her to perform ‘umrah from al-Tan‘īm, the nearest point outside the Sacred Precinct.

Likewise, the authentic hadiths about him state that he traversed the course between al-Safā and al-Marwah only once, in conjunction with his initial circumambulation. Those who reported that he performed Hajj alone spoke truthfully, because he performed a single set of Hajj rites and did not combine

---

## Page 11412

them with the rites of ‘umrah, as imagined by those who maintain that a pilgrim combining Hajj and ‘umrah must perform two circumambulations and traverse the course between al-Safā and al-Marwah twice. Nor did he perform tamattu‘ in a manner that involved leaving his state of ihrām, as does a pilgrim performing tamattu‘ who has not brought sacrificial animals. Rather, he instructed all his Companions who had not brought sacrificial animals to leave their state of ihrām, make their pilgrimage an ‘umrah, and enter ihrām for Hajj after completing their ‘umrah. End of quotation.

## Page 11413

The Shaykh—may Allah have mercy on him—said:

Section

“There are three kinds of opening formulas for prayer.”

These are also the categories of remembrance in general, apart from the Quran. The highest consists of praise of Allah, followed by statements in which the servant declares his worship of Allah. The third consists of supplication on the servant’s behalf. Speech is either declarative or non-declarative, and the finest declarative speech concerns Allah. Statements concerning Allah are superior to statements concerning anyone else and to non-declarative utterances. This is why

“Say: He is Allah, the One”

is equivalent to one-third of the Quran: it contains statements concerning Allah. Likewise, the Verse of the Throne is the greatest verse in the Quran because it speaks about Allah. Thus, remembrance of the same kind as this surah and this verse is the finest kind.

Making requests of the Lord ranks below remembrance devoted solely to Him, as in the hadith of Mālik ibn al-Huwayrith:

“Whoever is so occupied with remembering Me that he does not ask Me, I grant him better than what I grant those who ask.”

This is why al-Fātihah consists of two halves: half praise and half supplication. And the half

---

## Page 11414

that comes second is given precedence, and it is the half devoted to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Likewise, in the authentic hadith of intercession, he said:

“When I see my Lord, I will fall down before Him in prostration and praise Him with words of praise that He will inspire in me, which I cannot offer now. He will say, ‘O Muhammad, raise your head. Speak and you will be heard; ask and you will be granted what you ask; intercede and your intercession will be accepted.’”

Thus, he began by praising Allah until he was permitted to ask, and then he asked.

In Sahīh al-Bukhārī, the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“Whoever wakes during the night and says, ‘None has the right to be worshipped except Allah alone, without partner. His is the dominion, and to Him belongs all praise, and He has power over all things. Praise be to Allah; glory be to Allah; Allah is the Greatest. O Allah, forgive me.’ If he supplicates, his supplication will be answered; and if he performs ablution and prays, his prayer will be accepted.”

He also said:

“The best words that I and the prophets before me have spoken are: ‘None has the right to be worshipped except Allah alone, without partner. His is the dominion, and to Him belongs all praise, and He has power over all things.’”

For this reason, the tashahhud (the testimony recited while sitting in prayer) consists of praise of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Regarding its conclusion, he said, “Then let him choose whatever supplication he wishes.” The prescribed supplications come after the tashahhud; supplication while sitting before the tashahhud was not prescribed. Rather, praise was placed before supplication. In the hadith concerning the man who supplicated before offering praise, the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said, “This man has been hasty.”

Imam Ahmad, al-Tirmidhī and Abū Dāwūd narrated from Fadālah ibn ‘Ubayd, who said: “The Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—heard a man supplicating during his prayer without having praised Allah or invoked blessings upon

---

## Page 11415

the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said, ‘This man has been hasty.’ He then called him over and said to him—or to someone else—‘When any of you prays, let him begin by praising and extolling his Lord, then invoke blessings upon the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and then supplicate for whatever he wishes.’”

Remembrance of Allah is prescribed, by agreement of the Muslims, during bowing, prostration, and when returning to an upright posture. As for supplication during obligatory prayer, there is disagreement over whether it is disliked, although the correct view is that it is not disliked. Remembrance, however, is better, for it is commanded during both bowing and prostration in the words of the Most High:

“So glorify the name of your Lord, the Most Great,”

and:

“Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High.”

The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said concerning the first:

“Make this part of your bowing,”

and concerning the second:

“Make this part of your prostration.”

As for his saying—may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“When bowing, magnify the Lord; when prostrating, supplicate earnestly, for then your supplication is likely to be answered,”

this contains a command to magnify the Lord during bowing. His command to supplicate during prostration explains that supplication during prostration is more deserving of an answer than during bowing. Hence he said, “For then your supplication is likely to be answered,” just as he said:

“The closest a servant comes to his Lord is while he is prostrating.”

Thus, it is a command that supplication be made during prostration: a command concerning the manner of the act, not the act itself—or a command concerning both the manner and the act, even if glorifying Allah is better. For an act to be commanded, it is not necessary that nothing else be better

---

## Page 11416

than it; for supplication depends on what the servant seeks. He did not specify a particular supplication and command it, as he commanded the recitation of al-Fātihah, which includes His words:

“Guide us to the straight path.”

An obligatory supplication can only be a specified one, even if supplication as a general category is obligatory. It is well known that supplication is permissible both within prayer and outside it. Most of the supplications transmitted from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—were made at the end of prayer, as in the hadith reported from him—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—in which he stated:

“Supplication is most likely to be answered in the depths of the latter part of the night and at the end of prayer.”

Thus, supplication at the end of prayer—especially before the salutation, when the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—usually supplicated—is more likely to be answered than at any other stage of prayer, because it follows the completion of worship.

As for prostration, he mentioned it together with bowing because he said:

“I have been forbidden to recite the Quran while bowing or prostrating. When bowing, magnify the Lord; when prostrating, supplicate earnestly, for then your supplication is likely to be answered.”

Having forbidden recitation in these two postures, he mentioned a prescribed alternative for anyone who wished, assigning magnification of the Lord specifically to bowing and supplication to prostration. He thus brought together the three categories: recitation, remembrance, and supplication.

Among the evidence showing the superiority of remembrance over petition is what is authentically reported in Sahīh Muslim

---

## Page 11417

from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—that he said:

“The finest words after the Quran are four—and they are part of the Quran: Glory be to Allah; all praise is due to Allah; none has the right to be worshipped but Allah; and Allah is the Greatest.”

This is why he instructed anyone unable to recite in prayer to engage in remembrance. For praising Allah while standing upright after bowing is prescribed by the mass-transmitted Sunnah and the consensus of the Muslims. This is what the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—would do in every prayer. Sometimes, after praising Allah, he would supplicate, saying:

“O Allah, distance me from my sins.”

Thus, he placed petition after praise, commendation, and glorification. He also commanded praise, saying:

“When he says, ‘Allah hears whoever praises Him,’ say, ‘Our Lord, to You belongs all praise.’”

What he consistently practised, placed first, and commanded is superior to what he did only sometimes, placed afterwards, and did not command. Furthermore, the Lord has designated praise as His due and petition as His servant’s share. He said:

“When the servant says, ‘All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds,’ Allah says, ‘My servant has praised Me.’ When he says, ‘The Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful,’ He says, ‘My servant has extolled Me.’ When he says, ‘Master of the Day of Judgment,’ Allah says, ‘My servant has glorified Me.’ When he says, ‘You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help,’ He says, ‘This verse is divided into two halves between Me and My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks for.’ When he says, ‘Guide us to the straight path,’ through to the end of the surah, He says, ‘These verses are for My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks for.’”

Moreover, the vast majority of scholars hold praise to be obligatory, and therefore require the final tashahhud. Likewise, according to Mālik and Ahmad, the first tashahhud is obligatory when one remembers it. Thus, if someone omits it

---

## Page 11418

deliberately, his prayer is invalidated. According to Ahmad and others, the same applies to glorifying Allah when bowing and prostrating, and likewise to the declarations of Allah’s greatness when moving between postures.

Mālik’s position is that whoever deliberately omits three of these must repeat the prayer. Ahmad’s position is well known and applies without qualification. Ahmad’s followers state in their discussions of scholarly disagreement that requiring these remembrances is a position unique to Ahmad among the four imams. This is because Mālik’s followers call them sunnah practices. In their terminology, however, a sunnah practice may be obligatory, such that omitting it requires repeating the prayer; these practices fall into that category. Some mistakenly assume that, in their terminology, sunnah refers only to what may permissibly be omitted. That is not the case.

As for supplication, no supplication has been made obligatory on its own. Rather, the supplication required in al-Fātihah comes after praise. Likewise, those who require the prescribed supplication after the tashahhud—seeking refuge from the punishment of Hell and the grave, the trials of life and death, and the Dajjāl—require it only after the tashahhud, which is praise. This is the position of Tāwūs and one opinion within Ahmad’s school.

Furthermore, supplication has not been prescribed on its own; it has only been prescribed together with praise. Praise, however, has been prescribed on its own without any disapproval. Thus, if someone confines himself to praise while standing upright after bowing, and to glorifying Allah while bowing and prostrating, that is prescribed without any disapproval. But if he confines himself to supplication in these postures, that is not prescribed, and there is disagreement over whether his prayer is invalidated.

Moreover, praise encompasses the purpose of supplication, as in the hadith: “The best

---

## Page 11419

remembrance is ‘There is no god but Allah,’ and the best supplication is ‘Praise be to Allah.’” For praising the One whom one invokes in terms that imply the fulfillment of one’s request may be more effective than stating the request itself. As the poet said:

When a man praises you one day,
His praise suffices in place of asking.

Hence the words of the transmitted supplication:

“I ask You by virtue of the fact that all praise belongs to You. You are Allah, the Bestower of favors, the Originator of the heavens and the earth.”

He thus asks Him on the grounds that all praise belongs to Him. This shows that acknowledging His worthiness of praise is a means of obtaining what one seeks. This is like the words of Job, peace be upon him:

“Adversity has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful.”

Saying this is better than saying, “Have mercy on me.”

The supplication for the Night of Decree reported by ‘Ā’ishah says:

“O Allah, You are Pardoning and love to pardon, so pardon me.”

In the two Sahīh collections, Ibn ‘Abbās reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to say in times of distress:

“There is no god but Allah, the Forbearing, the Magnificent. There is no god but Allah, Lord of the Mighty Throne. There is no god but Allah, Lord of the seven heavens and Lord of the earth, Lord of the Noble Throne.”

Another indication of the superiority of praise over supplication is that prescribed praise necessarily entails faith in Allah, whereas supplication does not necessarily entail it, for the disbelievers ask Allah

---

## Page 11420

and He grants them what they ask, as Allah has stated in several places in the Quran. Asking for provision, well-being, and similar things is among the prescribed supplications offered by believers and disbelievers alike. This is unlike praise, such as the words:

“Glory and praise be to You, O Allah. Blessed is Your name, exalted is Your majesty, and there is no god but You.”

And:

“All greetings, prayers, and good things belong to Allah. Peace be upon you, O Prophet, and Allah’s mercy and blessings.”

Only a believer offers praise in these terms. The same applies to the words:

“O Allah, our Lord, to You belongs all praise, filling the heavens, filling the earth, filling all that lies between them, and filling whatever else You will.”

Nevertheless, disbelievers may acknowledge some forms of praise, such as acknowledging that Allah is the Creator of the heavens and the earth, that He answers the distressed when they call upon Him, and similar things.

Yet the polytheists had no prescribed form of praise with which to praise Allah. Even in their talbiyah they would say: “Here I am at Your service. You have no partner—except a partner who belongs to You: You own him and whatever he owns.” Likewise, the Christians’ praise includes associating partners with Allah. As for the Jews, their worship contains no praise except whatever has been transmitted from the prophets, which belongs to the praise offered by the people of faith. The same applies to the Christians, if they possess anything of that kind. Whatever Allah has prescribed of praise for Himself, however, entails faith.

There is abundant evidence that praise, as a category, is superior to supplication. One example is the Prophet’s instruction that whoever hears the muezzin should repeat what he says, then invoke blessings upon the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, then ask that he be granted al-wasīlah, and only afterward make requests for himself. He thus gave praise precedence over

---

## Page 11421

supplication. The same applies after the tashahhud (the testimony of faith in prayer): he placed praise of Allah first, then supplication for His Messenger, then supplication for oneself. The same applies here, and I know of no disagreement among the scholars on this point. Nevertheless, what is generally less meritorious may sometimes be superior. Prayer is superior to reciting the Quran, reciting the Quran is superior to remembrance, and remembrance is superior to supplication. Yet circumstances may arise in which the less meritorious act becomes superior, for various reasons: either generally—as reciting the Quran is superior to prayer during the times when prayer is prohibited—or in a particular circumstance. This is discussed at length elsewhere.

The point here is that praise, as a category, is superior to asking, as Allah Most High says:

“Whoever is so occupied with remembering Me that he does not ask of Me, I will give him better than what I give those who ask.”

Reciting the Quran is superior to both, as stated in the hadith narrated by al-Tirmidhī from Abū Saʿīd, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ‘Whoever is so occupied with reciting the Quran that he does not remember Me or ask of Me, I will give him better than what I give those who ask.’”

Al-Tirmidhī graded it “fair and singular.”

This is clear upon reflection, for the ultimate aim of the person asking is to obtain what he seeks and desires. He thus desires something from Allah, even if what he seeks is beloved to Allah—for example, asking Him for help in remembering Him, thanking Him, and worshipping Him well. He desires from Him this very thing that is beloved to Allah.

---

## Page 11422

As for the one who offers praise, he is remembering the very things Allah loves—His names and attributes. The aim here is to know Allah, love Him, and worship Him. This is sought for its own sake, not for anything else, and it is the purpose for which creation was brought into being. As Allah Most High says:

“I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me.”

Asking is a means to this end. Hence He says in al-Fātihah:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.”

He places “You alone we worship” first, because it is the end sought for its own sake, before “You alone we ask for help,” because that is a means to it. Ends take precedence over means in intention and speech. Moreover, this worshipper who offers praise obtains what the petitioner seeks through supplication, while occupying himself with the nobler of the two.

As for the one who supplicates, when he is preoccupied with his need to obtain some benefit or avert some harm—such as his need for provision and essential support—this very preoccupation distracts him from other things. When he supplicates to Allah, glorified is He, his supplication may bring him such knowledge of Allah, love for Him, praise of Him, servitude to Him, and dependence upon Him as is better and more beneficial than what he sought.

As one of the early Muslims said:

“O son of Adam, blessed indeed is a need that has led you to knock repeatedly at your Master’s door.”

Another said:

“I may have a need that I ask Allah to fulfil, and as I supplicate to Him, He opens for me a door to knowing Him such that I wish He would not hasten to fulfil my need, lest my heart turn away from supplication.”

Once the petitioner obtains what he asks for, his ardour cools, for he wanted nothing but what he requested. When he obtains it, he turns away from Allah. This is the condition of the disbelievers whom Allah censures in the Quran, as in His words:

“When adversity touches man, he calls upon Us, lying on his side or sitting or

---

## Page 11423

standing. But when We remove his adversity, he goes on as though he had never called upon Us concerning any adversity that touched him.” The Most High also says:

“Say, ‘Who rescues you from the darkness of land and sea, when you call upon Him humbly and in secret: “If He saves us from this, we will surely be among the grateful”?’”

“Say, ‘Allah rescues you from it and from every distress; yet you associate others with Him.’”

The Most High also says:

“When adversity touches man, he calls upon his Lord, turning to Him. Then, when He bestows a blessing upon him, he forgets what he had previously prayed for and sets up rivals to Allah to lead others astray from His path. Say, ‘Enjoy your disbelief for a little while; you are indeed among the inhabitants of the Fire.’”

His words, glorified is He,

“He forgets what he had previously prayed for,”

mean that he forgets what he had called upon Allah for: the need he had sought to have met. His supplication was directed towards it—that is, his attention and intention were directed towards it—so it was the end he sought. If mā (“what”) is understood as a nominalizing particle, the sense would be: “He forgot that he had been calling upon Allah regarding his need.”

As the Most High says in the other verse:

“But when We remove his adversity, he goes on as though he had never called upon Us concerning any adversity that touched him.”

On this interpretation, however, the pronoun in ilayhi (“for it”) would still refer to something not explicitly mentioned. This is not the case if mā is understood to mean “that which,” for the sense would then be: “He forgot his need, concerning which he had previously called upon Me.” Thus he forgot his supplication to Allah, which had been the cause of the need. The preposition ilā (“to”) indicates the end sought.

As the Most High says in the other verse:

“Say, ‘Tell me: if Allah’s punishment came upon you, or the Hour came upon you, would you call upon anyone other than Allah, if you are truthful?’”

“Rather, it is Him alone you would call upon; then, if He wills, He would remove what you called upon Him about, and you would forget those you associate with Him.”

For indeed,

---

## Page 11424

the Most High has stated that He removes what they call upon Him about: the hardship concerning which they supplicated.

As for the believer, once his need has been met, he must worship Allah sincerely, as He has commanded him. If he fulfills only what is obligatory, he is among the righteous; if he fulfills both what is obligatory and what is recommended, he is among those brought near to Allah. Whoever neglects some of what he has been commanded after his need has been met is among the sinners. This may involve minor association of partners with Allah, which afflicts most people—whether concerning His lordship or His exclusive right to be worshipped—as explained at length elsewhere. In places and times of ignorance, many people may fall into major association of partners with Allah without knowing it.

The supplicant’s aim is to obtain what he asks for. Even if he attains what the Lord loves—turning to Him, loving Him, and repenting to Him—this is incidental. It may endure, but usually it does not, unless what the Lord loves is itself what he asks for. For example, he may ask Allah to grant him repentance and help him remember Him, thank Him, and worship Him well. Here, what he seeks is beloved to the Lord. This is why Allah condemns those who seek only this world, saying:

“Among the people are those who say, ‘Our Lord, give us in this world,’ but they will have no share in the Hereafter.”

As for the one who praises Allah, his very praise is beloved to the Lord, while what the supplicant seeks is attained implicitly and as a secondary consequence. This is therefore more exalted. Yet this is fully realized only by one who purifies his faith

---

## Page 11425

and thus comes to love Allah and to love praising, extolling, and remembering Him. These are dearer to his heart than the provision and victory sought by supplicants. As for someone more concerned with such requests, he benefits more from supplication, even though praise as a category is superior—just as reciting the Quran is superior to remembrance and supplication. Because of shortcomings in his spiritual state, a person may benefit more fully from remembrance and supplication. They are therefore better for him given his circumstances, though not superior in themselves.

The purpose here is to explain what Allah has prescribed for His servants generally and without qualification. Thus, most scholars do not consider those utterances of remembrance in prayer that constitute supplication to be obligatory. As for praise, such as the opening supplication and other utterances, they differed over whether it is obligatory. A group of Ahmad’s followers held that utterances of remembrance consisting of praise, such as the opening supplication, are obligatory. This was the view chosen by Ibn Battah and others, and it has also been reported as a position held by Ahmad. Likewise, according to the well-known position reported from him, it is obligatory to glorify Allah when bowing and prostrating, to declare that Allah hears those who praise Him, to praise Him, and to say “Allah is greatest” when moving between postures. These, then, are two categories, the superiority of one over the other having become clear.

As for the category intermediate between them, it consists of a person declaring his worship of Allah Most High, as in the words:

“I have turned my face towards Him who created the heavens and the earth,”

and:

“Indeed, my prayer, my sacrifice, my life and my death are for Allah, Lord of all worlds,”

and:
