“To You I have prostrated, You I have worshipped, in You I have believed, and through You I have submitted,”

and similar expressions. This is

---

## Page 11426

superior to supplication but inferior to praise, for it both expresses and declares what Allah loves and commands His servant to do. Its aim is therefore what Allah loves, making it superior to that whose aim is what the servant seeks. Yet praise as a category is superior to it, as Muslim narrated in his Sahīh that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“The best words after the Quran are four, and they are part of the Quran: Glory be to Allah; praise be to Allah; there is no god but Allah; and Allah is greatest.”

He thus declared these words, which constitute remembrance of Allah, superior to all other speech after the Quran. Likewise:

“He said to the man who said, ‘I cannot learn any of the Quran, so teach me something I can do that will suffice’: ‘Glory be to Allah; praise be to Allah; there is no god but Allah; and Allah is greatest.’”

He thus made these words a substitute for the Quran.

Section

The surah beginning “Say, ‘He is Allah, One’” is superior to the surah beginning “Say, ‘O disbelievers.’” The former commands one to speak words describing the Lord, while the latter commands one to make a declaration of the servant’s devotion to Allah alone. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, used to give precedence to the former category, as in his words in the authentic hadith:

“O Allah, to You belongs all praise. You are the Lord of the heavens and the earth and all who are in them. To You belongs all praise. You are the Sustainer of the heavens and the earth and all who are in them. To You belongs all praise. You are the Light of the heavens and the earth and all who are in them. You are the Truth; Your word is the truth; Your promise is true; Paradise is real; and Hell is real;

---

## Page 11427

and the prophets are true, and Muhammad is true. O Allah, to You I have submitted; in You I have believed; upon You I have relied; to You I have turned; with Your help I have argued my case; and to You I have referred judgment. So forgive my past and future sins, what I have concealed and what I have made public. You are my God; there is no god but You.”

This remembrance comprises all three categories. It begins with statements about Allah, the Last Day, and His Messenger, then proceeds to statements about the servant’s devotion to Allah alone and his faith, and concludes with supplication. This is because a person’s statement about himself is part of his spiritual journey, in which he remains conscious of himself, and an actualization of his worship of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. In pure praise, however, he contemplates only Allah, Mighty and Majestic, through His names and attributes. What is devoted exclusively to the remembrance of Allah Most High is also superior to what is devoted exclusively to created beings. This is why the surah beginning “Say, ‘He is Allah, One’” was given precedence and made equivalent to one-third of the Quran: it describes the Most Merciful and is devoted purely to His remembrance, unmixed with mention of anyone else.

At the beginning of the spiritual journey, however, remembrance must include a declaration. Thus, entry into Islam begins with:

“I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger.”

This differs from the state of pure worship, in which one says:

“Glory be to Allah; praise be to Allah; there is no god but Allah; Allah is greatest.”

It is through the testimony of faith that a person becomes Muslim, and this is the root and foundation. Hence it has been made an essential component of addresses: the addresses within prayer, namely the tashahhud, conclude with the words:

“I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger.”

It is also included in addresses outside prayer, such as the sermon for

---

## Page 11428

a particular need—the address narrated by Ibn Masʿūd—and the prescribed sermons, such as the Friday sermon and others.

The Sunan collections report that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Every address that contains no testimony of faith is like a severed hand.”

Many of those who require mention of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in the sermon, such as the followers of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, say that invoking blessings upon him is obligatory alongside praising Allah. Others say that he must be mentioned either by invoking blessings upon him or through the testimony of faith. This was the view preferred by my grandfather, Abū al-Barakāt.

The correct view is that mentioning him through the testimony of faith is obligatory, as this hadith indicates. Moreover, bearing witness to his messengership expresses faith in him, whereas invoking blessings upon him is a supplication for him. What a difference there is between the two! The testimony to his messengership is indispensable in both the first and final tashahhud of the prayer. Invoking blessings upon him, however, has been prescribed alongside supplication.

The testimony of faith is prescribed in addresses and expressions of praise. Thus, the tashahhud in prayer is praise of the True One, and the testimony of faith has been prescribed within it. The sermon is an address to people, and the testimony of faith has been prescribed within it. The call to prayer is remembrance of Allah intended to announce the time for worship and its performance, so the testimony of faith has been prescribed within it as well.

As for invoking blessings upon him, the reports indicate that this accompanies supplication, as in the hadith in which he said:

“This man has been hasty,”

and similar reports. For invoking blessings

---

## Page 11429

upon him is a form of supplication, and he has a greater claim upon the believers than they have upon themselves. Supplication for him therefore takes precedence over supplication for others, just as greetings of peace to him in the tashahhud precede greetings to others—even to the person praying. This illustrates the perfection of the religion’s underlying wisdom. Thus, praise precedes the testimony of faith in sermons, just as praise precedes the affirmation of Allah’s oneness in al-Fātihah, expressed in His words:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.”

In Sunan Abī Dāwūd and elsewhere, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is reported to have said:

“Every important matter that is not begun with praise of Allah is cut short.”

Praise of Allah thus belongs at the beginning. This is why the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would open his sermons with praise of Allah. Likewise, prayer begins with praise: all Muslims begin it with the Surah of Praise, for this is the Sunnah established through mass transmission from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. According to the majority of Muslims, it begins with the word “Praise” recited aloud.

If, according to the majority of them, the invocation “In the name of Allah” is intended, it serves as a means. For the reciter’s words, “In the name of Allah,” mean “In the name of Allah, recite,” or “I am reciting in the name of Allah.” This is why invoking Allah’s name is prescribed at the beginning of all actions: one invokes His name when eating and drinking, entering and leaving the home, entering and leaving the mosque, and performing other actions. At the time of slaughter, it is one of the rites affirming Allah’s oneness. Prayer and recitation are themselves actions, so they begin with the invocation of Allah’s name.

---

## Page 11430

For this reason, Allah revealed the invocation of His name only at the beginning of each surah. It is part of the Quran wherever it is written, as recorded by the Companions, but it is an independent verse at the beginning of the surah, not part of the surah itself. This is the most balanced of the three scholarly positions on the matter.

Since it is subordinate and serves as a means, whereas praise is intended for its own sake and the invocation of Allah’s name serves that end, the intended end is recited aloud and proclaimed, while the means is recited quietly. This is the position of the majority of scholars and is supported by the authentic hadiths. Do you not see that, by agreement of the Muslims—and as established by the Sunnah transmitted through mass transmission from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace—it is not recited aloud in sermons? Rather, the sermon begins with praise, even though it is not Quran.

This is also why the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not mention it in the authentic hadith concerning the division of prayer between the servant and the Lord. The Friday sermon begins with praise, as established by the Sunnah through mass transmission and by scholarly agreement. As for the sermon for seeking rain, there are three positions within the school of Ahmad and elsewhere:

The first: it begins with praise of Allah, like the Friday sermon.

The second: with proclaiming Allah’s greatness, like the Eid sermon.

The third: with seeking forgiveness, because this is more particularly associated with seeking rain.

Regarding the Eid sermon, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUqbah mentioned that it begins with proclaiming Allah’s greatness, and this view was adopted by some

---

## Page 11431

of the jurists. However, no one has reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, began any sermon with anything other than praise—whether an Eid sermon, a sermon for seeking rain, or any other sermon. He said:

“Every important matter that is not begun with praise is incomplete.”

He delivered sermons during Hajj, as well as occasional sermons on other occasions, yet no one has reported that he began any sermon with anything other than praise. What is indispensable in a sermon, therefore, is praise of Allah and the testimony of faith. Praise is followed by glorification, and the testimony of faith is followed by proclaiming Allah’s greatness. These are the enduring good deeds. Allah Most High says:

“So call upon Him, sincere in your devotion to Him. All praise is for Allah, Lord of all worlds.”

Section

Once this principle is clear, the best opening invocations for prayer are those consisting entirely of praise, such as:

“Glory and praise be to You, O Allah. Blessed is Your name, exalted is Your majesty, and there is no god but You.”

And:

“Allah is truly the greatest; all praise is for Allah in abundance; and glory be to Allah morning and evening.”

The former, however, contains praise that the latter does not. It includes the expressions known as the “enduring good deeds,” which are the best words after the Quran, as well as the words, “Blessed is Your name, exalted is Your majesty,” both of which also occur in the Quran. This is why most of the early generations used it to begin their prayers, and why ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb would recite it aloud to teach it to the people.

---

## Page 11432

Next in merit comes the second type: a statement of the servant’s worship, such as his saying:

“I have turned my face towards the One who created the heavens and the earth,” and so forth.

This also includes supplication. If the servant recites this after the preceding invocation when beginning the prayer, he combines all three types. This is the best form of opening invocation, as is explicitly stated in a hadith. It is the choice of Abū Yūsuf and the minister Ibn Hubayra, a follower of Ahmad and the author of Al-Ifsāh. This is how I myself begin the prayer.

Next comes the third type, such as his saying:

“O Allah, distance me from my sins as You have distanced the east from the west,” and so forth.

The same applies to the remembrance recited when bowing and prostrating: glorifying Allah in these positions is better than saying, “To You I have bowed, and to You I have prostrated.” This, in turn, is better than supplication. As far as I know, this ranking is agreed upon, for I know of no one who has said that supplication during bowing and prostration is better than glorifying Allah, although such a view has been expressed concerning the opening invocation.

If you say: “This ranking is the reverse of the ranking of the chains of transmission. In the two Sahīh collections, the only hadith from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, concerning the opening invocation in an obligatory prayer is this supplication: ‘O Allah, distance me from my sins.’ His saying, ‘I have turned my face,’ is in Sahīh Muslim, whereas the hadith beginning, ‘Glory be to You, O Allah,’ is in the Sunan collections and has been subject to criticism. It has also been narrated that this was used in the night prayer, as was his saying, ‘I have turned my face.’”

---

## Page 11433

I reply:

The fact that one of these has reached us through a more authentic chain of transmission than another does not give the remembrance itself an inherent merit that makes it superior to the other. Rather, the chain is a means by which we learn of it. Its merit was already established by the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, during his lifetime, before knowledge of it reached us.

It is established in the Sahīh that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, would recite aloud, “Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You. Blessed is Your name, exalted is Your majesty, and none is worthy of worship but You,” to teach it to the people. Had this not been one of the prescribed practices of the Sunnah, ʿUmar would not have done so with the Muslims’ approval. The hadith of Abū Hurayra shows that the opening invocation is not restricted to “Glory be to You, O Allah,” “I have turned my face,” or other particular forms. Rather, any of the reported forms may be used to begin the prayer. The superiority of some forms over others, however, is established by other evidence, as we explained above.

Moreover, the invocation:

“Glory be to You, O Allah,” and so forth,

includes the enduring acts of righteousness that constitute the best words after the Quran. As related in Sahīh Muslim, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The best words after the Quran are four, and they are themselves part of the Quran: Glory be to Allah; praise be to Allah; none is worthy of worship but Allah; and Allah is the Greatest.”

It is also related in Sahīh Muslim: “The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked:

---

## Page 11434

‘Which words are best?’ He replied, ‘Those Allah has chosen for His angels: Glory be to Allah, and praise be to Him.’” This expression comes first in the opening invocation, and it is the best of speech. Moreover, Allah has commanded that He be glorified with praise, and has referred to prayer in these terms, saying:

“And glorify your Lord with praise when you rise.”

It is therefore more fitting to begin fulfilling this command with this remembrance. A number of Quran commentators, including al-Dahhāk, have explained this verse as referring to the worshipper’s words: “Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You. Blessed is Your name, exalted is Your majesty, and none is worthy of worship but You.” Elsewhere, I have discussed the meaning of this expression at length and explained that it encompasses declaring Him free of imperfection, praising Him, and magnifying Him through His attributes of permanence and affirmation and all His acts—glory be to Him, and praise be to Him.

Section

Proclaiming “Allah is the Greatest” is prescribed in elevated places, when a person ascends, and wherever a public proclamation is intended. Examples include proclaiming it in the call to prayer, during the festivals, when ascending high ground, when climbing al-Safā and al-Marwa, and when mounting an animal. Glorifying Allah, by contrast, is prescribed in low places and whenever a person descends. Thus, it is related in the Sunan collections that Jābir said:

“When we were with the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, we would proclaim Allah’s greatness whenever we ascended and glorify Him whenever we descended. Prayer was therefore arranged according to this pattern.”

---

## Page 11435

Praise is the opening of every matter of importance, whether intimate communion with the Lord or people addressing one another. The testimony of faith accompanies both praise and the proclamation of Allah’s greatness. In the call to prayer and in sermons, it concludes the words of praise. In the call to prayer, it follows the proclamation of Allah’s greatness; then the people are addressed with the muezzin’s words: “Come to prayer; come to success.” In sermons, it is followed by the words addressed to the people: “To proceed.” It is also recited in the tashahhud (the testimony recited in prayer), after which one chooses whichever supplication one likes best. Thus, praise and affirmation of Allah’s oneness come first when created beings address their Creator, with praise at the very beginning.

When Allah created Adam, peace be upon him, the first words He caused him to utter were words of praise. Adam sneezed and said, “Praise be to Allah, Lord of all worlds.” Allah said, “May your Lord have mercy on you.” Thus, his first utterance was praise, and the first words he heard from Allah were words of mercy. Allah likewise began the Mother of the Quran with praise, while the testimony of faith comes at the end. The beginning of al-Fātihah is:

“Praise be to Allah,”

and the last part devoted to the Lord is:

“You alone we worship.”

The same applies to the tashahhud. In sermons, too, the testimony of faith follows the opening praise. Its affirmation of the Lord’s divinity—that the Lord is the One worshipped—is the ultimate end toward which His servants’ deeds lead:

“Had there been in the heavens and the earth gods besides Allah, both would have been ruined.”

Yet praise is placed first because praise comes from Allah as well as from His creation. It also continues in Paradise: their final invocation will be, “Praise be to Allah, Lord of all worlds.” This is unlike worship, for worship through prostration and similar acts belongs only to this world. Affirming His oneness and remembering Him, however, continue in Paradise: He inspires its people to do so just as He inspires them to breathe.

---

## Page 11436

These forms of remembrance are verbal utterances, not physical acts of worship such as prostrating, standing, or entering ihrām (the consecrated state for pilgrimage). The Lord Most High praises Himself, but He does not worship Himself. Praise is thus the most comprehensive of the sciences concerning Allah, and it serves as both an opening and a conclusion.

It is therefore the Sunnah for someone who has eaten or drunk to praise Allah. In Sahīh Muslim, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Indeed, Allah is pleased with a servant who eats a meal and praises Him for it, and takes a drink and praises Him for it.”

Allah Most High says:

“Judgment will be passed between them in truth, and it will be said, ‘Praise be to Allah, Lord of all worlds.’”

He Most High also says:

“So the people who did wrong were utterly destroyed. And praise be to Allah, Lord of all worlds.”

And He says:

“Their final invocation will be, ‘Praise be to Allah, Lord of all worlds.’”

Section

The only regular supplication made obligatory upon the servant—repeated with every prayer, indeed with every unit of prayer, whether obligatory or voluntary—is the supplication contained in the Mother of the Quran, namely His words, Most High:

“Guide us to the straight path—the path of those You have blessed, not of those who have incurred anger, nor of those who have gone astray.”

For every servant is always in desperate need of what this supplication seeks: guidance to the straight path. There is no salvation from punishment except through this guidance, nor any attainment of happiness except through it. Whoever lacks this guidance is therefore either among those who have incurred anger or among those who have gone astray.

---

## Page 11437

And such guidance can only be attained through Allah’s guidance:

“Whoever Allah guides is truly guided; but whoever He leaves astray, you will never find for him a protecting guide.”

This verse demonstrates the falsity of the doctrine of the Qadariyyah, who claim that the servant does not depend upon Allah to attain this guidance. Rather, according to them, every servant possesses what enables both obedience and disobedience. They make no distinction in this respect between the believer and the disbeliever, and hold that Allah has not singled out the believer for guidance through which he becomes rightly guided. Their views are discussed at length elsewhere.

The point here is that every servant constantly needs to receive this guidance. As for the objection, “He has already guided them to faith, so there is no need for guidance,” and the response, “What is sought is the continuation of guidance,” both reflect a failure to understand the human condition and what people have been commanded to do.

For the reality of the straight path is that, at every moment, you fulfil what you have been commanded to know and do at that moment, refrain from what you have been forbidden, and acquire a firm resolve to perform what is commanded and a firm aversion that leads you to abandon what is forbidden. Such detailed knowledge and resolve cannot conceivably be acquired by the servant all at once. Rather, at every moment he needs Allah to place in his heart the knowledge and intentions by which he will be guided at that moment.

Certainly, he has received general guidance: that the Quran is true, that the religion of Islam is true, that the Messenger is true, and so forth. But this general guidance will not suffice him unless he receives detailed guidance concerning every particular matter that he undertakes or leaves aside—matters that bewilder

---

## Page 11438

the minds of most people in many instances. Whims and desires overpower most people because doubts and desires dominate their souls. Man was created unjust and ignorant. His original condition is therefore one of ignorance and an inclination toward the evil he desires. He constantly needs detailed knowledge to dispel his ignorance, and justice in his love and hatred, pleasure and anger, action and abstention, giving and withholding. In everything he says and does, he needs justice to counter his injustice. Unless Allah graciously grants him knowledge and justice in every particular matter, his ignorance and injustice will lead him away from the straight path.

Allah Most High said to His Prophet after the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyah and the Pledge of al-Ridwān:

“Indeed, We have granted you a clear triumph,

so that Allah may forgive you your past and future sins, complete His favor upon you, and guide you to a straight path,

and so that Allah may grant you a mighty victory.”

He thus states that He did this to guide him to a straight path. If this was the Prophet’s situation, what then of others? The straight path has been interpreted as the Quran, Islam, and the path of servitude to Allah. All these interpretations are true: it can be described in these and other ways.

This guidance is an absolute necessity for a person’s happiness and salvation, unlike provision and victory. Allah provides for him, and when his provision ceases, he dies. Death is inevitable. If he is among the rightly guided, he will enjoy happiness after death, and death will lead him to everlasting, eternal happiness. It will therefore be a mercy for him.

---

## Page 11439

The same applies to victory: if it is decreed that a person is overpowered and defeated, even to the point of being killed, then, provided he is rightly guided and steadfast, he dies a martyr, and his being killed completes Allah’s favor upon him. It is thus clear that people’s need for guidance is greater than their need for provision and victory; indeed, there is no comparison between them. This is why this supplication has been made obligatory upon them.

Moreover, this supplication also encompasses provision and victory. For whoever is guided to the straight path will be among those who fear Allah:

“And whoever fears Allah—He will make for him a way out,”

“And will provide for him from where he does not expect.”

He will also be among those who rely upon Allah:

“And whoever relies upon Allah—then He is sufficient for him. Indeed, Allah will accomplish His purpose.”

He will be among those who support Allah and His Messenger, and whoever supports Allah, Allah will support him. He will also belong to Allah’s forces, and Allah’s forces are victorious. Complete guidance thus entails attaining the greatest means of securing provision and victory.

It is therefore clear that this supplication encompasses everything one seeks: through it every benefit is attained and every harm is averted. This is why it has been made obligatory upon the servant. This also shows that nothing else can take the place of al-Fātihah, and that its superiority over other speech is greater than the superiority of bowing and prostration over all other acts of humble submission. If those specific acts are required, then this is all the more deserving of being required.

All praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds. May Allah’s blessings and peace be upon our master Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

---

## Page 11440

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

“Is the opening supplication in prayer obligatory or recommended? What do the scholars say about this?”

He replied:

The opening supplication after the takbīr (declaration of Allah’s greatness) is a Sunnah according to the majority of imams, including Abū Hanīfah, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad. This is established in authentic hadiths, such as the hadith of Abū Hurayrah recorded in both Sahīh collections. He said:

“I asked, ‘O Messenger of Allah, during your silence between the takbīr and the recitation, what do you say?’ He replied, ‘I say: “O Allah, put distance between me…”’”

He then related the supplication. This makes clear that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would pause between the takbīr and the recitation to supplicate.

Various forms of this opening supplication have been reported, most of them concerning night prayer. Whoever begins with the following has done well:

“Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You. Blessed is Your name, exalted is Your majesty, and there is no god but You.”

It is established in Sahīh Muslim that ʿUmar would recite this aloud in the obligatory prayer. It has also been reported in the Sunan collections in narrations traced back to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

---

## Page 11441

And whoever begins with the words “I have turned my face…” has done well, for it is established in Sahīh Muslim that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would begin his prayer with this supplication. It has been reported that this was in obligatory prayer, and also that it was in night prayer.

Whoever combines the two, beginning with “Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You” to its end, followed by “I have turned my face…,” has also done well. A hadith traced back to the Prophet has been reported concerning this.

The first is the preferred practice of Abū Hanīfah and Ahmad; the second is that of al-Shāfi‘ī; and the third is that of a group of scholars from the schools of Abū Hanīfah and Ahmad. All these forms are good, just like the various forms of the tashahhud (testimony of faith in prayer) and the seven Quranic readings, from which a person may recite whichever he chooses.

As for whether the opening supplication is obligatory, the majority hold that it is recommended, not obligatory. This is the position of Abū Hanīfah and al-Shāfi‘ī, and the well-known position reported from Ahmad. There is another view within his school, which some scholars mention as a report from him, that the opening supplication is obligatory. Allah knows best.

He was asked:

“What about a man who leads the people in prayer and, after the opening takbīr, recites aloud the formula seeking refuge with Allah, then says ‘In the name of Allah’ and recites the Quran, doing this in every prayer?”

---

## Page 11442

He replied:

If he does this occasionally for teaching or a similar purpose, there is nothing wrong with it, just as ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb used to recite the opening supplication aloud for a time, and Ibn ‘Umar and Abū Hurayrah would sometimes recite the formula seeking refuge with Allah aloud. However, consistently reciting it aloud is an innovation contrary to the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his rightly guided caliphs. They did not regularly recite it aloud. Indeed, no one has reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, recited the formula seeking refuge with Allah aloud. Allah knows best.

Shaykh al-Islām, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Section

As for the manner of performing prayer, one matter concerning its distinctive observances is the basmalah, the formula “In the name of Allah.” People have differed sharply over it, affirming and denying both its status as a verse of the Quran and its recitation. Works have been written on both sides, some of whose discussions display a measure of ignorance and injustice, although the matter itself is a minor one.

Partisanship over these and similar questions is among the marks of division and discord that we have been forbidden. What motivates it is the desire to champion the distinctive practices that divide the Muslim community. Otherwise, these questions are among the very slightest matters of disagreement, were it not for the incitement

---

## Page 11443

of Satan to display the outward marks of division.

As for whether it is a verse of the Quran, one group, including Mālik, said that it is not part of the Quran except in Sūrat al-Naml. They accepted the implication that the Companions had included in the written Quran something that was not Allah’s speech, for the sake of seeking blessing. Some of Ahmad’s followers transmitted this as a position reported from him, and some may even have believed it to be his settled view.

Another group, including al-Shāfi‘ī, said that the Companions would not have written it in the written Quran, in the same script as the Quran itself, while excluding everything that was not Quran, unless it formed part of the surah. They also cited other evidence.

Most jurists of the hadith tradition, such as Ahmad, together with the discerning scholars among Abū Hanīfah’s followers, took a middle position. They said that its inclusion in the written Quran establishes that it is part of the Quran, since it is known that the Companions did not write anything in it that was not Quran. This does not, however, establish that it forms part of the surah. Rather, it is a separate verse revealed at the beginning of each surah, just as the Companions wrote it on a separate line. As Ibn ‘Abbās said:

“The boundary between surahs was not known until ‘In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful’ was revealed.”

According to these scholars, then, it is a verse of Allah’s Book at the beginning of every surah in which it is written, but it does not form part of those surahs. This is the position explicitly stated by Ahmad on more than one occasion, and no explicit report conveying the contrary has been found from him. It is also the position of ‘Abd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak and others. It is the most balanced and fairest of the views.

---

## Page 11444

The same applies to reciting it in prayer. One group, including Mālik and al-Awzā‘ī, does not recite it either silently or aloud. Another group, including the followers of Ibn Jurayj and al-Shāfi‘ī, recites it aloud. The third, middle group—the great majority of jurists of the hadith tradition, together with the jurists of the legal-reasoning tradition—recites it silently, as reported from the great majority of the Companions. Ahmad, however, acts on the reports transmitted from the Companions concerning this matter and recommends reciting it aloud when doing so serves an overriding benefit. Indeed, he explicitly stated that someone praying in Madinah should recite it aloud. Some of his followers explained that this was because the people there used to object to those who recited it aloud.

It is recommended that a person seek to foster harmony by forgoing such recommended practices, because the religious benefit of fostering harmony is greater than the benefit of performing such acts. Thus, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, refrained from altering the structure of the Ka‘bah because leaving it as it was would foster harmony. Likewise, Ibn Mas‘ūd objected to ‘Uthmān’s performing the prayer in full while travelling, yet then prayed behind him without shortening it, saying, “Discord is evil.”

Although this is a reasonable explanation, Ahmad’s point was that the people of Madinah did not recite it, so it should be recited aloud to make clear that reciting it is Sunnah—just as Ibn ‘Abbās recited the Mother of the Book aloud during the funeral prayer and said, “So that you may know that it is Sunnah,” and just as ‘Umar recited aloud

---

## Page 11445

the opening supplication on more than one occasion, and just as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would sometimes recite a verse aloud during the noon and afternoon prayers. Thus, silent recitation has also been reported from most of the Companions who are reported to have recited it aloud. It would seem that they recited it aloud to make clear that they were reciting it, just as some of them also recited the supplication seeking refuge in Allah aloud.

Moderation in every matter consists in giving the transmitted reports their proper application. It is categorically impossible that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, always recited it aloud when most of the Companions neither reported nor practised this. Indeed, more than one Companion is reliably reported to have denied that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did so. No established report contradicts this without admitting of more than one interpretation.

To hold that reciting it aloud is never prescribed—despite its being reliably reported from more than one Companion—is to attribute to the Companions both doing and approving of something disliked. Moreover, reciting aloud during a silent prayer is prescribed for an incidental reason, as explained above.

Likewise, regarding its recitation as disliked is open to serious objection, given the established reports from the Companions concerning its recitation, some of which are traced back to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace; the fact that the Companions included it in the written Quran; and the fact that it would be revealed along with the surah. Furthermore, if it is recited at the beginning of Solomon’s letter, then reciting it at the beginning of Allah’s Book is entirely fitting. Following the transmitted reports in this matter therefore brings moderation, harmony, and the middle course, which is the best course of all.

As for the length of the prayer, the jurists of the hadith tradition prefer the prayer of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace

---

## Page 11446

which he usually performed: a balanced prayer whose postures were comparable in duration, in which he shortened the standing and sitting, prolonged the bowing and prostration, and made the bowing, prostration, and upright postures after each equal in duration. This is established from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. His recitation at dawn was between sixty and one hundred verses, at noon about thirty verses, and in the afternoon and night prayers half that amount. Yet he might shorten the prayer further for a particular reason, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“I begin the prayer intending to prolong it, but then I hear a child crying and shorten it, knowing how distressed his mother is on his account.”

Likewise, he might prolong it beyond this for a particular reason, as when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, recited the longer of the two long surahs—al-A'rāf—in the sunset prayer.

It is recommended to make the first unit of every prayer longer than the second. It is also recommended to prolong the first two units and shorten the last two, as Sa'd ibn Abī Waqqās related concerning the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. This is the position of the great majority of jurists of the hadith tradition.

Some jurists, however, do not recommend prolonging the upright postures after bowing and prostration. Some consider each of these an essential element to be kept brief, on the grounds that it is prescribed merely as an intervening separation, rather than being intended in its own right. Some make the first two units equal in length, while others recommend that the imam repeat the glorification of Allah no more than three times during bowing and prostration. They have expressed various other views as well.

---

## Page 11447

He was asked about the hadith of Nu'aym al-Mujammir, who said:

“I was praying behind Abū Hurayra. He recited, ‘In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy,’ then recited al-Fātiha until he reached ‘nor of those who go astray.’ He said, ‘Āmīn,’ and the people said, ‘Āmīn.’ Whenever he prostrated, he would say, ‘Allah is Most Great.’ When he ended the prayer with the salutation, he said, ‘By Him in whose hand is my soul, my prayer resembles that of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, more closely than any of yours.’”

Al-Mu'tamir ibn Sulaymān used to recite “In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy” aloud before and after al-Fātiha, saying, “I spare no effort to follow my father’s manner of prayer. My father said, ‘I spare no effort to follow Anas’s manner of prayer,’ and Anas said, ‘I spare no effort to follow the manner of prayer of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.’” This, then, is an established hadith supporting its recitation aloud. Al-Hākim Abū 'Abd Allāh stated that every narrator of this hadith is trustworthy.

Should Anas’s statement, “I prayed behind the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, Abū Bakr, 'Umar, and 'Uthmān, and I did not hear any of them recite ‘In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy,’” be understood as referring to his not having heard it? What is the precise assessment of this issue, and what is the correct position?

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds. As for the hadith of Anas denying its recitation aloud, it is

---

## Page 11448

explicit and does not admit this interpretation. Muslim narrated it in his Sahīh with the wording:

“I prayed behind the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, Abū Bakr, ‘Umar, and ‘Uthmān. They would begin with ‘All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds,’ and would not recite ‘In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy,’ either at the beginning of their recitation or at its end.”

Such a denial can only be made with knowledge of the matter. It cannot be based merely on his not having heard it, if it remained possible that they recited aloud without him hearing.

The other wording in Muslim’s Sahīh is:

“I prayed behind the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, Abū Bakr, ‘Umar, and ‘Uthmān, and I did not hear any of them recite aloud—or he said, pray reciting—‘In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy.’”

This wording denies having heard it. Even if this were the only wording transmitted, it could not be interpreted to mean that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, recited aloud but Anas did not hear him, for several reasons.

First: Anas related this only to explain to them what the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to do. People have no interest in knowing whether Anas heard or did not hear except to infer, from his not hearing it, that what would have been heard did not occur. Had his account not been evidence negating that practice, Anas would not have related something of no benefit to them, nor would they have transmitted such an account that benefited them in no way.

Second: In customary usage, wording of this kind has come to indicate the absence of what has not been

---

## Page 11449

perceived. Thus, when someone says, “We did not hear” or “We did not see,” concerning something he would ordinarily hear or see, he intends thereby to deny its occurrence; mentioning that it was not perceived serves as evidence of that. It is well known that this constitutes evidence regarding things that would ordinarily be perceived.

This becomes clear from the third reason: Anas served the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, from his arrival in Madinah until his death. He would enter the presence of his wives before the command to observe the veil, and accompany him both at home and on journeys. When the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, performed Hajj, Anas was beneath his she-camel, with its saliva dripping onto him. Given such close association and lengthy companionship, could he possibly have failed to hear the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, recite it aloud, if he had indeed been reciting it aloud? Ordinary experience makes the impossibility of this self-evident.

He then accompanied Abū Bakr, ‘Umar, and ‘Uthmān, and held administrative posts under Abū Bakr and ‘Umar. Over their lengthy terms, it would likewise have been impossible for them to recite it aloud without his hearing it. It is therefore clear that this is distortion, not interpretation. This would be so even if only this wording had been transmitted. How much more so when the other wording explicitly denies reciting it—and he gives preference to this other version.

Both versions also rule out the interpretation of those who take his statement, “They would begin the prayer with ‘All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds,’” to mean that he intended the surah. For his statement, “They would begin with ‘All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds,’ and would not recite ‘In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy,’ either at the beginning of their recitation or at its end,” explicitly shows that he means beginning with the verse, not with Sūrat al-Fātihah, which

---

## Page 11450

begins with “In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy.” Had that been his intended meaning, his two reports would have contradicted one another. Moreover, beginning the prayer with al-Fātihah before reciting another surah is a matter of common knowledge, familiar to learned and ordinary people alike, just as they know that bowing precedes prostration. All prayer leaders other than the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, Abū Bakr, ‘Umar, and ‘Uthmān also do this. There is no benefit in reporting something like this, nor does it require a report from Anas. They had questioned him about the matter, whereas this is not something anyone would ask about. All the prayer leaders whom Anas lived to see—city governors, army commanders, Umayyad and Zubayrid caliphs, and others—began with al-Fātihah. No one was confused about this or had any doubt concerning it. How, then, could anyone suppose that Anas intended to inform them of this, or that this was what they had asked him about?

That would be like saying, “They used to pray four rak‘ahs for Zuhr, four for ‘Asr, and three for Maghrib”; or, “They used to recite aloud in Maghrib, ‘Ishā’, and Fajr, and quietly in Zuhr and ‘Asr”; or, “They used to recite aloud in the first two rak‘ahs, but not in the last two.”

Similar to the hadith of Anas is the hadith of ‘Ā’ishah, also recorded in the Sahīh:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to begin the prayer by saying ‘Allah is the Greatest,’ and his recitation with ‘All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds.’”

And so on to the end of the hadith. Another narration reads:

“He would begin his recitation with ‘All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds, the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy, Master of the Day of Judgment.’”

This explicitly indicates that he means

---

## Page 11451

the verse. Nevertheless, the hadith of Anas does not deny that it was recited quietly, for he narrated:

“They would not recite ‘In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy’ aloud.”

This only rules out audible recitation. As for the other wording, “They did not say it,” he could only deny something whose absence he could ascertain. This applies to audible recitation: if he did not hear it despite being nearby, he would know that they had not recited it aloud. But he could not ascertain that the imam had not recited it at all unless there was no pause between the opening takbīr and the recitation during which it could have been recited quietly. Hence, those who held that there was no pause at that point, such as Mālik and others, cited the hadith of Anas as evidence that it was not recited. Yet it is established in the two Sahīh collections that Abū Hurayrah said:

“O Messenger of Allah, during your silence between the opening takbīr and the recitation, what do you say?”

He replied, “I say such and such,” and so on to the end of the hadith.

The Sunan collections also contain reports from ‘Imrān, Ubayy, and others that he would pause before reciting. They also report that he would seek refuge with Allah. If he paused, Anas could not deny that he recited it during that pause. Thus, his statement that they did not say it, and his account of how they began their recitation, concern only what was recited aloud.

Just as refraining from speaking aloud while saying something quietly is called “silence,” as in the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, it is appropriate to say, “He did not recite it” or “He did not say it”—meaning aloud. Here, “silence” and the denial of saying or reciting something have the same meaning.

---

## Page 11452

This is further supported by the hadith of ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mughaffal recorded in the Sunan collections:

“He heard his son reciting it aloud and objected, saying, ‘My son, beware of introducing innovations.’ He mentioned that he had prayed behind the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), Abū Bakr, ‘Umar, and ‘Uthmān, and that they had not recited it aloud.”

This agrees with the hadiths of Anas and ‘Ā’ishah found in the Sahīh. Moreover, it is well known that reciting it aloud is something people would have had ample reason and motivation to report. Had the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) recited it aloud as he recited the rest of al-Fātihah, neither ordinary practice nor religious obligation would have allowed this to go unreported. Indeed, had only one or two people reported something of this kind, their report would certainly have been judged false. For collusion to conceal something whose concealment is precluded by ordinary practice and religious obligation is like collusion to fabricate it. An illustration of this is the falsity of the Rāfidah’s claim that ‘Alī was explicitly designated for the caliphate, and similar claims.

Those versed in hadith have agreed that there is no explicit hadith concerning reciting it aloud. The compilers of the well-known Sunan collections, such as Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī, and al-Nasā’ī, narrated nothing of the kind. Explicit mention of reciting it aloud is found only in fabricated hadiths related by al-Tha‘labī, al-Māwardī, and others like them in Quranic commentary, or in some works by jurists who do not distinguish fabricated reports from others, but instead cite such reports as the hadith of al-Humayrā’ as evidence.

---

## Page 11453

More astonishing still is that one distinguished jurist attributed no hadith in his book to al-Bukhārī except a hadith concerning the basmalah (“In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful”)—yet that hadith is not in al-Bukhārī. If this is the extent of someone’s knowledge of hadith, how competent can such people be in this field?

Alternatively, these reports are narrated by those who compiled material on this subject, such as al-Dāraqutnī, al-Khatīb, and others. They collected whatever had been narrated; when asked about its authenticity, they answered according to their knowledge. For example, when al-Dāraqutnī came to Egypt, he was asked to compile the hadiths concerning reciting the basmalah aloud. After he had collected them, he was asked, “Is any of this authentic?”

He replied, “As for reports from the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), no. As for reports from the Companions, some are authentic and some are weak.”

Abū Bakr al-Khatīb was asked a similar question and mentioned two hadiths. One concerned Mu‘āwiyah when he led the prayer in Medina. Al-Shāfi‘ī (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated it, saying:

“‘Abd al-Majīd narrated to us from Ibn Jurayj, who said that ‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Uthmān ibn Khuthaym had informed him that Abū Bakr ibn Hafs ibn ‘Umar had informed him that Anas ibn Mālik said:

‘Mu‘āwiyah led the prayer in Medina, reciting the Mother of the Quran aloud. He recited “In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful” with the Mother of the Quran, but did not recite it with the surah that followed it. Nor did he say “Allah is the Greatest” when lowering himself, throughout that prayer. When he concluded with the salutation, those of the Emigrants who had heard this called out to him from every direction: “Mu‘āwiyah! Have you stolen from the prayer, or did you forget?” When he next led the prayer, he recited “In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful” with the surah following the Mother of the Quran, and said “Allah is the Greatest” as he lowered himself into prostration.’”

---

## Page 11454

Al-Shāfi‘ī also said: “Ibrāhīm ibn Muhammad informed us, saying: ‘Ibn Khuthaym narrated to me, from Ismā‘īl ibn ‘Ubayd ibn Rifā‘ah, from his father, that Mu‘āwiyah came to Medina and led them in prayer. He did not recite “In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful,” nor did he say “Allah is the Greatest” when lowering or raising himself. When he concluded with the salutation, the Emigrants and the Helpers called out to him: “Mu‘āwiyah! Have you stolen from the prayer?”’ He then related the rest of the report.”

Al-Shāfi‘ī also said: “Yahyā ibn Sulaym informed us, from ‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Uthmān ibn Khuthaym, from Ismā‘īl ibn ‘Ubayd ibn Rifā‘ah, from his father, from his grandfather, concerning Mu‘āwiyah and the Emigrants and Helpers, relating the same report, or one to the same effect, without contradicting it. I consider this chain of transmission more accurately preserved than the first. It is in the book of Ismā‘īl ibn ‘Ubayd ibn Rifā‘ah, narrated from his father, from his grandfather, concerning Mu‘āwiyah.”

Al-Khatīb mentioned that this was the strongest evidence adduced on the matter. Yet it does not constitute proof, as will be explained. Thus, if the experts in hadith agree that there is no authentic hadith, nor any explicit one, supporting reciting the basmalah aloud—let alone widely transmitted or mass-transmitted reports—it is impossible that the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) used to recite it aloud. Likewise, it is impossible that he used to recite the opening supplication and the invocation seeking refuge in Allah aloud without this being transmitted.

If it is objected:

“This argument is countered by his refraining from reciting it aloud, since people would likewise have had every reason and incentive to transmit that. Yet it has not been mass-transmitted; indeed, scholars have disputed it. Moreover, assuming that he refrained from reciting it aloud, he would have done so consistently, yet this has not been transmitted conclusively; rather, it has become a matter of dispute.”

---

## Page 11455

The reply is:

There are several answers to this.

First, what people ordinarily have every reason and incentive to transmit, and are religiously obliged to transmit, is what actually occurs. As for what does not occur, there is nothing to report. Its nonoccurrence is transmitted only when people suppose that it occurred or need to know whether it did; it is then reported because of that need.

For this reason, scholars have said that if someone reported that a sixth prayer had been made obligatory, or that obligatory fasting extended beyond Ramadan, or that a pilgrimage other than pilgrimage to the House had been prescribed, or that there was an addition to the Quran, the number of units of prayer, the obligatory zakat dues, or anything similar, we would know with certainty that his report was false. Had any such thing existed, ordinary practice and religious duty would have required its conclusive transmission. The absence of transmission indicates that it was not transmitted conclusively, as ordinary practice and religious duty would require. Indeed, the absence of any report, despite every ordinary and religious reason and incentive to transmit it, is evidence that it did not occur.

Scholars have illustrated this with the example of someone reporting that the preacher fell from the pulpit on Friday and did not perform the Friday prayer, or that some people fought with swords in the mosque. If only one, two, or three people reported this, while everyone else did not, we would know that their reports were false, since such an event is something people would ordinarily have every reason and incentive to report—even though they do not report the absence of fighting or other things that did not occur.

This is further clarified by the fact that they did not transmit that he recited the opening supplication and the invocation seeking refuge in Allah aloud. The Muslim community has taken this as evidence that he did not recite them aloud, even though his refraining from doing so was not itself widely transmitted. Thus, the same reasoning by which we know that he did not recite these aloud establishes that he did not recite the basmalah aloud. And this

---

## Page 11456

provides an answer to the objection raised by some speculative theologians against this principle: that matters which people have every reason and incentive to transmit cannot go unreported. They have challenged it by citing the hadiths concerning recitation aloud, the qunūt supplication, the call to prayer, and the call to commence the prayer. As for the call to prayer and the call to commence it, both practices have been transmitted. As for qunūt, he sometimes performed it and sometimes omitted it. As for recitation aloud, a report of it would concern a positive act, yet it has not been transmitted; it therefore falls under the principle.

Second, when the need arose to transmit reports of things not done, they were transmitted. Once the era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs had ended and some prayer leaders, such as Ibn al-Zubayr and others, began reciting the basmalah aloud, some people questioned the surviving Companions, such as Anas. Anas then reported to them that it had not been recited aloud. While the caliphs were still alive, however, the Sunnah was manifest and well known, and none of them recited it aloud. There was therefore no need to ask about things not done so that their nonoccurrence might be reported.

Third, the absence of recitation aloud has been transmitted authentically and explicitly in the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, whereas reciting it aloud has not been transmitted authentically and explicitly—even though ordinary practice and religious duty require that things actually done should be more deserving of authentic, explicit transmission than things not done.

Anyone who reflects on these arguments and is knowledgeable about conclusive evidence will conclude with certainty

---

## Page 11457

that the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) did not habitually recite it aloud. Indeed, even someone untrained in distinguishing conclusive evidence from other evidence would also say: If there is no authentic, explicit hadith establishing its recitation aloud, how could the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) have recited it aloud without the Muslim community transmitting this Sunnah—instead neglecting it and allowing it to be lost?

Is this any different from someone reporting that he used to recite the opening supplication and the invocation for refuge aloud, just as some of them recited the basmalah aloud? Yet we know with unavoidable certainty that the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) did not recite the opening supplication and the invocation for refuge aloud as he recited al-Fātihah aloud. Likewise, we know with unavoidable certainty that the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) did not recite the basmalah aloud as he recited al-Fātihah aloud. It is possible, however, that he recited it aloud occasionally, or that he did so earlier and later discontinued the practice, as Abū Dāwūd related in his Marāsīl from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, and al-Tabarānī related in his Muʿjam from Ibn ʿAbbās:

“The Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) used to recite it aloud in Mecca. When the polytheists heard it, they would revile the Most Merciful, so he stopped reciting it aloud and never did so again until he died.”

This, then, is possible.

As for occasional recitation aloud, examples include the report in al-Sahīh that he would sometimes recite a verse audibly, and some of the Companions saying aloud behind him:

“Our Lord, to You belongs all praise—abundant, good and blessed praise.”

Another example is ʿUmar saying aloud: “Glory and praise be to You, O Allah. Blessed is Your name, exalted is Your majesty, and there is no god but You.” Likewise, there is the example of Ibn ʿUmar and Abū

---

## Page 11458

Hurayrah reciting the invocation for refuge aloud, and Ibn ʿAbbās reciting aloud during the funeral prayer so that people would know that it is Sunnah. It may be said that those Companions who recited the basmalah aloud did so for this reason: to make it known that reciting it is Sunnah, not because reciting it aloud is Sunnah.

Anyone who reflects on the established reports on this subject as a whole will recognize that it is a verse from the Book of Allah, and that they recited it to demonstrate this—not to demonstrate that it forms part of al-Fātihah or that reciting it aloud is Sunnah. An example is what Ibn Wahb mentioned in his Jāmiʿ:

“Men of learning informed me on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū Hurayrah and Zayd ibn Aslam; Ibn Shihāb related the same through a different report from Ibn ʿUmar: he used to begin his recitation with ‘In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.’”

Ibn Shihāb said: “His intention was to show that it is a verse of the Quran, for Allah revealed it.” He added: “The scholars of jurisprudence used to do this in earlier times.”

The report from Ibn ʿUmar is well known through the narration of Hammād ibn Zayd, from Ayyūb, from Nāfiʿ, from Ibn ʿUmar: when he prayed, he would recite aloud, “In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.” Then, after saying:

“Not of those who have incurred Your anger, nor of those who have gone astray,”

he would say: “In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.”

This explanation given by Ibn Shihāb al-Zuhrī—the most knowledgeable person of his time concerning the Sunnah—clarifies the actual situation. For the principal reports concerning its recitation are those transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū Hurayrah and Ibn ʿUmar. He knew the true nature of Abū Hurayrah’s practice in this matter, and likewise that of the others—may Allah be pleased with them all.

---

## Page 11459

For this reason, hadith scholars who transmit reports of its being recited aloud have no explicit hadith to support them, since they know that such reports are fabricated and falsely attributed to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. They rely only on wording open to interpretation, as when they invoke the previously mentioned hadith of Nuʿaym al-Mujammir from Abū Hurayrah, reported by al-Nasā’ī. Those knowledgeable about hadith say that this is their principal evidence on this issue, yet it provides no proof for their position. For [what] (1) is reported from Abū Hurayrah in Sahīh Muslim more clearly indicates that it is not recited than this report indicates that it is recited aloud.

In Sahīh Muslim, Abū Hurayrah reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah says: ‘I have divided the prayer into two halves between Myself and My servant: half is for Me and half is for My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks for.’ When the servant says, ‘All praise is for Allah, Lord of all worlds,’ Allah says, ‘My servant has praised Me.’ When he says, ‘The Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful,’ He says, ‘My servant has extolled Me.’ When he says, ‘Master of the Day of Judgment,’ He says, ‘My servant has glorified Me’—or He said, ‘My servant has entrusted his affairs to Me.’ When he says, ‘You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help,’ He says, ‘This verse is between Me and My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks for.’ When he says, ‘Guide us along the straight path, the path of those You have blessed, not of those who have incurred Your anger, nor of those who have gone astray,’ He says, ‘These are for My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks for.’”

Abd Allāh ibn Ziyād ibn Samʿān—who is a liar—narrated that the following was said at its beginning: “When he says, ‘In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful,’ He says, ‘My servant has remembered Me.’”
