> Usāma ibn al-Zahrā’ — coordinator of the book for al-Mawsū‘a al-Shāmila.

---

## Page 11460

For this reason, the scholars agree that this addition is a fabrication. Fabrications concerning recitation aloud proliferated because the Shīʿah favor reciting it aloud, and they are the most mendacious of all sects. They therefore fabricated hadiths on this subject, thereby confusing people about their religion. Thus, in the statements of the leading Sunni scholars of Kufa, such as Sufyān al-Thawrī, we find that they list wiping over leather socks and refraining from reciting the basmalah aloud among the practices of the Sunnah, just as they mention giving precedence to Abū Bakr and ʿUmar and similar matters. This is because reciting it aloud was among the distinguishing marks of the Rāfidah.

For this reason, Abū ʿAlī ibn Abī Hurayrah, one of the leading scholars of the Shāfiʿī school, held that it should not be recited aloud. He said: “Because reciting it aloud has become a distinguishing mark of our opponents.” Likewise, some scholars of the Shāfiʿī school favored making graves mound-shaped, because making them flat had become a distinguishing mark of the people of innovation.

The hadith of Abū Hurayrah therefore demonstrates that the basmalah is neither part of the obligatory recitation nor part of the recitation divided between Allah and His servant. Its indication that it is not to be recited at all is clearer than the indication in the hadith of Nuʿaym al-Mujammir that it should be recited aloud. For the hadith of Nuʿaym al-Mujammir states that he recited, “In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful,” and then recited the Mother of the Quran. This indicates that, in their view, it is not part of the Quran. Abū Hurayrah’s hadith in Muslim corroborates this, for he said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘Whoever offers a prayer in which he does not recite the Mother of the Quran, it is deficient; it is deficient.’ A man said to him, ‘O Abū Hurayrah, I am sometimes praying behind the imam.’ He replied, ‘Recite it

---

## Page 11461

silently, O Persian, for I heard the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, say: “Allah Most High said, ‘I have divided the prayer between Myself and My servant into two halves.’”’” To the end of the hadith.

This explicitly establishes that, according to Abū Hurayrah, the Mother of the Quran that must be recited in prayer is the divided recitation he mentioned. The Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, also indicate this. This rules out the recitation of the basmalah being obligatory in Abū Hurayrah’s view. Thus, even if he recited it, he did so as something recommended, not obligatory.

Reciting it aloud while holding that it is not part of al-Fātihah is a position held by none of the four imams or the other well-known imams; indeed, I know of no one who holds it. However, the view that it is part of al-Fātihah and must be recited, but silently, is held by a group of hadith scholars and is one of the two positions reported from Ahmad.

If Abū Hurayrah recited it only as something recommended, not obligatory—and on this view, consistently reciting it aloud is not prescribed—then his reciting it aloud would all the more appropriately be taken as evidence that he intended to teach them that reciting it is recommended and prescribed. This is similar to ʿUmar’s reciting the opening supplication aloud, Ibn ʿAbbās’s reciting the Opening of the Book aloud during the funeral prayer, and other such instances. Abū Hurayrah would thus have intended to teach them that it is to be recited in general, even if not aloud. In that case, this would not contradict the hadith of Anas recorded in the Sahīh, the hadith of ʿĀʾishah recorded in the Sahīh, or other reports.

All this assumes that the hadith indicates that he recited it aloud; its wording, however, does not explicitly establish this, for two reasons:

---

## Page 11462

First, he said: “He recited ‘In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy,’ then recited the Mother of the Quran.” The word “recited” allows for the possibility that he recited it quietly, and that Nuʿaym knew this because he was close to him. Quiet recitation, if sufficiently audible, can be heard by someone next to the reciter. It is also possible that Abū Hurayrah told him that he had recited it. Abū Qatādah reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to recite the Opening of the Book and another surah in the first two rakʿahs, and the Opening of the Book in the last two, although this was quiet recitation. How, then, could he have intended thereby to establish that reciting it is obligatory—when he made clear in the hadith that it is not part of al-Fātihah—let alone that reciting it aloud is Sunnah? The grounds for disputing the latter are weaker still.

Second, he did not report that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, recited it before the Mother of the Book. Rather, he said at the end of the prayer:

“Of you all, my prayer most closely resembles that of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.”

The hadith mentions that he said “Amen” and “Allah is the Greatest” as he lowered and raised himself. These and similar practices were among those that the prayer leaders used to omit. Thus, his prayer would most closely resemble that of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in these respects, which included things that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had done but they had abandoned. His prayer being the closest to that of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, does not necessarily mean that it matched his prayer in every respect.

Perhaps, in Abū Hurayrah’s view, reciting it aloud was preferable to omitting its recitation altogether. Those prayer leaders did not recite it at all, so reciting it aloud would, in his view, more closely resemble the prayer of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, even if others disputed this.

---

## Page 11463

As for the report transmitted by Muʿtamir ibn Sulaymān from his father, it should first be understood that al-Hākim’s authentication and endorsement of reliability, when he alone provides them, cannot be trusted even in lesser matters. How, then, can they be trusted in a case such as this, where his endorsement is invoked against what the scholars agree is established to the contrary in the authentic collections? Anyone with even the slightest knowledge of hadith and its scholars would not invoke al-Hākim’s endorsement against something whose contrary is established in the authentic collections.

The scholars agree that al-Hākim is so lenient and permissive in grading hadiths as authentic that his authentication is indisputably less reliable than that of al-Tirmidhī, al-Dāraqutnī and others like them—let alone that of al-Bukhārī and Muslim. Indeed, it is less reliable than that of Abū Bakr ibn Khuzaymah, Abū Hātim ibn Hibbān al-Bustī and others like them. Even the authentication of the hadith master Abū ʿAbd Allāh Muhammad ibn ʿAbd al-Wāhid al-Maqdisī in his selected collection is better than al-Hākim’s. Anyone who knows hadith has no doubt that his book is better in this respect than al-Hākim’s. Al-Tirmidhī’s grading of a hadith as sound is sometimes equivalent to, or more reliable than, al-Hākim’s grading it as authentic. Al-Hākim frequently grades as authentic hadiths that are unquestionably fabricated and entirely baseless. So much for that.

It is well known that Sulaymān al-Taymī and his son Muʿtamir used to recite the basmalah aloud. It is the report attributing this to Anas, however, that is rejected. How could it be otherwise, when Anas’s trustworthy, thoroughly reliable students report the contrary from him? Indeed, Shuʿbah asked Qatādah about this, saying:

“Did you yourself hear Anas mention that?”

He replied, “Yes,” and related it to him in explicit wording incompatible with reciting aloud. Shuʿbah’s transmission from Qatādah of what he heard from Anas is of the utmost authenticity and of the highest

---

## Page 11464

grades of authenticity recognized by hadith specialists, for Qatādah had the strongest memory of anyone in his time, or was among those who did. Likewise, Shuʿbah’s precision and accuracy were unsurpassed in their estimation. This refutes the claim that some narrators transmitted Anas’s hadith according to their own understanding of its meaning, and that his actual wording was merely:

“They would begin the prayer with ‘Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.’”

According to this claim, some narrators understood this to mean that they did not recite the basmalah, and then introduced that meaning into their narration themselves. Such a claim could only come from someone utterly ignorant of the hadith narrators, of the explicit wording of their reports—which admits of no alternative interpretation—and of their utmost integrity and accuracy, which leave no room for such careless reporting. Otherwise, he is someone who stubbornly denies the truth, follows his own desires, and abandons what knowledge and evidence require.

It may then be said: Suppose that Muʿtamir learned his manner of prayer from his father, his father from Anas, and Anas from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. This is still a general statement open to more than one interpretation. Not every particular ruling concerning prayer can be established through such a broadly stated chain of transmission. It is well known that, over a long period and through multiple links in transmission, the particulars of numerous separate actions cannot be preserved with complete accuracy except through a detailed report, rather than a general one.

After all, it is well known that Mansūr ibn al-Muʿtamir, Hammād ibn Abī Sulaymān, al-Aʿmash and others learned their manner of prayer from Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī and his peers. Ibrāhīm learned it from ʿAlqamah, al-Aswad and others like them; they learned it from Ibn Masʿūd; and Ibn Masʿūd learned it from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The transmitters in this chain are more eminent than those in

---

## Page 11465

that chain. Abū Hanīfah, al-Thawrī, Ibn Abī Laylā and other jurists of Kufa learned their manner of prayer from these men. Is it therefore permissible, on the strength of this chain, to identify the precise manner in which these jurists prayed with the prayer of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, even in disputed matters? If that were permissible, these jurists did not recite the basmalah aloud, raised their hands only for the opening takbīr, performed the dawn prayer when daylight had grown bright, and observed other such practices followed by the Kufans.

A similar argument is advanced by some in support of reciting the basmalah aloud: the Meccans among the students of Ibn Jurayj used to recite it aloud, having learned their manner of prayer from Ibn Jurayj, who learned it from ʿAtāʾ, who learned it from Ibn al-Zubayr, who learned it from Abū Bakr al-Siddīq, who learned it from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. There is no doubt that al-Shāfiʿī, may Allah be pleased with him, first learned jurisprudence concerning this and other matters from the students of Ibn Jurayj, such as Saʿīd ibn Sālim al-Qaddāh and Muslim ibn Khālid al-Zinjī. Yet such broadly stated chains of transmission cannot establish detailed rulings over which people have disagreed.

Were that admissible, Mālik’s position would certainly carry greater weight than theirs. No reasonable person doubts that the Companions, the Successors and their followers who lived in Medina were more eminent, more knowledgeable about the Sunnah and more faithful in following it than those who lived in Kufa, Mecca and Basra.

Mālik’s followers have argued against reciting the basmalah aloud on the basis of the uninterrupted practice in Medina, saying:

“This is

---

## Page 11466

the prayer place where the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to pray, followed by Abū Bakr, then ʿUmar, then ʿUthmān, then the successive imams. Their account of the prayer of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, rests on mass transmission. They all witnessed his prayer and then that of his successors. They were more diligent than others in preserving the Sunnah and more vigorous in censuring those who departed from it. It is therefore inconceivable that they would have altered the prayer of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

“This practice is further supported by that of all the Umayyad and Abbasid caliphs, none of whom recited the basmalah aloud. They could not all have had an interest in unanimously changing the Sunnah in such a matter, nor could all the imams have acquiesced in their departure from it. Indeed, we know beyond doubt that Muslim caliphs and kings do not alter a Sunnah that has no bearing on their rule or the desires associated with it. This issue is not one in which rulers have any vested interest.”

When advanced, this argument is no weaker than the other; indeed, we know that it is stronger. No Muslim doubts that there are firmer grounds for asserting with certainty that the prayer of the Successors in Medina more closely resembled that of the Companions there, and that the prayer of those Companions more closely resembled that of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, than for asserting with certainty that the prayer of one or two individuals more closely resembled that of another, through a succession reaching back to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. For this reason, no one has ever held that the practice of people outside Medina

---

## Page 11467

or their consensus constitutes authoritative proof. The dispute has concerned only whether the practice and consensus of the people of Medina constitute authoritative proof, with disagreement over this no less extensive than that concerning the practice and consensus of others, if not more so. Thus, the practice attributed to Sulaymān al-Taymī, Ibn Jurayj, and others like them is countered by the practice of the people of Medina, even if there were no authentic, explicit report from Anas contradicting it. How much more so, then, when the report from Anas is too clear, well known, authentic, and firmly established to be opposed by this broadly worded hadith, which has not been established as authentic and has only been graded as such by the likes of al-Hākim and his peers.

A similar consideration also reveals the weakness of the hadith concerning Muʿāwiyah, which states that he led the Companions in prayer in Medina and that they objected to his omission of the basmalah at the beginning of al-Fātihah and at the beginning of the surah, until he resumed reciting it. Although al-Dāraqutnī said of this hadith, “The narrators in its chain are trustworthy,” and al-Khatīb said, “It is the best evidence to rely upon in this matter,” as Nasr al-Maqdisī related from him, its weakness is evident on several grounds:

First, there is also an authentic, explicit, widely transmitted report from Anas that refutes this.

Second, the chain of this hadith rests on ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUthmān ibn Khuthaym

---

## Page 11468

, whom a number of scholars have judged weak. As noted above, his report has been transmitted with inconsistencies in both its chain of transmission and its wording. This shows that it has not been reliably preserved.

Third, it has no chain in which direct hearing is established throughout. Rather, it contains weaknesses and inconsistencies that leave open the possibility of a break in the chain or poor retention.

Fourth, Anas was living in Basra. When Muʿāwiyah came to Medina, no one known to us mentioned that Anas was with him. Indeed, it appears that he was not.

Fifth, assuming this incident occurred, it took place in Medina, whereas its narrator, Anas, was in Basra. It was also the kind of incident that people would have had ample interest and reason to transmit. Yet it is known that neither Anas’s associates, who were well known for keeping his company, nor the people of Medina transmitted it. Rather, what is transmitted from Anas and the people of Medina is the opposite, while the person transmitting this report belongs to neither group.

(Sixth, had Muʿāwiyah resumed reciting the basmalah aloud at the beginning of al-Fātihah and the surah, this practice of his would also have been known among the people of Syria who kept his company. Yet no one has transmitted this from Muʿāwiyah. Rather, all the Syrians—their caliphs and their scholars—held that it should not be recited aloud. Indeed, al-Awzāʿī’s position on it was the same as Mālik’s: it should be recited neither silently nor aloud. Thus, when a scholar carefully considers these and similar points,

---

## Page 11469

he concludes with certainty that the report concerning Muʿāwiyah is either false, with no basis in fact, or has been distorted, and that its narrator transmitted it through an unsound channel, the defect arising from a break in its chain of transmission.

It has also been said: Even if this hadith could serve as evidence, it would be anomalous, because it contradicts what reliable, firmly established transmitters narrated from Anas, the people of Medina, and the people of Syria. For a hadith to be established as authentic, it must be neither anomalous nor affected by a hidden defect. This report is both anomalous and defective, if it is not the result of poor retention on the part of one of its narrators.

The principal evidence relied upon by those who wrote in support of reciting the basmalah aloud and of the obligation to recite it is that it was written in the Quran manuscript in the same script as the Quran, and that the Companions kept the Quran free of anything that was not part of it.

Their opponents rejected this evidence without justification, saying, for example: Something can be established as Quran only by conclusive proof; if this were conclusive proof, anyone who disagreed with it would be an unbeliever. Abū Bakr ibn al-Tayyib al-Bāqillānī and others adopted this approach. Relying on this argument, they claimed to know with certainty that al-Shāfiʿī was mistaken in considering the basmalah part of the Quran. They argued that nothing may be established as Quran except through mass transmission, that no such mass transmission exists here, and that one must therefore conclude with certainty that it is not part of the Quran.

The correct assessment is that this argument can be countered with an equivalent argument. They may be told: On the contrary, one can be certain

---

## Page 11470

that it is part of the Quran wherever it is written, just as you have categorically denied that it is not part of it. Of the same kind is the mass-transmitted report from the Companions that everything between the two covers is Quran. Distinguishing between one verse and another undermines confidence that the Quran written between the covers of the manuscript is Allah’s speech. We know beyond doubt that the Companions who wrote the Quran manuscripts transmitted to us that everything they wrote between their covers was Allah’s speech, which He revealed to His Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. They did not write therein anything that was not Allah’s speech.

If an opponent says, “If you are certain that the basmalah is part of the Quran wherever it is written, then declare anyone who denies this an unbeliever,” the reply is: “The same objection applies to your own judgment: if you are certain that it is not part of the Quran, then declare your opponents unbelievers.”

The Muslim community has agreed that no one is to be declared an unbeliever over this issue, even though many on both sides claim certainty for their respective positions. This is because not everything that one person considers certain must be certain to someone else, nor must everything that a group claims to be certain actually be certain in itself.

Rather, a person may mistakenly claim certainty where certainty is unwarranted, just as he may err in what he hears, understands, transmits, or otherwise experiences. Even the outward senses can sometimes err. Accordingly, we may say:

There are three positions concerning whether the basmalah is part of the Quran: two extremes and a middle position.

---

## Page 11471

The first extreme:
The view that the basmalah is not part of the Quran except in Sūrat al-Naml. This was the position of Mālik, a group of Hanafī scholars, and some of Ahmad’s followers, who either claim that it is his position or transmit it as a reported view of his.

The opposite extreme:
The view that it constitutes a verse, or part of a verse, of every surah. This is the well-known position of al-Shāfiʿī and those who agree with him. However, it has also been transmitted from al-Shāfiʿī that it is not part of the opening of any surah other than al-Fātihah; rather, the surahs are begun with it to seek blessing through it. As for its being part of al-Fātihah, no proof for this has been reliably transmitted from him.

The middle position:
It is part of the Quran wherever it is written, but is nevertheless not part of the surahs. Rather, it was written as a verse at the beginning of each surah and is likewise recited as an independent verse at the beginning of each surah, just as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, recited it when the surah “Indeed, We have granted you abundant good” was revealed to him, as established in Sahīh Muslim, [and] (1) as indicated by his saying:

“A surah of the Quran consisting of thirty verses interceded for a man until he was forgiven. It is the surah ‘Blessed is He in Whose Hand is the dominion.’”

This was narrated by the compilers of the Sunan, and al-Tirmidhī graded it sound. This position was held by ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak and is explicitly stated in the reports from Ahmad ibn Hanbal. Abū Bakr al-Rāzī mentioned that, in his view, this is what Abū Hanīfah’s position entails.

> **Footnotes:**
> (1) The text in square brackets is absent from the printed edition, and I could not find it in Siyānat Majmūʿ al-Fatāwā min al-Saqt wa-l-Tashīf (Protecting Majmūʿ al-Fatāwā from Omissions and Scribal Errors).
> Usāma ibn al-Zahrāʾ — book coordinator for al-Mawsūʿa al-Shāmila.

---

## Page 11472

and this is also the position of all others who have examined this question thoroughly and adopted a middle course, reconciling the implications of the evidence with the fact that it is written on a separate line from the surah. This is supported by the statement of Ibn ʿAbbās:

“Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would not know where a surah ended until ‘In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful’ was revealed to him.”

Narrated by Abū Dāwūd.

Those who hold this position have two views concerning al-Fātihah, both reported from Ahmad. The first is that the basmalah is part of al-Fātihah alone, and must therefore be recited whenever reciting al-Fātihah is obligatory.

The second, which is the sounder view, is that there is no distinction in this respect between al-Fātihah and the other surahs: reciting it at the beginning of al-Fātihah is like reciting it at the beginning of the other surahs. The authentic hadiths accord with this view and do not contradict it.

Accordingly, there are also three views concerning its recitation in prayer:

The first is that reciting it is obligatory, just as reciting al-Fātihah is obligatory. This is the position of al-Shāfiʿī, of Ahmad according to one of the two reports from him, and of a group of hadith scholars, on the basis that it is part of al-Fātihah.

The second is that reciting it is disliked, whether silently or aloud, as is the well-known position in Mālik’s school.

The third view is that reciting it is permissible—indeed, recommended. This is the position of

---

## Page 11473

Abū Hanīfah, Ahmad according to the well-known report from him, and most hadith scholars. Some of these scholars regard reciting it and omitting it as equally acceptable, allowing either, since they consider one practice to accord with one of the two Quranic readings and the other with the other reading.

If it is recited, there are then three views on whether reciting it aloud is recommended:

One view is that reciting it aloud is recommended. This is the position of al-Shāfiʿī and those who agree with him.

Another is that reciting it aloud is not recommended. This is the position of the majority of scholars of hadith and juristic reasoning, and the jurists of the major cities.

A third is that either practice may be chosen. This is reported from Ishāq and is the position of Ibn Hazm and others.

Nevertheless, the correct view is that reciting aloud what is normally recited silently may be prescribed when a greater benefit warrants it. Thus, it is prescribed for the imam to do so occasionally for such purposes as teaching those praying behind him. Worshippers may also occasionally say a few words aloud. It is likewise permissible to forgo the preferable course in order to bring hearts together and preserve unity, for fear of driving people away from what is beneficial. Thus, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, refrained from rebuilding the House upon Abraham’s foundations because Quraysh had only recently emerged from the pre-Islamic age of ignorance, and he feared alienating them by doing so

---

## Page 11474

and he considered the benefit of unity and concord to take precedence over the benefit of rebuilding upon Abraham’s foundations.

When Ibn Masʿūd prayed the full prayer behind ʿUthmān despite objecting to his doing so, he was asked about this and replied, “Discord is evil.” For this reason, leading scholars such as Ahmad and others explicitly endorsed this approach regarding the basmalah, joining the units of the witr prayer, and other matters in which one forgoes the preferable practice for a permissible but less preferable one, in order to preserve harmony among those praying behind the imam, teach them the Sunnah, or serve similar purposes. And Allah knows best.

---

## Page 11475

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was also asked:

“Is ‘In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful’ a verse at the beginning of every surah? Please give us your ruling; may you be rewarded.”

He replied:

Praise be to Allah.

Muslims agree that it is part of the Quran in His words:

“It is from Solomon, and it is”

However, they differ concerning its occurrence at the beginnings of the surahs where it is written, holding three views:

The first is that it is not part of the Quran, but was written only to seek blessing through it. This is the view of Mālik and a group of Hanafi scholars. It is also reported as a position transmitted from Ahmad, but this attribution to him is not authentic, although it is a view held within his school.

The second is that it is part of every surah, either as a complete verse or as part of a verse. This is the view of al-Shāfiʿī—may Allah be pleased with him.

The third is that it is part of the Quran wherever it is written—a verse from the Book of Allah at the beginning of each surah—but is not part of the surah itself. This is the view of Ibn al-Mubārak and Ahmad

---

## Page 11476

ibn Hanbal—may Allah be pleased with him—and others. Al-Rāzī stated that, in his view, this is what Abū Hanīfah’s position entails. This is the most balanced of the views.

Its inclusion in the Quranic manuscript in the same script as the Quran indicates that it is part of the Quran, while its being written separately, detached from what precedes and follows it, indicates that it is not part of the surah. This is also supported by what the compilers of the Sunan narrated from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—that he said:

“A surah of the Quran consisting of thirty verses interceded for a man until he was forgiven. It is ‘Blessed is He in whose hand is dominion.’”

This is not contradicted by the report in the Sahīh:

“The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—dozed briefly, then said, ‘A surah has just been revealed to me.’ He then recited, ‘In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. Indeed, We have granted you abundance.’”

That report does not state that it is part of the surah; rather, it indicates that it is recited at the beginning of the surah. This is sunnah: it is recited at the beginning of every surah, even though it is not part of the surah. Similar to this is the hadith of Ibn ‘Abbās:

“The Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—would not know where one surah ended until ‘In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful’ was revealed.”

Abū Dāwūd narrated it. It indicates that this formula was revealed to separate the surahs, but does not state that it is a verse of the surah. Moreover, “Blessed is He in whose hand is dominion” consists of thirty verses without the opening formula.

A further reason is that none of those who enumerate the verses of the Quran counted the opening formula as part of the surah. They did, however, differ concerning al-Fātihah: is it a verse of that surah alone, but not of the others? There are two views, both transmitted from Ahmad:

---

## Page 11477

The first is that it is part of al-Fātihah but not of any other surah. This is the position of a group of hadith scholars; I believe it is the view of Abū ‘Ubayd. They cite as evidence the reports stating that the opening formula is part of al-Fātihah. According to their view, reciting it in prayer is obligatory, even if they do not recite it aloud.

The second is that it is not part of al-Fātihah, just as it is not part of any other surah. This is the more evident view.

It is established in the Sahīh that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“Allah Most High says, ‘I have divided the prayer between Myself and My servant into two halves: half is for Me and half is for him, and My servant shall have what he asks for.’

“The servant says, ‘All praise is for Allah, Lord of all worlds.’ Allah says, ‘My servant has praised Me.’

“The servant says, ‘The Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.’ Allah says, ‘My servant has lauded Me.’

“The servant says, ‘Master of the Day of Judgment.’ Allah says, ‘My servant has glorified Me.’

“The servant says, ‘You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.’ Allah says, ‘This verse is divided into two halves between Myself and My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks for.’

“The servant says, ‘Guide us to the straight path,’ through to the end of the surah. Allah says, ‘These verses are for My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks for.’”

If the opening formula were part of al-Fātihah, He would have mentioned it as He mentioned the other verses. It does appear in a fabricated hadith transmitted by ‘Abd Allāh ibn Ziyād ibn Sam‘ān, which was cited by the likes of al-Tha‘labī in his Quran commentary and by those who compiled the hadiths about reciting it aloud—all of which are weak or fabricated. Moreover, if it were part of al-Fātihah, the Lord would not have

---

## Page 11478

three and a half verses, with three and a half for the servant.

The apparent meaning of the hadith is that this division concerns the verses, for He said:

“These verses are for My servant.”

“These” is a plural demonstrative. Thus, the passage from “Guide us to the straight path” to the end of the surah comprises three verses according to those who do not count the opening formula as one of its verses. Those who do count it as a verse regard this passage as two verses.

Furthermore, al-Fātihah is one of the surahs of the Quran, and the opening formula is written at its beginning. In this respect, there is no distinction between it and the other surahs. This is one of the clearest lines of reasoning.

Moreover, if the opening formula were part of al-Fātihah, it would be recited aloud in prayer just as the surah’s other verses are. This is the position of those who advocate reciting it aloud, such as al-Shāfi‘ī and a group of scholars from Mecca and Basra. They said that it is a verse of al-Fātihah and should be recited aloud like its other verses. Support for this was drawn from transmitted reports, some from the Companions and others from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

As for the reports from Companions such as Ibn al-Zubayr and others, some are authentic and some are weak. The reports from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—are weak or fabricated, as the hadith masters, including al-Dāraqutnī and others, have stated. For this reason, the compilers of the well-known Sunan and Musnad collections did not transmit from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—

---

## Page 11479

a single hadith supporting its audible recitation. Such reports are transmitted only by those who lack discernment in assessing hadith, including Quran commentators such as al-Tha‘labī and others like him, and some hadith scholars who have written on this subject. Some jurists also cite them in their works on jurisprudence.

The view that it should be recited aloud has been attributed to Ahmad and others on the basis of one of the two reports from him: that it forms part of al-Fātihah and should therefore be recited aloud like the rest of the surah. This, however, is not his position. Rather, according to him, it is recited quietly, even if he holds that it forms part of al-Fātihah.

In his view, however, it is recited aloud when doing so serves an overriding benefit—for example, when the worshippers do not recite it at all, so that reciting it aloud teaches them that its recitation is Sunnah. Similarly, Ibn ‘Abbās recited al-Fātihah aloud in the funeral prayer, and ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb recited the opening supplication aloud. It is also reported that Abū Hurayrah recited the opening formula and then the Mother of the Book, saying:

“Of all of you, my prayer most closely resembles that of the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace.”

This was narrated by al-Nasā’ī, and it is the strongest evidence they have cited.

Some of Ahmad’s followers likewise explained his differing position as referring to his reciting it aloud when those praying behind him objected to anyone who did not recite it aloud, and in similar circumstances. Both reciting it aloud and reciting it quietly are Sunnah. Thus, if someone who normally recites it quietly were to recite it aloud, his prayer would undoubtedly be valid.

The majority of scholars, including Abū Hanīfah, Mālik, Ahmad and al-Awzā‘ī, do not favour reciting it aloud. Some of them, such as Abū Hanīfah, Ahmad and others, recite it quietly, while others, such as Mālik, recite it neither quietly nor aloud.

---

## Page 11480

The majority’s evidence is the report established in the Sahīh:

“The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—Abū Bakr and ‘Umar did not recite ‘In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful’ aloud.” Another wording states: “They did not mention ‘In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful’ at the beginning or end of their recitation.”

And Allah knows best.

He was asked:

“Is the prayer of someone who makes errors when reciting al-Fātihah valid?”

He answered:

If an error in reciting al-Fātihah does not change the meaning, the prayer of the person making it is valid, whether he is leading the prayer or praying alone. Examples include saying “rabbi l-‘ālamīn” (Lord of all worlds), “wa-l-dāllīn” (and those who have gone astray), and the like.

As for forms transmitted as Quranic readings, such as “al-hamdu lillāhi rabba,” “rabbi,” and “rabbu” (praise belongs to Allah, Lord…); or “al-hamdu lillāh” and “al-hamdi lillāh” (praise belongs to Allah), with the letter dāl pronounced with u or i; or “‘alayhimu,” “‘alayhim,” and “‘alayhumu” (upon them), and similar examples—these are not considered errors.

As for an error that changes the meaning, if the person making it understands its meaning—for example, saying “sirāt alladhīna an‘amta ‘alayhim” (the path of those whom You have blessed), knowing that this is a first-person pronoun—his prayer is invalid. If, however, he does not know that it changes the meaning and believes it to be a second-person pronoun, there is disagreement concerning his prayer’s validity. And Allah knows best.

---

## Page 11481

He was asked:

“Regarding someone who recites the Quran but has no one to ask about errors in recitation and the like: if he gets stuck on something and consults a copy of the Quran, does he incur any sin?”

He answered:

If he needs to recite the Quran, he should recite it to the best of his ability and consult a copy of the Quran wherever he encounters difficulty. “Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity.” He should not abandon the recitation he needs and brings to completion because of occasional mistakes, provided it does not entail an overriding harm. And Allah knows best.

He was asked:

“What if someone pronounces a word in the accusative instead of the genitive during his prayer?”

He answered:

If he does so knowingly, his prayer is invalid, because he is treating his prayer frivolously. If he does so out of ignorance, his prayer is not invalid according to one of the two views.

---

## Page 11482

He was asked:

“Regarding a man who leads people in prayer and recites according to the reading of Shaykh Abū ‘Amr: if he recites according to Warsh or Nāfi‘, with the differences among the transmitted versions, while his usual recitation follows Abū ‘Amr, does he incur any sin, or is his prayer deficient or rejected?”

He answered:

It is permissible to recite part of the Quran according to the reading of Abū ‘Amr and part according to the reading of Nāfi‘, whether within a single unit of prayer or across two units, and whether during prayer or outside it. And Allah knows best.

He was asked:

“Has it been narrated that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, recited Sūrat al-A‘rāf or Sūrat al-An‘ām in its entirety during the Maghrib prayer or another prayer? If Ahmad narrated this, is it authentic or not?”

He answered:

Praise be to Allah. Yes, it is established in the authentic hadith collections that he recited Sūrat al-A‘rāf during the Maghrib prayer, but he did not do so regularly. On another occasion, he recited Sūrat al-Mursalāt during it, and on yet another occasion, Sūrat al-Tūr. All of this is recorded in the authentic hadith collections. And Allah knows best.

---

## Page 11483

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

“Does raising the hands after bowing invalidate the prayer or not?”

He answered:

Praise be to Allah. It does not invalidate the prayer, by agreement of the imams. Indeed, most leading Muslim scholars recommend it, as is abundantly attested in the Sunnah of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, through reports from Ibn ‘Umar, Mālik ibn al-Huwayrith, Wā’il ibn Hujr, Abū Humayd al-Sā‘idī and Abū Qatādah al-Ansārī among a group of ten Companions, as well as reports from ‘Alī, Abū Hurayrah and others.

It is recommended according to the majority of scholars. This is the position of al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad and Mālik, according to one of the two reports from him. Abū Hanīfah said that it is not recommended; he did not say that it invalidates the prayer. And Allah knows best.

He was asked:

“Regarding the words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ‘Nor can wealth avail its possessor against You’: should it be read in the genitive or the nominative? Please give us a ruling; may you be rewarded.”

---

## Page 11484

He answered:

Praise be to Allah. The first occurrence is in the genitive, while the second is in the nominative. The meaning is that a person’s wealth cannot avail him against You: it cannot save or deliver him from You. Rather, what saves him is faith and righteous deeds. The word jadd means wealth, eminence, and possessions.

He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained that worldly authority and wealth cannot save a person or deliver him from Allah. Only his faith and piety can save him from His punishment. For he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“O Allah, none can withhold what You give, and none can give what You withhold, nor can wealth avail its possessor against You.”

In this hadith, he explained two great principles. The first is Allah’s oneness in lordship: none can give what Allah withholds, and none can withhold what He gives; none but Him is to be relied upon, and none but Him is to be asked.

The second is Allah’s exclusive right to worship. This explains what benefits a person and what does not: not everyone granted wealth, worldly advantages, or authority thereby receives something that benefits him before Allah and saves him from His punishment. Allah grants worldly things to those He loves and those He does not love, but He grants faith only to those He loves. The Most High said:

“As for man, when his Lord tests him by honoring him and granting him favors, he says, ‘My Lord has honored me.’ But when He tests him by restricting his provision, he says, ‘My Lord has humiliated me.’ No!”

That is: “Not everyone whose provision I have expanded have I honored, nor have I humiliated everyone whose provision I have restricted.” Rather, this is a test, so that the servant may be thankful in prosperity and patient in adversity. Thus, whoever is granted thankfulness

---

## Page 11485

and patience will find that every decree Allah ordains is good for him, as stated in the authentic hadith in which the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah decrees nothing for the believer except that it is good for him. This is true of no one but the believer: if prosperity comes his way, he is thankful, and that is good for him; if adversity befalls him, he is patient, and that is good for him.”

Affirming Allah’s exclusive right to worship means worshipping Allah without associating anything with Him, obeying Him and His messengers, and doing what He loves and is pleased with. As for affirming Allah’s oneness in lordship, this encompasses whatever He has determined and decreed, even if it is not something He has commanded, made obligatory, or been pleased with. The servant is commanded to worship Allah and do what He has commanded—this is affirming His exclusive right to worship—and to seek Allah’s help in doing so, which is affirming His oneness. Thus, he says:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.”

And Allah knows best.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

If someone takes two steps backward when he wishes to prostrate during prayer, is that disliked or not?

He answered:

Stepping backward when prostrating is not a sunnah and should not be done, unless the space is cramped, in which case one may step backward to make room to prostrate.

---

## Page 11486

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

In prayer, should one support oneself when lowering to the ground by placing one’s knees before one’s hands, or one’s hands before one’s knees?

He answered:

Both ways are permissible in prayer by scholarly agreement. The worshipper may place his knees before his hands if he wishes, or his hands before his knees. His prayer is valid in either case by scholarly agreement. However, the scholars differed over which is preferable.

Some held that the first is preferable. This is the position of Abū Hanīfah and al-Shāfiʿī, and one of the two positions reported from Ahmad.

Others held that the second is preferable. This is the position of Mālik and the other position reported from Ahmad. A hadith supporting each practice has been narrated from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in the Sunan collections.

It is reported of him in the Sunan collections:

“When he prayed, he would place his knees down, then his hands; when he rose, he would lift his hands, then his knees.”

In Sunan Abī Dāwūd and elsewhere, he is reported to have said:

“When one of you prostrates, he should not go down as a camel does, but should place his hands down, then his knees.”

The opposite has also been narrated, and it has been said that it was abrogated. And Allah knows best.

---

## Page 11487

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was also asked:

Concerning the report that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“I have been commanded to prostrate on seven bones and not to hold back any of my clothing or hair.”

In another narration:

“And not to gather up any of my clothing or hair.”

What is meant by “holding back” (kaff) and “gathering up” (kaft)? Does braiding the hair count as gathering it up?

He answered:

Kaft means gathering and drawing together. Kaff is similar: it means preventing the hair and clothing from prostrating. A man is instructed not to pray with his hair tucked up on his head or coiled and tied up. Concerning this, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“One who prays with his hair tied up is like one who prays with his hands bound.”

This is because the clothing of the one whose hands are bound does not prostrate, and the hair of the one whose hair is tied up does not prostrate. As for braiding the hair while leaving it hanging down, this does not count as gathering it up. And Allah knows best.

---

## Page 11488

He was also asked:

Concerning a man who prays behind an imam and sits briefly to rest between units of prayer, although the imam does not do so: is this permissible for him? If it is permissible, does it diminish his reward because he has not kept pace with the imam?

He answered:

It is established in the Sahīh collection that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, observed this brief sitting for rest. However, scholars have differed over whether he did so out of need owing to advanced age, or because it is part of the Sunnah of prayer.

Those who hold the latter view consider it recommended. This is the position of al-Shāfiʿī and of Ahmad according to one of the two reports from him. Those who hold the former view consider it recommended only when needed. This is the position of Abū Hanīfah, Mālik, and Ahmad according to the other report.

Anyone who observes it is not to be censured, even when praying behind an imam. According to those who consider it recommended, a delay of this duration does not constitute the prohibited lagging behind the imam. Is this not simply an action in a matter open to scholarly judgment? For him, performing this act, which he regards as Sunnah, conflicts with promptly following the imam.

---

## Page 11489

for doing so is preferable to lagging behind, although the delay is slight. This is thus like the case where the imam rises from the first tashahhud before the follower has completed it, while the follower considers it recommended; or where the imam gives the salutation while the follower still has a little supplication left: should he give the salutation or finish it? Such questions are matters open to scholarly judgment. The stronger view is that following the imam takes precedence over lagging behind to perform a recommended act. Allah knows best.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was also asked:

Is raising the hands after rising from the sitting following the first two units of prayer recommended? Did the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, or any of the Companions do this?

He answered:

Yes, it is recommended according to the discerning scholars versed in the Sunnah of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. This is one of the two reports from Ahmad and the position of a group of his followers, followers of al-Shāfiʿī, and others. This practice is established from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in the Sahīh and Sunan collections. Al-Bukhārī and the Sunan collections of Abū Dāwūd and al-Nasāʾī contain the following report:

“Nāfiʿ reported that when Ibn ʿUmar began the prayer, he would say ‘Allah is the Greatest’ and raise his hands. When he bowed, he would raise his hands; when he said ‘Allah hears those who praise Him,’ he would raise his hands; and when he rose after the first two units of prayer, he would raise his hands.”

Ibn ʿUmar attributed this

---

## Page 11490

to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

ʿAlī ibn Abī Tālib reported:

“When the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, stood to perform an obligatory prayer, he would say ‘Allah is the Greatest’ and raise his hands level with his shoulders. He would do the same when he finished his recitation and when he intended to bow, and again when he rose from bowing. He would not raise his hands at any point in the prayer while seated. When he stood after the first two units of prayer, he would likewise raise his hands and say ‘Allah is the Greatest.’”

This was narrated by Ahmad, Abū Dāwūd—whose wording is given here—Ibn Mājah, and al-Tirmidhī, who said: “It is a sound and authentic hadith.”

Abū Humayd al-Sāʿidī described the Prophet’s prayer, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. His account includes:

“When he rose after the two prostrations, he would say ‘Allah is the Greatest’ and raise his hands level with his shoulders, just as he had done when beginning the prayer.”

This was narrated by Imam Ahmad, Abū Dāwūd, Ibn Mājah, al-Nasāʾī, and al-Tirmidhī, who graded it authentic.

These are authentic, firmly established hadiths, in addition to the other transmitted reports on this matter. There is no counterevidence strong enough to match them, let alone outweigh them. Allah knows best.

---

## Page 11491

Shaykh al-Islam was asked about the words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You sent blessings upon the family of Abraham. Indeed, You are Praiseworthy, Glorious”—and the rest of the hadith;

and his words:

“O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You sent blessings upon Abraham and the family of Abraham.”

Are the two hadiths equally authentic? What is the ruling on mentioning the family without mentioning Abraham?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. This hadith is recorded in the authentic collections through four chains of transmission. The best-known is the report of ʿAbd al-Rahmān ibn Abī Laylā, who said: Kaʿb ibn ʿUjrah met me and said, “Shall I offer you a gift?”

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, came out to us, and we said, ‘We have learned how to greet you with peace, but how should we invoke blessings upon you?’

“He said, ‘Say: O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You sent blessings upon the family of Abraham. Indeed, You are Praiseworthy, Glorious. O Allah, bless—or, in another wording, “and bless”—Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed the family of Abraham. Indeed, You are Praiseworthy, Glorious.’”

It was narrated by the compilers of the authentic collections, the Sunan collections, and the Musnad collections, including al-Bukhārī, Muslim, Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī, al-Nasāʾī, Ibn Mājah, and Imam Ahmad in his Musnad, as well as others.

---

## Page 11492

This is the wording used by all these compilers, except that al-Tirmidhī has “upon Abraham” in both places, without mentioning his family. This is also a version transmitted by Abū Dāwūd and al-Nasā’ī. Another version reads, “as You sent blessings upon the family of Abraham,” followed by “as You blessed Abraham,” mentioning the family in the first instance and Abraham in the second.

In the two Sahīh collections and the three Sunan collections, Abū Humayd al-Sāʿidī reported:

> They said, “O Messenger of Allah, how should we invoke blessings upon you?”
>
> He replied, “Say: O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad, his wives and his descendants, as You sent blessings upon the family of Abraham. And bless Muhammad, his wives and his descendants, as You blessed the family of Abraham. Indeed, You are Praiseworthy, Glorious.”

This is the well-known wording. It has also been transmitted with the wording “as You sent blessings upon Abraham” and “as You blessed Abraham,” without mentioning the family in either place.

In Sahīh al-Bukhārī, Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī said:

> We said, “O Messenger of Allah, we know how to greet you with peace, but how should we invoke blessings upon you?”
>
> He replied, “Say: O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad, Your servant and Messenger, as You sent blessings upon the family of Abraham. And bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed the family of Abraham.”

In Sahīh Muslim, Abū Masʿūd al-Ansārī said:

> The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, came to us while we were gathered with Saʿd ibn ʿUbādah. Bashīr ibn Saʿd said to him, “Allah has commanded us to invoke blessings upon you. How should we invoke blessings upon you?”
>
> He continued: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, remained silent until we wished that he had not asked him. Then the Messenger of Allah said

---

## Page 11493

, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Say: ‘O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You sent blessings upon the family of Abraham. And bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed the family of Abraham among all peoples. Indeed, You are Praiseworthy, Glorious.’ The greeting of peace is as you have learned.”

Others besides Muslim also transmitted this report, including Mālik, Ahmad, Abū Dāwūd, al-Nasā’ī and al-Tirmidhī, with different wording. Some chains of transmission have “as You sent blessings upon Abraham” and “as You blessed Abraham,” without mentioning “the family.” Another version has “as You sent blessings upon Abraham” and “as You blessed the family of Abraham.”

Thus, in these hadiths found in the Sahīh collections, and in the reports transmitted, I have not found the wording “Abraham and the family of Abraham.” Rather, the well-known wording in most of the hadiths and their chains of transmission is “the family of Abraham,” while some have “Abraham.” Sometimes “the family of Abraham” occurs in one of the two places and “Abraham” in the other.

The wording “Abraham and the family of Abraham” has been transmitted in a hadith reported by al-Bayhaqī, from Yahyā ibn al-Sabbāq, from a man of Banū al-Hārith, from Ibn Mas‘ūd, from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who said:

“When any of you recites the tashahhud in prayer, let him say: ‘O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, and bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, and bless Muhammad and have mercy on Muhammad, as You sent blessings, bestowed blessings and had mercy upon Abraham and the family of Abraham. Indeed, You are Praiseworthy, Glorious.’”

Its chain of transmission is weak. However, Ibn Mājah transmitted it in his Sunan as a statement of Ibn Mas‘ūd himself, who said: “When you invoke blessings

---

## Page 11494

upon the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, offer them in the finest manner, for you do not know: they may be presented to him.” He said: “Then say to him, ‘Teach us.’” He said:

“Say: ‘O Allah, bestow Your blessings, mercy and bounty upon the master of the messengers, the leader of the God-fearing and the Seal of the Prophets, Muhammad, Your servant and Messenger, the leader in goodness, the guide to goodness and the Messenger of mercy. O Allah, raise him to a station of praise that those of earlier and later generations will look upon with longing. O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You sent blessings upon Abraham and the family of Abraham. Indeed, You are Praiseworthy, Glorious. O Allah, bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed Abraham and the family of Abraham. Indeed, You are Praiseworthy, Glorious.’”

I do not have the chain of transmission of this report at hand. Nor, to date, has any Prophetic hadith with an established chain of transmission reached me containing the wording, “as You sent blessings upon Abraham, and as You blessed Abraham and the family of Abraham.” Rather, the hadiths in the Sunan collections agree with those in the two Sahīh collections. Thus, in Sunan Abī Dāwūd, Abū Hurayrah reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever wishes to receive the fullest measure when invoking blessings upon us, the members of the household, should say: ‘O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad the Prophet, his wives—the Mothers of the Believers—his descendants and the members of his household, as You sent blessings upon the family of Abraham. Indeed, You are Praiseworthy, Glorious.’”

Al-Shāfi‘ī transmitted in his Musnad, from Abū Hurayrah, who said: “We asked, ‘O Messenger of Allah, how should we invoke blessings upon you?’”—meaning during prayer. He said:

“Say: ‘O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You sent blessings upon Abraham. And bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed Abraham.’ Then greet me with peace.”

## Page 11495

Some later scholars have adopted a newly introduced approach to certain supplications and remembrances which the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would recite and practise using different wordings—and which have been transmitted with different wordings. They combine these wordings, recommend doing so, and consider the resulting formula the best wording to recite.

An example is the hadith in the two Sahīh collections, in which Abū Bakr al-Siddīq, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

“O Messenger of Allah, teach me a supplication to recite during my prayer.” He replied: “Say: ‘O Allah, I have greatly wronged myself, and none forgives sins but You. So grant me forgiveness from You, and have mercy on me. Indeed, You are the All-Forgiving, the Most Merciful.’”

The wording has been transmitted as “greatly” and also as “grievously.” Someone following this approach therefore says that it is recommended to say “greatly and grievously.”

The same applies when one narration reads:

“O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad and the family of Muhammad,”

and another reads:

“O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad, his wives and his descendants,”

and in similar cases. This is a newly introduced approach, unprecedented among any of the recognized imams.

Following this approach consistently would entail reciting the tashahhud (testimony of faith) using all its transmitted wordings, and likewise reciting the opening supplication using all its transmitted wordings. Besides being contrary to the practice of the Muslims, this was never recommended by any of their imams; rather, their practice was the opposite. It is therefore a religious innovation and rationally unsound.

---

## Page 11496

As for the former:

The variations in the wording of remembrances and supplications are like the variations in Quranic wording, such as ta‘lamūna (“you know”) and ya‘lamūna (“they know”); bā‘idū and ba‘‘idū (two forms meaning “make distant”); and arjulakum and arjulikum (two grammatical forms of “your feet”). It is well known that Muslims agree that combining these variant readings is not recommended for someone reciting during prayer, or outside prayer for worship and reflection. Some reciters combine them on certain occasions only to test their memorization of the variants and their ability to distinguish the readings. This practice has been a subject of discussion. As for combining them in any prescribed and enjoined recitation, this is not prescribed, by agreement of the Muslims. Rather, one may choose between these variants, and it is good to recite one on one occasion and another on another occasion.

The same applies to remembrances: it is good to say “greatly” on one occasion and “grievously” on another. Likewise, it is good to say “upon the family of Muhammad” on one occasion and “upon his wives and his descendants” on another.

Similarly, in the tashahhud, it is good to recite the version transmitted by Ibn Mas‘ūd on one occasion, that transmitted by Ibn ‘Abbās on another, and that transmitted by ‘Umar on another. For the opening supplication, it is good to use the version transmitted by ‘Umar on one occasion, that transmitted by ‘Alī on another, and that transmitted by Abū Hurayrah on another, and so forth.

More than one scholar, including al-Shāfi‘ī and others, has supported the permissibility of the various transmitted forms of the tashahhud and similar formulas by citing the hadith in the Sahīh collections reported from

## Page 11497

the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who said:

They argued: If permission has been given to recite the Quran in seven modes, then other remembrances and supplications are all the more deserving of permission to be recited in several forms. It is well known that what is prescribed is to recite one of these forms, or to alternate between them on different occasions—not to combine them. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not combine these wordings on a single occasion. Rather, he used one on one occasion and another on another occasion—if he did indeed utter both. Where reports differ over a particular wording, however, he may have uttered both, or permitted both; alternatively, one narrator may have retained the wording accurately while the other did not. This applies, for example, to the words “grievously” and “greatly.”

As for such expressions as “and upon the family of Muhammad” and, in the other version, “and upon his wives and his descendants,” there is no doubt that he said one on one occasion and the other on another. Hence, some scholars have cited this as evidence when explaining the meaning of “family.” There are two well-known views on this.

The first is that they are the members of his household who are forbidden to receive charity. This is the expressly stated position of al-Shāfi‘ī and Ahmad. On this view, two positions are reported from Ahmad concerning whether charity is forbidden to the Prophet’s wives and whether they are members of his household:

The first is that they are not members of his household. This is the view of Zayd ibn Arqam, as reported from him by Muslim in his Sahīh.

## Page 11498

The second is that they are members of his household, on the evidence of this hadith, in which he said:

and Allah’s words:

And His words in the account of Abraham:

Sarah was included in this address. Similarly, the Prophet’s statement concerning the mosque founded upon piety—“It is this mosque of mine”—indicates that his mosque has the greater claim to this description, while the mosque of Qubā’ is also founded upon piety, as indicated by the circumstances of the verse’s revelation and its context. Likewise, his wives are included in his family and household, as indicated by the circumstances of the verse’s revelation and its context.

It has thus become clear that the sounder view is that his wives are included in his household, even though their freed slaves are not counted among the freed slaves of his family. This is evidenced by charity being given to Barīrah, the freedwoman of ‘Ā’ishah, whereas he forbade Abū Rāfi‘, the freedman of al-‘Abbās, to receive it.

According to this view, are the descendants of al-Muttalib included among his family and the members of his household who are forbidden to receive charity? Two positions are reported from Ahmad:

The first is that they are included. This is the view of al-Shāfi‘ī.

The second is that they are not included. This is the position of Abū Hanīfah and Mālik.

The second view is that Muhammad’s family consists of his community, or the God-fearing members of his community. This view

and at other times said:

Whoever uses either wording, or alternates between them, has done well. But whoever combines them has departed from the Sunnah. Moreover, doing so is unsound from a rational standpoint, since one wording substitutes for the other, and a substitute is not combined with what it replaces. Anyone who reflects upon what he is saying and understands it will recognize this.

As for the judgment on this matter, we may say: whenever the expression “the family of so-and-so” occurs without qualification in the Quran and Sunnah, it includes that person himself, as in Allah’s words:

“Indeed, Allah chose Adam and Noah, the family of Abraham, and the family of ‘Imrān above all people.”

And His words:

“Except the family of Lot, whom We saved before dawn.”

And His words:

“Admit Pharaoh’s people into the severest punishment.”

And His words:

“Peace be upon Il Yāsīn.”

Another example is the statement of the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace):

The same applies to the expression “members of the household,” as in the words of Allah Most High:

“May Allah’s mercy and blessings be upon you, O members of the household.”

Abraham is included among them. Likewise, his statement:

“Whoever wishes

---

## Page 11500

to receive the fullest measure when invoking blessings upon us, the members of the household, should say: ‘O Allah, bestow blessings upon Muhammad the Prophet’”—and so on, to the end of the hadith.

The reason for this is that the word āl (family) was originally awal: the wāw carried a vowel and was preceded by a short a, so it was changed into an alif, yielding āl. The same applies to bāb (door) and nāb (canine tooth), and, among verbs, qāla (he said), ‘āda (he returned), and similar examples. Whoever says that its original form was ahl, with the hā’ changed into an alif, is mistaken. He has made an unsupported assertion and claimed an irregular letter substitution without evidence, contrary to the original rule.

Moreover, ahl is used in association with inanimate things and people of no elevated standing, as when one says “the members of the household,” “the inhabitants of the city,” “the poor man’s family,” and “the needy man’s family.” By contrast, āl is used only in association with someone of elevated standing whose role is to take charge of others or govern them, so that their affairs ultimately rest with him. From the same root comes iyālah, meaning governance. A person’s āl are those whom he governs and who turn and refer back to him. His own self comes first and has the greatest claim to his governance, and its affairs rest with him. Thus, the expression “the family of so-and-so” includes the person himself. This does not mean that it refers exclusively to him; rather, it includes both him and those whom he governs.

This is why most versions contain the wording, “as You bestowed blessings upon Abraham’s family, and as You blessed Abraham’s family.” Some versions name “Abraham” himself, because he is the primary recipient of blessings and purification; the other members of his household receive these only by virtue of their association with him. Some versions mention both him and his family, drawing attention to both aspects.

If it is asked: Why, then, does it say, “Bestow blessings upon Muhammad and upon Muhammad’s family, and bless

---

## Page 11501

Muhammad and Muhammad’s family,” thus mentioning both Muhammad and his family here, whereas there it uses the wording “Abraham’s family” or “Abraham”?

(The answer is: Blessings upon Muhammad and his family are mentioned by way of request and supplication, whereas blessings upon Abraham are mentioned by way of reporting and recounting. The words “upon Muhammad and upon Muhammad’s family” express a request, while “You bestowed blessings upon Abraham’s family” is a statement of fact. It is fitting to expand a request, because what is sought increases as the request is expanded and decreases as it is curtailed. A statement of fact, however, reports something that has already occurred and passed, admitting neither increase nor decrease. Adding words therefore adds nothing to its meaning, so brevity and concision are more complete, more adequate, and more fitting.

This is why the wording sometimes mentions Abraham’s family and sometimes Abraham: each expression conveys what the other conveys, namely, the blessings already bestowed. It is known that the blessings bestowed upon Abraham were blessings upon Abraham’s family, and that blessings upon Abraham’s family are blessings upon Abraham. Thus, both expressions convey the same meaning, with brevity and concision.

In a request, however, if one were to say, “O Allah, bestow blessings upon Muhammad,” nothing in this would indicate blessings upon Muhammad’s family. It is a request and supplication made through these words, not a report of something that has already occurred and been established. And if one were to say, “Bestow blessings upon

---

## Page 11502

Muhammad’s family,” one would be invoking blessings upon him only within that general designation. Hence the wording, “upon Muhammad and upon Muhammad’s family,” invokes blessings upon him specifically as well as through the blessings invoked upon his family.

If it is said that he is included among his family when the two are mentioned together, just as he is included when his family is mentioned alone, then blessings have been invoked upon him twice: specifically and generally. This follows the view that a general term conjoined to a particular term includes the particular referent. Even if it is said that he is not included, this makes no difference, since invoking blessings upon him specifically suffices.

Furthermore, this wording makes clear that blessings upon the rest of his family are sought only in conjunction with him: he is the primary recipient, on whose account blessings are sought for his family. This explanation is completed by answering the familiar question concerning the words:

“Just as You bestowed blessings upon Abraham.”

These suggest Abraham’s superiority, because what is being compared is inferior to that with which it is compared. Various weak answers have been given to this question.

One answer is that the comparison relates only to the blessings upon the first-mentioned. Thus, the words “Bestow blessings upon Muhammad” constitute a separate statement, while the words “and upon Muhammad’s family, just as You bestowed blessings upon Abraham” begin a new statement. Al-ʿUmrānī transmitted this from al-Shāfiʿī, but its attribution to al-Shāfiʿī is certainly false: it is unworthy of his learning and eloquence. Such wording is awkward and exceedingly strained, and it raises questions of Arabic grammar whose discussion would be out of place here.

---

## Page 11503

Second:

Some deny that the standard of comparison must be superior to what is compared with it, maintaining that the two may be equal. The proponent of this view says that the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) is superior to Abraham in respects other than the blessings bestowed upon them, while they are equal in those blessings.

This, too, is weak. Receiving blessings from Allah is among the highest honours, if not the highest, and Muhammad is foremost among all creation in this regard. How could it be otherwise, when Allah commanded us to invoke blessings upon him after declaring that He and His angels bestow blessings upon him? Furthermore, Allah and His angels bestow blessings upon those who teach goodness, and he is the best of all who teach goodness. The evidence is abundant, beyond what this answer can accommodate.

Third:

Some say that Abraham’s family includes prophets whose equals are not found among Muhammad’s family. Thus, when one asks for blessings equal to those bestowed upon these prophets, his household receives the share befitting them, since they rank below the prophets, while the remainder goes to Muhammad (may Allah bless him and grant him peace). He thereby receives a distinction in the blessings bestowed upon him that neither Abraham nor anyone else receives. This answer is better than the preceding ones.

Better still is to say:

Muhammad himself belongs to Abraham’s family, as ʿAlī ibn Abī Talhah narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning Allah’s words:

“Indeed, Allah chose Adam, Noah, the family of Abraham and the family of ʿImrān above all people.”

Ibn ʿAbbās said: “Muhammad belongs to Abraham’s family.” This is clear: if other prophets are included among Abraham’s family, then he has an even greater claim to inclusion among them. Thus, our words:

“Just as You bestowed blessings upon the family of

---

## Page 11504

Abraham” encompass blessings upon him and upon all the other prophets descended from Abraham’s family. Allah Most High said:

“And We placed among his descendants prophethood and the Scripture.”

He then commanded us to invoke blessings specifically upon Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, equal to those we invoked upon him together with the rest of Abraham’s family collectively. His household receives the share befitting them, while the remainder goes to him. Thus, this immense measure of blessings is sought for him.

Clearly, this is a tremendous distinction through which he receives more than Abraham or anyone else. For if what is sought through the supplication is merely equal to the blessings used as the standard of comparison, while he has an ample share of the blessings being compared and receives most of what is sought, then his share of the blessings being compared alone exceeds that of Abraham or anyone else—even if the total sought equals the blessings being compared. Added to this is his share of the blessings used as the standard of comparison. This reveals his superiority over each of the prophets in a manner befitting him. May Allah bestow blessings and abundant peace upon him, and reward him on our behalf with the finest reward He has granted a messenger on behalf of his community.

O Allah, bestow blessings upon Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, just as You bestowed blessings upon the family of Abraham. You are indeed Praiseworthy, Glorious. And bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, just as You blessed the family of Abraham. You are indeed Praiseworthy, Glorious.

## Page 11505

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

When invoking blessings upon the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is it better to do so quietly or aloud? Has it been reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, “Stir your limbs by invoking blessings upon me,” or not? And what of the report attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās that “he instructed them to raise their voices so that those who had not heard could hear”? Please give us a ruling; may you be rewarded.

He answered:

The aforementioned report is a fabricated lie, by scholarly consensus. The same applies to the other report, and likewise to all other reports about raising the voice when invoking blessings upon him, such as those narrated by vendors to promote their wares, or by beggars—storytellers and others—to gather people and collect money from them, and similar purposes.

Invoking blessings upon him is a form of supplication, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, taught his community when they said:

“We have learned how to greet you with peace, but how should we invoke blessings upon you?”

He replied: “Say: ‘O Allah, bestow blessings upon Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, just as You bestowed blessings upon the family of Abraham. You are indeed Praiseworthy, Glorious. And bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, just as You blessed the family of Abraham. You are indeed Praiseworthy, Glorious.’”

This was recorded in the two Sahīh collections. The Sunnah in all supplication is to recite quietly, unless there is a reason for which raising the voice is prescribed.

## Page 11506

Allah Most High says:

“Call upon your Lord humbly and privately. Indeed, He does not love those who transgress.”

And He says of Zechariah:

“When he called upon his Lord in a quiet voice.”

Indeed, this is the Sunnah for all remembrance of Allah, as He, Most High, says:

“Remember your Lord within yourself, humbly and fearfully, without raising your voice, morning and evening.”

It is reported in the two Sahīh collections that the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, were travelling with him and began raising their voices. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“O people, be gentle with yourselves! You are not calling upon one who is deaf or absent. Rather, you are calling upon One who is All-Hearing and Near. The One you call upon is closer to each of you than the neck of his mount.”

What we have mentioned concerning invoking blessings upon him and supplication is a matter of scholarly agreement. All scholars instruct a person, when supplicating, to invoke blessings upon the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in the same manner as he supplicates, without raising his voice more when invoking blessings upon him than when supplicating. This applies whether he is praying—as in the full ritual prayer or the funeral prayer—or is outside prayer, even immediately after the talbiyah (pilgrimage invocation). He raises his voice for the talbiyah, then afterwards invokes blessings upon the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and supplicates quietly.

Likewise, between the proclamations of Allah’s greatness at Eid, if he remembers Allah and invokes blessings upon the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, he does not recite these aloud, even though he proclaims Allah’s greatness aloud.

Similarly, if he confines himself to invoking blessings upon him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, outside prayer—for example, when the Prophet is mentioned and he invokes blessings upon him—no scholar has recommended raising

He was asked about someone who says:

“O Allah, send blessings upon our master Muhammad and the family of Muhammad until none of Your blessings remain. He answered:

All praise is due to Allah. This supplication has not been transmitted from any of the early generations.

As for the words, “until none of Your blessings remain, and none of Your mercy remains”: if the speaker means that what Allah possesses of these should be exhausted, then he is ignorant, for the goodness that Allah possesses is inexhaustible. If he means that, through his supplication, he is giving him everything he could possibly be given, this too is ignorance, for his supplication is not what makes that possible.

“Indeed, the angels invoke blessings upon any one of you as long as he remains

Shaykh al-Islām, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Section

The well-known, explicitly stated position of Imam Ahmad is that one should supplicate during prayer only with prescribed supplications transmitted in the reports. Al-Athram said:

I asked Ahmad, “What should I supplicate with after the tashahhud?”

He replied, “What has been transmitted in the reports.”

I said to him, “Did the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, not say, ‘Then let him choose whatever supplication he wishes’?”

He replied, “He should choose from what has been transmitted in the reports.”

I asked him again, and he said, “What is in the reports.”

I say: I have already explained part of the basis for this in light of His words:

“Indeed, He does not love the transgressors.”
