## Page 11598

to say it like this’—and he pointed with his finger—‘greeting his brother on his right and on his left.’” In another version, he said:

“Is it not enough for one of you—or one of them—to place his hand on his thigh, then greet his brother on his right and on his left?”

Muslim’s wording is:

“We prayed with the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. When we gave the salutation, we would gesture with our hands, saying, ‘Peace be upon you.’ The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, looked at us and said: ‘Why are you gesturing with your hands as though they were the tails of unruly horses? When one of you gives the salutation, let him turn towards his companion without gesturing with his hand.’”

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, thus commanded stillness in prayer. This requires stillness throughout the prayer, and stillness requires coming to rest. Whoever does not come to rest has not remained still in prayer. His command to remain still in prayer accords with Allah Most High’s command to observe humble devotion in it. Those most bound to follow this are the people of hadith.

Whoever supposes that his prohibition against raising the hands refers to raising them to shoulder level when bowing and when rising from bowing, and interprets it accordingly, is mistaken. The hadith itself explains that, when they gave the concluding salutation in prayer, they would gesture with their hands towards those they were greeting on their right and left. This is clarified by his words:

“Why do I see you raising your hands as though they were the tails of horses

---

## Page 11599

that are unruly?”

Shums (“unruly”) is the plural of shamūs, commonly pronounced shamūs with a sād. It describes a horse that swishes its tail to the right and left—a movement without stillness. As for raising the hands when bowing and when rising from bowing, just as they are raised at the opening of the prayer, this is prescribed by agreement of the Muslims. How, then, could the hadith prohibit it?

His words, “Remain still in prayer,” encompass this as well. Thus, one of the imams who did not regard this raising of the hands as prescribed once prayed beside ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak. When Ibn al-Mubārak raised his hands, he asked him, “Are you trying to fly?” He replied, “If I am flying the first time, then I am flying the second time; otherwise, I am not.” This refutes the reasoning he had put forward.

Moreover, reports from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his Companions establishing this raising of the hands have been mass-transmitted. Thus, the hadith cannot be a prohibition of it, nor can it contradict those reports. Even if they did conflict, the hadiths establishing this raising of the hands are numerous and mass-transmitted, and must be given precedence over a report that is not mass-transmitted, were it to contradict them.

This raising of the hands is accompanied by stillness. His words, “Remain still in prayer,” therefore do not preclude it, just as they do not preclude raising the hands at the opening of the prayer or the other actions of prayer. Rather, his command, “Remain still,” requires stillness in every

---

## Page 11600

part of the prayer. This entails the obligation to remain still when bowing, prostrating, standing after bowing, and sitting between prostrations. This makes clear that stillness is prescribed in all the actions of prayer as far as possible. Thus, one maintains composure even during its transitions, which culminate in movement; stillness in these consists of moving at a measured rather than a rapid pace, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, instructed when walking to prayer. If this applies to movement towards prayer, how much more so to movement within it? He said:

“When you come to prayer, do not come rushing. Come with tranquility. Pray whatever you catch, and make up whatever you miss.”

This also constitutes independent evidence on the issue. Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, said: I heard the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, say:

“When the call to commence prayer is given, do not come rushing. Come walking, with tranquility. Pray whatever you catch, and make up whatever you miss.”

This was narrated by al-Bukhārī, Muslim, Abū Dāwūd, and Ibn Mājah. Abū Dāwūd said—and al-Tirmidhī said likewise—that Ibn Abī Dhi’b, Ibrāhīm ibn Sa‘d, Ma‘mar, and Shu‘ayb ibn Abī Hamzah narrated from al-Zuhrī the wording:

“And complete whatever you miss.”

Ibn ‘Uyaynah narrated from al-Zuhrī the wording, “Make it up.” Muhammad ibn ‘Amr, reporting from Abū Salamah, from Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, and Ja‘far ibn Abī Rabī‘ah, reporting from al-A‘raj, from Abū Hurayrah, related the wording, “Complete it.” Ibn Mas‘ūd also related from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the wording, “Complete it.” Abū Dāwūd narrated from Abū

---

## Page 11601

Hurayrah, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who said:

“Come to prayer with tranquility. Pray whatever you catch, and make up whatever you miss.”

Abū Dāwūd said: Ibn Sīrīn likewise narrated from Abū Hurayrah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—the wording, “Let him make it up.” Abū Rāfi‘ likewise narrated this from Abū Hurayrah. Both “Complete it” and “Make it up” were reported from Abū Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him; the reports from him differed.

Since the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded tranquility when going to prayer and prohibited rushing—which means moving quickly in this context—because going to prayer is a means to performing it, then prayer itself has an even greater claim to tranquility being commanded within it and haste being prohibited. It follows, all the more certainly, that someone bowing or prostrating is commanded to remain tranquil and forbidden to hurry. This is especially so because he commanded tranquility after hearing the call to commence prayer, which obliges a person to go to it, and forbade him to occupy himself instead with voluntary prayer—even if proceeding tranquilly meant missing part of the prayer. He commanded him to remain tranquil and to pray whatever he had missed on his own after the imam’s salutation, giving this precedence over rushing to prayer. This indicates how emphatically rushing to prayer is forbidden; how much more so rushing within it!

This is clarified by what Abū Dāwūd narrated from Abū Thumāmah al-Hannāt, from Ka‘b ibn ‘Ujrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When one of you performs ablution thoroughly and then sets out for the mosque, he must not interlace his fingers, for he is in prayer.”

Thus, while a person is walking to prayer, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, forbade him to do what

---

## Page 11602

he forbade him to do in prayer, whether in speech or action, even when praying alone. How, then, should someone actually praying conduct himself with regard to such walking and other actions? If he is forbidden to walk hurriedly and hastily, and commanded to proceed with tranquility—even if he misses part of the prayer with the imam and must make it up—then he is all the more clearly commanded to observe tranquility within the prayer itself.

Further evidence for this is that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, commands tranquility and moderation in movement and walking generally in His Book, saying:

“Be moderate in your pace and lower your voice.”

And He, Most High, says:

“The servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth humbly, and when the ignorant address them, they say words of peace.”

Al-Hasan and others explained this as “with tranquility and dignity.”

Thus, He tells us that these are the servants of the Most Merciful. If a person is commanded to observe tranquility and dignity in ordinary actions involving movement, how much more does this apply to acts of worship? And how much more to those acts within worship that involve stillness, such as bowing and prostration?

These proofs require tranquility during transitions, such as raising and lowering oneself, rising and descending. As for the actual postures that these transitions are intended to reach—bowing itself, prostration itself, and standing and sitting themselves—these are, by their very nature, states of stillness. Whoever does not remain still in them has not performed them. He is merely like someone who lowers himself to sit but never actually sits, or someone who reaches for food without eating any of it, or puts it to his mouth without tasting it.

Moreover, Allah Most High has enjoined bowing and prostration in the Book

---

## Page 11604

and when an action of his is performed in compliance with a command or to explain something stated without detail, it carries the same ruling as that which it fulfils and explains. Thus, since he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, performed one bow and two prostrations in every unit of prayer, both were obligatory. By doing so, he fulfilled Allah’s command to bow and prostrate and explained what the Quran had mentioned without elaboration. Likewise, his Sunnah is the reference for how to prostrate.

He used to offer obligatory and voluntary prayers, and people prayed during his lifetime. He never prayed without returning to an upright posture after bowing and prostrating and coming to rest in all the postures of prayer. Everyone who transmitted accounts of his obligatory and voluntary prayers reported this. People prayed during his lifetime, and he never prayed without returning to an upright posture after bowing and prostrating and coming to rest. His Companions likewise prayed in this manner during his lifetime. This establishes the obligation to pause and come to rest in these movements, just as it establishes their required number: two prostrations for every bow.

Furthermore, his constant observance of this in every prayer, every day, despite the great number of prayers, is among the strongest proofs that it is obligatory. Had it not been obligatory, he would have omitted it at least once to demonstrate that doing so was permissible, or he would have explained verbally that it could be omitted. Since he never indicated, either by word or deed, that it could be omitted, while consistently observing it himself, this is evidence that it is obligatory.

Furthermore, it is authentically reported from him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in Sahīh al-Bukhārī:

## Page 11605

that he said to Mālik ibn al-Huwayrith and his companion:

“When the time for prayer comes, give the call to prayer and announce its commencement, and let the older of you lead you both. And pray as you have seen me pray.”

He thus commanded them to pray as they had seen him pray. This entails that the imam must lead people in prayer as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to lead them. Nothing contradicts this or restricts its scope, for the imam has obligations that do not apply to someone following an imam or praying alone.

An authentic report in the two Sahīh collections relates that Sahl ibn Sa‘d said:

“I saw the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, stand on the pulpit and proclaim ‘Allah is the Greatest.’ The people behind him did likewise while he was on the pulpit. He then stepped backwards down from it and prostrated at its base. He then returned and continued until he had finished his prayer. Then he turned towards the people and said, ‘O people, I did this only so that you would follow my example and learn how I pray.’”

In the Sunan collections of Abū Dāwūd and al-Nasā’ī, Sālim al-Barrād said:

“We came to Uqbah ibn Āmir al-Ansārī, Abū Mas‘ūd, and said to him, ‘Tell us about the prayer of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.’ He stood before us in the mosque and proclaimed ‘Allah is the Greatest.’ When he bowed, he placed his hands on his knees, with his fingers below them, and held his elbows apart until every part of his body had come to rest. Then he said, ‘Allah hears whoever praises Him,’ and stood until every part of his body had come to rest. Then he proclaimed ‘Allah is the Greatest’ and prostrated, placing his palms on the ground and holding his elbows apart until every part had come to rest.

---

## Page 11606

of his body. Then he raised his head and sat until every part of his body had come to rest. He did the same again, then prayed four units of prayer like this one, completing his prayer. Then he said, ‘This is how we saw the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, pray.’”

This represents the consensus of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. They would only pray with composure. Whenever any of them saw someone praying without composure, he would rebuke him and forbid him from doing so. None of them objected to anyone who rebuked this. Their words and actions thus establish their consensus that stillness and composure are obligatory in prayer. Had this not been obligatory, they would sometimes have omitted it, just as they sometimes omitted what was not obligatory.

Furthermore, in the Arabic language, bowing and prostration require a person to remain still when bending down and when placing his face on the ground. Merely lowering oneself and rising again is not called bowing or prostration. Whoever calls it bowing and prostration has misunderstood the language. He must therefore provide linguistic evidence that someone doing this is described as bowing and prostrating before that person can be considered to have fulfilled the command, and before it can be said that this required command is fulfilled by performing whatever falls within the scope of those terms.

Such an argument is valid only once it is known that these movements alone are called bowing and prostration in the language. Yet there is no way to establish this, nor any evidence for it. Whoever makes this claim therefore speaks without knowledge concerning the Book of Allah and the Arabic language.

If doubt arises as to whether a person is prostrating or not, he cannot, by unanimous agreement, be regarded as having fulfilled the command. For the obligation is known, whereas the performance of

---

## Page 11607

the obligatory act is uncertain. This is like someone who is certain that he owes a prayer or zakah but doubts whether he has performed it. This is a principle that ought to be understood, for it cuts off the argument of the disputant who says, “Such a person is called prostrating and bowing in the Arabic language.” He has spoken without knowledge or proof, and when asked for evidence, he has no answer. The sound argument belongs to the one who says, “We cannot know that he has discharged his obligation except through prostration and bowing in their recognized forms.”

It may then be said: If the expressions “bowing and prostration” were used in Arabic for merely bringing the face into contact with the ground without composure, someone rubbing his cheek in the dust would be prostrating. So too would someone pressing his nose into the dust—that is, bringing his nose into contact with raghām, meaning dust. This would be especially true according to the disputant who says that prostration is accomplished by placing the nose on the ground, without the forehead and without composure. Pecking at the ground with the nose would thus be prostration. Yet it is well known that this is not how the Arabs use their language, just as they do not call a crow’s pecking, or anything similar, prostration. Were that the case, someone placing his face on the ground to suck, bite, or move something lying there, or to do anything similar, would be called prostrating.

Furthermore, Allah has commanded that prayer be observed carefully and consistently, and has condemned neglecting it and being heedless of it. He says at the beginning of Surah al-Mu’minūn:

“Successful indeed are the believers.”

“Carefully observe the prayers, especially the middle prayer, and stand before Allah in devout obedience.”

## Page 11609

And these verses entail censure of anyone who neglects any obligation of prayer, even if he outwardly performs it—for example, by failing to pray at its prescribed time or failing to fulfil its conditions and pillars, whether outward or inward acts. This is how the early generations explained them.

In the Tafsīr of ‘Abd ibn Humayd—and he also cited it from Ibn al-Mundhir in his Tafsīr through ‘Abd’s narration—it is reported: Rawh narrated to us from Sa‘īd, from Qatādah, concerning the words,

“and who carefully observe their prayers,”

that this means observing the ablution required for them, their prescribed times and their bowing.

Abū Bakr ibn al-Mundhir also reported in his Tafsīr, through Abū ‘Abd al-Rahmān, from ‘Abd Allāh, who said:

‘Abd Allāh was told, “Allah frequently mentions prayer in the Quran:

‘who are constant in their prayer,’

‘who are humble in their prayer,’

and ‘who carefully observe their prayer.’”

‘Abd Allāh replied, “That refers to observing their prescribed times.”

They said, “Abū ‘Abd al-Rahmān, we thought that referred only to abandoning prayer.”

He replied, “Abandoning it is disbelief.”

Sa‘īd ibn Mansūr reported: Abū Mu‘āwiyah narrated to us: al-A‘mash narrated to us from Muslim, from Masrūq, concerning Allah’s words,

“and who carefully observe their prayer.”

He said, “At their prescribed times.”

They said, “Abū ‘Abd al-Rahmān, we thought that referred only to abandoning prayer.”

He replied, “Abandoning it is disbelief.”

It was also reported through Sa‘īd ibn Abī Maryam that the words,

“yet are heedless of their prayer,”

mean neglecting its prescribed time.

He also narrated from Abū Thawr, from Ibn Jurayj, concerning the words,

“and who carefully observe their prayers,”

that these are the obligatory prayers, whereas those mentioned in Surah Sa’ala Sā’il are voluntary prayers. This is a weak opinion.

---

## Page 11610

Section

As for the prescribed length of prayer when leading others, the model is the prayer of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. In Sahīh al-Bukhārī, Abū Qilābah reports from Mālik ibn al-Huwayrith:

“When the time for prayer comes, let one of you give the call to prayer, and let the eldest of you lead you. Then pray as you have seen me pray.”

As for standing, Sahīh Muslim contains the report of Jābir ibn Samurah:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would recite ‘Qāf. By the glorious Quran’ and similar surahs in the dawn prayer, and his subsequent prayers were shorter.”

That is, he would make the prayers following the dawn prayer brief. As also reported from him in Sahīh Muslim:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would recite ‘By the night when it covers’ in the noon prayer, a similar amount in the afternoon prayer, and more than that in the dawn prayer.”

In the two Sahīhs, Abū Barzah al-Aslamī said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would perform the midday prayer—which you call the first prayer—as soon as the sun passed its zenith. He would perform the afternoon prayer, after which one of us could return to his dwelling at the farthest end of Medina while the sun was still bright—the narrator said, ‘I have forgotten what he said about the sunset prayer’—and he preferred to delay the night prayer, which you call the nightfall prayer.

---

## Page 11611

and he disliked sleeping before it and conversing after it. He would finish the dawn prayer when a man could recognize the person sitting beside him, and he would recite between sixty and a hundred verses in it.”

Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

“We estimated how long the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, stood in the noon and afternoon prayers. We estimated his standing in the first two units of the noon prayer to be the time needed to recite thirty verses—the length of Sūrat Alif Lām Mīm al-Sajdah. We estimated his standing in the first two units of the afternoon prayer to be as long as his standing in the last two units of the noon prayer, and his standing in the last two units of the afternoon prayer to be half that.”

Reported by Muslim, Abū Dāwūd and al-Nasā’ī.

In the two Sahīhs and elsewhere, Jābir ibn Samurah reported that Umar said to Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqās:

“The people have complained about you in everything, even the prayer.”

He replied, “As for me, I lengthen the first two units and shorten the last two, sparing no effort to follow the example of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in prayer.”

Umar said, “That is what we would expect of you, Abū Ishāq.”

Also in Sahīh Muslim, Abū Saʿīd, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

“The noon prayer would begin, and a man could go to al-Baqīʿ, relieve himself, perform ablution and then return while the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was still in the first unit, so long did he make it.”

Also in Sahīh Muslim, Abū Wā’il said:

“One day, Ammār ibn Yāsir delivered a sermon to us, speaking concisely and eloquently. We said, ‘Abū al-Yaqzān, you have spoken eloquently and concisely; if only you had spoken a little longer!’

“He replied, ‘I heard the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, say: “Indeed, the length of a man’s prayer and the brevity of

---

## Page 11612

his sermon are a sign of his understanding. So lengthen the prayer and shorten the sermon, for some eloquence is indeed magic.”’”

In Sahīh Muslim, Jābir ibn Samurah, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

“I used to offer the prayers with the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his prayer was moderate.”

That is, it was of medium length. The practice he established for his community falls within the lightening of prayer prescribed for prayer leaders, for lightening is relative. The Sunnah therefore determines its proper measure.

An example is the report narrated by al-Bukhārī and Muslim in their two Sahīhs from Jābir, may Allah be pleased with him, who said:

“Muʿādh used to pray with the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, then return and lead us in prayer—on one occasion he said, ‘Then return and lead his people in prayer’—and he informed the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace—on one occasion he said, ‘The night prayer: Muʿādh prayed with the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, then came to lead his people in prayer’—and he recited al-Baqarah. A man withdrew from the congregation and prayed separately. He was told, ‘You have acted hypocritically.’

“He replied, ‘I have not acted hypocritically.’ He then went to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and said, ‘Muʿādh prays with you, then returns and leads us in prayer. Messenger of Allah, we are people who work with water-drawing camels and labour with our own hands. He came to lead us in prayer and recited Sūrat al-Baqarah.’

“He said, ‘Are you driving people away, Muʿādh? Recite such-and-such; recite such-and-such.’”

Abū al-Zubayr said: “‘Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High’ and ‘By the night as it envelops.’”

In a narration recorded by al-Bukhārī, Jābir, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

“A man came with two water-drawing camels after night had fallen and found Muʿādh

---

## Page 11613

praying—and he related a similar account, concluding: ‘Why did you not recite “Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High,” “By the sun and its brightness,” and “By the night as it envelops” in prayer? For behind you pray the weak, the elderly, and those who have matters to attend to.’”

In the two Sahīhs, Abū Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

“A man came to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and said, ‘I stay away from the dawn prayer because so-and-so makes the prayer so long for us.’ I never saw the Messenger of Allah angrier when delivering an admonition than he was that day. He said, ‘People! Some of you drive others away. Whoever leads the people in prayer should keep it brief, for behind him are the elderly, the weak, and those who have matters to attend to.’”

In another narration: “For among them are the weak and the elderly.” In another: “Let him lighten the prayer, for among them are the sick, the weak, and those who have matters to attend to.”

In Sahīh al-Bukhārī, Abū Qatādah reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“I begin the prayer intending to make it long, but then I hear a child crying, so I shorten it, not wishing to cause hardship to his mother.”

As for “the duration of the remaining essential acts of prayer, together with standing,” al-Bukhārī and Muslim narrated in their two Sahīhs, through Sharīk ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Namir, that Anas ibn Mālik, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

“I have never prayed behind an imam whose prayer was lighter or more complete than that of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.”

In another narration through Sharīk, Anas said:

“He would hear a child crying and lighten the prayer for fear that his mother would become distressed.”

They also narrated in their two Sahīhs, on the authority of

---

## Page 11614

ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Suhayb, from Anas ibn Mālik, may Allah be pleased with him, who said:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, kept the prayer brief yet complete.” In another wording: “He kept the prayer brief and performed it fully.”

They also narrated from Qatādah, from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“I begin the prayer intending to make it long, but then I hear a child crying and shorten my prayer, knowing how deeply his crying distresses his mother.”

Muslim related it through Thābit, from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, who said:

“When the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, heard a child crying while accompanying his mother during the prayer, he would recite a brief surah—or a short surah.”

Muslim also narrated that Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

“I have never prayed behind anyone whose prayer was briefer or more complete than that of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The different parts of his prayer were proportionate in length, as were those of Abū Bakr’s prayer. When ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, took over, he lengthened the dawn prayer.”

Qatādah also narrated from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was among those whose prayers were lightest while remaining complete.”

Thus, when Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, said, “I have never prayed behind an imam whose prayer was lighter or more complete than that of the Messenger of Allah,” he meant that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, offered the lightest

---

## Page 11615

prayer of any imam, as well as the most complete. This was because the different parts of his prayer were balanced and proportionate, as in the other wording, “His prayer was balanced,” and another wording, “The different parts of his prayer were similar in length.” Its lightness came from keeping the standing and sitting brief, while its completeness came from prolonging the bowing and prostration. Had he meant that the very same act—such as standing—was both the briefest and the most complete, that would have been contradictory. This is why he explained how the Prophet shortened the prayer when a child cried: by reciting a short surah. He also explained that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb lengthened the dawn prayer. What he lengthened was the recitation, for ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, would recite Surah Yūnus, Surah Hūd and Surah Yūsuf in the dawn prayer.

This is clarified by the report that Abū Dāwūd narrated in his Sunan from Anas ibn Mālik, may Allah be pleased with him, who said:

“I have never prayed behind anyone whose prayer was briefer, yet complete, than that of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. When the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘Allah hears those who praise Him,’ he would remain standing until we would say, ‘He has become forgetful.’ Then he would say ‘Allah is greatest’ and prostrate. He would also sit between the two prostrations until we would say, ‘He has become forgetful.’”

Likewise, al-Bukhārī and Muslim narrated in their two Sahīh collections through Hammād ibn Zayd, from Thābit, from Anas, who said:

“I spare no effort to lead you in prayer as the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to lead us.”

Thābit said:

“Anas used to do something that I do not see you doing: when he raised his head from bowing, he would stand upright until someone would say, ‘He has forgotten.’”

Al-Bukhārī also narrated through

---

## Page 11616

Shuʿba, from Thābit, who said:

Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, said, describing to us the prayer of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“When he prayed, after raising his head from bowing, he would remain standing until someone would say, ‘He has forgotten.’”

These authentic reports from Anas explicitly state that, in the prayer which the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, kept brief yet complete—the briefest and most complete of prayers—he would remain standing after bowing until someone would say, “He has forgotten,” and would sit between the two prostrations until someone would say, “He has forgotten.”

If he did this in such a prayer, then it is established by the agreement of the Muslims and the mass-transmitted Sunnah that his bowing and prostration were no shorter than these two upright postures. Indeed, many scholars say that it is neither prescribed nor permissible to make these two upright postures as long as the bowing and prostration; rather, they should be shorter.

In the two Sahīh collections, Shuʿba narrated from al-Hakam, who said:

“A man—whose name he mentioned, and whom Ghundar identified in one narration as Matar ibn Nājiya—took control of Kufa during the time of Ibn al-Ashʿath. He ordered Abū ʿUbayda ibn ʿAbd Allāh to lead the people in prayer. When he prayed, after raising his head from bowing, he would remain standing for as long as it takes me to say: ‘O Allah, our Lord, to You belongs all praise, filling the heavens, filling the earth, and filling whatever else You will. You are worthy of praise and glory. None can withhold what You give, and none can give what You withhold; nor can worldly fortune avail its possessor before You.’”

Al-Hakam said: “I mentioned this to ʿAbd al-Rahmān ibn Abī

---

## Page 11617

Laylā, who said: ‘I heard al-Barā’ ibn ʿĀzib say: “In the prayer of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, his standing, bowing, standing after raising his head from bowing, prostration, and sitting between the two prostrations were nearly equal in duration.”’”

Shuʿba said: “I mentioned this to ʿAmr ibn Murra, who said, ‘I have seen ʿAbd al-Rahmān ibn Abī Laylā, and his prayer was not like that.’”

Matar’s wording, narrated from Shuʿba, is:

“The Prophet’s bowing, prostration, sitting between the two prostrations, and standing after raising his head from bowing—excluding the standing and sitting—were nearly equal in duration.”

It also appears in the Sahīh and the Sunan collections, through Hilāl ibn Abī Humayd, from Ibn Abī Laylā, from al-Barā’ ibn ʿĀzib, who said:

“I closely observed the prayer with Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. I found that his standing, then his bowing, then his standing upright after bowing, then his prostration, then his sitting between the two prostrations, then his prostration, then his sitting between the final salutation and leaving were nearly equal in duration.”

This is supported by what Muslim, Abū Dāwūd and al-Nasā’ī narrated from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, may Allah be pleased with him: when the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, raised his head from bowing, he would say:

“Allah hears those who praise Him. O Allah, our Lord, to You belongs all praise, filling the heavens, filling the earth, and filling whatever else You will. You are worthy of praise and glory—the truest words a servant has spoken—and we are all Your servants. None can withhold what You give, and none can give what You withhold; nor can worldly fortune avail its possessor before You.”

His words, “The truest words a servant has spoken,” appear exactly thus in the hadith. This phrase is

---

## Page 11618

the predicate of an omitted subject.

As for the wording cited by some jurists and Sufi authors:

“What the servant says is true,”

this is a distortion, as the scholars of hadith and Sunnah unanimously agree. It has no basis in the transmitted reports, and its meaning is also unsound. A servant may speak both truth and falsehood, whereas the Lord, glorified and exalted is He, speaks the truth and guides to the right way. As He, exalted is He, says:

“The truth—and the truth I speak.”

Moreover, prayer is founded solely upon praising Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Muslim and others narrated from ‘Atā’, from Ibn ‘Abbās, may Allah be pleased with them both:

“When the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, raised his head from bowing, he would say: ‘O Allah, our Lord, to You belongs all praise, filling the heavens, filling the earth, filling all that is between them, and filling whatever else You will. You are worthy of praise and glory. The truest words a servant has spoken—and we are all Your servants—are: None can withhold what You give, and none can give what You withhold; nor can worldly fortune avail its possessor before You.’”

Muslim and others narrated that ‘Abd Allāh ibn Abī Awfā said:

“When the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, raised his head from bowing, he would say: ‘Allah hears those who praise Him. O Allah, our Lord, to You belongs all praise, filling the heavens, filling the earth, and filling whatever else You will.’”

In another narration, Muslim adds after this that he

---

## Page 11619

would say:

“O Allah, purify me of sins and misdeeds as a white garment is cleansed of dirt.”

If it is asked: “If this was the prayer of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, which the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, unanimously transmitted from him, and which the compilers of the Sahīh, Sunan, and Musnad collections transmitted through these and other routes—and prayer is the pillar of religion—how did this escape some jurists of Iraq and elsewhere? They did not regard standing upright after bowing and sitting between the two prostrations as actions comparable in duration to bowing and prostration, nor did they recommend any remembrance during this standing beyond the words of praise, ‘Our Lord, to You belongs all praise.’ Some students of jurisprudence even said that if a person prolonged it considerably, his prayer would become invalid.”

The answer is: The reason for this and other such matters is that the established practice of the Sunnah was for rulers and military commanders to lead the Muslims in prayer. The commander responsible for jihad was also the leader of prayer during the time of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, his rightly guided caliphs, and thereafter, into the period of Abbasid rule. The caliph himself would lead the people in the five daily prayers and the Friday prayer; the Muslims knew no other practice.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, foretold the changes that would occur among the rulers after him, even saying:

“After me there will be rulers who delay the prayer beyond its appointed time. So offer the prayer at its appointed time, and let your prayer with them be voluntary.”

Among these rulers were some who would delay it

---

## Page 11620

beyond its appointed time, until the prescribed time for it had passed. Some of them also failed to complete the takbīrs (“Allah is Most Great”)—that is, they did not pronounce them aloud when moving into bowing and other postures—and some did not properly complete the two upright postures. These practices spread among the people: the young grew up with them, and the old grew elderly observing them, until even many of the elite thought that nothing else was the Sunnah. When rulers came who revived the Sunnah, however, this became apparent.

Thus al-Bukhārī narrated in his Sahīh, from Qatāda, from Ikrima, who said:

“I prayed behind an elderly man in Mecca, and he pronounced twenty-two takbīrs. I said to Ibn Abbās, ‘He really is a fool!’ He replied, ‘May your mother be bereaved of you! This is the Sunnah of Abū al-Qāsim, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.’”

In Abū Bishr’s narration from Ikrima, he said:

“I saw a man at the Station of Abraham pronouncing the takbīr whenever he lowered or raised himself, stood up or went down. I told Ibn Abbās, and he said, ‘Was that not the prayer of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace? May you be motherless!’”

What this means is that this imam pronounced the takbīrs aloud. The imams behind whom Ikrima prayed did not do so, while Ibn Abbās had not been an imam whose practice in this regard would have been known. Ikrima therefore objected to it until Ibn Abbās explained it to him. As for saying the takbīr itself, no one was in any doubt about that.

Similarly, most imams of later times do not pronounce the takbīrs aloud; rather, the muezzin or someone else does so. Most people therefore suppose that this is the Sunnah. Yet there is no disagreement

---

## Page 11621

among the scholars that this is not the Sunnah. Rather, they agree on what has been established among them through mass transmission from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: that neither the muezzin nor the other worshippers following the imam regularly pronounce the takbīrs aloud.

Bilāl likewise did not pronounce them aloud behind the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. However, when this is needed because the imam’s voice is weak or because of the distance, they have argued that it is permissible on the grounds that “Abū Bakr al-Siddīq, may Allah be pleased with him, would make the takbīrs audible to the people behind the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, during his illness.” Indeed, the jurists have even disagreed over whether a worshipper’s pronouncing them aloud behind the imam without any need invalidates his prayer.

A similar example is the report recorded in the two Sahīhs and the Sunan collections from Mutarrif ibn Abd Allāh ibn al-Shikhkhīr, who said:

“Imrān ibn Husayn and I prayed behind Alī ibn Abī Tālib. Whenever he prostrated, he pronounced the takbīr; whenever he raised his head, he pronounced the takbīr; and whenever he rose after the two rakʿahs, he pronounced the takbīr. When he had completed the prayer, Imrān ibn Husayn took my hand and said, ‘This man has reminded me of the prayer of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace’—or he said, ‘He has led us in prayer as Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prayed.’”

Thus, when he pronounced the takbīrs aloud, Imrān and Mutarrif heard him, just as others did.

Another similar example is the report also recorded in the two Sahīhs and the Sunan collections from Abū Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him:

“He used to pronounce the takbīrs in every prayer, whether obligatory or otherwise: he would pronounce the takbīr

---

## Page 11622

when he stood up, then pronounce the takbīr when he prostrated, then pronounce the takbīr when he raised his head, then pronounce the takbīr when he rose after sitting following the two rakʿahs. He would do this in every rakʿah until he completed the prayer. Then, when he finished, he would say, ‘By Him in Whose hand is my soul, my prayer most closely resembles the prayer of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. This was indeed how he prayed until he departed this world.’”

Abū Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, used to do this when he was governor of Medina. Muʿāwiya alternated between him and Marwān ibn al-Hakam in the governorship of Medina, appointing one at one time and the other at another. Marwān would appoint a deputy, while Abū Hurayra would lead them in a prayer that more closely resembled the prayer of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, than did the prayer of Marwān and the other governors of Medina.

The words “whether obligatory or otherwise” refer to voluntary prayers, such as the night prayers of Ramadan. Thus, al-Bukhārī recorded, through al-Zuhrī from Abū Bakr ibn Abd al-Rahmān ibn al-Hārith and Abū Salama:

“Abū Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, used to pronounce the takbīrs in every prayer, whether obligatory or otherwise, during Ramadan and at other times. He would pronounce the takbīr when he stood up and when he bowed, then say, ‘Allah hears whoever praises Him,’ then, ‘Our Lord, to You belongs all praise.’” He then related a similar account.

The people had grown accustomed to what others did, so they did not recognize this practice and asked him about it, as Muslim related through Yahyā ibn Abī Kathīr from Abū Salama:

---

## Page 11623

“Abū Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, used to pronounce the takbīr in prayer whenever he rose or lowered himself. I said, ‘Abū Hurayra, what is this takbīr?’ He replied, ‘This is indeed the prayer of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.’”

All of this refers to the imam pronouncing the takbīr aloud. This is why they called it “completing the takbīrs”: completing them involved raising the voice and pronouncing them at every downward and upward movement.

This is made clear by what al-Bukhārī mentions in the “Chapter on Pronouncing the Takbīr When Rising after Two Rakʿahs.” He says, “Ibn al-Zubayr used to pronounce the takbīr as he rose.” Al-Bukhārī then relates through Fulayh ibn Sulaymān, from Saʿīd ibn al-Hārith, who said:

“Abū Saʿīd led us in prayer and pronounced the takbīr aloud when he raised his head from prostration, when he prostrated, when he rose, and when he stood up after two rakʿahs. He said, ‘This is how I saw the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.’”

Al-Bukhārī then follows this with the hadith of Mutarrif, who said:

“Imrān ibn Husayn and I prayed behind Alī ibn Abī Tālib, may Allah be pleased with him. Whenever he prostrated, he pronounced the takbīr; whenever he rose, he pronounced the takbīr; and whenever he stood up after two rakʿahs, he pronounced the takbīr. When he concluded the prayer with the salām, Imrān ibn Husayn took my hand and said, ‘This man has indeed led us in the prayer of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace,’ or he said, ‘This man has indeed reminded me of the prayer of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.’”

This makes clear that the discussion concerns only pronouncing the takbīr aloud. As for the practice of pronouncing the takbīr itself, no one was unaware of it. Nor, moreover, is it unclear

---

## Page 11624

whether the imam does it or not. They therefore cannot validly deny that the imams pronounced it, just as they cannot deny that they recited in prayers performed silently, glorified Allah during bowing and prostration, or recited in the final two rakʿahs, and so forth.

For this reason, some who did not complete the takbīrs or pronounce them aloud cited the report narrated by Saʿīd ibn Abd al-Rahmān ibn Abzā from his father:

“He prayed with the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who did not complete the takbīrs.”

This was related by Abū Dāwūd and by al-Bukhārī in al-Tārīkh al-Kabīr.

Abū Dāwūd al-Tayālisī is reported to have said: “In our view, this is unsound.”

If this report has indeed been accurately preserved, perhaps Ibn Abzā prayed behind the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, at the rear of the mosque, while the Prophet’s voice was faint. He therefore did not hear his takbīrs and thought that he had not completed them. Otherwise, the mass-transmitted hadiths from him establish the contrary. Were this report to contradict them, it would be anomalous and carry no weight.

Nevertheless, many later jurists believe that completing the takbīrs means simply pronouncing them, even silently, and that Alī ibn Abī Tālib, Abū Hurayra, and the other imams merely taught people to pronounce the takbīr during the transitions between postures. This would imply that Muslims generally did not know that no takbīr was being pronounced during the prayer’s downward or upward movements.

This is undoubtedly mistaken, and those familiar with the circumstances do not dispute this. If what was meant were pronouncing the takbīr silently, neither its omission nor its performance could validly be established, for one praying behind an imam

---

## Page 11625

cannot tell whether his imam does so. Nor does omitting the takbīr here mean abandoning it altogether, for the imams used to pronounce it at the beginning of the prayer but not during the transitions. That, however, is not the Sunnah. Rather, the transmitted hadiths show that all the imam’s upward and downward movements were accompanied by the takbīr.

Ishāq ibn Mansūr said:

“I asked Ahmad ibn Hanbal: ‘Which takbīrs did they omit?’

“He replied: ‘When descending from bowing into prostration, and when about to perform the second prostration of each rakʿah.’”

Imam Ahmad thus explained that the imams did not complete the takbīrs; rather, they omitted the takbīr when lowering themselves from standing and from sitting. This was indeed the case—and Allah knows best—because downward movements can be seen. They therefore thought that someone praying behind the imam did not need to hear his takbīr, since he could see him bowing and prostrating. Rising from bowing and prostration, however, is different: someone praying behind the imam cannot see him and therefore needs to know that he has risen by hearing his takbīr.

The report of Ibn Abzā supports the accuracy of Ahmad’s statement:

“He prayed behind the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who did not complete the takbīrs and did not pronounce the takbīr when lowering himself.”

This is how Abū Dāwūd al-Tayālisī narrated it from Shuʿbah, from al-Hasan ibn ʿImrān, from Saʿīd ibn Abd al-Rahmān ibn Abzā, from his father. Abū ʿUmar ibn Abd al-Barr, like others, assumed that these

---

## Page 11626

early Muslims did not pronounce the takbīr when lowering or raising themselves. This was taken as evidence that it is not obligatory, since they would not allow the Muslim community to persist in abandoning an obligation. It was even narrated from Ibn ʿUmar that “when praying alone, he would pronounce the takbīr in obligatory prayers, but not in voluntary prayers.”

Abū ʿUmar said: “Ahmad would only report from Ibn ʿUmar what he considered authentic, Allah willing.”

He continued: “As for Mālik’s report from Nāfiʿ, from Ibn ʿUmar, that ‘he would pronounce the takbīr in prayer whenever he lowered or raised himself,’ its apparent meaning indicates that he did this whether leading the prayer or not.”

I say: There is no doubt about what Mālik narrated. What Ahmad mentioned does not contradict it; rather, Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr misunderstood Ahmad’s words. Ahmad was speaking only about the takbīr after prayer during the days of Eid al-Adhā, not the takbīr within the prayer. This is why Ahmad distinguished between obligatory and voluntary prayers, saying: “I prefer that one pronounce the takbīr after obligatory prayers, but not after voluntary prayers.”

Neither Ahmad nor anyone else distinguished between obligatory and voluntary prayers regarding the takbīr within the prayer. Rather, the apparent position of his school is that the takbīr within voluntary prayers is obligatory, just as it is within obligatory prayers. If it is held to be Sunnah in obligatory prayers, then it is likewise held to be Sunnah in voluntary prayers. As for distinguishing between the two, that is neither his position nor anyone else’s.

As for what he reported from Ibn ʿUmar concerning his pronouncing the takbīr after prayer when praying alone:

---

## Page 11627

this is widely reported from him. It is also a well-known point of disagreement among the scholars.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr cited Abū Salama’s report:

“Abū Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, used to lead them in prayer, pronouncing the takbīr whenever he lowered or raised himself. When he finished, he said: ‘By Allah, my prayer most closely resembles that of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.’”

Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr then said: “Not everyone used to do this. This is indicated by what Ibn Abī Dhiʾb narrated in his Muwattaʾ, from Saʿīd ibn Samʿān, from Abū Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, who said:

‘There are three things that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to do which people have abandoned: when he stood for prayer, he raised his hands outstretched; he paused briefly before reciting, asking Allah for His bounty; and he pronounced the takbīr whenever he raised or lowered himself.’”

I say: A number of imams and jurists have abandoned these three practices: those who neither raise their hands nor regard the takbīr as obligatory; those who do not consider the opening supplication and seeking refuge in Allah recommended; and imams who do not pronounce the takbīr aloud when moving between postures.

He said:

Some scholars have said: “The takbīr serves only to signal the imam’s movements and is a distinguishing feature of prayer. It is a Sunnah practice only in congregational prayer. As for someone praying alone, there is no harm in his omitting the takbīr.”

For this reason, Mālik cited this report, as well as the report of Ibn Shihāb from ʿAlī ibn Husayn, who said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to pronounce the takbīr in prayer whenever he lowered or raised himself. He continued to pray in this manner until he met Allah, Mighty and Majestic.”

And the report of Ibn ʿUmar and Jābir, may Allah be pleased with them

---

## Page 11628

that “they both used to pronounce the takbīr whenever they lowered or raised themselves in prayer, and Jābir used to teach them this.”

He said: Mālik cited all these reports to show you that the takbīr is among the Sunnah practices of prayer.

I say: What Mālik mentioned is indeed as he stated. As for the disagreement mentioned by Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr, I have not found him cite any basis for it other than what Ahmad reported from the Muslim scholars: that the takbīr is prescribed in the prayers. Mālik and others mentioned this—and Allah knows best—only because of the objectionable conduct of imams who did not fully observe the practice of takbīr.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said:

Ibn Wahb narrated: “ʿIyād ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Fihrī informed me that ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar used to say: ‘Everything has an adornment, and the adornment of prayer is the takbīr and raising the hands during it.’”

If Ibn ʿUmar said this, how could anyone suppose that he did not pronounce the takbīr when praying alone? No reasonable person would think this of Ibn ʿUmar.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said:

It has been narrated from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, Qatāda, and others that “they did not fully observe the practice of takbīr.” Al-Qāsim, Sālim, and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr also related this from him.

It was narrated through Abū Salama, from Abū Hurayra, that “he used to pronounce these takbīrs, saying: ‘This is indeed the prayer of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.’”

He said: This indicates that people had abandoned pronouncing the takbīr whenever lowering or raising themselves. And the people’s abandonment

---

## Page 11629

of it, without any of them objecting, indicates that they regarded the matter as optional.

I say: All that can be known is that they omitted saying it aloud. As for the imam omitting the takbīr silently, one cannot claim that he omitted it if the imam did not proceed to perform it; none of the imams has said this. Nor has anyone said that they omitted it whenever lowering or raising themselves. Rather, they said that they did not observe it fully. “Not observing it fully” means reducing it, and this reduction consists in not pronouncing it while lowering oneself, as stated earlier in his discussion. The deficiency lies either in not raising the voice when pronouncing it or in omitting it at certain points.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr narrated that Anas ibn Mālik, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

“I prayed behind the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and behind Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, and ʿUthmān, may Allah be pleased with them. All of them would pronounce the takbīr whenever they raised their heads or lowered themselves.”

He said: This conflicts with the report that ʿUmar “did not fully observe the practice of takbīr.”

It was narrated through Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz that al-Zuhrī said:

“I said to ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz: ‘What prevents you from observing the takbīr fully, when your official, ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, observes it fully?’ He replied: ‘That is how the earlier generations prayed,’ and refused to accept what I said.”

I say: What ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz and these others were unaware of was only the practice of pronouncing the takbīr aloud, just as various groups in our own time have been unaware of it. An earlier instance is what was related by Ibn

---

## Page 11630

Abī Shaybah: Jarīr informed us, from Mansūr, from Ibrāhīm, who said:

“The first to curtail the takbīr was Ziyād.”

I say: Ziyād was a governor during the time of ʿUmar, so this report may be correct. Ziyād may have established that practice when others had abandoned it. It was also narrated from al-Aswad ibn Yazīd, from Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī, who said:

“ʿAlī has reminded us of a prayer that we used to perform with the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, which we either forgot or deliberately abandoned. He would pronounce the takbīr whenever he rose, lowered himself, or prostrated.”

It is well known that the governors in Iraq observed the practices of the local governors, who were also imams, and had received no report from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, indicating otherwise. They saw that the people of knowledge and religious devotion whom they encountered knew no other practice, so they thought that this was part of the original Sunnah. This resulted in shortcomings concerning both the timing of prayer and its performance. They believed that delaying prayer was better than offering it earlier, as this was what the imams used to do.

The same applied to not observing the takbīr fully and to other practices that fell short of those of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Indeed, Ibn Masʿūd understood some of the governors of his time to be among the successors of whom Allah Most High said:

“But they were succeeded by generations who neglected prayer and followed their desires; so they will meet ruin.”

He would therefore say: “What will become of you when a trial engulfs you, amid which the young grow up and the old grow decrepit, and in which, if there is any abandonment

---

## Page 11631

of anything, people say, ‘You have abandoned the Sunnah.’”

He was asked, “When will that be, Abū ʿAbd al-Rahmān?”

He replied, “When your scholars have gone, your jurists have become few, worldly gain is sought through deeds meant for the Hereafter, and religious learning is pursued for purposes other than religion.”

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd also used to say:

“I fear for you something other than the Dajjāl more than I fear the Dajjāl: things that will come from your leaders. Any man or woman who lives to see that time must hold fast to the original way—hold fast to the original way.”

Another example concerns ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. When he became governor of Medina during the caliphate of his cousin al-Walīd—this ʿUmar was the one who built the Prophet’s chamber at that time—Anas ibn Mālik, may Allah be pleased with him, prayed behind him. He then said, as narrated by Abū Dāwūd and al-Nasāʾī from Anas ibn Mālik, may Allah be pleased with him:

“After the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, I have never prayed behind anyone whose prayer more closely resembled that of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, than this young man”—meaning ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz.

He said, “We estimated that his bowing lasted long enough to glorify Allah ten times, and his prostration long enough to glorify Him ten times.”

This was in Medina, even though its governors adhered more closely to the Sunnah than the governors of the other cities. The other cities were governed according to the judgment of kings, whereas Medina was governed only according to the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace—or something to that effect. Nevertheless, they too had altered some aspects of the Sunnah.

Anyone who believes that this occurred during the caliphate of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz is mistaken, for Anas ibn Mālik, may

---

## Page 11632

Allah be pleased with him, did not live to see the caliphate of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz; rather, he died two years before it.

This accords with the well-known hadith recorded in the Sunan collections of Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī, and Ibn Mājah, from ʿAwn ibn ʿAbd Allāh, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him, who said that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When one of you bows, let him say three times, ‘Glory be to my Lord, the Magnificent’—and that is the minimum. When he prostrates, let him say three times, ‘Glory be to my Lord, the Most High’—and that is the minimum.”

Abū Dāwūd said, “This report has a disconnected chain: ʿAwn did not live to meet ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd.” Al-Bukhārī said the same in his History.

Al-Tirmidhī said, “Its chain of transmission is not connected: ʿAwn ibn ʿAbd Allāh did not live to meet Ibn Masʿūd.” ʿAwn was one of the well-known scholars of Kufa and belonged to ʿAbd Allāh’s family. It has been said that he received this report from the scholars of his own family.

For this reason, the jurists relied on this hadith concerning the repetitions of glorification, because of its supporting reports. They came to describe three repetitions as “the minimum degree of completeness” or “the minimum for bowing.” This indicates that the fullest degree involves more than this.

Thus, the assertion made by some jurists following the principles of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad—may Allah be pleased with them both—and others, that the Sunnah is for the imam to limit himself to three repetitions of glorification, is like the assertion that the Sunnah is not to prolong standing upright after bowing, or to delay the prayer until the end of its allotted time, and similar claims. For

---

## Page 11633

those who said this have no basis whatsoever in the Sunnah to which they can refer. Rather, the widely transmitted hadiths from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, established in the collections of authentic hadith, the Sunan, the Musnads, and elsewhere, show that in most of his prayers he repeated the glorifications more often than that, as the evidence of the hadiths has already demonstrated.

They said this, however, because they heard that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When one of you leads the people in prayer, let him keep it brief; when he prays alone, let him prolong it as much as he wishes.”

Yet they did not know how long the prayer should be, nor did they understand the prolongation he forbade when he said to Muʿādh:

“Are you putting people to trial, O Muʿādh?”

Thus, on the basis of their own opinion, they made this the measure of what is recommended. It is well known that the duration of prayer—its obligatory and recommended elements alike—must be determined by reference to the Sunnah alone. This is knowledge that Allah and His Messenger have not left to people’s opinions. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to lead the Muslims in five prayers every day, as did his rightly guided caliphs, whom we have been commanded to follow. We must therefore investigate what the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, established as Sunnah, rather than formulate a ruling on it through personal opinion. Independent reasoning based on opinion applies only where no Sunnah has been established from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, [and] (1) it is impermissible to take something established by the Sunnah and reject it on the basis of opinion and analogy.

This is further clarified by the fact that brevity is relative and comparative: it has no fixed measure in either language or customary usage. Some may find lengthy what others find brief, and may find brief

> **Footnotes:**
> (1) The text in square brackets is absent from the printed edition, and I could not find it in Siyānat Majmū‘ al-Fatāwā min al-Saqt wa-al-Tashīf (Safeguarding the Collected Fatwas against Omissions and Scribal Errors).
> Usāma ibn al-Zahrā’ — coordinator of the book for al-Maktaba al-Shāmila.

---

## Page 11634

what others find lengthy. It therefore varies with people’s habits and the duration of acts of worship; nor is there a fixed measure in every act of worship that is not prescribed by the Sharia.

It is thus clear that the Muslim must refer to the Sunnah to determine how brief or lengthy the prayer should be. This also makes clear that the Prophet’s command to keep it brief does not contradict his command to prolong it, as in the hadith of ʿAmmār recorded in the Sahīh, where he said:

“A man’s lengthy prayer and brief sermon are a sign of his understanding of religion. So prolong the prayer and keep the sermon brief.”

Elsewhere, he commanded them to keep the prayer brief, and there is no contradiction between the two. Here, the prayer is to be lengthy relative to the sermon; there, it is to be brief relative to what some imams did during his lifetime, such as reciting Surah al-Baqarah in the ʿIshāʾ prayer. Hence he said:

“When one of you prays alone, let him prolong it as much as he wishes.”

He thus made clear that someone praying alone is not subject to a limit on the length of his prayer that would keep it brief, unlike the imam, who must take account of those praying behind him. Among them are the sick, the elderly, and those with pressing needs. Accordingly, the established Sunnah is to shorten the prayer rather than prolong it when something arises that affects the congregation or some of its members. As he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“I begin the prayer intending to prolong it, but then I hear a child crying and shorten it, knowing the distress his mother feels.”

This was also the reason the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, gave in the previously cited hadith of Ibn Masʿūd.

---

## Page 11635

Likewise, in the two Sahīhs, Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When one of you leads people in prayer, let him keep it brief, for among them are the weak, the elderly, and those with pressing needs. When he prays alone, let him prolong it as much as he wishes.”

Another version reads: “For among them are the sick, the very elderly, and those with pressing needs.”

For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would sometimes make the prayer shorter than he usually did. Muslim reported in his Sahīh that ‘Amr ibn Hurayth, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

“It is as though I can hear the voice of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, reciting in the dawn prayer: ‘So I swear by the retreating stars, those that run their courses and disappear.’”

It is also reported that he “recited Surah al-Zalzalah in the Fajr prayer during one of his journeys.”

At other times, he would prolong the prayer. Indeed, it is established in the Sahīh, on the authority of Ibn ‘Abbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that Umm al-Fadl bint al-Hārith heard him reciting “By those sent forth in succession,” and said:

“My son, your recitation of this surah has brought back a memory: it was the last surah I heard the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, recite in the Maghrib prayer.”

In the two Sahīhs, Muhammad ibn Jubayr ibn Mut‘im reported from his father that he said:

“I heard the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, reciting Surah al-Tūr in the Maghrib prayer.”

Al-Bukhārī and the Sunan collections also report that Marwān ibn al-Hakam said:

“Zayd ibn Thābit said to me, ‘Why do you recite the short surahs of the Mufassal in the Maghrib prayer, when I saw the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, recite the longer of the two long surahs in Maghrib?’

“I asked, ‘Which is the longer of the two long surahs?’

“He replied, ‘Al-A‘rāf.’”

---

## Page 11636

These hadiths are among the most authentic. They establish that he would sometimes recite al-A‘rāf in Maghrib, sometimes al-Tūr, and sometimes al-Mursalāt, although the jurists agree that the Sunnah is for the recitation in Maghrib to be shorter than that in Fajr. What, then, of the recitation in Fajr and the other prayers?

Another example is what Wakī‘ narrated from Mansūr, from Ibrāhīm al-Nakha‘ī, who said:

“Abū ‘Ubaydah ibn ‘Abdullāh ibn Mas‘ūd would prolong his standing to match the duration of his bowing, and they used to criticize him for that.”

Abū Muhammad ibn Hazm said:

“The blame lies with those who criticize the practice of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and rely on those whose example carries no authority.”

I say:

Abū ‘Ubaydah’s practice, as reported in the Sahīh, and its agreement with the practice of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, have already been discussed. Those who criticized him were people of Kufa who lived during the time of al-Hajjāj and the uprising of Ibn al-Ash‘ath. They were not Companions, nor were they known to be among the leading Successors. Although some of them may have lived in Ibn Mas‘ūd’s lifetime, Ibn Mas‘ūd’s son was not the regular imam at the time; someone else held that position. Moreover, Ibn Mas‘ūd’s son was more likely to follow his father than these unidentified men. Those who objected to Abū ‘Ubaydah did so only because he departed from the custom

---

## Page 11637

to which they had grown accustomed, even if it conflicted with the Prophetic Sunnah. But this objection did not come from the jurists. This is demonstrated by the fact that the most eminent jurist under whom Ibrāhīm al-Nakha‘ī studied was ‘Alqamah, who died before the uprising of Ibn al-Ash‘ath during which Abū ‘Ubaydah ibn ‘Abdullāh prayed. ‘Alqamah died in 61—or 62—AH, early in Yazīd’s rule, whereas Ibn al-Ash‘ath’s uprising occurred during the rule of ‘Abd al-Malik. Likewise, Masrūq is said to have died before 70 AH. Similar statements were made about both of them, as were made about Masrūq and others like him.

It is therefore clear that the leading jurists among the students of ‘Abdullāh ibn Mas‘ūd were not those who objected to this practice. Yet some people, upon hearing this unqualified statement, take it to refer to Ibrāhīm al-Nakha‘ī. You have already learned that, according to the well-known account, ‘Alqamah thought that Ibrāhīm and others like him objected to it. They had witnessed it, and they had acquired knowledge from ‘Abdullāh and others like him. It has thus become clear that this was not the case.

---

## Page 11638

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked about a man who does not come to rest in his prayer.

He replied:

Coming to rest in prayer is obligatory, and all the imams agree that whoever omits it is at fault. Indeed, the majority of the imams of Islam—such as Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad, Ishāq, and Abū Yūsuf, the associate of Abū Hanīfah—as well as Abū Hanīfah and Muhammad, do not dispute that whoever omits this is acting wrongly and not performing the prayer properly. Rather, he is sinning, disobeying, and neglecting an obligation. Others require anyone who omits coming to rest to repeat the prayer.

The evidence that repeating it is obligatory is the report in the two Sahīh collections:

“A man prayed two units of prayer in the mosque, then came and greeted the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, told him two or three times: ‘Go back and pray, for you have not prayed.’

“The man said: ‘By Him who sent you with the truth, I do not know how to do any better than this. Teach me what will suffice for my prayer.’

“He said: ‘When you stand for prayer, proclaim Allah’s greatness, then recite whatever you can of the Quran. Then bow until you come to rest in bowing. Then rise until you are standing upright. Then prostrate until you come to rest in prostration. Then sit until you come to rest in sitting. Do this throughout your prayer.’”

This man was ignorant, yet the Prophet commanded him

---

## Page 11639

—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—to repeat the prayer and told him that he had not prayed. This makes it clear that whoever omits coming to rest has been declared by Allah and His Messenger not to have prayed, and has been commanded by Allah and His Messenger to repeat the prayer. Whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger will suffer a painful punishment.

In the Sunan collections, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah does not accept the prayer of a man who does not straighten his back in bowing and prostration.”

This means straightening his back when rising from bowing and when rising from prostration.

It is reported in the Sahīh that Hudhayfah ibn al-Yamān—may Allah be pleased with him—saw a man who did not straighten his back in bowing and prostration. He asked him: “How long have you been praying like this?”

He replied: “For such-and-such a time.”

Hudhayfah said: “If you were to die, you would die upon something other than the natural disposition with which Allah endowed Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.”

Ibn Khuzaymah also related this meaning in his Sahīh in a report traced back to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: he said to someone who pecked hurriedly through his prayer:

“If you were to die in this state, you would die upon something other than the natural disposition with which Allah endowed Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.”

Or he said words to that effect. He also said:

“The one who prays without completing his bowing and prostration is like someone who eats a mouthful or two—what nourishment can that give him?”

In Sahīh Muslim, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“That is the hypocrite’s prayer! That is the hypocrite’s prayer! He watches the sun until it is between the two horns of

---

## Page 11640

Satan, then he rises and pecks hurriedly through four units of prayer, remembering Allah only a little during them.” Elsewhere we have presented evidence from the Quran and Sunnah on this subject that would take too long to recount here. Allah knows best.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was also asked:

“What about someone who is sometimes attentive during prayer and at other times troubled by intrusive thoughts? What can help him remain attentive throughout the prayer? Do such thoughts invalidate the prayer, detract from it, or neither?

“And regarding ʿUmar’s statement, ‘I make preparations for my army while I am praying,’ did that distract him from his state of inner concentration, or not?”

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds. The scholars agree that a small amount of distraction does not invalidate the prayer, but it does diminish the reward. As Ibn ʿAbbās said: “You are credited only with the part of your prayer to which you were attentive.”

It is reported in the Sunan collections that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“A servant may finish his prayer with only half of it recorded for him, or a third, a quarter, a fifth, a sixth, a seventh, an eighth, a ninth, or a tenth.”

---

## Page 11641

It is also said that voluntary prayers were prescribed to make up for deficiencies in obligatory prayers, as reported in the Sunan collections from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“The first deed for which a servant will be called to account is prayer. If he has performed it completely, well and good; otherwise it will be said: ‘See whether he has any voluntary prayers.’ If he has voluntary prayers, his obligatory prayer will be completed through them. The same will then be done with the rest of his deeds.”

This completion encompasses deficiencies of every kind.

[As for intrusive thoughts that dominate the prayer, a group of scholars—including Abū Abd Allah ibn Hāmid, Abū Hāmid al-Ghazālī, and others—said that this also necessitates assistance, citing the report transmitted in the two Sahīh collections from Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When the caller gives the call to prayer, Satan retreats, passing wind so that he cannot hear the call. When the call is finished, he returns. When the call to commence the prayer is made, he retreats; when it is finished, he returns and intrudes between a person and his thoughts, saying: ‘Remember such-and-such; remember such-and-such,’ reminding him of things he had not been thinking about, until the man no longer knows how many units he has prayed. If any of you experiences this, let him perform two prostrations before giving the salutation.”

There is also an authentic report from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: “Prayer with intrusive thoughts, without qualification.” He made no distinction between a little and a great deal.] (*)

There is no doubt that the fewer the intrusive thoughts during prayer, the more complete it is. Thus, in the two Sahīh collections, Uthmān, may Allah be pleased with him, reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever performs ablution as I have just done, then prays two units of prayer without engaging

> **Footnotes:**
> (*) Shaykh Nāsir ibn Hamad al-Fahd stated (p. 189):
> Several points should be noted:
> First: This passage contains an omission, as indicated by two things:
> 1. The context: Ibn Hāmid and Abū Hāmid, mentioned here, hold that a person troubled by intrusive thoughts must repeat the prayer. Yet the evidence cited for their position plainly supports the view that repetition is not required.
> 2. He mentions both views in 22/612: he first presents the view of Ibn Hāmid and Abū Hāmid, then the view of those who do not require repetition, and then cites this evidence in support of the second view.
> Thus, the omitted material consisted of the evidence for the first view and the statement of the second view. For the views and their evidence, see 22/611–613.
> Second: The statement attributed here to the Shaykh—“It has been authentically reported from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: ‘Prayer with intrusive thoughts, without qualification.’ He made no distinction between a little and a great deal”—appears to be a textual corruption, likewise indicated by two things:
> 1. No authentic hadith exists with this wording.
> 2. Elsewhere, commenting on the hadith about Satan and his whispering to someone praying, he states (22/613): “The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained that Satan reminds him of things until he no longer knows how much he has prayed. He instructed him to perform two prostrations for forgetfulness, but did not instruct him to repeat the prayer, nor did he distinguish between a little and a great deal.” This passage effectively explains what he stated briefly in the earlier passage.
> Accordingly, the correct wording—and Allah knows best—is:
> “The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, declared prayer valid despite intrusive thoughts, without qualification, and made no distinction between a little and a great deal.”
> Third: This defect also occurs in al-Fatāwā al-kubrā, 2/24.

---

## Page 11642

in inner conversation during them, will have his past sins forgiven.”

Likewise, an authentic report records that he said:

“Whoever performs ablution thoroughly, then prays two units, devoting himself to them with both face and heart, will have his past sins forgiven.”

There have always been people who pray in this manner. Saʿd ibn Muʿādh, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

“There are three situations in which, if I were in all my circumstances as I am in them, I would truly be the man I should be: when praying, I think of nothing other than the prayer; when I hear a statement from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, no doubt enters my heart that it is the truth; and when attending a funeral, I think of nothing other than what the deceased says and what is said to him.”

Maslamah ibn Bashshār was praying in the mosque when part of it collapsed. The people sprang up, but he remained unaware as he prayed. Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with him, was prostrating when a catapult projectile carried away part of his garment, yet he did not raise his head from prayer.

They asked ʿĀmir ibn Abd al-Qays, “Do you think about anything during prayer?”

He replied, “Is there anything dearer to me than prayer that I should occupy my thoughts with it?”

They said, “We do think about other things during prayer.”

He asked, “Paradise, its maidens, and the like?”

They replied, “No, our families and our wealth.”

He said, “I would rather be pierced by spears!”

There are many similar examples.

Two things help one achieve this: a strong motivating force and diminished distractions.

As for the first, it consists in the servant striving to understand what he says and does, and to reflect upon

---

## Page 11643

the recitation, remembrance, and supplication, keeping in mind that he is speaking intimately with Allah Most High as though he sees Him. For when a person stands in prayer, he is speaking intimately with his Lord.

Excellence in worship is “to worship Allah as though you see Him; and although you do not see Him, He sees you.” The more the servant tastes the sweetness of prayer, the more strongly he is drawn to it. This depends on the strength of his faith, and there are many means of strengthening faith. Thus the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to say:

“Women and perfume from this world of yours have been made dear to me, and the delight of my eyes has been placed in prayer.”

Another hadith records that he said:

“O Bilāl, bring us rest through prayer.”

He did not say, “Bring us rest from it.” Another report states:

“One whose worries persist until he rises to pray has not attained complete faith.”
