Or words to that effect. This is a vast subject. People differ enormously in what their hearts contain of knowledge of Allah, love for Him, awe of Him, sincere devotion to Him, fear of Him, hope in Him, belief in what He has conveyed, and other such qualities.

These qualities grow stronger as the servant reflects more deeply on the Quran, increases in understanding and knowledge of Allah’s names, attributes, and greatness, acknowledges his utter need for Him in worship, and occupies himself with Him. He thus feels that his need for Allah Most High as the One he worships and calls upon for help is greater than his need for food and drink. For he cannot be sound unless Allah is the One he worships, in whom he finds peace and comfort, in whose remembrance he takes pleasure, and with whom he finds rest. This can only be attained with Allah’s help. And whenever there is

---

## Page 11644

a god other than Allah that the heart worships, the heart becomes corrupt and is ruined beyond repair. Without Allah’s help in this, the heart cannot be set right. There is neither power nor strength except through Him, and there is no refuge or escape from Him except with Him.

For this reason, it is reported that Allah revealed one hundred and four books, gathered their knowledge into the four Books, and gathered the four Books into the Quran. He gathered the knowledge of the Quran into the Mufassal section, the knowledge of the Mufassal into the Opening of the Book, and the knowledge of the Opening of the Book into His words:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.”

Similar to this are His words:

“So worship Him and put your trust in Him.”

And His words:

“In Him I put my trust, and to Him I turn.”

And His words:

“Whoever fears Allah, He will make a way out for him and provide for him from where he does not expect. And whoever puts his trust in Allah, He is sufficient for him.”

Allah Most High has also said:

“I did not create jinn and mankind except to worship Me.”

For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The head of the matter is Islam, its pillar is prayer, and its pinnacle is jihad in the cause of Allah.”

A full explanation of this would be lengthy and is beyond the scope of this discussion.

As for removing the impediment, this requires striving to ward off whatever preoccupies the heart, such as thinking about matters that do not concern one and dwelling on the attractions that draw the heart away from the purpose of prayer. This varies according to each servant’s circumstances. The abundance of intrusive thoughts corresponds to the abundance of doubts and desires, and to the heart’s attachment to things it loves, which turn it toward pursuing them, and things it dislikes, which turn it toward warding them off.

---

## Page 11645

Intrusive thoughts may relate either to love, as when something that has happened comes to mind, or to seeking something, as when a person thinks of what he wants to do. Some intrusive thoughts concern disbelief and hypocrisy, causing the believer’s heart intense distress. Thus, the Companions said:

“O Messenger of Allah, one of us finds within himself thoughts that he would rather fall from the sky than utter.” He asked, “Have you experienced this?” They replied, “Yes.” He said, “That is pure faith.”

In another wording:

“One of us finds within himself thoughts that he considers too terrible to utter.” He said, “Praise be to Allah, who has reduced his scheming to mere whispering.”

Many scholars have said: Disliking and hating these thoughts, and the heart’s recoiling from them, constitute pure faith. Praise be to Allah that Satan’s scheming has amounted to no more than whispering. For a devil among the jinn whispers when he gains the upper hand, while a devil among mankind lies when he gains the upper hand.

Intrusive thoughts inevitably assail everyone who turns to Allah Most High through remembrance or other acts of worship. The servant should therefore remain steadfast and patient, persist in his remembrance and prayer, and not become exasperated. By persisting, he will drive Satan’s scheming away from himself:

“Indeed, Satan’s scheming is ever weak.”

Whenever the servant seeks to turn his heart toward Allah Most High, further intrusive thoughts arise. Satan is like a highway robber: whenever the servant seeks to journey toward Allah Most High, he tries to block his way. For this reason, one of the early generations was told: “The Jews and Christians say, ‘We do not

---

## Page 11646

experience intrusive thoughts.’” He replied, “They speak the truth. What would Satan do with a ruined house?” A detailed account of what befalls those journeying to Allah would require a lengthy discussion of its own.

As for the report that Umar ibn al-Khattāb—may Allah be pleased with him—said, “I prepare my army while I am praying,” this was because Umar was commanded to wage jihad. As Commander of the Faithful, he was also responsible for leading jihad. In some respects, therefore, he was like someone offering the prayer of fear with the enemy in sight, whether during actual combat or otherwise. He was commanded both to pray and to wage jihad, and thus had to fulfil both obligations to the extent possible.

Allah Most High says:

“O you who believe, when you encounter an enemy force, stand firm and remember Allah much, so that you may succeed.”

It is well known that the heart is not as tranquil during jihad as it is in safety. Thus, even if the prayer is diminished in some respect because of jihad, this does not detract from the completeness of the servant’s faith and obedience. This is why the requirements of the prayer of fear are eased compared with prayer offered in safety.

After mentioning the prayer of fear, Allah, glorified and exalted be He, says:

“Then, when you are secure, establish prayer. Indeed, prayer has been prescribed for the believers at fixed times.”

The full observance of prayer commanded in a state of security is not required in a state of fear.

Nevertheless, people differ in this regard. When a servant’s faith is strong, his heart remains attentive in prayer even while he thinks through other matters during it. Indeed, in Umar’s case,

---

## Page 11647

Allah had established truth upon his tongue and in his heart, and he was a man granted inspiration. It is therefore not surprising that someone like him, even while planning the deployment of his army during prayer, could have a degree of attentiveness that others did not possess. Yet there is no doubt that his attentiveness would be greater without this. Nor is there any doubt that, in its outward actions, the prayer of the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—was more complete in a state of security than in a state of fear. If Allah has waived certain outward obligations in a state of fear, what, then, of the inward ones?

In short, thinking during prayer about an obligation for which time may be running short is not like thinking about something that is not obligatory, or about an obligation for which time is not running short. Umar may have had no opportunity to think about managing the army except at that moment, since he was the leader of the Muslim community and faced many demands.

Everyone encounters such situations according to his station. A person continually recalls during prayer things that he does not recall outside it. Some of this comes from Satan. For example, it is related that a man told one of the early Muslims that he had buried some money but had forgotten where. He told him, “Get up and pray.” The man got up and prayed, and remembered the place. When asked, “How did you know that?” he replied:

“I knew that Satan would not leave him alone during prayer without reminding him of something to distract him, and nothing mattered more to him than remembering where he had buried the money.”

Nevertheless, the discerning servant strives for complete attentiveness while fully carrying out everything else he has been commanded to do. There is no power and no strength except through Allah, the Most High, the Magnificent.

---

## Page 11648

He was asked:

About distracting thoughts during prayer: What degree of them invalidates the prayer? What degree is disliked? Are any such thoughts permissible during prayer? Can a person be punished for any of them? What constitutes sincerity in prayer? And what is meant by the Prophet’s saying—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—“Each of you has only that part of his prayer to which he was attentive”?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. Distracting thoughts are of two kinds:

The first does not prevent the reflection one is commanded to give to the good words and righteous deeds within prayer. Rather, these are merely passing thoughts. They do not invalidate the prayer, but someone whose prayer is free of them is better than someone whose prayer is not. The former resembles those brought near to Allah, while the latter resembles those who follow a moderate course.

The second kind prevents understanding and attentiveness of heart, leaving a person heedless. This undoubtedly deprives him of reward, as Abū Dāwūd narrated in his Sunan from Ammār ibn Yāsir that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said: “A man may finish his prayer with only half of it recorded for him, or a third of it;

---

## Page 11649

or a quarter of it, or a fifth, or a sixth,” until he said, “or a tenth.” Thus, he—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—explained that a person may have only a tenth of his prayer recorded for him.

Ibn Abbās said: “You have only that part of your prayer to which you were attentive.” But does this invalidate the prayer and require it to be repeated? This requires a distinction.

If heedlessness occupies less of the prayer than attentiveness, and attentiveness predominates, the prayer need not be repeated, although its reward is diminished. For the transmitted texts abundantly establish that forgetfulness does not invalidate prayer; rather, certain instances of it are remedied by the two prostrations for forgetfulness. If, however, heedlessness predominates over attentiveness, the scholars hold two views:

The first is that the prayer is not valid inwardly, even if it is valid outwardly—for purposes such as safeguarding one’s life—because the purpose of prayer has not been achieved. It resembles the prayer of someone who prays to show off, which, by agreement, does not inwardly discharge his obligation. This is the view of Abū Abd Allāh ibn Hāmid, Abū Hāmid al-Ghazālī, and others.

The second is that the obligation is discharged, so he need not repeat the prayer, even though he receives no reward or recompense for it. This is like the fast of someone who does not abandon false speech and acting upon it: he gains nothing from his fast but hunger and thirst.

This is the view transmitted from Imam Ahmad and other imams. They cited as evidence the report in the two Sahīh collections, narrated by Abū Hurayrah from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—that he said:

“When the muezzin gives the call

---

## Page 11650

to prayer, Satan turns and flees, passing wind so that he cannot hear the call. When the call ends, he returns. When the call to commence the prayer is given, he flees again, then returns when it ends, intruding upon a person’s thoughts and saying: ‘Remember this, remember that,’ reminding him of things he had not been thinking about, until he no longer knows how many units he has prayed. If any of you experiences this, let him perform two prostrations.”

The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—thus explained that Satan reminds a person of things until he no longer knows how many units he has prayed. He instructed him to perform two prostrations for forgetfulness, but did not instruct him to repeat the prayer, nor did he distinguish between a little distraction and a great deal. This view is more fitting and balanced, for the scriptural texts and transmitted reports establish only that reward and recompense depend on attentiveness. They do not establish an obligation to repeat the prayer, whether with regard to its inward or outward validity. And Allah knows best.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

What if a person praying enters a state of ritual impurity before the closing salutation?

He replied:

If a person praying enters a state of ritual impurity before the closing salutation, his prayer is invalid, whether obligatory or non-obligatory.

---

## Page 11651

He was asked:

If a man laughs during prayer, is his prayer invalidated?

He replied:

Smiling does not invalidate the prayer. Laughing aloud during prayer, however, invalidates it, but does not invalidate his ablution according to the majority of scholars, including Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad. Nevertheless, according to the stronger of the two views, it is recommended that he renew his ablution, because he has committed a sin and to take account of the scholarly disagreement: according to Abū Hanīfa’s school, his ablution is invalidated. And Allah knows best.

---

## Page 11652

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

About clearing the throat, coughing, blowing, groaning and similar actions during prayer: do they invalidate it or not? Which of these actions, or others, invalidate prayer? According to which school, and what is the evidence for that?

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds.

The foundational principle in this matter is the Prophet’s statement—may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“No ordinary human speech is permissible in this prayer of ours.”

He also said:

“Allah introduces such commands as He wills, and among the commands He has introduced is that you must not speak during prayer.”

Zayd ibn Arqam said: “We were commanded to remain silent and forbidden to speak.” This is a matter on which the Muslims agree.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: “The scholars unanimously agree that whoever speaks deliberately during his prayer, without intending to correct any aspect of it, has invalidated his prayer. A person speaks deliberately when he knows that he is praying and that speaking is prohibited.”

(I say: The scholars have differed concerning someone who speaks forgetfully, out of ignorance, under coercion, or for the benefit of the prayer. All these cases are disputed within Ahmad’s school and among other scholars.

---

## Page 11653

With this understood, vocal utterances fall into three categories.

The first conveys meaning by linguistic convention, either independently or in combination with another word, as with fī (“in”) and 'an (“about”). This constitutes speech, as do yad (“hand”), dam (“blood”), fam (“mouth”), and khadd (“cheek”).

The second conveys meaning naturally, such as sighing, groaning, weeping, and the like.

The third conveys no meaning, either naturally or by linguistic convention, such as clearing the throat. Ahmad used to do this during his prayer. His followers transmitted two opinions from him concerning whether clearing the throat invalidates prayer. If we adopt the opinion that it does, there are two views concerning someone who does so out of necessity.

Thus, there are three opinions on the matter:

The first is that it does not invalidate prayer under any circumstances. This is the position of Abū Yūsuf and one of the two opinions reported from Mālik; indeed, it is the apparent position of his school.

The second is that it invalidates prayer in all circumstances. This is the position of al-Shāfi'ī and one of the two opinions within the schools of Ahmad and Mālik.

The third is that if a person does so for a valid excuse, the prayer is not invalidated; otherwise, it is. This is the position of Abū Hanīfa, Muhammad, and others. They said that if he does so to improve and clear his voice

---

## Page 11654

the prayer is not invalidated. They explained that the need for this arises frequently, so it is permitted on account of that need.

Those who hold that it invalidates prayer argue that it involves two letters and is not a form of remembrance prescribed in prayer, making it comparable to loud laughter. The first opinion, however, is more correct.

This is because the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) prohibited only speaking during prayer, saying:

“No ordinary human speech is appropriate in this prayer.”

Other statements of this kind likewise refer to speech. Clearing the throat does not fall within the meaning of speech at all: neither by itself nor in combination with other utterances does it convey a meaning, nor is someone who clears his throat described as speaking. His intention is understood only through contextual clues, making it comparable to a gesture.

As for loud laughter and similar sounds, there are two responses.

The first is that it conveys meaning naturally.

The second is that we do not concede that it invalidates prayer because it constitutes speech. This is supported by the fact that loud laughter invalidates prayer by consensus, as reported by Ibn al-Mundhir, whereas these other kinds of sounds are disputed. Indeed, it may be argued that loud laughter involves raised sounds incompatible with the state of prayer and the reverent humility required in it. It is thus comparable to a loud, sustained sound unaccompanied by any articulated letter. Moreover, it involves treating prayer lightly and trifling with it in a manner contrary to its purpose, and therefore invalidates it for that reason

---

## Page 11655

, not because the person is speaking. For prayer to be invalidated by something of this kind, it need not constitute speech; mere sound is not speech. It is reported that ‘Alī (may Allah be pleased with him) said:

“I had two times for visiting the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him), by night and by day. Whenever I entered upon him while he was praying, he would clear his throat for me.”

This was narrated by Imam Ahmad and Ibn Mājah, and by al-Nasā’ī with similar wording.

As for the second category—sounds that convey meaning naturally rather than by convention—it includes blowing. Two opinions concerning it are likewise reported from Mālik and Ahmad.

The first is that it does not invalidate prayer. This is the view of Ibrāhīm al-Nakha‘ī, Ibn Sīrīn and other early scholars, as well as Abū Yūsuf and Ishāq. The second is that it invalidates prayer. This is the view of Abū Hanīfah, Muhammad, al-Thawrī and al-Shāfi‘ī. According to this view, blowing invalidates prayer when it produces two distinct letters.

It has also been reported from Ahmad that blowing is treated as speech even if it does not produce two distinct letters.

Those who hold this view cited as evidence the report from Umm Salamah that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said:

“Whoever blows during prayer has spoken.”

This was narrated by al-Khallāl. However, a report like this is not authentically established as a statement of the Prophet and therefore cannot be relied upon. Ahmad did, however, relate this wording from Ibn ‘Abbās. Another wording reported from him states: “Blowing during prayer is speech.” This was narrated by Sa‘īd in his Sunan.

They also argued that it comprises two letters and is not among the prescribed remembrances of

---

## Page 11656

prayer, and thus resembles loud laughter. The evidence supports the same position as in the case of clearing the throat, and the disagreement is of the same kind. For this is not called speech in the language in which the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) addressed us, so it does not fall within the general prohibition against speaking during prayer. If someone swore not to speak, doing these things would not break his oath; and if he swore that he would speak, doing such things would not fulfil his oath.

Speech necessarily involves an utterance that signifies a meaning by convention, a connection understood through reason. Mere sounds indicating the condition of those producing them, however, convey meaning naturally, through sensory perception. Although they share with ordinary speech the capacity to convey meaning, not everything that conveys meaning is prohibited during prayer. Gestures, for example, convey meaning and take the place of verbal expression. Indeed, they convey meaning intentionally and are called speech, yet they do not invalidate prayer. For:

“When people greeted the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), he would respond to them with a gesture.”

It is thus clear that he did not prohibit everything that conveys meaning and can be understood. Likewise, it is permissible to draw someone’s attention by reciting the Quran or glorifying Allah, as the texts indicate. Yet since this is prescribed during prayer, it does not invalidate it. If someone deliberately conveys something to a listener without thereby invalidating his prayer, how much more should this apply to something that conveys meaning naturally, when he does not intend to communicate anything to anyone? The listener merely learns his condition from it, just as one learns it from his movements or his silence. When someone sees him trembling, shaking, shedding tears or smiling, he understands his condition. The only distinguishing feature here is that it takes the form of sound.

This would hold even if no Sunnah report had been transmitted concerning it. How much more so, then, when the Musnad contains a report from al-Mughīrah ibn Shu‘bah that “the Prophet

---

## Page 11657

(peace and blessings be upon him) was performing the eclipse prayer and began blowing. When he finished, he said, ‘The Fire was brought so close to me that I blew its heat away from my face.’” And does not the report in the Musnad and Abū Dāwūd’s Sunan, from ‘Abd Allah ibn ‘Amr, state that “during the solar eclipse prayer, the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) blew near the end of his prostration, saying, ‘Uff! Uff! Uff! My Lord, did You not promise me that You would not punish them while I am among them?’”?

Some of our fellow jurists have answered this by interpreting it as something he did before speaking during prayer was prohibited, or something he did out of fear of Allah or of the Fire. They said: “This does not invalidate prayer according to our school, as Ahmad explicitly stated, just as sighing and groaning do not invalidate it in his view.” Both answers, however, are weak.

(As for the first, the eclipse prayer took place towards the end of the Prophet’s life (peace and blessings be upon him), on the day his son Ibrāhīm died. Ibrāhīm’s mother was Māriyah the Copt, whom al-Muqawqis had given to the Prophet after the Prophet sent al-Mughīrah to him. This was after the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyyah, for it was after al-Hudaybiyyah that he sent his envoys to the kings. It is well known, by the consensus of the Muslims, that speaking during prayer had been prohibited before this. Indeed, the majority of scholars rejected the claim that the incident involving Dhū al-Yadayn occurred before speaking during prayer was prohibited, because Abū Hurayrah witnessed it. How, then, could such a claim be made about the eclipse prayer? It has even been said that the solar eclipse occurred after the Farewell Pilgrimage, shortly before his death (peace and blessings be upon him).

As for the explanation that he did so out of fear, the report states that he blew its heat away from his face. This was blowing to ward off something harmful coming from outside, just as someone blows on a lamp to extinguish it

---

## Page 11658

or blows on dust. Blowing out of fear is akin to weeping and groaning; this, however, is something different.

As for coughing, sneezing, yawning, weeping that can be suppressed, sighing, and groaning, these are like blowing: they convey meaning by their very nature. There is even greater reason for them not to invalidate prayer, since blowing resembles speech more closely than they do. Blowing resembles saying “uff” in annoyance, as Allah says:

“Do not say to them even ‘uff.’”

However, those among Ahmad’s fellow jurists who discussed these matters, such as Abū al-Khattāb and his followers, stated that they invalidate prayer if two letters are distinctly articulated, without mentioning any disagreement. Some then mentioned Ahmad’s explicit ruling on clearing the throat, while others mentioned the alternative report from him concerning blowing. This gave the misleading impression that the disagreement was confined to those cases. That is not so. Indeed, one cannot maintain that these invalidate prayer while blowing does not.

Consistent with his underlying principle, Abū Yūsuf holds that sighing and groaning do not invalidate prayer in any case. This is the soundest opinion on this issue.

Mālik, despite the differing reports of his position on clearing the throat and blowing, said: “Groaning does not invalidate a sick person’s prayer, but I dislike it for a healthy person.” There is no doubt that groaning without need is disliked, but he did not consider it to invalidate prayer.

---

## Page 11659

As for al-Shāfiʿī, he followed his own principle, with which many later jurists among Ahmad’s followers agreed: any of these sounds in which two letters are distinctly articulated constitutes speech that invalidates prayer. This is the strictest opinion on this issue and the furthest removed from the evidence. If they establish that these sounds invalidate prayer because they fall within the meaning of “speech” in the words of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, it is self-evident that these sounds do not fall within that meaning. If their ruling rests on analogy, that analogy is unsound: when speaking, a person intends meanings that he expresses in words, and this distracts the worshipper. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Prayer demands one’s full attention.”

These sounds, however, are natural, like breathing. It is well known that even if a person breathes more than necessary, his prayer is not invalidated. These sounds differ from breathing only in being audible. To invalidate prayer merely because of a sound is to establish a ruling without any basis or parallel. Moreover, hadiths concerning clearing the throat and blowing have been reported, as mentioned earlier. Furthermore, the prayer is certainly valid, so it is not permissible to invalidate it on the basis of doubt. We do not know that the reason for prohibiting speech is the supposed feature common to speech and these sounds. Rather, this amounts to establishing a ruling on the basis of doubt unsupported by evidence.

This disagreement concerns someone who makes such sounds for a reason other than fear of Allah. If he makes them out of fear of Allah, the position of Ahmad and Abū Hanīfa is that his prayer is not invalidated, whereas al-Shāfiʿī’s position is that it is invalidated because this constitutes speech. The former opinion is more correct, for when this arises from fear of Allah, it belongs to the same category as remembering Allah and supplicating to Him, for it is speech

---

## Page 11660

that expresses dread of Allah and longing for Him. This is fear of Allah within prayer. Allah praised Abraham as awwāh, a term interpreted as referring to one who sighs out of fear of Allah. Were a person to express that meaning explicitly by seeking refuge from the Fire or asking for Paradise, his prayer would not be invalidated. This differs from groaning and sighing because of illness or affliction: explicitly expressing their meaning would constitute speech that invalidates prayer.

It is reported in the two Sahīhs that Ā’isha said to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Abū Bakr is a tender-hearted man; when he recites, he is overcome by weeping.”

He said: “Tell him to lead the prayer. You women are indeed like the women in Joseph’s story.”

Umar’s sobbing could be heard from behind the rows when he recited:

“I only complain of my suffering and my grief to Allah.”

Sobbing means weeping aloud, as explained by Abū Ubayd. This report from Umar is well established and was mentioned by Mālik, Ahmad and others. This disagreement concerns cases in which the person is not overcome involuntarily.

As for sneezing, weeping or yawning that a worshipper cannot control, the correct view according to the majority is that it does not invalidate prayer. This is the explicit position of Ahmad and others. Some of his followers, however, held that it invalidates prayer even though the person is excused, as with someone who speaks out of forgetfulness. Regarding speech uttered out of forgetfulness, two opinions are reported from Ahmad. The first, which is also Abū Hanīfa’s position, is that it invalidates prayer.

---

## Page 11661

And the second, which is the position of Mālik and al-Shāfi‘ī, is that it does not invalidate prayer. This is the stronger view. Involuntary sneezing and similar occurrences warrant this ruling even more than forgetful speech, since they are ordinary occurrences that a person cannot prevent. It is authentically established that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Yawning is from Satan. When one of you yawns, let him suppress it as much as he can.”

There is also the established report of the man who sneezed during prayer and for whom Mu‘āwiya ibn al-Hakam al-Sulamī invoked Allah’s mercy. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, forbade Mu‘āwiya to speak during prayer, but said nothing to the man who sneezed. To hold that sneezing invalidates prayer is to impose a burden; it is one of the newly introduced views with no basis in what is transmitted from the early generations, may Allah be pleased with them.

It has thus become clear that these throat sounds, which convey no conventionally assigned meaning, are disputed within the schools of Abū Hanīfa, Mālik and Ahmad. The stronger view concerning all of them is that they do not invalidate prayer. Sounds are comparable to movements: just as minor movement does not invalidate prayer, neither does a slight sound. Loud laughter, however, is different, for it is comparable to minor movement, and that is incompatible with prayer. Indeed, loud laughter is even more incompatible with the purpose of prayer. Hence it is never permissible during prayer, unlike extensive movement, which is permitted in cases of necessity. And Allah knows best.

---

## Page 11662

He was asked:

If someone recites the Quran during prayer and keeps count using prayer beads, does this invalidate his prayer?

He replied:

If the question means using prayer beads to count verses or repetitions of a single surah, such as “Say: He is Allah, the One,” there is nothing wrong with that. If something else is intended by the question, let the questioner clarify it. And Allah knows best.

He was asked:

When someone enters the mosque while people are praying, may he greet them aloud, or should he refrain for fear that someone unaware of the ruling might return his greeting verbally?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. If the person praying knows how to respond with a gesture, there is nothing wrong with greeting him, just as the Companions used to greet the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and he would respond to them with a gesture. But if he does not know how to respond and might speak instead, one should not put him in a situation where he either invalidates his prayer or fails to give the response required of him. And Allah knows best.

---

## Page 11663

He was asked:

Does the prohibition against passing in front of someone praying apply to a person praying behind an imam, just as it applies to the imam and someone praying alone?

He replied:

The prohibition applies only to passing in front of the imam or someone praying alone. They cited as evidence the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās—may Allah be pleased with them both. And Allah knows best.

> End of Volume Twenty-Two.
